C-3.overview: Bill C-3 changes Canada's rules on "citizenship by descent" — that is, who automatically becomes a Canadian citizen because of a parent, even though they were born abroad. Under the law as it stood, citizenship generally stopped after the first generation born outside Canada; this bill gives citizenship to everyone born abroad to a Canadian parent before the new rules take effect, and, going forward, extends citizenship past the first generation whenever the Canadian parent has a "substantial connection" to Canada — spelled out in the bill as at least 1,095 days (the equivalent of three years) of physical presence in Canada before the child's birth. Parallel rules are created for children adopted abroad by Canadian parents. The bill also restores citizenship to people who lost it under an old rule requiring them to apply to keep it, and it gives people who gain citizenship automatically under these changes a simplified way to give it up if they don't want it. The bill is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Lena Metlege Diab and has received royal assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Citizenship Act in several connected ways. First, it removes the cut-off that limited citizenship by descent to the first generation born outside Canada, for everyone born abroad to a Canadian parent before the new rules come into force — those people are recognized as citizens. Second, for children born abroad after the new rules take effect, citizenship can pass beyond the first generation as long as the Canadian parent meets a physical-presence test in Canada before the birth.

It also makes matching changes for adoption (section 5.1 of the Act), restores citizenship to a group of people who lost it under a repealed "retention" rule, and creates a simplified renunciation process for people who become citizens because of the new law but do not wish to be Canadian citizens.

deepDive.heading: The "substantial connection" test
deepDive.body:
For births (and adoptions) happening on or after the day the new rules come into force, a Canadian parent who was themselves born outside Canada can pass on citizenship only if that parent was physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days before the child's birth or adoption. If neither citizen parent meets that threshold, the child is not covered by the automatic descent rule.

The bill sets out in detail which categories of citizen parents this test applies to, including parents who hold citizenship under various provisions of the current Act and under earlier versions of Canadian citizenship legislation going back to 1946. The same 1,095-day requirement is written into the adoption provisions.

deepDive.heading: Restoring and clarifying citizenship for past cases
deepDive.body:
The bill restores citizenship to people who lost it because they did not apply to retain it under the former section 8 of the Citizenship Act, or whose application to retain it was refused. It also contains provisions dealing with deceased parents: if a person would qualify only because a parent (or grandparent) is treated as a citizen under the new law, the fact that the parent or grandparent died before the law came into force does not block the claim — they are treated as if they would have been citizens.

Other technical amendments address people who were previously granted citizenship but would now qualify automatically (they are generally treated as never having been citizens "by way of grant"), and confirm that people covered by the descent rule are considered citizens from the moment of birth. Exceptions remain for people who formally renounced their citizenship or made a declaration of alienage.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The main groups affected are Canadians living abroad and their children and grandchildren; people born outside Canada in past decades who were excluded by the first-generation limit; children adopted overseas by Canadian parents; and people sometimes described as "lost Canadians" who lost status under the old retention requirement. Because some people will gain citizenship automatically without asking for it, the bill includes a simplified process to renounce it.

Going forward, Canadian citizens born outside Canada who wish to pass citizenship to children born abroad will need to be able to show the required 1,095 days of physical presence in Canada before the child's birth or adoption.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill is drafted as a series of amendments to the existing Citizenship Act, replacing and repealing provisions added by earlier reforms (the text references amendments made in 2008 and 2014, and the April 17, 2009 date when major changes took effect). Its structure is highly technical because it must slot into decades of layered citizenship legislation dating back to the Canadian Citizenship Act of 1946.

Bill C-3 is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Lena Metlege Diab and has received royal assent. Note that many of its rules are tied to "the day on which this Act comes into force" rather than the day of royal assent, so the exact date on which the new descent and adoption rules begin to apply is set separately in the legislation's coming-into-force arrangements. This summary is based on the bill text provided, which is partially truncated.

C-4.overview: Bill C-4, the Making Life More Affordable for Canadians Act, is a federal government bill (sponsored by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne) that has received royal assent. It bundles together four separate measures: a cut to the income tax rate on the lowest tax bracket (to 14.5% for 2025 and 14% starting in 2026), a temporary GST rebate of up to $50,000 for first-time buyers of newly built homes, the repeal of the federal consumer fuel charge (the part of the carbon pricing law that applied to fuels), and changes to the rules requiring federal political parties to have privacy policies protecting personal information. The first three measures are aimed at reducing costs for households — through smaller tax bills, cheaper new-home purchases for first-time buyers, and the removal of the fuel charge. Because the tax cut and housing rebate involve spending or forgoing public revenue, the bill carries a royal recommendation, meaning it could only be introduced by the government.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act is an omnibus-style package with four parts. Part 1 amends the Income Tax Act to lower the tax rate on the first (lowest) income bracket. Part 2 amends the Excise Tax Act and related regulations to create a temporary GST rebate for first-time home buyers of new homes. Part 3 repeals Part 1 of the Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act along with the Fuel Charge Regulations. Part 4 amends the Canada Elections Act with respect to political parties' policies for protecting personal information.

The long title acknowledges the mixed nature of the package: "An Act respecting certain affordability measures for Canadians and another measure" — the "other measure" being the elections-related privacy changes, which are not an affordability item.

deepDive.heading: Part 1: Lower tax rate on the lowest income bracket
deepDive.body:
The rate applied to the lowest bracket of taxable income — income up to $57,375 (indexed) — drops to 14.5% for the 2025 tax year and to 14% for 2026 and later years. The other brackets and rates listed in the Act are unchanged: 20.5% on income between $57,375 and $114,750, 26% up to $177,882, 29% up to $253,414, and 33% above that. Because Canada's system is progressive, everyone who pays income tax benefits on the first portion of their income, with the maximum dollar benefit reached once income exceeds the first bracket.

The bill also requires the Minister of Finance to prepare a report on how the lower rate affects tax credits that are calculated using the "appropriate percentage" (many non-refundable credits, such as the basic personal amount, are valued at that lowest-bracket rate, so lowering the rate also lowers the value of those credits). The report must be tabled in both the House and Senate within 90 days of that section coming into force and published on the Department of Finance website within 10 days of tabling.

deepDive.heading: Part 2: GST rebate for first-time home buyers of new homes
deepDive.body:
The bill creates an additional GST new housing rebate, on top of any existing rebate, worth up to $50,000 for eligible first-time buyers. For a purchase from a builder, the full amount is available where the price is $1,000,000 or less; between $1,000,000 and $1,500,000 the rebate is gradually reduced to zero using a formula, and there is no rebate at $1,500,000 or above. Parallel versions of the rebate exist for owner-built or building-only situations and for shares in a cooperative housing corporation, using thresholds of $1,050,000 and $1,575,000 and a calculation based on 4.77% of the consideration.

The measure is temporary and tied to strict timing: the purchase agreement must be signed after March 19, 2025 and before 2031, construction must begin before 2031 and be substantially completed before 2036, and ownership or possession must transfer before 2036. The buyer must be acquiring the home as their primary residence and be the first person to occupy it. A "first-time home buyer" is defined as someone at least 18 years old who is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident and who, in the current and four preceding calendar years, has not lived as an owner-occupant in a home they owned — in Canada or abroad — and who has also not lived in a home owned by their spouse or common-law partner during that period. These provisions are deemed to have come into force on March 20, 2025.

deepDive.heading: Part 3: Repeal of the federal fuel charge
deepDive.body:
Part 3 repeals Part 1 of the Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act and the Fuel Charge Regulations. Part 1 of that Act is the section that imposed the federal fuel charge — the levy applied to fuels such as gasoline and natural gas in provinces and territories covered by the federal system. Repealing it removes that charge and its associated regulatory framework from the statute books.

The bill as summarized repeals only Part 1 of that Act; it does not, on its face, address Part 2 of the Greenhouse Gas Pollution Pricing Act, which deals with the output-based pricing system for large industrial emitters.

deepDive.heading: Part 4: Political parties and personal information
deepDive.body:
Part 4 amends the Canada Elections Act to change requirements relating to the policies federal political parties must have for protecting personal information. The detailed wording of these amendments is not included in the excerpt of the bill text available here, so the specific obligations being added, removed or modified cannot be described precisely from this material.

This is the one component of the package that is unrelated to household costs, which is why the long title refers separately to "another measure."

deepDive.heading: Who is affected and status
deepDive.body:
The income tax change affects essentially all individual income tax filers. The housing rebate affects a narrower group: first-time buyers of newly built or substantially renovated homes purchased within the specified window and under the price ceilings. The fuel charge repeal affects consumers and businesses in jurisdictions where the federal fuel charge applied, as well as the administration of that charge. Part 4 affects registered federal political parties and how they handle voters' personal information.

The bill has received royal assent, meaning it has passed the House of Commons and the Senate and is law, with individual measures taking effect on the dates set out in the Act (for example, the housing rebate provisions are deemed effective March 20, 2025, and the tax rate changes apply to the 2025 and 2026 tax years respectively).

C-2.overview: Bill C-2, the Strong Borders Act, is a large "omnibus" government bill that changes 16 different areas of federal law at once, all grouped under the theme of border and national security. It touches border inspections and exports, fentanyl precursor chemicals, mail opening by Canada Post, Coast Guard security duties, information sharing about immigrants, major changes to the asylum and refugee claim system, new government powers to pause or cancel immigration applications and documents, tougher anti-money-laundering rules including a ban on cash payments of $10,000 or more, expanded sex offender registry obligations, and new police and CSIS powers to obtain subscriber and other data from companies that serve the public. It also creates an entirely new law, the Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act, requiring electronic service providers to be able to help authorities access information when legally authorized. Because it bundles border enforcement, immigration, financial-crime and digital-investigation measures together, the bill affects a wide range of people — refugee claimants, banks and businesses, telecom and online service providers, and anyone sending mail or moving money. The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet been studied in committee or passed.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Strong Borders Act is framed as a package of measures relating to the Canada–U.S. border and "other related security measures." Rather than creating one new program, it amends more than a dozen existing statutes — including the Customs Act, Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, Cannabis Act, Canada Post Corporation Act, Oceans Act, Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, Sex Offender Information Registration Act, Criminal Code, and Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act — and enacts one new Act.

The bill is divided into 16 parts. Broadly, Parts 1–5 deal with border operations, drugs and mail; Parts 6–9 deal with immigration and asylum; Parts 10–12 and 16 deal with money laundering and financial oversight; Part 13 deals with the sex offender registry; and Parts 14–15 deal with police and intelligence access to electronic data.

deepDive.heading: Border, drugs, mail and coast guard measures
deepDive.body:
Part 1 requires that the Canada Border Services Agency be given facilities free of charge to carry out its work, and gives officers access to goods destined for export at certain locations. Part 2 creates a temporary fast-track process letting the Minister of Health add precursor chemicals (ingredients used to make illegal drugs) to a schedule under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act. Part 3 confirms the Governor in Council can make regulations exempting police from certain drug-related Criminal Code offences during lawful investigations.

Part 4 amends the Canada Post Corporation Act so that mail in the course of post can only be demanded, seized, detained or retained under an Act of Parliament, and expands Canada Post's authority to open mail to include opening letters. Part 5 states that Coast Guard services include security-related activities and allows the responsible minister to collect, analyze and disclose information and intelligence.

deepDive.heading: Immigration and asylum changes
deepDive.body:
Part 6 lets the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration share personal information held by the department internally and with certain other federal and provincial bodies, subject to regulations. Part 7 makes significant changes to the in-Canada asylum system: it eliminates the "designated countries of origin" regime; lets the minister specify what documents refugee claimants must provide; allows claims not yet referred to the Refugee Protection Division to be declared abandoned or withdrawn in certain circumstances; requires proceedings to be suspended if a claimant is not in Canada; and allows regulations on appointing representatives for claimants under 18 or unable to understand the proceedings.

Part 8 would let the federal Cabinet (Governor in Council), when it considers it in the public interest, order that certain immigration applications not be accepted, be suspended or be terminated, and cancel, suspend or vary documents already issued or impose conditions — with people required to appear for examination, answer truthfully and produce documents. Part 9 adds two new grounds making a refugee claim ineligible, with regulations to allow exceptions, and includes a transitional provision applying those grounds retroactively.

deepDive.heading: Money laundering, financial rules and the sex offender registry
deepDive.body:
Parts 10 through 12 and 16 tighten Canada's anti-money-laundering framework. Maximum administrative penalties and criminal punishments increase; the voluntary compliance agreement system becomes mandatory, with compliance orders if a business refuses or fails to comply; more businesses must enroll with FINTRAC (the federal financial intelligence agency); and FINTRAC may share certain information with the Commissioner of Canada Elections and with financial regulators. Part 11 bans certain entities from accepting third-party cash deposits and bans accepting cash payments, donations or deposits of $10,000 or more. Part 16 allows regulated businesses to collect and use personal information without consent when it comes from a government or law enforcement agency and is used to detect or deter money laundering, terrorist financing or sanctions evasion.

Part 13 updates the Sex Offender Information Registration Act: changing when and what offenders must report, allowing identifying physical characteristics to be recorded, clarifying excuses for late travel notice, letting CBSA share entry and exit information with police, and permitting disclosure of registry information where there are reasonable grounds to believe it will help prevent or investigate a sexual crime.

deepDive.heading: Police and intelligence access to electronic information
deepDive.body:
Part 14 modernizes investigative powers across several statutes. Under the Criminal Code, it creates an "information demand" and a judicial production order to obtain basic information from persons who provide services to the public, clarifies response times for production orders and the use of voluntarily provided or publicly available information, sets out when officers may obtain evidence such as subscriber information in urgent circumstances, expands warrants to cover tracking or transmission data for similar things unknown when the warrant was issued, clarifies authority to examine computer data, and allows judges to authorize requests to foreign telecom providers. Similar information-demand and judicial-order tools are added for CSIS, and the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act is amended to help enforce foreign orders for transmission data or subscriber information held in Canada.

Part 15 creates a new statute, the Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act, establishing a framework to ensure electronic service providers can facilitate lawful access to information by authorized persons under the Criminal Code or the CSIS Act. Together these parts would affect telecommunications companies, online platforms and other service providers, as well as the privacy interests of their users.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
Bill C-2 is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Gary Anandasangaree, and carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money. As of this summary it is at second reading in the House of Commons — the stage where MPs debate the bill in principle before it can go to committee for detailed study, then to report stage, third reading, the Senate and royal assent. Its contents can change, and it is not law unless and until it completes all of those steps.

Because the bill combines many unrelated statutes into one package, different parts are likely to draw attention from different groups — for example, refugee and civil-liberties organizations regarding the immigration and data-access provisions, and financial institutions and service providers regarding the compliance and reporting obligations. This explainer describes only what the bill text says; it does not assess whether the measures will achieve their stated goals.

C-5.overview: Bill C-5, the One Canadian Economy Act, is a federal law (it has received royal assent) that creates two new statutes. The first, the Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act, is meant to reduce federal red tape that gets in the way of selling goods and services across provincial borders and of workers practising their trade or profession in another part of the country: in general, if a good, service or worker already meets a province's or territory's rules, that will count as meeting a comparable federal rule. The second, the Building Canada Act, lets the federal Cabinet designate certain projects as being "in the national interest" and place them on a schedule; for those listed projects, various approvals required under other federal laws are treated as already decided in the project's favour, and a designated minister issues a single document setting out the conditions that apply. The bill matters because it changes both how federal rules apply to interprovincial commerce and how major projects such as energy or infrastructure developments move through federal permitting. It also builds in oversight measures, including a public registry, annual independent reviews of each listed project, and parliamentary review of the legislation.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The One Canadian Economy Act is an umbrella law that enacts two separate pieces of legislation. Part 1 enacts the Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act, aimed at removing federal barriers to moving goods and services between provinces and to workers moving across the country. Part 2 enacts the Building Canada Act, which sets up a streamlined federal approval route for projects the Governor in Council (Cabinet) decides are in the national interest.

The two parts come into force differently: Part 1's Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act comes into force on a day set by order of the Governor in Council. The bill also carries a royal recommendation, meaning it involves the spending of public money.

deepDive.heading: Part 1: Interprovincial trade and labour mobility
deepDive.body:
Under the new Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act, a good that is produced, used or distributed according to a provincial or territorial rule is considered to meet any comparable federal rule, and the same idea applies to services (so long as the provincial or territorial rule keeps applying to the service provider). A provincial rule only counts as "comparable" if it deals with the same aspect of the good or service, aims at a similar objective, and meets any conditions set out in regulations. The relevant federal regulator decides whether the rules are in fact comparable. Importantly, these provisions apply only where a federal requirement relates to the interprovincial movement of the good or provision of the service.

For workers, federal regulatory bodies must recognize a provincial or territorial authorization to practise an occupation as comparable to a federal one, and must issue a federal authorization when a holder of a provincial or territorial authorization applies. Cabinet can make regulations creating exceptions and conditions, and must consult the affected federal regulator before recommending an exception. The Act prevails over other federal laws where they conflict, protects the Crown and federal regulators from civil lawsuits for good-faith actions under these sections (while leaving judicial review and Canadian Free Trade Agreement dispute processes available), and requires a ministerial review and report to Parliament within five years. Its preamble states the government intends to remove federal exceptions under the Canadian Free Trade Agreement and to keep working with provinces toward a national mutual-recognition system, while continuing to protect health, safety, security, well-being and the environment.

deepDive.heading: Part 2: National interest projects
deepDive.body:
The Building Canada Act allows the Governor in Council to add a project's name and a brief description to a schedule if, having regard to certain factors, it considers the project to be in the national interest. Once a project is listed in Schedule 1, determinations, findings and opinions that federal decision-makers would otherwise have to make under certain Acts and regulations before granting an authorization are deemed to have been made in favour of allowing the project to go ahead in whole or in part.

The designated minister must then, if certain conditions are met, issue the project's proponent a single document setting out the conditions that apply; that document is deemed to be the authorizations, specified within it, that would normally be required under other federal laws. The minister can later amend those conditions. The Act's table of provisions indicates specific consultation requirements and limits tied to the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and the Canadian Energy Regulator Act, provisions relating to the Atlantic and Nova Scotia offshore accord implementation Acts, and non-application of certain provisions of the Impact Assessment Act.

deepDive.heading: Transparency and oversight
deepDive.body:
The Building Canada Act includes several accountability mechanisms: a public registry, provisions making information available to the public, an Office with a defined role, and a requirement that the designated minister cause an independent review of the status of each national interest project to be conducted every year. The schedule of projects can be added to, amended or deleted, and regulations may be made under the Act.

Both new statutes include review clauses. The Free Trade and Labour Mobility in Canada Act must be reviewed by the minister within five years, with a report tabled in both Houses of Parliament, while the Building Canada Act provides for review by a Parliamentary Review Committee.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
Part 1 mainly affects businesses that sell goods or services across provincial lines and workers in regulated occupations who hold a provincial or territorial licence, as well as the federal regulators that will have to assess comparability and issue authorizations. Part 2 affects proponents of large projects — the referenced statutes point to areas such as nuclear, energy and offshore development — along with the federal departments and agencies that would normally issue the separate approvals.

The bill was sponsored by the Hon. Dominic LeBlanc, introduced in 2025 during the 45th Parliament, and has received royal assent. This summary is based on the bill's summary and the text provided, which is truncated; the detailed wording of the Building Canada Act's sections, including the factors Cabinet must consider and the exact scope of consultation and limits, is not fully reproduced in the material available here.

C-6.overview: Bill C-6, the Appropriation Act No. 1, 2025-26, is a routine but essential money bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $149,771,149,015 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) to pay for departmental and agency operations during the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026. The money is tied to the Main Estimates for 2025-26 — the government's detailed spending plan — and covers only amounts that were not already released through two special warrants issued in April and May 2025 while Parliament was not in session to approve spending. Each dollar is attached to a specific 'vote' for a specific organization and purpose, listed in two schedules covering everything from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to the Canadian Space Agency and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. The bill received royal assent, meaning the spending authority is now law. Appropriation bills like this one are how Parliament exercises its constitutional control over public money: without them, departments have no legal authority to spend.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) permission to spend a maximum of $149,771,149,015 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026, on expenses 'not otherwise provided for' — that is, spending that isn't already authorized by other legislation. It does not create new programs or change any policy; it simply releases funds for purposes already set out in the Main Estimates tabled in Parliament.

The total is split into two parts: $144,228,741,594 under Schedule 1 (ordinary annual spending) and $5,542,407,421 under Schedule 2 (amounts that may be spent over a longer window). Although the bill was passed later in the year, its provisions are deemed to take effect as of April 1, 2025, the start of the fiscal year.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 is the core accountability rule: money approved for a given item can only be spent for the purposes and under the conditions written into that item. Departments cannot shift funds to unrelated uses. Each entry in the schedules names an organization, a vote number, a description of what the money is for (operating expenditures, capital expenditures, grants and contributions, payments to a Crown corporation, and so on), and the dollar amount.

Sections 4 and 5 deal with bookkeeping. They allow appropriations to be charged to the accounts of Canada after the fiscal year ends — up until the Public Accounts are tabled — for accounting adjustments that don't involve actual cash leaving the Fund. Schedule 2 amounts get extra flexibility: they may be paid out any time up to March 31, 2027, with a rule that older appropriations must be used up first, and any unused balance lapses at the end of that second year.

deepDive.heading: The role of the special warrants
deepDive.body:
The bill's amounts are net of money already advanced. Two Governor General's special warrants — issued under Orders in Council P.C. 2025-462 (April 1, 2025) and P.C. 2025-467 (May 2, 2025) — had already released a portion of the Main Estimates funding. Special warrants are a mechanism that allows urgent government spending when Parliament is dissolved or not sitting and cannot pass an appropriation bill.

This is why the schedules show three dollar columns for each item: the full amount in the Main Estimates, the amount already covered by special warrants, and the remaining balance granted by this Act. For example, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's operating vote of $1,307,346,411 in the Estimates had $326,836,602 released by warrant, leaving $980,509,809 authorized here.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Effectively every federal department, agency and Crown corporation that relies on parliamentary appropriations. The schedules cover a wide cross-section of government: economic development agencies (Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency), Crown corporations (Canada Post, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation), regulators (Canadian Energy Regulator, CRTC, Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission), research and cultural bodies (Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Canada Council for the Arts, the national museums), and security organizations (CSIS, Communications Security Establishment).

Indirectly, it affects the public: these votes fund food inspection, air transport security screening, housing programs, health research grants, public broadcasting and much more. Some votes also carry specific authorities, such as permission to recover costs or to spend revenues earned from providing internal support services to other departments.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
Appropriation acts are tabled several times a year and are among the most predictable pieces of legislation Parliament passes. They flow from the Estimates process: the government tables its spending plan, committees review it, and the House then votes the funds. A vote against supply is traditionally treated as a confidence matter.

This particular bill was sponsored by Hon. Shafqat Ali and has received royal assent, so the spending authority it contains is in force. Note that the text reproduced here appears truncated partway through Schedule 1 — the complete schedules list every voted item across the federal administration, and the totals cited in sections 2, and at the head of Schedule 1, are the authoritative figures.

C-7.overview: Bill C-7, the Appropriation Act No. 2, 2025-26, is a routine but essential spending bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $8,580,271,678 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026. The money corresponds to the items listed in the Supplementary Estimates (A) for 2025-26 — extra funding requested after the main budget-year spending plan was already approved. Nearly all of it, about $8.21 billion, goes to the Department of National Defence, with a further $370 million for the Communications Security Establishment (Canada's signals intelligence and cyber security agency). The bill matters because, under Canada's constitutional rules, the government cannot spend public money without Parliament's explicit approval; bills like this are how that approval is granted. It has received royal assent, meaning it is now law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) permission to spend a maximum of $8,580,271,678 during the fiscal year running from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2026, on expenses "not otherwise provided for" — that is, spending not already authorized by earlier appropriation acts or standing legislation.

The total is not a new policy decision in itself; it is the sum of the individual line items (called "votes") set out in the Supplementary Estimates (A) for 2025-26 and reproduced in the bill's schedule. Supplementary estimates are used when departments need funding beyond what was approved in the Main Estimates earlier in the year.

deepDive.heading: Where the money goes
deepDive.body:
Two organizations appear in the schedule. The Communications Security Establishment receives $370,060,088 for program expenditures, along with authority to spend revenues it earns from its own operations (including internal support services provided to other departments) to offset its costs.

The Department of National Defence receives $8,210,211,590, split across three votes: $3,966,131,556 for operating expenditures, $804,619,191 for capital expenditures, and $3,439,460,843 for grants and contributions. The grants-and-contributions vote allows payments to be made in money or, alternatively, in the form of goods, services or the use of facilities, and includes contributions approved by the Governor in Council for transferring defence equipment, supplies, facilities or services under the Defence Appropriation Act, 1950.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and spending authorities
deepDive.body:
Beyond the dollar figures, the bill carries several standing authorities attached to the Defence votes. It permits total commitments of up to $86,760,127,023 across Defence Votes 1, 5 and 10 regardless of when payment falls due — with an estimated $52,954,717,761 expected to come due in future years. This reflects long-term contracts and multi-year procurement rather than cash to be spent this year. Defence is also authorized to make recoverable expenditures or advances for materials and services supplied to individuals, companies, outside agencies, other departments and other governments; to make payments for pension, insurance and social security arrangements for staff hired locally outside Canada; and to pay a salary to ministers without portfolio or ministers of State who do not preside over a ministry, capped at the level set under the Salaries Act.

Three procedural rules apply throughout: money voted for a given item may only be used for the purpose and on the terms stated in that item; the items are deemed to take effect retroactively as of April 1, 2025, the start of the fiscal year; and appropriations may be charged after the fiscal year ends, up until the Public Accounts are tabled, solely for bookkeeping adjustments that do not involve actual payments out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and why it matters
deepDive.body:
The most direct effects are on the Department of National Defence and the Communications Security Establishment, which gain legal authority to spend the amounts listed — covering operations, equipment purchases, and grants and contributions. Suppliers, contractors and recipients of defence-related grants and contributions are indirect beneficiaries.

More broadly, the bill is part of Parliament's core "power of the purse." Appropriation acts are the mechanism by which the House of Commons and Senate authorize government spending, and votes on them are traditionally treated as confidence matters in the House. Because the bill has received royal assent, the authorized funds are now available to be spent.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The bill was introduced by Hon. Shafqat Ali as a government bill and follows the standard structure of Canadian appropriation acts: a short preamble noting the Governor General's message transmitting the Estimates, a clause setting the maximum amount, clauses on the conditions and effective date, and a schedule listing each vote.

As "Appropriation Act No. 2" for 2025-26, it follows an earlier appropriation act for the same fiscal year and draws on Supplementary Estimates (A). Additional supplementary estimates and further appropriation bills are typically brought forward later in a fiscal year as departmental needs are updated. The bill itself does not create or change any program, policy or law beyond authorizing the spending described in its schedule.

C-9.overview: Bill C-9, the Combatting Hate Act, amends the Criminal Code to expand how hate-motivated conduct is prosecuted in Canada. It creates a new offence for publicly displaying certain symbols — such as the Nazi Hakenkreuz, SS bolts, a noose, or symbols associated with listed terrorist entities — when done to wilfully promote hatred against an identifiable group; it creates a standalone "hate crime" offence that adds higher maximum penalties when any federal offence is motivated by hatred; and it makes it a crime to intimidate people out of entering, or to block access to, places of worship, community and cultural buildings, schools, seniors' residences and cemeteries. The bill also removes the existing defence based on expressing opinions on religious subjects or texts for the wilful promotion of hatred and antisemitism offences, while adding a statutory definition of "hatred" and several clarifications and defences aimed at protecting journalism, education, art and public-interest debate. It received royal assent and comes into force 30 days later. It matters because it changes what can be prosecuted, raises potential penalties, and touches directly on the line between hateful conduct and protected expression and protest.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act amends the Criminal Code in four main ways: it adds a hate-symbol display offence, it repeals a religious-opinion defence in the existing hate propaganda provisions, it creates a new general hate crime offence with escalated maximum sentences, and it criminalizes intimidation and obstruction that block access to religious and community places.

It also makes supporting technical changes — for example, adding the new intimidation offence to the list of offences for which wiretap authorizations and DNA orders can be available, and to bail provisions requiring courts to consider certain conditions. The Act comes into force on the 30th day after royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Hate symbols and hate propaganda changes
deepDive.body:
New subsection 319(2.2) makes it an offence to wilfully promote hatred against an identifiable group by displaying, in a public place, a symbol principally used by or associated with a listed terrorist entity, the Nazi Hakenkreuz, the Nazi double Sig-Rune (SS bolts), a noose, or a symbol closely resembling these. The maximum penalty is two years on indictment, or it can be prosecuted as a summary offence. There are defences where the display served a legitimate purpose — including journalism, education or art — that is not contrary to the public interest, or where it was made in good faith to point out hate-producing material for the purpose of removal.

The bill repeals the defence based on expressing an opinion on a religious subject or a text believed to be religious, for both the wilful promotion of hatred and the wilful promotion of antisemitism offences. It adds a definition of "hatred" as "an emotion of an intense and extreme nature that is clearly associated with vilification and detestation," and states for greater certainty that a statement does not incite or promote hatred solely because it discredits, humiliates, hurts or offends. Separate clarification provisions say nothing in these offences prohibits communicating statements on matters of public interest — educational, religious, political or scientific — made in discussion, publication or debate, so long as the person is not wilfully promoting hatred (or antisemitism). Prosecutions for these offences require the consent of the Attorney General.

deepDive.heading: The new hate crime offence
deepDive.body:
New section 320.1001 creates a distinct offence of committing any other federal offence when that offence is motivated by hatred based on race, national or ethnic origin, language, colour, religion, sex, age, mental or physical disability, sexual orientation, or gender identity or expression. Rather than a fixed sentence, the maximum penalty is scaled to the seriousness of the underlying ("included") offence: five years where the underlying maximum is two to under five years; 10 years where it is five to under 10; 14 years where it is 10 to under 14; and life where the underlying maximum is 14 years or more.

The offence cannot be prosecuted by indictment if the underlying offence is summary-only. As with the propaganda provisions, conduct is not treated as hate-motivated solely because it discredits, humiliates, hurts or offends. If the hate motivation is not proven but the underlying offence is, the accused can still be convicted of that underlying offence, and courts must endorse the proven included offence on the charging document.

deepDive.heading: Access to religious and cultural places
deepDive.body:
New section 423.3 creates two offences. The first covers conduct intended to provoke fear in a person in order to impede their access to a place primarily used for religious worship, or used by an identifiable group for administrative, social, cultural or sports activities, as an educational institution (including daycares), or as a seniors' residence — as well as cemeteries. The second covers intentionally obstructing or interfering, without lawful authority, with someone's lawful access to those same places.

Both carry a maximum of 10 years on indictment, or can proceed summarily. The obstruction offence includes an exception: a person is not guilty by reason only of attending at or near, or approaching, such a place for the sole purpose of obtaining or communicating information.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The changes apply to anyone in Canada whose conduct falls within the new offences, and are relevant to police, prosecutors and courts, who gain new charging options and higher potential penalties for hate-motivated conduct. Communities that gather at places of worship, community centres, schools, daycares, seniors' residences and cemeteries are the intended beneficiaries of the access provisions, while journalists, educators, artists, protesters and participants in public debate are addressed through the bill's express defences, exceptions and clarification clauses.

The Attorney General's consent requirement acts as a filter on hate propaganda prosecutions, including the new symbol-display offence. Because several provisions turn on intent, motivation and the defined threshold of "hatred," how they operate in practice will depend on prosecutorial decisions and court interpretation once the Act is in force.

C-10.overview: Bill C-10 would create a new independent watchdog — the Commissioner for Modern Treaty Implementation — whose job is to check whether federal departments and agencies are actually living up to the modern treaties Canada has signed with Indigenous peoples since 1974. The Commissioner would be able to conduct reviews and 'performance audits' of government institutions, demand information from them, and report publicly to Parliament, including through an annual report. The bill also sets up an Office to support the Commissioner, and amends several other federal laws to fit the new office into existing rules on access to information, privacy, public service pensions and official languages. Modern treaties are constitutionally protected agreements, and the bill's stated purpose is to give Parliament and Indigenous treaty partners an independent way to hold the federal government accountable for implementing them. The bill is a government bill sponsored by the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations and has reached third reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates the Commissioner for Modern Treaty Implementation Act. Its central feature is a new independent officer, appointed by the Governor in Council, who assesses whether federal government institutions are carrying out Canada's modern treaty commitments. A 'modern treaty' is defined as a treaty under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 between Canada and an Indigenous people that came into force after 1974 — and the Commissioner's scope also extends to related agreements, including associated self-government agreements.

The Commissioner's mandate is framed around three benchmarks: strengthening relationships between Canada and Indigenous modern treaty partners; fulfilling Canada's treaty obligations, interpreted broadly and purposively; and upholding the 'honour of the Crown' through timely and effective implementation. The bill also establishes an Office of the Commissioner with staff and a head office to support that work.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Appointment: the Commissioner is appointed only after the Minister consults Indigenous modern treaty partners, after consultation with party leaders in both the Senate and House, and after both chambers approve the appointment by resolution. The term is up to seven years during good behaviour, renewable once, with removal only for cause on address of both houses. The Governor in Council must consider a candidate's knowledge and experience with modern treaties, and being a beneficiary or member under a treaty is expressly not a conflict of interest.

Powers: the Commissioner may launch reviews or performance audits on their own initiative, or when a matter is referred by the Minister, another minister, or an Indigenous modern treaty partner. The bill provides for access to information from government institutions, security and non-disclosure rules, draft reports shared with the institutions involved before a final report, briefings, annual reports and special reports. Immunity provisions protect the Commissioner from being summoned, from prosecution, and from defamation claims in connection with the role. The bill also includes regulation-making powers, a parliamentary review, an independent review, and a schedule listing Indigenous modern treaty partners that can be amended by order in certain cases.

deepDive.heading: Limits on the role
deepDive.body:
The bill draws boundaries around what the Commissioner does. Where a modern treaty, a related agreement, or an implementing statute already provides for a specific review or audit, the Commissioner is not responsible for conducting it — though the Commissioner retains discretion to look at the matter on their own initiative.

The bill also states for greater certainty that a review or performance audit is not a substitute for any dispute resolution process set out in a modern treaty, related agreement, or implementing legislation. In other words, the office is designed as an oversight and reporting mechanism rather than a court or arbitrator.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are Indigenous modern treaty partners — the entities named in the bill's schedule — who gain a formal channel to refer implementation problems to an independent officer and to be consulted on appointments and on legislative changes to the Act, including changes to the schedule.

Federal government institutions (entities listed in Schedules I, I.1, II or III to the Financial Administration Act) would be subject to reviews and audits and to requirements to provide information. Parliament also gains a new stream of public reporting on how well modern treaties are being implemented across government.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The bill's lengthy preamble situates it within reconciliation policy: it references nation-to-nation, Inuit-Crown and government-to-government relationships, the constitutional status of modern treaties, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and the related federal implementation Act, and Canada's Collaborative Modern Treaty Implementation Policy, under which Canada and Indigenous treaty partners support creating an independent oversight mechanism accountable to Parliament.

The preamble also notes that because Canada enters treaties on behalf of the Crown as a whole, implementation requires a 'whole-of-government approach' — the rationale for an officer able to examine any federal institution rather than a single department. Because the bill involves spending public money, it carries a royal recommendation from the Governor General. As of this summary, it is at third reading in the House of Commons and would still need to pass the Senate and receive royal assent to become law.

C-8.overview: Bill C-8 is a federal cyber security law that gives the government new powers to protect Canada's telecommunications networks and other critical digital systems from hacking, sabotage and foreign interference. Part 1 amends the Telecommunications Act to make security of the telecom system an official policy goal and lets Cabinet and the Industry Minister order phone and internet companies to take (or stop taking) specific actions — for example, banning equipment from a particular supplier or requiring its removal. Part 2 creates a brand-new law, the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act, which requires companies in federally regulated sectors deemed "vital" — such as telecommunications, banking, energy, nuclear and transportation — to build cyber security programs, manage risks from suppliers, report cyber incidents and follow government cyber security directions. Both parts come with enforcement tools, including inspections, compliance orders, financial penalties and, in some cases, criminal offences. The bill has received royal assent, and Parliament must review how the new rules are working within five years.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has three parts. Part 1 changes the existing Telecommunications Act: it adds "promoting the security of the Canadian telecommunications system" to the list of national telecom policy objectives, and creates authority for the Governor in Council (Cabinet) and the Minister of Industry to direct telecommunications service providers to do — or not do — whatever is considered necessary to secure the system. It also sets up administrative monetary penalties for companies that don't comply, and rules governing how those orders can be challenged in court through judicial review.

Part 2 enacts a separate statute, the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act, which builds a compliance framework for protecting the computer systems behind services considered vital to national security or public safety, within areas Parliament has authority over. Part 3 requires a review of everything enacted or amended by the bill after five years.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: telecom orders
deepDive.body:
Under new section 15.1, Cabinet may, after consulting appropriate parties, prohibit a telecom provider from using products or services from a specified supplier, or order the removal of that supplier's products from its networks. The order must be "necessary and reasonable" in relation to the gravity of the threat, and before making it Cabinet must consider the operational and financial impact on providers, the effect on telecom services including confidentiality and security, potential impacts on Canadians' privacy, and any other relevant factor. Orders must normally be published in the Canada Gazette within 90 days, though Cabinet can direct otherwise, and no compensation is payable for financial losses caused by an order.

An order can also include a secrecy provision barring anyone from disclosing that it exists or what it says. Before doing so, Cabinet must weigh whether disclosure would undermine the order's purpose, the nature of the threat, whether a narrower ban would suffice, the impact on government transparency and accountability, and any representations from affected providers. A separate clause (15.01) makes clear that "interference, manipulation, disruption or degradation" refers to technical actions that impede a telecom system — not lawful expression, persuasion or political debate. The Minister of Industry has parallel ordering powers under section 15.2, exercisable after consulting the Minister of Public Safety.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the Critical Cyber Systems Protection Act
deepDive.body:
The new Act lets Cabinet designate services or systems as "vital" and create classes of operators responsible for them. Designated operators must establish a written cyber security program within set timelines and share it with their regulator, implement and maintain it, review it periodically, take steps to mitigate risks arising from their supply chains and third-party providers, report cyber security incidents, and comply with government-issued cyber security directions. Cyber security directions can be kept confidential, and the Act includes rules for exchanging information between government bodies and operators, restrictions on disclosure, and requirements for disposing of personal information.

Enforcement is delegated to existing sector regulators rather than one central body: the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, the Minister of Industry, the Bank of Canada, the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission, the Canadian Energy Regulator and the Minister of Transport each get powers to enter premises (with special protections for dwelling-houses), order internal audits, issue compliance orders, and impose administrative monetary penalties, with review or appeal processes attached. Directors and officers can be held liable, a due diligence defence is available, compliance agreements are possible, and separate summary offences exist for obstruction and providing false or misleading information. The Act also requires a report to Parliament.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected are telecommunications service providers — phone, internet and wireless carriers — who can be ordered to drop specific suppliers or stop serving specified persons, and who face penalties for non-compliance. Beyond telecom, the new Act reaches operators in federally regulated sectors implied by the list of enforcement bodies: federally regulated financial institutions, banking and payment/clearing systems, nuclear facilities, interprovincial energy infrastructure, and federally regulated transportation. Exactly which services and operators are covered will be set out by Cabinet through designations and regulations rather than being fixed in the bill itself.

Ordinary Canadians are affected indirectly, through the reliability and security of these services. The bill explicitly requires decision-makers to consider potential privacy impacts, and includes limits on how information — including personal information — can be disclosed, used and retained.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill is a government bill sponsored by Hon. Gary Anandasangaree and has received royal assent. Different provisions of Part 2 come into force by order in council, meaning the government sets the timing. The bill also makes consequential amendments to the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act, the Nuclear Safety and Control Act and the Transportation Appeal Tribunal of Canada Act to fit the new enforcement roles into existing structures.

Some features of the bill — the breadth of the order-making powers, the ability to impose secrecy on orders, the bar on compensation for affected companies, and the amount of detail left to future regulations — are the kinds of provisions that typically draw scrutiny from industry, privacy advocates and parliamentarians. The built-in five-year review in Part 3 is the mechanism the bill provides for revisiting how these powers are working in practice.

C-11.overview: Bill C-11, the Military Justice System Modernization Act, changes how the Canadian Armed Forces handles criminal and disciplinary matters, mainly by amending the National Defence Act. Its biggest change is that sexual offences under the Criminal Code alleged to have happened in Canada can no longer be investigated by the military or tried by court martial — those cases go to civilian police and civilian courts. The bill also reworks how three senior military justice officials are appointed to strengthen their independence, renames the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal the "Provost Marshal General," widens who can become a military judge, and broadens the rules about complaints of interference in military police investigations. The government says the changes respond to two major outside reviews of the military justice system: the Third Independent Review Authority report and the Independent External Comprehensive Review of the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces. The bill has received Royal Assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the National Defence Act — the law that sets up the separate justice system governing members of the military — along with the Criminal Code and other Acts. It is a response to recommendations from two independent reviews of military justice and of the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces.

The changes fall into a few broad buckets: shifting sexual offence cases out of the military system, strengthening the independence of key military justice officials, adjusting who can serve as a military judge and how military judges interact with the summary hearing system, expanding supports for victims, and aligning military sex offender registry and publication ban rules with recent Criminal Code changes.

deepDive.heading: Sexual offences move to the civilian system
deepDive.body:
The bill removes court martial jurisdiction over Criminal Code offences of a sexual nature, or committed for a sexual purpose, that are alleged to have occurred in Canada. It lists a long set of specific offences — including sexual assault, sexual assault with a weapon or causing bodily harm, aggravated sexual assault, sexual interference, sexual exploitation, child pornography, luring a child, voyeurism, non-consensual distribution of intimate images, and certain human trafficking and sex-work-related offences — plus a catch-all for any other Criminal Code offence of a sexual nature, historical versions of those offences, and related conspiracy, attempt, accessory and counselling charges.

A new section also removes the Canadian Armed Forces' authority to investigate these offences when they are alleged to have happened in Canada. The bill spells out what the military can still do before civilian police arrive: make an arrest, conduct a search incident to that arrest, and secure or preserve evidence, all to the extent needed to prevent an offence from being committed, continued or repeated. Anyone arrested and any evidence gathered must be handed over to the civilian authorities as soon as feasible. The bill also clarifies that these limits do not block a member from initiating a private prosecution.

deepDive.heading: Independence and appointments
deepDive.body:
The bill changes the appointment process for three senior officials — the Provost Marshal General (formerly the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal, who heads the military police), the Director of Military Prosecutions, and the Director of Defence Counsel Services — with the stated aim of enhancing their independence. For the Provost Marshal General, the Governor in Council may appoint an officer with at least 10 years as a member of the military police, the appointment must be made within 120 days of the office becoming vacant, the officer must hold a rank of at least brigadier-general, and the term runs up to four years. A similar 120-day deadline applies to appointing the Director of Military Prosecutions, who must be a lawyer with at least 10 years at a provincial bar. If the Provost Marshal General position is vacant or the officeholder is unable to act, the Minister may authorize another military police officer to fill in, but beyond 90 days that requires Governor in Council approval.

The bill also adds a clarifying provision stating that, in supervising the administration of military justice, the Judge Advocate General respects the independence of authorities in the system, including the Provost Marshal General and the two directors. Separately, it expands who may file an "interference" complaint about improper interference in a military police investigation, and requires military police members (or those performing policing duties under the Provost Marshal General's supervision) to make such a complaint in certain circumstances. The Minister may issue public written general instructions or guidelines to the Provost Marshal General, and the Provost Marshal General must file an annual report to the Minister within three months of each fiscal year's end.

deepDive.heading: Military judges, summary hearings and victims
deepDive.body:
The bill widens the pool of people eligible to be appointed as military judges. It also removes military judges from the summary hearing system: a military judge may not conduct a summary hearing, and a military judge is not to be charged with having committed a "service infraction" (the lower-level disciplinary category dealt with at summary hearings).

On the victim side, the bill provides that a person acting on a victim's behalf — not just the victim — may request that a commanding officer appoint a victim's liaison officer. That liaison officer's job includes explaining how service offences are charged and tried, and obtaining and passing along information the victim is entitled to. The commanding officer must appoint one on request unless it is not possible for operational reasons, and should, where possible, appoint the specific person requested.

deepDive.heading: Sex offender registry and Criminal Code changes
deepDive.body:
The bill harmonizes the National Defence Act's sex offender information and publication ban provisions with earlier amendments made to the Criminal Code, the Sex Offender Information Registration Act and the International Transfer of Offenders Act. It also adjusts how certain failures to report to the registry can be proven in military proceedings, by allowing a certificate from a designated person to serve as evidence without needing to prove the signature or the signer's official position.

On the Criminal Code side, the bill gives superior courts of criminal jurisdiction the power to hear applications for exemptions from sex offender registry compliance orders made under the National Defence Act, and applications to vary how long such orders last.

deepDive.heading: Who is affected and context
deepDive.body:
The changes most directly affect members of the Canadian Armed Forces, military police, military prosecutors and defence counsel, military judges, and people who report sexual offences involving military members. For complainants in sexual offence cases arising in Canada, the practical effect is that investigation and prosecution move to civilian police forces and civilian courts rather than the military chain.

The bill is framed as a government response to the Report of the Third Independent Review Authority to the Minister of National Defence and the Report of the Independent External Comprehensive Review of the Department of National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces. Note that this summary is based on the portion of the bill text available above, which appears to be truncated; some provisions — including the full details on the Director of Defence Counsel Services, military judge eligibility and the interference complaint rules — are described in the bill's own summary rather than reproduced in the excerpt. The bill has received Royal Assent, meaning it has passed both the House of Commons and the Senate and become law, though specific provisions may come into force at different times.

C-12.overview: Bill C-12, the Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act, is a large government "omnibus" bill that changes a dozen different federal laws touching on border control, drugs, the coast guard, asylum claims, money laundering and the national sex offender registry. On the immigration side, it rewrites parts of the asylum system \u2014 scrapping the "designated countries of origin" list, adding new reasons a refugee claim can be ruled ineligible, and giving Cabinet broad new power to pause, cancel or refuse to process immigration applications and documents when it considers doing so to be in the public interest. On the security and enforcement side, it expands the Canada Border Services Agency's access to export-bound goods and to free facilities at ports and crossings, speeds up the listing of chemicals used to make illegal drugs, moves the Canadian Coast Guard under the Minister of National Defence, and toughens penalties and compliance rules for businesses covered by anti\u2011money\u2011laundering law. It also broadens information sharing between immigration officials and other government bodies. The bill has received royal assent, and Parliament must review how the changes are working after five years.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body: C-12 is a package of 12 parts, each amending a different area of federal law rather than creating one new program. Roughly speaking, it covers four themes: border and customs powers (Part 1), drug enforcement (Parts 2 and 3), maritime security (Part 4), immigration and asylum (Parts 5 through 8), financial crime (Parts 9 and 10), and the sex offender registry (Part 11). Part 12 requires a parliamentary review of how all of these amendments are operating five years after they take effect.\n\nBecause it is a money-related bill, it carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes spending of public funds for the purposes it sets out. It has completed the legislative process and received royal assent, though many of its details \u2014 particularly the exceptions and procedures under the immigration parts \u2014 are left to be filled in later through regulations made by Cabinet or by ministers.

deepDive.heading: Immigration and asylum changes
deepDive.body: Part 6 reworks the in-Canada asylum system. It eliminates the designated countries of origin regime (a list of countries whose nationals faced a faster, more restricted claim process), lets the Immigration Minister specify what information and documents a claimant must supply, and creates new ways for claims that have not yet reached the Refugee Protection Division to be treated as abandoned or withdrawn. It also blocks the Refugee Protection Division and Refugee Appeal Division from proceeding \u2014 or requires claims to be deemed abandoned \u2014 in certain cases where the claimant is not in Canada, and allows regulations requiring a designated representative for claimants under 18 or who cannot understand the proceeding.\n\nPart 7 gives Cabinet (the Governor in Council) power, when it believes it is in the public interest, to order that certain immigration applications not be accepted, or that their processing be suspended or terminated, and to cancel, suspend or vary documents issued under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or change the conditions attached to them. People affected by such an order can be required to appear for examination, answer truthfully and produce documents. Part 8 adds two new grounds on which a refugee claim is ineligible, requires officers to stop processing an ineligible claim, and includes a transitional provision applying the new grounds retroactively; regulations may set out exceptions. Part 5 separately allows the immigration department to share personal information internally and with other federal and provincial bodies for specified purposes.

deepDive.heading: Borders, drugs and the coast guard
deepDive.body: Part 1 amends the Customs Act so that owners and operators of international bridges, tunnels, railways, airports, wharves and docks must provide and maintain facilities for border services free of charge, and broadens their use to any program legislation administered by the CBSA. It also gives officers access to premises where export-bound goods are handled, including the ability to require packages be opened \u2014 but entry into a home requires the occupant's consent or a judicial warrant obtained on specified grounds.\n\nPart 2 creates a temporary fast-track process letting the Minister of Health add precursor chemicals (ingredients used to make illegal drugs) to a schedule under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act. Part 3 confirms that Cabinet may make regulations exempting police from drug-related \"inchoate\" offences (such as conspiracy or attempt) during lawful investigations. Part 4 transfers responsibility for the Canadian Coast Guard from the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to the Minister of National Defence, states that coast guard services include security activities, and authorizes the responsible minister to collect, analyze and share information and intelligence.

deepDive.heading: Financial crime and the sex offender registry
deepDive.body: Part 9 strengthens the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act by raising maximum administrative penalties and criminal punishments, replacing voluntary compliance agreements with a mandatory regime (with compliance orders if a business refuses or fails to comply, and a new violation for breaching such an order), requiring more entities to enroll with FINTRAC, and permitting FINTRAC to share certain information with the Commissioner of Canada Elections under set conditions. Part 10 adds FINTRAC's Director to the federal financial-institutions supervisory committee and allows information exchange with its other members.\n\nPart 11 updates the Sex Offender Information Registration Act: it adjusts when offenders must report and what information they must provide, allows identifying physical characteristics to be recorded, clarifies what counts as a reasonable excuse for not giving 14 days' notice before a trip of seven or more days, lets the CBSA share travel arrival and departure information with police for administering the Act, and permits disclosure of registry information where there are reasonable grounds to believe it will help prevent or investigate a sexual crime.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and what to watch
deepDive.body: The most direct effects fall on refugee claimants and other immigration applicants, who face new eligibility bars, new document requirements, new abandonment and withdrawal rules, and the possibility that Cabinet could pause or cancel processing of categories of applications or existing documents. Operators of international bridges, tunnels, ports, airports and railways, exporters and warehouse operators face expanded obligations to accommodate and cooperate with border officers. Businesses regulated under anti-money-laundering rules face higher penalties and mandatory compliance agreements, and registered sex offenders face changed reporting rules and broader information sharing.\n\nMuch of the bill's practical impact will depend on regulations still to be written \u2014 for example, the exceptions to the new ineligibility grounds, the limits on immigration information sharing, and the circumstances in which documents can be cancelled. The mandated five-year parliamentary review in Part 12 is the built-in checkpoint for assessing how the changes have worked in practice.

C-13.overview: Bill C-13 is the Canadian law needed to put into effect the July 2023 protocol that lets the United Kingdom join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), the trade pact Canada already shares with countries such as Japan, Australia, Mexico and Vietnam. The bill does not rewrite the trade agreement itself; instead it updates Canadian statutes so they recognize the UK's membership and so Canada can meet the commitments it made under the protocol. Its most concrete effect is on customs duties: it creates a new tariff category, the "Comprehensive and Progressive United Kingdom Tariff" (CPUKT), under which most goods imported from the UK enter Canada duty-free immediately and a smaller list of goods sees tariffs phased out over several years. It also adjusts banking and financial-sector rules and updates references to the CPTPP in several other Acts. The bill is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Maninder Sidhu and has received royal assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The CPTPP is an existing trade agreement among Canada and ten other Pacific-Rim countries. In 2023, the members signed a protocol in Auckland and Bandar Seri Begawan admitting the United Kingdom as a new member. Before that protocol can take effect for Canada, Canadian laws that refer to the CPTPP or that govern tariffs and financial institutions have to be brought into line with it.

Bill C-13 is that housekeeping-and-implementation law. As the bill's own summary puts it, it works by "updating how that Agreement is defined or referred to in certain Acts and by amending other Acts to bring them into conformity with Canada's obligations under that Agreement and Protocol." In practical terms, it amends the Financial Administration Act, the Commercial Arbitration Act, the Trust and Loan Companies Act, the Bank Act, the Insurance Companies Act and the Customs Tariff.

deepDive.heading: The new UK tariff and how it phases in
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new preferential tariff category to the Customs Tariff called the Comprehensive and Progressive United Kingdom Tariff, abbreviated "CPUKT," and adds it to the list of tariff treatments available to the United Kingdom, the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. For most tariff items, the CPUKT rate is set at "Free" — meaning no customs duty — right away, with certain listed exceptions set out in schedules to the bill.

For those exceptions, the bill sets out staged reductions using codes "X78," "X79" and "X80." Depending on the code, duties either begin dropping the day the agreement takes effect between Canada and the UK and disappear by January 1, 2028; stay unchanged for a year and then fall in equal steps to zero by January 1, 2029; or drop immediately to a quarter of the original rate and reach zero on January 1, 2029. The bill also includes technical rules for rounding fractional rates down, and a rule that any remaining rate under two per cent (except on certain motor vehicles) drops immediately to "Free." None of these reductions can apply retroactively to a period before the agreement is in force between Canada and the UK.

deepDive.heading: Other changes: safeguards, cabinet powers and financial institutions
deepDive.body:
The bill lets the Governor in Council (the federal cabinet) extend CPUKT treatment by order to goods originating in any CPTPP country, and to make such an order retroactive — but never earlier than the day the agreement takes effect between Canada and the UK. It also updates the Customs Tariff's safeguard provisions (section 76), setting time limits for temporary protective measures on UK goods that run to the third anniversary of the agreement's entry into force for the UK, or until the relevant duty reaches "Free," depending on the good.

On the financial side, the bill amends the Bank Act, the Trust and Loan Companies Act and the Insurance Companies Act. It reworks the definition of a "regulated foreign entity," ties several exceptions for foreign bank subsidiaries and bank holding companies to a list of countries and territories in Schedule IV of the Bank Act, replaces that Schedule IV entirely, and gives cabinet a general power to amend Schedule IV by order "for the purpose of implementing Canada's international trade obligations." Similar updating is done in the Financial Administration Act and the Commercial Arbitration Act, where references to the CPTPP are broadened to include any accession protocol listed in the CPTPP Implementation Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Importers and exporters trading between Canada and the United Kingdom are the most directly affected: Canadian businesses buying UK goods will generally pay lower or no duties, with a set of goods facing a multi-year phase-out instead of immediate elimination. Canadian producers who compete with UK imports in those staged categories will see tariffs fall gradually rather than all at once.

Financial institutions — banks, bank holding companies, trust and loan companies and insurers with foreign ownership links — are affected by the changes to how "regulated foreign entity" and the Schedule IV country list work. Customs brokers and anyone classifying goods will need to work with the new CPUKT column added to the List of Tariff Provisions.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Maninder Sidhu, and it has received royal assent, meaning it has completed the parliamentary process and become law. That said, many of its tariff effects are tied to the date the CPTPP actually enters into force between Canada and the United Kingdom, and several provisions expressly cannot apply before that day.
