One caution for readers: the text reproduced above is marked as possibly truncated, and the bill refers to detailed schedules (Schedules 1, 2 and 3) listing the specific tariff items and the revised Bank Act Schedule IV. This summary describes only what appears in the available text; the precise list of goods subject to staged tariff reductions is contained in those schedules.

C-14.overview: Bill C-14, the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, is a federal government bill (sponsored by Justice Minister Sean Fraser) that has received royal assent. It makes a broad set of changes to the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act and the National Defence Act, generally tightening the rules around bail (called "judicial interim release") and increasing the severity of sentencing for certain offences. On bail, it clarifies that the "principle of restraint" does not require release, expands "reverse onus" situations where an accused must prove why they should be released, and requires judges to impose or consider specific release conditions for offences such as extortion, auto theft and break-ins. On sentencing, it adds new aggravating factors, requires some sentences to be served one after another rather than at the same time, limits conditional (community-based) sentences for sexual offences, and directs courts to prioritize denunciation and deterrence for repeat auto theft, repeat break-ins and organized crime. It also changes youth justice rules, including publication of a young person's identity by police in urgent public-safety situations, and requires the Justice Minister to publish an annual report on the state of bail in Canada.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act amends three federal statutes at once. In the Criminal Code, it reshapes how police officers, justices of the peace and judges decide whether to release or detain a person awaiting trial, and it changes how courts sentence people convicted of a range of offences. In the Youth Criminal Justice Act, it adjusts definitions, custody rules, publication rules and record-keeping for young people. In the National Defence Act, it mirrors several of the sentencing changes in the military justice system.

A notable clarifying provision states that the existing "principle of restraint" — the direction to use the least restrictive approach to pre-trial detention — does not require that an accused be released. Police must not release someone if detention is necessary in the public interest, including for the safety of victims or witnesses; where release does occur, the least onerous appropriate conditions must be imposed; and a judge must not release an accused where detention is justified under the Criminal Code's existing grounds, including protection of the public.

deepDive.heading: Bail changes in detail
deepDive.body:
The bill expands "reverse onus" bail, meaning the accused (rather than the Crown) must show why they should be released. New reverse-onus categories include auto theft involving violence or committed for a criminal organization, extortion involving violence, breaking and entering a dwelling-house, certain human trafficking and smuggling offences, certain alleged choking, suffocation or strangulation offences, and a third or subsequent violent indictable offence. It also extends reverse onus to people charged with a serious violent offence involving a weapon who were convicted of a similar offence within the past 10 years, and creates a reverse onus where the Crown applies to cancel someone's existing release order after a finding of guilt.

Other bail provisions require a justice to consider whether the alleged offence involved random and unprovoked violence, and to weigh the number and gravity of any outstanding charges when deciding if detention is needed to maintain public confidence in the justice system. For extortion and criminal-organization charges, a weapons prohibition condition becomes mandatory; for auto theft and break-and-enter charges, judges must consider specified conditions. A person convicted of an indictable offence within the past 10 years generally cannot act as a surety (the person who vouches for an accused), and the rules for cancelling release documents are broadened, with appeal court review available.

deepDive.heading: Sentencing changes
deepDive.body:
The bill creates new aggravating factors — circumstances that push a sentence upward — for repeat violent offending, offences against first responders, retail theft and theft, mischief to property, and assaults on public transit employees (with the definition widened to cover anyone working or contracted to work for a public transit organization). Additional aggravating factors apply where theft or robbery-type offences were committed to sell, barter or fraudulently return stolen goods, or where an offence interfered with essential infrastructure.

It also adds consecutive-sentence rules (sentences served back-to-back) for repeat violent offences, auto theft, break-and-enter, and extortion combined with arson; directs courts to give primary consideration to denunciation and deterrence for repeat auto theft, repeat break-ins and organized crime offences; restricts conditional sentence orders for sexual assault and sexual offences against victims under 18; restores driving prohibitions for manslaughter and criminal negligence causing bodily harm or death; and increases the penalty for contempt while strengthening fine enforcement and allowing more remote appearances in the mental disorder regime.

deepDive.heading: Youth justice and military justice
deepDive.body:
Under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, the definition of "violent offence" is clarified to include offences where a young person causes bodily harm or that involve using or trafficking a firearm. Time a young person spends unlawfully at large will not count toward time served on a custody and supervision order. Police gain the ability to publish identifying information about a young person in urgent situations involving imminent danger to public safety. The bill also clarifies detention and release procedures for young people remanded for allegedly breaching a custody-sentence condition, sets access periods for records of extrajudicial measures, clarifies rules for police records of investigations that led to no charge, and makes technical sentencing amendments.

In the National Defence Act, the changes largely parallel the civilian ones: a higher penalty for contempt, a requirement that courts martial give primary consideration to denunciation and deterrence for criminal-organization offences, and new aggravating circumstances for repeat violent offending, offences against first responders, stealing for commercial purposes and certain property offences.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The bill most directly affects people charged with or convicted of the listed offences — including violent offences, auto theft, break-and-enter, extortion, human trafficking and smuggling, and sexual offences — as well as young people in the youth justice system and Canadian Armed Forces members subject to military justice. It also affects the day-to-day work of police officers, justices of the peace, judges, prosecutors and defence counsel, and it changes who can serve as a surety for an accused person. Victims and witnesses are referenced explicitly in the new direction to police and courts about release decisions and conditions.

For transparency and monitoring, the bill amends the Department of Justice Act to require the Minister of Justice to prepare an annual report on the state of judicial interim release (bail) in Canada. The Act also contains transitional provisions and coordinating amendments, plus a number of housekeeping changes such as updating references to which courts count as superior courts in various provinces and territories. Because the bill has received royal assent, it is law, though specific provisions take effect according to the Act's own coming-into-force and transitional rules.

C-15.overview: Bill C-15 is the government's first bill to put into law measures announced in the federal budget tabled on November 4, 2025. It is a large "omnibus" budget bill: it changes income tax rules for individuals and businesses, repeals the Digital Services Tax, ends the Underused Housing Tax and the luxury tax on aircraft and boats, creates a legal framework for a high-speed rail line between Quebec and Ontario, authorizes billions in spending on housing and infrastructure entities, and rewrites a range of banking and financial-institution rules. The bill received royal assent, meaning it has been passed by Parliament and is now law (though individual measures take effect on their own timelines set out in the legislation). Because it touches everything from tax credits for personal support workers to how quickly a cheque clears at your bank, it affects most Canadians in some way, even if indirectly.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill implements budget commitments across five parts. Part 1 amends the Income Tax Act and regulations with dozens of changes. Part 2 repeals the Digital Services Tax Act and its regulations. Part 3 changes the Excise Tax Act (GST/HST), ends the Underused Housing Tax starting with the 2025 calendar year and eventually repeals that Act entirely, and ends the luxury tax on aircraft and vessels. Part 4 amends the First Nations Goods and Services Tax Act. Part 5 is a grab-bag of measures enacting or amending numerous other statutes, from transportation and postal rates to banking regulation.

As a budget implementation act, it carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money for the purposes it sets out.

deepDive.heading: Tax changes for individuals and businesses
deepDive.body:
For individuals, Part 1 exempts the Canada Disability Benefit from being counted as income, broadens the list of expenses eligible under the Disability Supports Deduction, creates a Personal Support Workers Tax Credit, streamlines the Home Accessibility Tax Credit, extends the deadline for certain 2024 charitable donations, and adds a temporary non-refundable credit for people whose non-refundable credit amounts exceed the first tax bracket threshold. The Lifetime Capital Gains Exemption limit rises to $1.25 million for dispositions on or after June 25, 2024, with indexation resuming in 2026.

For businesses, the bill exempts the first $10 million in capital gains on a sale to a worker cooperative (with a matching change for employee ownership trusts), enhances the SR&ED research credit (higher expenditure limits, extension to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restored capital expenditure eligibility), reinstates the accelerated investment incentive and immediate expensing for certain assets, adds a 10% accelerated capital cost allowance for new purpose-built rental projects, and reforms transfer pricing rules. Resource and clean-economy measures include extending the Mineral Exploration Tax Credit to March 31, 2027, expanding the Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit to 14 additional minerals, extending full Carbon Capture credit rates to 2035, and broadening clean technology and clean electricity investment credits. Several anti-avoidance and integrity measures are also included, such as removing the tax-indifferent investor exception to the synthetic equity arrangement rule and narrowing trust reporting requirements.

deepDive.heading: Taxes being removed and sales tax changes
deepDive.body:
Three taxes are wound down. The Digital Services Tax Act and its regulations are repealed outright. The Underused Housing Tax ends for 2025 and future years, and the Act itself is later repealed. The luxury tax stops applying to aircraft and vessels (regulations are made to clarify treatment of remaining subject items).

On the GST/HST side, the bill clarifies that osteopathic services provided by people who are not osteopathic physicians are taxable, extends the Enhanced (100%) GST Rental Rebate to qualifying cooperative housing corporations and to student residences built by universities, public colleges and school authorities, and limits input tax credits for redeemed coupons to payments made exclusively in commercial activities. Part 4 sets up an opt-in framework allowing interested Indigenous governments to levy their own value-added sales tax on fuel, alcohol, cannabis, tobacco and vaping products on reserves or settlement lands, with administrative streamlining.

deepDive.heading: Infrastructure, spending and government operations
deepDive.body:
Division 1 of Part 5 enacts the High-Speed Rail Network Act, a framework for a high-speed passenger rail network between Quebec and Ontario. It deems the rail lines approved under section 98 of the Canada Transportation Act, confirms that construction, operation, decommissioning and abandonment remain subject to the Impact Assessment Act, allows notices of right of first refusal or prohibition on work for certain land, modifies expropriation procedures for the project, protects Indigenous knowledge shared in confidence, and applies parts of the Official Languages Act to certain operators.

Other measures authorize up to $11.5 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for Build Canada Homes and up to $1.515 billion for Canada Lands Company Limited, and raise the ceiling on payments to the Canada Infrastructure Bank to $45 billion. Canada Post gains the authority to set postage rates and terms directly, replacing the regulation-making power. The Red Tape Reduction Act is amended to let ministers grant temporary exemptions from certain laws to support regulatory experimentation in clean technology and financial technology. Two divisions amend the Public Service Superannuation Act to widen early retirement eligibility for some operational-service employees and to create a temporary early retirement option during workforce reduction initiatives. The Farm Credit Canada Act gains periodic review requirements.

deepDive.heading: Banking and consumer finance
deepDive.body:
Part 5 rewrites significant portions of financial sector law. The existing Consumer-Driven Banking Act is repealed and replaced with a new one covering open banking: accreditation of participants, data sharing, consent and authentication, security safeguards, liability, complaints, enforcement, and screen scraping. Financial institution statutes (Bank Act, Trust and Loan Companies Act, Insurance Companies Act) are amended to extend institutions' sunset dates, remove certain prudential limits on borrowing, loans and investments, permit electronic delivery of documents without prior consent (with paper copies on request), and raise the public holding requirement threshold from $2 billion to $4 billion. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions gains clarified powers over integrity and security policies, authority to direct compliance where practices are unsafe or unsound, and greater latitude to share information with federal bodies.

For everyday consumers, the bill raises the amount that can be withdrawn immediately after depositing a cheque and removes the hold delay for cheques not deposited in person. It also requires express consent before certain personal deposit account capabilities are activated, lets account holders deactivate capabilities and adjust transaction limits, requires banks to have policies for detecting and preventing consumer-targeted fraud, and requires annual fraud reporting by institutions and by the Commissioner of the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada. Note: the text provided here is truncated partway through Division 17, so additional divisions of Part 5 may exist that are not described above.

C-16.overview: Bill C-16, the Protecting Victims Act, is a large government bill that amends the Criminal Code and several other laws dealing with criminal justice, corrections and the military justice system. Its main themes are protecting children, responding to gender-based and intimate partner violence, reducing court delays, and strengthening the rights of victims. Among other things, it creates a new offence of coercive or controlling behaviour toward an intimate partner, makes certain murders — including those the bill identifies as femicide when the victim is female — automatically first-degree murder, tightens rules around child sexual offences and non-consensual intimate images (including realistic fakes), and gives judges a limited power to go below mandatory minimum sentences where those minimums would be cruel and unusual for a particular offender. The bill received royal assent, and most of it comes into force 30 days after that date.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Protecting Victims Act is an omnibus criminal justice bill. It amends the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act, the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights, the National Defence Act, the federal law on mandatory reporting of online child sexual abuse material, the Firearms Act, the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, and the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act.

Rather than addressing a single issue, it bundles together changes grouped around four stated themes in its long title: child protection, gender-based violence, court delays, and "other measures." It also includes transitional rules explaining how the changes apply to cases already underway, coordinating provisions with several other bills before Parliament, and a requirement that the Senate and House of Commons review the legislation.

deepDive.heading: Gender-based and intimate partner violence
deepDive.body:
The bill creates a new offence prohibiting a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct toward an intimate partner — behaviour that may not involve physical assault but that dominates or restricts a partner's life. It also makes murder automatically first-degree murder (the most serious classification) in four situations: when an intimate partner is killed in the context of a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct, when the killing occurs in the context of sexual violence, when it occurs in the context of human trafficking, or when it is motivated by hate. The bill notes that murder of a female person is known as femicide. Where manslaughter is committed in those same circumstances, a court must consider imposing a life sentence, with parole ineligibility of 10 to 25 years for adult offenders.

The criminal harassment (stalking) offence is changed so prosecutors no longer must prove the victim personally felt afraid; instead, they must show the conduct could reasonably be expected to make the victim believe someone's safety is threatened. The Firearms Act is amended so that a person is ineligible for a firearms licence if the chief firearms officer has reasonable grounds to suspect they may have engaged in domestic violence or stalking, and it clarifies that someone whose licence is revoked must hand over their firearm to police or a firearms officer. Victims of offences such as those committed against an intimate partner become entitled to testimonial aids — supports that make testifying in court easier.

deepDive.heading: Child protection and online material
deepDive.body:
Several child-focused changes are included. Existing child sexual offences are expanded to cover inviting a child to expose their own sexual organs for a sexual purpose, and the Criminal Code adds a definition of "sexual organs." A new offence targets recruiting a person under 18 to take part in an offence. The bill also criminalizes distributing visual representations of bestiality, and broadens the offence of non-consensual distribution of intimate images to cover fabricated or altered depictions — images likely to be mistaken for a real recording of an identifiable person.

The law requiring internet service providers to report child sexual abuse and exploitation material is updated: it clarifies which services are covered, requires transmission data to accompany reports where the material is clearly abuse material, lengthens how long related data must be preserved, and extends the time limit for prosecuting offences under that Act. Under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, youth justice courts may order a young person to enter into a recognizance (a court-ordered promise with conditions) where there is a reasonable fear the young person will commit a child sexual offence.

deepDive.heading: Court delays, sentencing and trial procedure
deepDive.body:
A new Part of the Criminal Code addresses unreasonable delay. It requires courts to weigh specific factors when assessing how complex a case is, directs them to exclude certain time periods tied to particular applications, and provides that a stay of proceedings (ending a prosecution because of delay) may be ordered only where the court is satisfied, considering a list of factors, that no other remedy would be appropriate and just. Parallel rules are added for courts martial under the National Defence Act.

On sentencing, the bill lets a court impose a term below a mandatory minimum, but only where the minimum would amount to cruel and unusual punishment for that specific offender. A new Part sets out a framework for alternative measures and restorative justice processes in appropriate cases. The bill also streamlines the rules governing sexual offence trials — specifically when a complainant's past sexual activity can be raised and when private records such as therapy records can be produced or used — with matching changes for the military justice system. Affidavit evidence becomes available in some identity theft and identity fraud cases, and the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act is amended to allow cooperation with supranational investigative or prosecuting bodies.

deepDive.heading: Victims' rights and who is affected
deepDive.body:
The Canadian Victims Bill of Rights is amended to affirm victim-centred and trauma-informed approaches, to give victims a right to be treated with respect, courtesy, compassion and fairness, and to provide information automatically rather than only on request. Victims gain the right to be told about their own rights and about available protection measures and restorative justice options, and the right to present a victim impact statement at sentencing and a victim statement in parole and corrections decisions is clarified. Similar rights are added to the National Defence Act's Declaration of Victims Rights, and the Corrections and Conditional Release Act is amended to expand information sharing with victims and within the justice system.

The people most directly affected include victims of intimate partner violence, sexual offences, harassment and human trafficking; accused persons and offenders, who face new offences and sentencing rules but also a new judicial discretion around mandatory minimums; children and young people; internet service providers; firearms licence holders; and courts, police, prosecutors and corrections officials. The Youth Criminal Justice Act changes also modernize the principle requiring consideration of young persons' needs, with particular attention to Aboriginal and Black young persons. Most provisions take effect 30 days after royal assent, and Parliament is required to review the legislation.

C-17.overview: Bill C-17, the Appropriation Act No. 3, 2025-26, is a routine but essential government spending bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $10,848,320,356 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026. The money corresponds to the Supplementary Estimates (B) for that year — extra funding requested for departments and agencies beyond what Parliament had already approved earlier in the year. The bill itself does not create new programs or change any laws; it simply gives legal permission to spend money on the specific items listed in its two schedules, such as top-ups for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Canadian Heritage, Agriculture and Agri-Food, and dozens of other federal bodies. Because governments cannot legally spend money without parliamentary approval, bills like this one are a core part of Parliament's control over public finances. The bill has received royal assent, meaning it is now law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) the authority to pay out a maximum of $10,848,320,356 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for expenses in the 2025-26 fiscal year that are "not otherwise provided for" — that is, spending not already covered by earlier appropriation acts or by standing legal authorities.

The total is broken into two schedules. Schedule 1 accounts for $10,662,579,153 based on the Supplementary Estimates (B) for 2025-26; Schedule 2 covers the remaining amount and operates under somewhat different timing rules. Each schedule lists individual "votes" assigned to specific departments, agencies and Crown corporations, with a dollar figure and a description of what the money may be used for.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 2 sets the overall spending ceiling and ties it to the Supplementary Estimates (B) tabled with the Governor General's message. Section 3 confirms that transfers of money between appropriations, as set out in those Estimates, are treated as authorized from April 1, 2025. Section 4 is a limiting rule: money approved for a given item may be spent only for the purposes and under the conditions written into that item, and each item is deemed to take effect from April 1, 2025 (the start of the fiscal year), even though the bill passed later.

Sections 5 and 6 deal with accounting mechanics. They allow appropriations listed in the schedules to be charged after the fiscal year has ended — up until the Public Accounts are tabled — purely to make bookkeeping adjustments that do not involve any actual cash leaving the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Schedule 2 amounts can be paid out any time up to March 31, 2027, with payments charged against the oldest available appropriation first; anything unspent lapses at the end of the following fiscal year, subject to adjustments under section 37 of the Financial Administration Act.

deepDive.heading: Who and what is funded
deepDive.body:
The schedules cover a wide cross-section of the federal government. Examples visible in the text include the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation ($101.1 million to reimburse the corporation for loans forgiven, grants, contributions and losses under the National Housing Act and other statutes), the Department of Canadian Heritage (about $124.1 million, mostly grants and contributions), the Department of Agriculture and Agri-Food (about $42.1 million), the Communications Security Establishment ($30 million), the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency ($22.5 million) and the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency ($11.2 million).

Smaller amounts go to bodies such as the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, Correctional Service of Canada, the Courts Administration Service, the Canadian Human Rights Commission, the Canada School of Public Service and several national museums. Some votes also carry non-dollar authorities — for instance, permission for an agency to spend revenues it earns from providing internal support services to other departments, or Correctional Service of Canada's authority to operate inmate canteens and deposit proceeds into the Inmate Welfare Fund. A few items appear as a token $1, a standard Estimates practice used to make a technical change to an existing authority without granting new money.

deepDive.heading: Context: how appropriation bills work
deepDive.body:
Under Canada's system of responsible government, the executive cannot spend public money without a vote of Parliament. Each year the government tables Main Estimates and, as needs change, one or more sets of Supplementary Estimates (labelled A, B and C). Each set is then given legal force through an appropriation act. Bill C-17 is the third such act for 2025-26 and corresponds to Supplementary Estimates (B).

The bill's preamble notes that it follows a message from Governor General Mary Simon transmitting the Estimates, reflecting the constitutional rule that spending measures originate with the Crown. Sponsored by the Hon. Shafqat Ali, the bill has passed both the House of Commons and the Senate and received royal assent. Appropriation bills of this kind are considered confidence matters in the House of Commons, since a government's ability to obtain supply is central to its ability to govern.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does not do
deepDive.body:
This is a spending authorization, not a policy statute. It does not amend existing legislation, create new programs, set tax rates, or change eligibility rules for any benefit. The programs the money supports were established under other laws and authorities; C-17 only permits the cash to flow to them.

It also does not oblige the government to spend the full amount. The figures are ceilings — the government may spend up to those limits for the stated purposes, and unspent amounts generally lapse at the end of the applicable period. Readers wanting detail on any individual line item would need to consult the Supplementary Estimates (B), 2025-26, which the bill's schedules reproduce.

C-18.overview: Bill C-18 is the federal law that puts into effect a new free trade deal between Canada and Indonesia — the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), signed in Ottawa on September 24, 2025. The bill formally approves the agreement, sets up and funds Canada's participation in the joint bodies that will oversee it, and gives Cabinet the authority to issue orders — including retaliatory measures if a trade dispute goes against Indonesia. It also amends several existing laws, including the Customs Act, Customs Tariff, Investment Canada Act and Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, so Canadian rules match what the agreement requires. The bill has received royal assent, though its provisions come into force by order in council. For businesses and consumers, the practical effect is lower or eliminated tariffs and clearer rules for trade and investment between the two countries.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act's core function is straightforward: section 9 states simply that "the Agreement is approved." Everything else in the bill is the machinery needed to make that approval work in Canadian law. Section 7 lists the agreement's stated objectives, which include establishing a free trade area, reducing or eliminating barriers to trade in goods and services, providing a predictable framework for business planning and investment, and increasing investment opportunities while preserving each country's right to regulate for legitimate policy goals.

The stated objectives also extend beyond tariffs. They include supporting small and medium-sized businesses, promoting environmental protection and enforcement of environmental laws, protecting labour rights and improving working conditions, encouraging companies to respect corporate social responsibility standards, combatting bribery and corruption, increasing participation by Indigenous Peoples in trade and investment, and preserving each country's right to maintain measures for cultural industries.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Several mechanical provisions structure how the agreement operates day to day. The Minister for International Trade is Canada's principal representative on the Joint Committee overseeing the agreement, and Canada agrees to pay its share of that committee's costs, plus the remuneration and expenses of panellists, experts and subsidiary bodies. The Minister appoints Canada's representatives to panels and working groups, with the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Labour appointing members to the Environment Sub-Committee and Labour Council respectively.

Two provisions stand out. Section 15 lets the Governor in Council (Cabinet) make orders suspending benefits Canada has granted Indonesia — including suspending rights or privileges, modifying federal laws as they apply to Indonesian goods, services or investors, or taking any other measure considered necessary — as a dispute-settlement remedy under Article 24.13. Section 8 restricts private lawsuits: no individual can sue to enforce rights arising solely from the agreement or from the funding and order-making provisions without the consent of the Attorney General of Canada, subject to certain carve-outs in the agreement itself. Section 4 clarifies that neither the Act nor the agreement applies to natural surface or ground water.

deepDive.heading: Accountability and review requirements
deepDive.body:
Section 15.1 requires the Minister for International Trade to ensure that Canadian companies operating in Indonesia comply with the responsible-business principles and guidelines referenced in Article 22.15 of the agreement. The Minister must set up a process for receiving and responding to complaints of non-compliance, and must prepare an annual report summarizing these activities — the first due on or before January 1, 2027 — and table it in both houses of Parliament.

Separately, section 15.2 requires a comprehensive review of how the Act and the agreement are working, and their effects, within three years of that section coming into force and every three years afterward. The review is to be conducted by a House of Commons committee designated for the purpose, which must report its findings and recommendations to the House within six months of finishing.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Canadian exporters and importers dealing with Indonesia are the most directly affected. Amendments to the Customs Act and Customs Tariff build the agreement into Canada's border rules — for example, importers claiming preferential tariff treatment under the new agreement (referred to as "CICEPA") can self-certify in writing that goods meet the rules of origin, using prescribed forms and supporting documents from the exporter or producer, similar to how the CPTPP and CUSMA already work.

Other affected parties include foreign investors, since the Investment Canada Act schedule is amended to include the agreement, which affects how investment review thresholds and rules apply. Amendments also touch the Financial Administration Act, the Commercial Arbitration Act and the Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act. Businesses operating in Indonesia will face the new corporate-conduct compliance and complaints process.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Maninder Sidhu, Minister for International Trade, and it has received royal assent. The bill carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money — in this case Canada's share of the costs of running the agreement's committees and dispute panels. The provisions come into force on a date set by order in council, which typically allows Canada to align the timing with Indonesia's own ratification steps.

Bill C-18 follows a familiar template used for Canada's other trade agreements: approve the treaty, fund the institutions, empower Cabinet to respond to disputes, and amend the customs and trade statutes to match. The added elements here are the corporate-conduct compliance obligation with annual reporting and the mandatory three-year parliamentary review cycle, both of which create ongoing oversight after the deal takes effect.

C-20.overview: Bill C-20, the Build Canada Homes Act, creates a new federal Crown corporation called Build Canada Homes. Its job is to increase the supply of affordable housing across Canada and to encourage new, faster and more efficient ways of building homes. The corporation gets broad business-style powers — it can lend money, invest, buy and sell land, build housing itself, partner with other governments, and collect housing data — and the bill authorizes up to $11.5 billion in federal funding for its operations, plus borrowing powers. The bill also lets Cabinet transfer assets from other Crown corporations to Build Canada Homes and direct the reorganization of Canada Lands Company Limited, the federal real-estate corporation. The bill has received Royal Assent, though most of it comes into force on a date set by order in council.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act establishes Build Canada Homes as a Crown corporation and an agent of the Crown, with the legal capacity of a natural person (meaning it can enter contracts, own property and sue or be sued). Its stated purpose is twofold: to promote, support and develop the supply of affordable housing in Canada, and to promote innovative and efficient building techniques in the housing construction sector.

Cabinet (the Governor in Council) designates which minister is responsible for the corporation and where its head office will be located. The corporation's share capital is nominal — $100 in 10 shares — all held by the minister on behalf of the Crown, confirming full public ownership.

deepDive.heading: Powers and money
deepDive.body:
Section 20 lists what Build Canada Homes can do: advise federal departments and Crown corporations; provide financial assistance to any person, entity or level of government; invest in housing-related businesses through shares, securities, loans or guarantees; acquire and develop property; develop land and construct housing directly; buy, hold, lease or sell property; charge fees for its services; deliver programs on behalf of or jointly with other governments; and collect and share housing data to monitor the sector. Cabinet can add further activities by order. Loan guarantees require the Finance Minister's approval.

On funding, the Minister of Finance may pay out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund up to an aggregate $11.5 billion (or other amounts set by an appropriation Act) to fund the corporation's operations. The corporation also has borrowing powers exercised at the Finance Minister's discretion (the provision is cut off in the text available here). Several standard Financial Administration Act constraints — sections 91, 99(2) and 100(1), which normally govern Crown corporation transactions such as creating subsidiaries and disposing of or leasing property — are made not to apply, giving the corporation more operational latitude.

deepDive.heading: Governance and accountability
deepDive.body:
Build Canada Homes is run by a board of a Chairperson plus eight to ten other directors. The Chairperson and the Chief Executive Officer are appointed by Cabinet to hold office 'during pleasure' (that is, they can be removed at any time); other directors are appointed by the responsible minister with Cabinet approval for terms of up to four years, staggered so no more than half turn over in a single year. The minister must consult the board before the Chairperson or CEO is appointed, and Cabinet can terminate, remove or suspend any of them.

Sitting senators, MPs and provincial legislators cannot be appointed, nor can anyone under 18 or an undischarged bankrupt. Remuneration rates are set by Cabinet. The Act also includes a review provision, regulation-making authority, and rules on accident compensation; the table of provisions indicates a consequential amendment to the Financial Administration Act and coordinating amendments tied to Bill C-15.

deepDive.heading: Transfers and Canada Lands Company
deepDive.body:
The Act allows Cabinet to transfer property, rights, interests and obligations held by any Crown corporation or its subsidiary to Build Canada Homes. It also empowers Cabinet to issue directives for the reorganization of Canada Lands Company Limited — the federal Crown corporation that manages and develops surplus federal real estate — or any of its subsidiaries, including amendments to corporate articles and authorities for the companies involved.

Transitional provisions cover matters such as the transfer of a 'special operating agency' and the initial appointment of the Chairperson and Chief Executive Officer, so the new corporation can begin operating without a gap.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The most direct effects fall on the federal housing and real-estate apparatus: the new corporation itself, Canada Lands Company and any Crown corporations whose assets are transferred. Beyond that, the corporation can deal with provinces, territories, municipalities, non-profit and private housing developers, builders and investors — as a funder, investor, landowner, partner or direct builder of housing.

The bill is a government bill sponsored by Hon. Gregor Robertson and has received Royal Assent, with coming into force set by order in council. Note that the text supplied here is truncated partway through the borrowing-power provision, so some details of the financial, miscellaneous, transitional and coordinating sections are not described above.

C-21.overview: Bill C-21 would put into Canadian law a treaty signed on November 30, 2024 between the Government of Canada and the Red River Métis, represented by the Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF). The treaty recognizes the Red River Métis right to govern themselves, and the bill declares it valid, gives it the force of law, and confirms it is a treaty under sections 25 and 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 — the sections that protect Aboriginal and treaty rights. It also approves a separate tax treatment agreement, sets out how courts are to handle Red River Métis laws, and makes small housekeeping changes to the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act so the MMF is treated like other Indigenous governments in those laws. The bill matters because Parliament's approval is the final step needed to ratify the treaty and make the self-government arrangement legally binding. It is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The core of the bill is short: it approves the Red River Métis Self-Government Recognition and Implementation Treaty, declares it valid, and gives it the force of law. The bill's preamble explains that ratification of the treaty requires an Act of Parliament, so this legislation is the mechanism that brings the treaty into effect.

Once in force, the treaty binds everyone and can be relied on by anyone — people and organizations named in it gain the powers and benefits it confers and take on the duties and liabilities it imposes. Section 3 confirms, for greater certainty, that the agreement counts as a "treaty" under sections 25 and 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982, which is the constitutional protection attached to Aboriginal and treaty rights.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Order of precedence: if the treaty conflicts with this Act or any other federal law, the treaty wins to the extent of the conflict. If this Act conflicts with another federal law, this Act wins. The bill also approves a separate tax treatment agreement and gives it the force of law while it is in effect, but clarifies that this tax agreement is not part of the treaty and is not itself a constitutionally protected treaty or land claims agreement.

Courts and legal process: judges must take "judicial notice" of the treaty, the tax agreement, and Red River Métis laws — meaning these do not have to be formally proven in court each time they come up. Copies published by the King's Printer, or deposited in the public registry described in the treaty, count as evidence. The Federal Court may review administrative decisions made by the MMF under Red River Métis law, but only after all appeal or review steps within Red River Métis law have been used up. Red River Métis laws and instruments made under the treaty are not treated as federal "statutory instruments," so the usual federal regulation-making rules do not apply to them.

Regulations and transition: Cabinet (the Governor in Council) may make orders and regulations needed to carry out the treaty, the Act, and related agreements, and must give the MMF a meaningful opportunity to collaborate on developing the policy behind those regulations. A transitional provision deems past MMF actions and decisions valid, to the extent they would have been valid under the treaty had it been in force at the time.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill directly affects the Red River Métis and the Manitoba Métis Federation, the body that represents them under the treaty and that will exercise governing authority through Red River Métis laws. It also affects the federal government, which takes on the treaty obligations and gains responsibility for implementing regulations.

More broadly, the bill affects courts (which must recognize Red River Métis laws and may review certain MMF decisions) and federal institutions that handle information. Amendments to the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act add the MMF to the lists of "aboriginal governments" and similar entities, allowing information-sharing arrangements for administering or enforcing laws and requiring that personal information obtained in confidence from the MMF generally be withheld from disclosure — the same treatment other Indigenous governments already receive.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The preamble frames the bill within the federal government's stated commitment to reconciliation through renewed government-to-government relationships, and states that Ottawa recognizes the inherent right of self-government as a right affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. It also says the government is committed to implementing the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and that both parties view the treaty as contributing to that implementation.

The bill is sponsored by the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations, the Hon. Rebecca Alty. A coordinating clause ties it to Bill C-10, the proposed Commissioner for Modern Treaty Implementation Act: if that bill becomes law, the Red River Métis would be added to its schedule, bringing this treaty within the oversight of that proposed commissioner. Note that the bill text itself does not spell out the treaty's substantive contents — the specific law-making powers, funding, and jurisdictions are set out in the treaty document, which the bill approves and requires to be published.

C-22.overview: Bill C-22, the Lawful Access Act, 2026, is a federal government bill that would update the rules for how police, other law enforcement officials and Canada's spy agency (CSIS) obtain digital data and subscriber information during investigations. It would let officers send "confirmation of service demands" to telecom companies to find out whether a company serves a particular customer, account or identifier; create new court-ordered production and warrant powers for subscriber information, tracking data, transmission data and computer data; and set out when officers can act in urgent ("exigent") circumstances or on information that is volunteered or publicly available. A second part creates a brand-new law, the Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act, requiring designated "core" electronic service providers to build in the capacity to assist with lawfully authorized access, backed by inspections, compliance orders, financial penalties and offences. The bill matters because it touches directly on the balance between investigative powers and the privacy of Canadians' online and phone records, and it would require Parliament to review the new powers after they are in force. As of this writing, the bill has passed the House of Commons stage and is awaiting first reading in the Senate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has three parts. Part 1 amends existing laws — the Criminal Code, the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act, the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act and the Cannabis Act (plus a consequential change to the Foreign Publishers Advertising Services Act) — to speed up and clarify how investigators get data and information. Part 2 enacts a new statute, the Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act, dealing with the obligations of electronic service providers. Part 3 requires a parliamentary review of Parts 1 and 2.

The overall theme, as described in the bill's own summary, is "modernizing" provisions about the "timely gathering and production of data and information during an investigation" — that is, making existing investigative tools work with today's telecommunications and computer systems, and adding new ones.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions in Part 1 (police and CSIS powers)
deepDive.body:
Several tools are created or clarified. A new "confirmation of service demand" (Criminal Code section 487.0121) would let a peace officer or public officer require a telecom provider to confirm whether it does or did provide service to a named subscriber, account or identifier. The officer must have "reasonable grounds to suspect" that an offence has been or will be committed and that the confirmation will help the investigation. The bill expressly states such a demand cannot be made if it would reveal medical information or information covered by solicitor-client privilege or the professional secrecy of advocates and notaries, and cannot be directed at a provider that is itself under investigation for the offence.

Other Part 1 measures include: judicial production orders for "subscriber information," which the bill defines broadly (name, pseudonym, address, phone number, email, account numbers, types and duration of services, and identifiers of devices used); a shortened review process to speed up responses to production orders; clarified rules on officers receiving voluntarily provided information and using publicly available information; rules for obtaining evidence, including subscriber information, in exigent (urgent) circumstances; warrants that can cover tracking or transmission data for similar things not yet known when the warrant was issued; new and clarified warrant powers to search, seize, copy and examine computer data, including a requirement that a copy of a computer-data examination warrant generally be given to the computer's owner and to a person under investigation whose data is examined (with exceptions and possible extensions of up to three years); and judicial authorization for officers to ask foreign telecommunications or online service providers to produce transmission data or subscriber information. Amendments to the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act would allow the Minister of Justice to authorize arrangements to enforce a foreign authority's order compelling production of transmission data or subscriber information held by someone in Canada. CSIS would get parallel confirmation-of-service demands and judicial orders against providers, plus clarified response times for production orders.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions in Part 2 (obligations on service providers)
deepDive.body:
The new Supporting Authorized Access to Information Act would create a framework so that electronic service providers can "facilitate the exercise, by authorized persons, of authorities to access information" already conferred under the Criminal Code or the CSIS Act. It provides for classes of "core providers," temporary exemptions, and ministerial orders — with a role for the Intelligence Commissioner and an opportunity for providers to make representations before orders take effect. Providers subject to the Act would have an "obligation to assist" and would face confidentiality rules, including a prohibition on disclosing certain information except as authorized, along with related amendments to the Intelligence Commissioner Act.

Enforcement tools are extensive: designated inspectors with authority to enter places (with special rules for dwelling-houses), audit orders requiring internal audits, compliance orders to stop contraventions with a review process, administrative monetary penalties for violations (including potential liability for corporate officers), compliance agreements as an alternative to paying penalties, ministerial review, debt recovery, and criminal offences for obstruction and for making false or misleading statements. The Minister would table an annual report, and regulations could set out further details.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Telecommunications companies and, under Part 2, designated "core" electronic service providers face the most direct obligations: responding to demands and orders, keeping matters confidential, submitting to inspections and audits, and facing penalties or prosecution for non-compliance. Police forces, other federal and provincial officials with enforcement duties ("public officers"), Crown prosecutors and CSIS would gain clearer and, in some cases, faster routes to obtaining subscriber, transmission, tracking and computer data.

Ordinary users are affected indirectly: the bill defines what counts as "subscriber information" that can be sought, sets the legal thresholds (reasonable grounds to suspect for confirmation demands; reasonable grounds to believe for various warrants), carves out medical and solicitor-client-privileged information from confirmation demands, and in some cases requires that a person whose computer data is examined be given a copy of the warrant. Judges and justices remain the gatekeepers for production orders and warrants, and the Intelligence Commissioner has a role in the Part 2 ministerial order process.

deepDive.heading: Status, cost and oversight
deepDive.body:
The bill is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Gary Anandasangaree and has cleared the House of Commons; it is awaiting first reading in the Senate, so it is not yet law and could still be amended or fail to pass. It carries a Royal Recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money — a signal that implementing the framework is expected to involve federal costs.

Built-in accountability measures include the Part 3 requirement for a parliamentary review of Parts 1 and 2, an annual report under the new Act, judicial authorization requirements for many of the powers, judicial review provisions with notice to the Minister, and regulation-making authority on confidentiality and security. This explainer is based on the bill's summary and the portions of the text available above; some later clauses are truncated, so details of specific sections may differ from this general description.

C-23.overview: Bill C-23, the Appropriation Act No. 4, 2025-26, is a routine but essential money bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $5,408,955,628 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) to cover spending for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2026 that was not already approved by earlier appropriation acts. The amounts come from the Supplementary Estimates (C) for 2025-26 — the final top-up request departments make near the end of a fiscal year — and are listed department by department in schedules attached to the bill. Notable items include $1.008 billion for Canada Post, $150 million for CBC/Radio-Canada operating expenditures, and various smaller amounts for departments and agencies ranging from Correctional Service of Canada to museums and Indigenous programs. Under Canada's system, the government cannot legally spend money without Parliament's approval, so bills like this are how the House of Commons and Senate exercise control over public spending. The bill has received Royal Assent, meaning it is now law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) permission to pay out a maximum of $5,408,955,628 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for the 2025-26 fiscal year, covering expenses "not otherwise provided for" — that is, spending not already authorized in the main estimates or earlier supplementary appropriation acts.

The money is not a lump sum the government can spend freely. Section 4 specifies that each amount may be used only for the purpose, and under the terms and conditions, set out in the corresponding item in Schedules 1 and 2. The spending is deemed to take effect as of April 1, 2025, the start of the fiscal year, and any transfers of appropriations described in the Estimates are treated as having been authorized on that same date.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 2 sets the dollar ceiling and ties it to the Supplementary Estimates (C) for 2025-26. Schedule 1 alone accounts for $5,358,660,919, with the remainder in Schedule 2.

Sections 5 and 6 deal with accounting mechanics. Amounts in Schedule 1 can be charged after the fiscal year ends — up until the Public Accounts are tabled — solely to make bookkeeping adjustments that do not involve any actual payment of cash. Schedule 2 items have a longer window: they may be paid or applied any time up to March 31, 2027, with a rule that payments must draw first on the oldest applicable appropriation before newer ones. Anything unused by the end of the following fiscal year lapses, subject to adjustments under section 37 of the Financial Administration Act.

deepDive.heading: What the money is for
deepDive.body:
The published schedule lists allocations by organization. The largest single item visible is $1,008,000,000 to Canada Post Corporation under section 31 of the Canada Post Corporation Act, followed by $150,000,000 in operating funding for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Other examples include roughly $138.3 million for Correctional Service of Canada, about $172.4 million across two votes for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, about $109 million for Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs, $7.3 million for CSIS, $6.75 million for the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency, and small amounts (from $12,000 to under $500,000) for several national museums.

Some votes authorize actions rather than new cash. Employment and Social Development Canada's Vote 10c, for instance, authorizes writing off 38,526 debts totalling $381,908,993 in student and apprentice loans (which includes $197,249,543 already written off under an earlier 2025-26 appropriation act), and Vote 15c covers writing off 377 debts worth $18,637 in Government Annuities Account overpayments. Several votes also carry standing authorities, such as permission for departments to re-spend revenues they earn from providing internal support services to other departments. Note that the text provided here is truncated, so the full schedule includes further organizations not listed above.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and why it matters
deepDive.body:
Directly, the bill affects the federal departments, agencies and Crown corporations named in the schedules, which need this authorization to complete planned spending before the fiscal year ends on March 31, 2026. Indirectly it affects anyone who relies on the programs funded — postal service, public broadcasting, immigration processing, corrections, Indigenous programs, research grants and more — as well as the roughly 38,500 student and apprentice loan borrowers whose uncollectible debts are being formally written off the government's books.

For taxpayers and Parliament, appropriation bills are the constitutional check on government spending: no money can leave the Consolidated Revenue Fund without an Act of Parliament. Debate on such bills is typically tied to confidence in the government, since a defeat would deny it the funds to operate.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
This is the fourth appropriation act of the 2025-26 fiscal year, sponsored by the Hon. Shafqat Ali, and it is based on Supplementary Estimates (C) — conventionally the last set of estimates tabled before a fiscal year closes, used to capture spending needs that emerged after the main estimates were approved.

The bill itself contains no new policy or program design; it is an authorization instrument. The substantive details of what each dollar buys are found in the Estimates documents that accompany it and in the underlying legislation cited in individual votes, such as the Canada Post Corporation Act and the Financial Administration Act. The bill has received Royal Assent and is in force.

C-24.overview: Bill C-24, the Appropriation Act No. 1, 2026-27, is a routine but essential money bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $86,422,679,148 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund to pay for federal operations during the fiscal year that ends March 31, 2027. It is what is commonly called an "interim supply" bill — rather than releasing a full year's funding, it advances departments and agencies a portion of what they have requested in the Main Estimates (anywhere from three twelfths to twelve twelfths of each item, depending on the schedule the item falls under) so that government can keep operating while Parliament continues to study the full spending plan. The money can only be spent for the specific purposes and under the conditions written into each item, which are listed vote-by-vote in the bill's schedules covering bodies such as the RCMP, Parks Canada, the Canadian Space Agency and the House of Commons. The bill has received Royal Assent, meaning the spending authority is now in force. For ordinary readers, this is the mechanism that keeps departments funded and public services running; it does not create new programs or change any laws.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) permission to spend a maximum of $86,422,679,148 out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund — the central account into which federal revenues flow — on expenses for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 that are "not otherwise provided for" by existing legislation. Much federal spending, such as certain statutory transfers, is already authorized by other laws; appropriation acts cover the rest, which Parliament must approve each year.

Because it is the first appropriation act of the year, it functions as interim supply. Instead of releasing the full amounts listed in the 2026-27 Main Estimates, it releases fractions of them so departments have cash on hand for the opening months of the fiscal year while Parliament finishes reviewing the Estimates.

deepDive.heading: How the amounts are calculated
deepDive.body:
Section 2 breaks the total into ten parts. The largest single component, $29,073,487,176, is three twelfths (a quarter) of the items in Schedules 1 and 2 — the default share for most government items. Other groups of items receive larger fractions because they need money earlier in the year: four twelfths for Schedule 1.1 ($9,749,461,296), five twelfths for Schedule 1.2 ($11,854,113,573), six twelfths for Schedule 1.3 ($12,340,997,391), seven twelfths for Schedule 1.4 ($359,445,528), eight twelfths for Schedule 1.5 ($5,369,743,750), nine twelfths for Schedule 1.6 ($15,746,169,976), ten twelfths for Schedule 1.7 ($93,026,910), eleven twelfths for Schedule 1.8 ($1,836,233,543), and the full twelve twelfths for Schedule 1.9 — which in this case totals just $5.

The published portion of Schedule 1.1 illustrates how this works item by item. For example, the RCMP's operating expenditures vote of $3,868,940,232 in the Main Estimates yields $1,289,646,744 in interim funding; Public Works and Government Services receives $1,183,597,938 of a $3,550,793,813 vote; the Department of Canadian Heritage's grants and contributions vote of $1,606,092,571 yields $535,364,191; and the House of Commons, including the cost of running MPs' constituency offices, receives $157,369,814 of $472,109,441.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and conditions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 states that money authorized for an item may be spent only for the purposes and subject to the terms and conditions written into that item. The schedule entries therefore include detailed authorities — for instance, letting Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada spend revenues it collects from International Experience Canada services, letting Innovation, Science and Economic Development recover costs from bankruptcy, corporate registration and merger-review services, and authorizing salary payments to ministers without portfolio or ministers of State in certain departments.

Sections 4 and 5 deal with accounting housekeeping. They allow appropriations to be charged after the fiscal year has ended, up until the Public Accounts are tabled, so the government's books can be adjusted without any new money leaving the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Items in Schedule 2 get a longer runway: they may be paid or applied up to March 31, 2028, drawing first on the oldest available appropriation, with any unused balance lapsing at the end of the following fiscal year.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and why it matters
deepDive.body:
The direct effect is on federal departments, agencies and Crown bodies named in the schedules — including the Canadian Space Agency, Canadian Heritage, Immigration, Finance, Global Affairs, Industry, Public Safety, Public Works and Government Services, the House of Commons, the National Film Board, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, Parks Canada, the Public Service Commission, the Registrar of the Supreme Court and the RCMP. Indirectly it affects anyone who relies on federal services, grants, contributions or transfers funded through these votes.

Appropriation bills are also constitutionally significant: only Parliament can authorize spending from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and in the House of Commons a defeat on a supply bill is treated as a matter of confidence in the government.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble notes that it follows a message from the Governor General, the Right Honourable Mary Simon, transmitting the Main Estimates for 2026-27 — the standard constitutional route by which the Crown asks Parliament for money. It was sponsored by Hon. Shafqat Ali and has received Royal Assent, so the spending authority it contains is in effect.

The numbering — "Appropriation Act No. 1" — signals that further appropriation bills for the same fiscal year are expected, typically to release the remaining amounts in the Main Estimates and to fund any Supplementary Estimates. The bill itself does not create programs, change policy or amend other statutes; it only authorizes payment of amounts already set out in the Estimates.

C-25.overview: Bill C-25, the Strong and Free Elections Act, updates Canada's federal election law (the Canada Elections Act) and also renames a number of federal ridings at the request of the MPs who represent them. The bill's main focus is tightening rules against foreign interference, bribery, hacking and the spread of false or misleading information about elections and the candidate nomination process. It also bans anonymous and certain other contributions to parties and third parties, requires political parties to meet new standards for protecting voters' personal information, and gives the Commissioner of Canada Elections stronger enforcement tools, including higher maximum financial penalties. The bill has received royal assent, meaning it has been passed by Parliament and is now law. For ordinary voters, the practical significance is that it changes what outside actors, parties and campaigns are allowed to do around elections, and how those rules are policed.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act has two parts. Part 1 amends the Canada Elections Act with a package of new and revised prohibitions, contribution rules, privacy requirements for parties, and enforcement powers. A second component enacts a separate statute changing the names of certain electoral districts, based on proposals from the MPs who represent those ridings.

According to the bill's own summary, the amendments cover: foreign influence in the electoral process; offering or accepting bribes; unauthorized use of a computer; making or publishing false or misleading information about elections and about the nomination process; new prohibitions related to voting in party nomination and leadership contests; restrictions on accepting or using certain contributions, including anonymous ones; new requirements for political parties' personal-information protection policies; and expanded administration and enforcement provisions.

deepDive.heading: Foreign interference provisions
deepDive.body:
The bill rewrites the rules on "undue influence by foreigners." It broadens who counts as a foreign actor by pointing to the definitions of "foreign economic entity," "foreign entity," "foreign power" and "foreign state" in the Foreign Interference and Security of Information Act, and it clarifies that a corporation organized outside Canada is covered if it does not carry on business in Canada or if one of its primary Canadian activities is influencing how electors vote. The prohibitions are extended to cover attempts to influence votes for "potential candidates" and "eligible parties," not just registered candidates and parties.

Related provisions bar selling advertising space to a foreign actor covered by these rules for election or partisan advertising, prohibit foreign entities from providing property, services or funds to a third party for partisan activities, advertising or election surveys, and prohibit foreign entities from circumventing that ban or colluding with others to do so. The existing ban on using a broadcasting station outside Canada to influence voters is extended to nomination contests and leadership contests.

deepDive.heading: Nominations, bribery and ballot handling
deepDive.body:
The bill adds new offences around candidate nomination papers: no one may convey false or misleading information to be included in a nomination paper, no one filing a nomination paper may include false or misleading information in it, and no elector may sign the nomination papers of more than one prospective candidate in the same election. At the same time, a nomination cannot be refused simply because one of the electors who signed also signed for someone else.

On bribery, the Act separates and restates two offences: offering a bribe, directly or indirectly, to influence how an elector votes, and accepting or agreeing to accept such a bribe. The bill also updates ballot-security rules, allowing candidates or their representatives to sign the seal on ballot boxes at the close of each of the four advance polling days, and requiring election officers to safeguard sealed ballot boxes, record any transfer of custody and notify candidates in writing. Prohibitions on defacing or destroying ballots and interfering with ballot boxes are expanded to expressly cover special ballots and related envelopes and packets.

deepDive.heading: Enforcement, parties and voter lists
deepDive.body:
The bill increases the maximum administrative monetary penalties that can be imposed for certain violations and gives the Commissioner of Canada Elections powers in relation to conspiring or attempting to break the Act, being an accessory after the fact, or counselling someone else to break it — in other words, extending enforcement beyond the person who directly commits a violation.

It also changes which parties can obtain preliminary lists of electors during a campaign: a registered or eligible party qualifies if it was represented in the House of Commons the day before the writ was issued, endorsed a candidate in that riding in one of the last two elections, or endorsed candidates in at least two-thirds of ridings in the last general election, with a rule accounting for redrawn boundaries. Separately, parties face new requirements for their personal-information protection policies. A minor administrative change requires the Chief Electoral Officer to publish the list of returning officers in the Canada Gazette between January 1 and 20 each year.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The rules apply most directly to political parties, candidates, nomination and leadership contestants, third-party advertisers, foreign entities and states, media and platforms that sell advertising space, and election officials. Voters are affected indirectly — through protections against bribery, disinformation and foreign influence, tighter handling of ballots, and new obligations on parties that hold their personal data.

The bill was introduced as a government bill sponsored by Hon. Steven MacKinnon and has received royal assent. Note that the text available here is truncated, so some details — including the specific penalty amounts, the full contribution and privacy rules, and the list of renamed electoral districts — are not reproduced above and would need to be checked against the final statute.

C-26.overview: Bill C-26 is a short government spending bill that lets the federal government transfer up to $1.713 billion from the Consolidated Revenue Fund — the government's main bank account — to the provinces and territories to help increase the supply of housing. Sponsored by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, the bill contains just one operative section: it sets the total dollar amount, states the purpose, and gives the Minister of Finance discretion over how much each province or territory receives and when the money is paid out. It does not itself build housing, set construction targets, or create a new program; it simply provides the legal authority to spend the money. The bill has received Royal Assent, meaning it is now law. Because Parliament must authorize any spending of public money, legislation like this is the necessary step before funds committed in a budget or announcement can actually flow.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill authorizes the Minister of Finance to make payments to the provinces and territories totalling $1.713 billion, drawn from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, "for the purpose of improving housing supply." The Consolidated Revenue Fund is the account into which federal revenues are deposited; by law, money can only be taken out of it when Parliament passes a statute permitting it. Bill C-26 is that permission.

The legislation is deliberately narrow. Its entire operative content is a single section with two subsections: one setting the total amount and purpose, and one confirming the money comes out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. There are no accompanying rules, application processes, eligibility criteria or reporting requirements written into the bill itself.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Subsection 1(1) caps total spending at $1.713 billion and states that the amount each province or territory receives "is to be determined by the Minister of Finance." The bill does not include a formula — for example, one based on population, housing starts, or need — so the allocation among jurisdictions is left to ministerial discretion.

Subsection 1(2) allows the Minister to pay the money out "at the times and in the manner that the Minister of Finance considers appropriate," giving flexibility over timing and mechanics of the transfers. The bill also carries a Royal Recommendation from the Governor General, a constitutional requirement for any bill that authorizes the spending of public funds; it means the measure could only be introduced by the government, not by an individual member of Parliament.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The direct recipients are provincial and territorial governments, which would receive the federal transfers. How the money ultimately reaches builders, municipalities, non-profit housing providers or homebuyers is not specified in the bill and would depend on decisions made by the federal government in setting the payments and by each province or territory in using them.

Indirectly, the bill is aimed at people affected by housing availability across Canada, since its stated purpose is improving housing supply. The bill text itself, however, does not define what counts as "improving housing supply" or attach conditions to how recipients spend the funds.

deepDive.heading: Context and limits of this summary
deepDive.body:
Bills of this kind are common vehicles for implementing spending commitments announced in a budget or fiscal update: the announcement signals the intent, and a statute like C-26 provides the legal authority to release the money. The bill's brevity is typical of standalone appropriation-style legislation.

Anything not stated in the text — such as the specific split among provinces and territories, conditions attached to the transfers, timelines, or how results will be measured — is not addressed by the bill and would be set out through subsequent government decisions or agreements. Readers looking for those details will need to consult the relevant federal budget documents or departmental announcements rather than the legislation itself.

C-28.overview: Bill C-28, the Canadian Space Launch Act, would amend the Aeronautics Act (and several related transportation laws) to create Canada's first dedicated legal framework for launching rockets into space and bringing spacecraft back down to Earth on Canadian soil. It does this largely by folding launch and re-entry vehicles into the existing aviation rulebook: they would count as "aircraft," the Minister of Transport could issue permits and certify launch and re-entry sites, and the Governor in Council could write detailed regulations covering these operations. The bill also sets up rules about who pays if something goes wrong — allowing the government to shield operators from certain third-party claims when it is in the public interest, while also allowing it to require operators to cover the government's own liability, including under the 1972 international treaty on damage caused by space objects. It gives the Minister emergency power to halt a launch or re-entry for safety or security reasons, and creates a zoning system to keep neighbouring land uses compatible with launch and re-entry sites. As introduced, it is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it is still early in the legislative process.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
Rather than creating a stand-alone space agency law, Bill C-28 builds a space launch regime inside the existing Aeronautics Act. The definition of "aircraft" would be broadened to include launch vehicles and re-entry vehicles, while "airport" would be defined to exclude certified launch and re-entry sites — so space facilities are treated as their own category. Until the government writes regulations defining the key terms, the bill supplies temporary definitions: a launch vehicle is a rocket or another vehicle designed to reach Earth orbit or beyond, and a re-entry vehicle is one designed to come back from orbit substantially intact. Those placeholder definitions are automatically repealed once permanent regulatory definitions take effect.
