The bill also expands the government's regulation-making powers so that Cabinet can set rules for launches, re-entries, and the operation of launch and re-entry sites, including rules applying international conventions Canada has signed and international standards more broadly.

deepDive.heading: Permits, certificates and oversight
deepDive.body:
The Minister of Transport would be able to issue, renew, amend, suspend, transfer or cancel permits and "notices of determination" for launches from Canada and re-entries into Canada, as well as certificates authorizing an aerodrome to be used as a launch or re-entry site. These documents are added to the list of Canadian aviation documents under the Act.

Notably, the summary states that certain launch- and re-entry-related decisions are removed from review by the Transportation Appeal Tribunal of Canada — meaning the usual aviation appeal route would not apply to them. Separately, the Minister gains emergency authority to order the stopping of a launch, a re-entry, or any related activity for safety or security reasons. The bill also clarifies that where launch rules conflict with regulations made under the Explosives Act, the Explosives Act rules prevail.

deepDive.heading: Liability, insurance and indemnification
deepDive.body:
Space launches carry a small but potentially very costly risk of damage to people and property on the ground. Bill C-28 addresses this in two directions. First, the Minister may indemnify (cover the costs of) the owner or operator of a launch or re-entry vehicle for their liability to third parties, if the Minister considers it in the public interest, on whatever terms the Minister sets. Second, the Minister may require owners and operators to indemnify the Government of Canada for third-party liability — expressly including claims arising under the 1972 Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, under which countries can be held responsible internationally for objects launched from their territory.

Because of the potential spending involved, the bill carries a Royal Recommendation. Standard aviation liability-insurance requirements would no longer apply to launch and re-entry vehicles; instead, Cabinet could create a separate "financial responsibility" regime for operators, set minimum amounts, define what financial responsibility means, and allow exemptions or adjustments in specific cases.

deepDive.heading: Land use and zoning near launch sites
deepDive.body:
The bill extends the Aeronautics Act's airport zoning system to space facilities. It defines "certified" launch and re-entry sites (those holding a ministerial certificate) and "designated" sites — land declared by Cabinet order to be needed for a future site, where the land either belongs to the Crown or is subject to a registered notice of intention to expropriate.

Cabinet could then make zoning regulations preventing nearby land from being used or developed in ways the Minister considers incompatible with the operation or safe operation of these sites or vehicles. For designated (not yet certified) sites, there is a precondition: the Minister must first have tried and failed to reach an agreement with the relevant provincial government, unless immediate action is needed. The bill also updates the Minister's authority to enter agreements with provincial authorities to regulate land use around airports, adjusting the wording to account for launch and re-entry vehicles.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The bill is aimed at companies and organizations that want to launch rockets from Canada or recover spacecraft returning to Canadian territory, at the communities and landowners near proposed or existing launch and re-entry sites, and at federal and provincial authorities that would share responsibility for land use around those sites. It also touches ordinary air travel indirectly, since the changes are woven into aviation law and include consequential amendments to the Carriage by Air Act, the Canada Transportation Act and the Secure Air Travel Act.

Much of the practical detail — including the final definitions of "launch," "launch vehicle" and "re-entry vehicle," the minimum financial responsibility amounts, and the operating rules for sites — would be set later through regulations rather than in the bill itself. The bill is a government bill sponsored by Hon. Steven MacKinnon and is at second reading in the House of Commons, so its contents could still change before it becomes law.

C-29.overview: Bill C-29 would create a new federal police-style body called the Financial Crimes Agency, reporting to the Minister of Finance, with a mandate to investigate serious and complex financial crimes — such as money laundering, dealing in proceeds of crime, and offences involving financial assets (including digital assets), financial services or markets — and to help recover the proceeds of crime. The agency would be led by a Commissioner appointed by the Governor in Council, could designate its own employees as investigators and as police officers with peace officer powers across Canada, and would be required to enter into an arrangement with the RCMP for services and assistance. The bill also gives the Attorney General of Canada authority to prosecute offences the agency investigates, including the power to issue a "fiat" that takes exclusive carriage of a case away from a province. It makes consequential amendments to a long list of statutes and regulations — from the Access to Information Act and Criminal Code to sanctions and immigration laws — so the new agency fits into existing federal rules. The bill is currently at committee stage in the House of Commons, and if passed it would come into force one year after royal assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill enacts the Financial Crimes Agency Act, which establishes the Financial Crimes Agency as a specialized federal law enforcement agency. Its stated object is to have the capability and expertise to investigate serious and complex financial crimes, contribute to the recovery of proceeds of crime, and take part in international efforts against financial crime.

"Financial crime" is defined broadly: any federal offence relating to financial assets (explicitly including digital assets) or to financial services or markets. That covers laundering, trafficking or possessing proceeds of crime; conduct that harms or could harm the security or integrity of Canada's economy, financial system or any Canadian financial market; "designated offences" under the Criminal Code that generate proceeds of crime; and offences under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.

deepDive.heading: How the agency would be structured and governed
deepDive.body:
The agency would be headquartered in the National Capital Region, with authority to open other offices in Canada with the Minister's approval. It would be led by a Commissioner appointed by the Governor in Council for terms of up to five years, renewable but capped at 10 years total. The Commissioner holds the rank and powers of a deputy head, is a peace officer everywhere in Canada, and may delegate powers to agency employees.

The Minister of Finance is responsible for the agency, and the Commissioner manages it "under the direction of the Minister." The Minister may issue directions on matters that materially affect public policy or the agency's strategic direction; such directions are not statutory instruments but must be made public as soon as feasible. On staffing, the Commissioner would have exclusive authority to hire, lay off and terminate employees and to set staffing rules, with certain Financial Administration Act provisions not applying; pay and hours would be set after consulting the President of the Treasury Board, and collective bargaining mandates would need Treasury Board approval.

deepDive.heading: Investigative and prosecution powers
deepDive.body:
The Commissioner may investigate financial crimes on their own initiative or at the request of, or with, any Canadian or foreign law enforcement agency or investigative public body. Before starting an investigation on their own initiative, the Commissioner must consult other relevant Canadian law enforcement agencies where they consider it appropriate. To keep the focus on serious and complex cases, the Commissioner may set criteria for which matters get investigated. Employees can be designated as "investigations officers" (public officers for purposes of Criminal Code section 25 and Part XV) or as "police officers," who become peace officers across Canada while designated.

On the prosecution side, the Attorney General of Canada may conduct proceedings for any federal offence that is a financial crime investigated under the Act, exercising the Criminal Code powers of the Attorney General. Provincial attorneys general keep their authority, except where the federal Attorney General issues a "fiat" — a formal notice served on a province that gives Ottawa exclusive carriage of a specific case. Factors that may be considered in issuing a fiat include whether the offence is transnational, spans more than one province, or engages the national interest.

deepDive.heading: Relationship with the RCMP and other laws
deepDive.body:
The bill requires the Commissioner and the RCMP Commissioner, with the approval of the Minister of Public Safety, to enter into an arrangement for the RCMP to provide services and assistance to the new agency; the arrangement can later be amended or terminated jointly. RCMP personnel working under that arrangement would not become agency employees and would be treated as acting under the RCMP Act, though the Commissioner may delegate investigative powers to them subject to the arrangement's terms.

Consequential amendments would fold the agency into a range of existing statutes and regulations, including the Access to Information Act, Privacy Act, Criminal Code, Financial Administration Act, Public Service Superannuation Act, Special Economic Measures Act, Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, Security of Canada Information Disclosure Act, the Sergei Magnitsky Law, and the Public Complaints and Review Commission Act, along with regulations on access to information, privacy, federal real property, citizenship, and national security review of investments. A transitional provision addresses complaints.

deepDive.heading: Accountability, timing and status
deepDive.body:
The Act provides for a special report and an annual report, as well as a five-year review, and allows the Governor in Council to make regulations (including in relation to designating police officers). Ministerial directions must be published, and the inclusion of the Public Complaints and Review Commission Act among the amended statutes indicates a complaints and review mechanism is contemplated.

Bill C-29 is a government bill sponsored by the Minister of Finance, Hon. François-Philippe Champagne, and carries a royal recommendation because it authorizes spending of public money. It is currently at consideration in committee in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading but is still subject to possible amendment and further votes in both chambers. If enacted, the Act would come into force on the first anniversary of royal assent, giving a year to stand up the agency.

C-27.overview: Bill C-27 is a federal government bill that would put into law the Final Self-Government Agreement for the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę, a Dene community in the Sahtu region of the Northwest Territories. The agreement was negotiated by the community (through The Tlegohli Got'ine Government Incorporated) with the governments of Canada and the Northwest Territories under the 1993 Sahtu Dene and Metis Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement, was ratified by the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę on March 31, 2025, and signed on September 18, 2025. Because the agreement itself says it only takes effect once Parliament passes a law giving it force, this bill is the final federal step: it declares the agreement valid, gives it the force of law, and confirms it is a treaty protected by sections 25 and 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. The bill also recognizes the new Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government as a legal entity whose laws have the force of law, ends the application of the Indian Act to that government and its citizens, and makes housekeeping amendments to several other federal statutes. Sponsored by Hon. Rebecca Alty, the bill has cleared the House of Commons and is awaiting first reading in the Senate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's core function is short and technical: section 4 approves the Final Self-Government Agreement, declares it valid and gives it "the force of law," meaning the agreement becomes legally binding on everyone and can be relied on in court. Section 3 states that the agreement is a treaty within the meaning of sections 25 and 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 — the constitutional provisions that recognize and affirm Aboriginal and treaty rights.

The preamble sets out the reasoning behind the bill: that Canada recognizes an inherent right of self-government under section 35; that the Sahtu Dene and Metis land claim agreement of 1993 called for self-government to be negotiated as close to the community level as reasonably possible; and that Canada and the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę view the agreement as contributing to Canada's implementation of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Beyond giving effect to the agreement, the bill sets out how the new arrangement fits into the existing legal system. The Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government becomes a legal entity with the capacity, rights and powers of a natural person (section 7), and laws it makes in accordance with the agreement have the force of law (section 8). The Indian Act will no longer apply to that government or its citizens, subject to an exception set out in the agreement itself (section 9), and Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę laws are not treated as federal "statutory instruments" (section 10).

The bill also creates a priority order for resolving conflicts: the agreement generally prevails over this Act and other federal laws, and this Act prevails over other federal laws — but the Sahtu Dene and Metis Land Claim Settlement Act and the Sahtu Agreement prevail over all of them (sections 5 and 6). On courts, the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government and its institutions are not federal boards or tribunals, and judicial review of their decisions goes exclusively to the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories, but only after all internal appeal routes under Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę law have been used (section 15). If a court case raises questions about the agreement's interpretation, validity or applicability, the party raising it must give at least 14 days' notice to the Attorney General of Canada, the Attorney General of the Northwest Territories and the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government, each of whom may join the case as a full party (section 16).

deepDive.heading: Taxes, timing and technical amendments
deepDive.body:
A separate Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Tax Treatment Agreement is also approved and given the force of law while it is in effect, but the bill is explicit that this tax agreement is not part of the main self-government agreement and is not itself a treaty or land claims agreement under the Constitution (sections 11 and 12).

On timing, the Act comes into force by order of the Governor in Council, who may also make the orders and regulations needed to carry out the agreement, including setting the "Effective Date" and "Transition Date" for different parts of the agreement (sections 18 and 44). One provision is retroactive: clause 2.7 and chapter 7 of the agreement are deemed to have had effect since November 20, 2024 (section 17). The bill further makes consequential amendments to other federal statutes, including the Access to Information Act and Privacy Act (adding the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government to provisions on information sharing with other governments), the Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act (recognizing it as a "taxing authority" if it levies property taxes on lands within Tłegǫ́hłı̨), the Mackenzie Valley Resource Management Act and the First Nations Goods and Services Tax Act, plus a coordinating amendment relating to Bill C-10. The published text available here is truncated, so the full detail of some of those amendments is not reproduced above.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The people most directly affected are the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę and their citizens, who will be governed by their own government and laws rather than by the Indian Act, and who gain the powers, rights and benefits — and the duties and liabilities — the agreement assigns. The new Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government itself is affected as a newly recognized legal entity with law-making authority.

The federal and Northwest Territories governments are affected as parties to the agreement, and territorial courts take on a defined judicial-review role. More broadly, anyone dealing with the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę Government or living or doing business on the lands covered by the agreement is affected, since the agreement is binding on all persons and entities and courts must take judicial notice of it and of registered Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę laws (both must be publicly available — the agreements through the King's Printer, and Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got'įnę laws through a public register).

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This bill follows a well-established pattern in Canada: when Canada, a province or territory, and an Indigenous government sign a modern treaty or self-government agreement, Parliament passes a short statute to bring it into legal effect. Here, the negotiations flowed from chapter 5 and appendix B of the 1993 Sahtu Dene and Metis Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement, which contemplated later, community-level self-government agreements. The bill preserves the primacy of that earlier land claim agreement where any conflict arises.

The bill carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money in connection with implementing the agreement. It is a government bill sponsored by Hon. Rebecca Alty, and its listed status is that it has moved through the House of Commons and is awaiting first reading in the Senate; it would come into force on a date set by order in council.

C-32.overview: Bill C-32, the Appropriation Act No. 2, 2026-27, is a routine but essential spending bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $144,032,017,964 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) to pay for departments, agencies and Crown corporations during the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027. The money is tied to the Main Estimates for 2026-27, and the amount is what remains after subtracting the interim funding Parliament already approved in Appropriation Act No. 1, 2026-27. Each dollar is attached to a specific 'vote' for a specific organization and purpose, so the government cannot legally spend it on something else. Bills like this are how Parliament exercises its control over the public purse, and they are required for the ordinary operations of government to continue. The bill has received royal assent, meaning it is now law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
This is an appropriation (supply) bill. It grants His Majesty — in practice, the federal government — permission to pay out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund a sum not exceeding $144,032,017,964 for expenses in the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 that are 'not otherwise provided for' (that is, spending not already authorized by other, standing legislation).

The total is made up of two parts: $140,396,109,102 from the items listed in Schedule 1 (based on Main Estimates Schedule 1, totalling $225,606,818,628, less the $85,210,709,526 in interim supply already granted by Appropriation Act No. 1, 2026-27) and $3,635,908,862 from the items listed in Schedule 2. The spending authority is deemed to take effect as of April 1, 2026, the start of the fiscal year.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 requires that money authorized for each item be spent only for the purposes, and under any terms and conditions, set out in that item. This is the core discipline of the estimates system: funds are voted line by line rather than as a general pot of money.

Sections 4 and 5 deal with accounting timing. Schedule 1 appropriations can be charged after the fiscal year ends, up until the Public Accounts for that year are tabled, but only for bookkeeping adjustments that do not involve actual payments out of the fund. Schedule 2 items are multi-year: they may be paid or applied any time up to March 31, 2028, with payments charged first against the oldest applicable appropriation before newer ones. Anything left unused lapses at the end of the fiscal year following March 31, 2027, subject to adjustments under section 37 of the Financial Administration Act.

deepDive.heading: Who and what it funds
deepDive.body:
The schedules cover a broad cross-section of the federal public administration. Examples visible in the text include the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation ($6.13 billion), the Canada Border Services Agency ($2.73 billion), the Communications Security Establishment ($1.92 billion), Atomic Energy of Canada Limited ($1.70 billion), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research ($1.48 billion), the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation ($1.38 billion), the Canadian Security Intelligence Service ($931 million), the Canadian Space Agency ($894 million), the Canadian Food Inspection Agency ($677 million), and smaller bodies such as museums, the Copyright Board, the Canadian Grain Commission and the Canadian Dairy Commission.

Individual votes are typically split into operating expenditures, capital expenditures, and grants and contributions. Some votes also carry special authorities — for instance, permission for an agency to spend certain revenues it collects to offset its own costs, or Correctional Service of Canada's authority to operate inmate canteens and deposit proceeds into the Inmate Welfare Fund. The published text provided here is truncated, so it does not list every organization in the schedules.

deepDive.heading: Context: how supply bills work
deepDive.body:
The federal spending cycle begins with the Estimates, which the government tables in Parliament with a message from the Governor General (here, the Right Honourable Mary Simon). Parliament then passes appropriation bills to convert those planned amounts into legal spending authority. Early in the fiscal year, an interim supply bill (Appropriation Act No. 1) provides a portion of the funds so government can keep operating; a later bill such as this one releases the remaining amounts for the full year.

The bill was sponsored by Hon. Shafqat Ali as a government bill and has received royal assent. Because confidence in the government is traditionally tied to its ability to obtain supply, votes on appropriation bills are treated as confidence matters in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does not do
deepDive.body:
An appropriation act authorizes spending; it does not create programs, change policy, or amend other statutes. The purposes and conditions attached to each vote come from the Estimates documents, not from new policy language in this bill.

It also does not cover all federal spending. Large amounts — such as statutory payments already authorized by other legislation — flow without appearing in this bill, which is why the text repeatedly refers to expenses 'not otherwise provided for.'

C-30.overview: Bill C-30 is the government's legislation to put into effect a package of tax and spending measures announced in the spring economic update tabled on April 28, 2026. It bundles together several unrelated changes: tweaks to income tax rules (a bigger deduction for tradespeople who travel for work, a permanent capital gains break for owners who sell a business to their employees, more time to repay Home Buyers' Plan withdrawals, and fast write-offs for new greenhouses), a temporary elimination of federal excise tax on gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel from April 20 to September 7, 2026, and an extension of alcohol excise duty relief for brewers and other producers. It also lowers Canada Pension Plan contribution rates starting in 2027 and makes a series of technical amendments to banking, payments, Employment Insurance, transportation, food inspection and pesticide laws. The bill has received royal assent, meaning it is now law. Because omnibus budget bills like this one touch many different areas of federal policy at once, its effects reach households, small businesses, farmers and financial institutions alike.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is an "implementation act" — the legal machinery that turns announcements in an economic update into enforceable law. It is organized into three parts: Part 1 amends the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations; Part 2 amends the Excise Tax Act, the Excise Act and the Excise Act, 2001 to deliver fuel and alcohol tax relief; and Part 3 contains eight separate divisions amending other federal statutes.

Because it appropriates public revenue, the bill carries a formal recommendation from the Governor General and was sponsored by the Minister of Finance, Hon. François-Philippe Champagne. It has already received royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Tax measures for individuals and businesses (Part 1)
deepDive.body:
Five income tax changes are included. The Labour Mobility Deduction for tradespeople becomes more generous: the annual limit on deductible expenses rises to $10,000 (and will be indexed to inflation for tax years beginning after 2026), and the distance test is set at 120 kilometres, making more workers eligible. These changes apply to the 2026 and later tax years. The capital gains exemption for selling a business to an employee ownership trust or worker co-operative is made permanent, applying to qualifying dispositions occurring after 2023.

The bill also extends the grace period for repaying money withdrawn under the Home Buyers' Plan, with relief now reaching completion dates before 2030 and repayment years running out to 2032. Owners of "eligible greenhouses" get temporary immediate expensing — a 100% first-year write-off for greenhouses available for use before 2030, then a declining rate of 75% in 2030–31, 55% in 2032–33 and none after 2033, with the rules deemed in force as of November 4, 2025. Finally, the Electric Vehicle Affordability Program announced on February 5, 2026 is added to the list of prescribed incentive programs so it interacts properly with existing tax rules.

deepDive.heading: Fuel and alcohol tax relief (Part 2)
deepDive.body:
The federal excise tax on gasoline and aviation gasoline, and on diesel and aviation fuel, is set to $0.00 for the period from April 20, 2026 to September 7, 2026 — a temporary holiday covering roughly the summer travel season.

On alcohol, the bill extends for another two years, effective April 1, 2026, two existing measures: the 2% cap on the annual inflation adjustment to alcohol excise duties, and the 50% reduction in excise duty rates on the first 15,000 hectolitres of beer brewed in Canada.

deepDive.heading: Other statutory changes (Part 3)
deepDive.body:
Division 5 reduces Canada Pension Plan contribution rates for employees, employers and the self-employed beginning in 2027 and for later years. Division 4 extends until October 7, 2028 the measure giving certain seasonal workers additional weeks of Employment Insurance benefits, removes the list of eligible regions from the Act itself so that regions will instead be set by regulation, and repeals one related provision on November 7, 2027.

The remaining divisions are largely technical or administrative. Division 1 provides that the Investment Canada Act does not apply to certain foreign bank transactions already requiring approval under financial institution legislation. Division 2 consolidates the Bank of Canada's cost-recovery powers into a single Act. Division 3 gives the Canadian Payments Association and certain individuals immunity from civil liability (other than in contract) for acts done in good faith. Division 6 requires specified individuals and entities to give the Minister of Transport information the Minister considers necessary for transportation policy, and sets out who that information may be shared with. Division 7 clarifies the Canadian Food Inspection Agency's mandate and lets Cabinet exempt certain persons, things or activities from laws the Agency enforces. Division 8 requires the Minister of Health to consider national or regional economic security and national food security under the Pest Control Products Act, and allows Cabinet, by order, to register or reinstate a pesticide for emergency infestation control or on economic or food-security grounds even after the Minister has found its environmental risks unacceptable, subject to any conditions Cabinet sets.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The measures touch a wide range of groups: tradespeople who relocate temporarily for work, business owners planning employee-ownership sales, first-time homebuyers using RRSP withdrawals, greenhouse growers, drivers and airlines during the summer fuel tax holiday, brewers and other alcohol producers, seasonal workers on EI, and all CPP contributors and employers from 2027 onward. Financial institutions, the Canadian Payments Association, transportation operators, food businesses and pesticide registrants are affected by the Part 3 amendments.

As an omnibus implementation bill, C-30 combines measures with fixed end dates (the fuel tax holiday, the two-year alcohol relief extension, the phasing-down greenhouse write-off) with permanent changes (the employee-ownership capital gains exemption, the lower CPP contribution rate). The bill text above is truncated, so some detailed provisions — including the full definitions and the specific new CPP contribution rates — are not reproduced here; readers seeking exact figures should consult the final published Act.

C-33.overview: Bill C-33, the Appropriation Act No. 3, 2026–27, is a routine but essential money bill: it authorizes the federal government to withdraw up to $11,127,236,516 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund (the government's main bank account) to cover spending for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 that was not already approved. The money corresponds to the Supplementary Estimates (A) for 2026–27 — a top-up request that departments and agencies make partway through the year for costs not included in the original budget plan. The bill lists, department by department, exactly how much each organization may spend and for what purpose, ranging from $673 million for Canada Post and $740 million for the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority to smaller amounts for museums, regional development agencies and tribunals. Sponsored by Treasury Board President Hon. Shafqat Ali, the bill has received Royal Assent, meaning the spending authority is now law. Bills like this matter because, under Canada's constitutional rules, the government cannot legally spend public money without Parliament's explicit approval.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act grants His Majesty (in practice, the federal government) permission to pay out a maximum of $11,127,236,516 from the Consolidated Revenue Fund for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, for expenses "not otherwise provided for" — that is, spending beyond what Parliament has already authorized in earlier appropriation acts for the same year.

The total matches the items listed in the Supplementary Estimates (A) for 2026–27, which are reproduced in Schedules 1 and 2 of the bill. Schedule 1 alone accounts for $11,109,703,047, with the small remainder in Schedule 2. The bill does not create new programs or change any policy; it simply provides the legal authority to spend money on plans already tabled in Parliament through the Estimates process.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 2 sets the spending ceiling. Section 3 states that transfers of appropriations described in the Estimates are deemed authorized as of April 1, 2026, and section 4 makes each item's spending authority retroactive to that same date — the start of the fiscal year — while requiring that each amount be used only for the purpose and under the terms and conditions written beside it in the schedules. In other words, money voted for one department's grants cannot simply be redirected elsewhere.

Sections 5 and 6 deal with accounting housekeeping. They allow appropriations listed in the schedules to be charged after the fiscal year ends, up until the Public Accounts are tabled, purely to make bookkeeping adjustments that do not involve actual cash leaving the treasury. Schedule 2 items are treated differently: they may be paid or applied any time up to March 31, 2028, with payments charged first against the oldest available appropriation, and any unused balance lapsing at the end of the following fiscal year.

deepDive.heading: Where the money goes
deepDive.body:
The schedules break the total down by organization and by "vote" (a category such as operating expenditures, capital expenditures, or grants and contributions). Among the larger amounts visible in the text: $740,178,150 to the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority for operating and capital costs, $673,000,000 to Canada Post Corporation, $154,096,867 to the Department of Canadian Heritage (mostly grants and contributions), and $83,694,310 to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.

Smaller allocations cover a wide cross-section of federal bodies: the Canadian Food Inspection Agency ($64.6 million), Correctional Service of Canada ($15.1 million), the Canadian Transportation Agency ($19.7 million), regional development agencies in Atlantic Canada and the North, the Canadian Energy Regulator, the Communications Security Establishment, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and several national museums. The listed text is truncated, so it does not show every organization receiving funds — including the Department of Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs, whose entry is cut off mid-figure.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Directly, the bill affects the federal departments, agencies and Crown corporations named in the schedules, which need this authority to pay salaries, fund programs, issue grants and contributions, and make capital purchases through the rest of the 2026–27 fiscal year.

Indirectly, it affects anyone who relies on the services and funding streams involved — for example, air travellers screened by CATSA, postal customers and Canada Post operations, recipients of Canadian Heritage grants, and clients of immigration services. It also affects taxpayers generally, since the money comes from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. Several items also carry specific administrative authorities, such as permission for certain agencies to spend revenue they earn from providing internal support services to other departments.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
Appropriation acts are among the most routine pieces of legislation Parliament passes. Each fiscal year typically sees several: one based on the Main Estimates and others tied to Supplementary Estimates (A), (B) and (C), which capture funding needs that emerge after the main spending plan is set. The numbering "No. 3" reflects its place in that sequence for 2026–27.

The bill's preamble notes that it follows a message from the Governor General accompanied by the Estimates — the constitutional convention that only the Crown may propose the spending of public money, and only Parliament may authorize it. Because the bill has received Royal Assent, the spending authority described is now in force. Note that the text provided here is truncated, so the full schedules contain additional line items not reproduced above.

C-34.overview: Bill C-34, the Safe Social Media Act, would create two new laws: the Digital Safety Act, which sets out online safety duties for large social media platforms, AI chatbot services and certain other online services, and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act, which creates a new federal regulator to oversee and enforce those duties. Under the bill, covered services would have to take steps to reduce users' exposure to harmful content, protect children (including age restrictions for pornographic content and design requirements set by regulation), label AI-generated "synthetic" content, give users tools to block others and flag harmful material, and file "digital safety plans" with the Commission. Platforms would also have to quickly remove content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor, and intimate images shared without consent — and people in Canada could complain to the Commission if a platform does not act. The Commission would have inspection powers, could issue compliance orders, and could impose administrative monetary penalties, with separate offence provisions for serious breaches. The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning MPs are still debating it in principle and many details would be filled in later through regulations.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is a framework law with two parts. Part 1 enacts the Digital Safety Act, which states that its purposes include promoting the safety of people in Canada — particularly children — reducing harms from harmful content online, and making operators of regulated services transparent and accountable. Part 2 enacts the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act, establishing a new arm's-length body with a chairperson, members, employees, the power to set rules and divisions, and a duty to report annually.

Much of the practical detail is left to future regulations. The Governor in Council can define categories of online services, set out required design features to protect children, specify age-verification and other measures, and extend the child-protection and transparency duties to online services beyond social media and chatbots. Most provisions come into force on a date set by order in council, and the Minister must later review both the Act as a whole and the minimum-age rules.

deepDive.heading: Key duties for platforms
deepDive.body:
For regulated social media services, operators would have a "duty to act responsibly": implementing measures adequate to reduce the risk that users are exposed to harmful content, giving users tools to block other users and to flag harmful content, labelling synthetic (AI-generated) content, flagging repeated automated posting, designating a resource person for users, and preserving certain harmful content. They would also have to submit a digital safety plan to the Commission.

All regulated services would owe a "duty to protect children," including building in prescribed design features and applying minimum-age restrictions for access to pornographic content; regulations could also set a minimum age for holding a social media account, with an exemption process. Separately, social media operators must make certain content inaccessible in Canada — content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor, and intimate content shared without consent — whether the operator identifies it or a user flags it, with a process for representations and reconsideration. Notably, the bill states that operators are not required to proactively search all content, and it excludes private messaging features and telecommunications service providers from certain rules.

deepDive.heading: New rules for AI chatbots
deepDive.body:
The bill treats conversational AI as its own category. A "chatbot service" is defined as an AI system available online in Canada that uses natural language to give adaptive, human-like responses, can simulate a sustained human-like relationship over multiple sessions (such as friendship, an intimate relationship or therapeutic support), and produces responses not fully predetermined by its developer or operator.

Operators of regulated chatbot services would have to take measures to reduce the risk the chatbot communicates harmful content, implement emergency measures for crisis intervention, guard against specified harmful chatbot behaviours, provide tools to flag harmful content, designate a resource person, and file a digital safety plan. The specific required measures would be spelled out in regulations and guidelines.

deepDive.heading: The regulator and enforcement
deepDive.body:
The Digital Safety Commission of Canada would administer the Act. People in Canada could make submissions about how an operator is meeting its duties, and could file complaints about child sexual victimization content or non-consensual intimate content — provided they first made best efforts to seek recourse from the platform. The Commission could then order the operator to make the content inaccessible in Canada.

Enforcement tools include holding hearings, designating inspectors who can enter premises under a warrant, requiring information or access, issuing compliance orders, and accrediting researchers for access to platform data inventories. There is an administrative monetary penalty regime with maximum penalties, factors for setting amounts, continued-violation provisions, negotiated undertakings, a due diligence defence, and publication of decisions. Separate offences apply to operators and to other persons, though imprisonment is expressly precluded. The Act also contains confidentiality protections and provides for information sharing and consultation with the CRTC, the Privacy Commissioner and the RCMP.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and where it stands
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are operators of large social media and chatbot services offered in Canada — the definitions reference thresholds such as gross global revenue and allow regulations to set service categories, so the rules are aimed at defined classes of platforms rather than every website. Users in Canada gain complaint and submission rights, blocking and flagging tools, and labelling of AI-generated content; parents and children are a stated focus, with "child" defined as anyone under 18. Researchers may benefit from accredited access to platform data.

The bill is sponsored by Hon. Marc Miller as Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes new government spending (the Commission would be funded partly through a cost-recovery regime set in regulations). It is at second reading in the House of Commons, so it has not been passed; it could still be amended at committee or later stages, and the text above is a summary of the bill as introduced.

C-31.overview: Bill C-31 is the second piece of legislation implementing measures from the federal budget tabled on November 4, 2025. Like most budget implementation bills, it is an omnibus bill: it changes dozens of federal laws at once, covering income tax, the global minimum tax on large multinationals, GST/HST and excise duties on products like tobacco, cannabis and vaping, plus a long list of unrelated policy changes ranging from banking rules and government procurement to a ban on non-compete clauses for federally regulated workers and a new Defence Investment Agency. Because it flows from the budget and involves spending public revenue, it carries a royal recommendation and is a confidence-style government bill sponsored by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue. As of this writing it is being studied by a House of Commons committee, meaning it has passed second reading but is not yet law and could still be amended.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is divided into four parts. Part 1 amends the Income Tax Act and related tax laws. Part 2 updates the Global Minimum Tax Act to bring Canada further in line with the OECD's international minimum tax rules for large multinational corporations. Part 3 makes changes to sales tax (GST/HST) and excise duty laws. Part 4 is the catch-all: it creates one new Act and amends more than a dozen others across banking, labour, health, northern lands, procurement and defence.

Because the measures were announced in the budget, the bill's function is to give them legal effect. Nothing in the summary above indicates the bill sets overall spending levels; rather, it changes the rules that govern taxes, regulators and certain federal programs.

deepDive.heading: Tax measures (Parts 1 to 3)
deepDive.body:
On income tax, the bill would allow temporary immediate write-offs for eligible manufacturing or processing buildings, deliver certain federal benefits automatically to lower-income people, clarify what counts as a Canadian exploration expense, and extend the clean hydrogen investment tax credit to hydrogen made through methane pyrolysis. It also tightens several anti-avoidance rules (including for trust-to-trust transfers, tiered corporate structures with mismatched year-ends, debt forgiveness for bankrupt entities and tax-debt avoidance), implements the international Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, gives the Canada Revenue Agency stronger information-gathering tools during audits, simplifies the rules on qualified investments, and sets a deadline of October 30, 2026 after which no Canada Carbon Rebate payments will be made in respect of returns or adjustment requests. It also suspends the operation of the Canada–Russia income tax agreement.

Part 2 implements the "UTPR" backstop under the global minimum tax, which can subject Canadian entities of certain multinational groups to top-up tax on low-taxed profits elsewhere in the group. Part 3 makes largely technical GST/HST changes affecting financial institutions, credit unions, investment plans, insurers and first home savings accounts, allows CRA to share information with international tax authorities under existing agreements, and adjusts excise rules for cigars, cannabis, vaping products, raw leaf tobacco imports and brewer licences.

deepDive.heading: Non-tax measures in Part 4
deepDive.body:
Part 4 contains a wide range of changes. In finance: banks and insurers would be barred from issuing bearer-form documents; the Crown and officials would be shielded from lawsuits for good-faith acts under financial institution statutes; banks would have to offer deposit products in a non-discriminatory manner in certain circumstances; and the caps on CMHC mortgage guarantees and insured loans would rise. Other divisions expand the Tax Court's informal (simpler) appeal thresholds, give cabinet new regulation-making power over government contracting and the Procurement Ombudsman's complaint process, protect confidential information under the Retail Payment Activities Act from disclosure, and give the Superintendent of Bankruptcy new powers against unlicensed trustees and misleading insolvency solicitation, with higher maximum fines.

Other notable items: the Canada Labour Code would prohibit non-compete clauses and similar employment restrictions except in defined circumstances; the Canadian Human Rights Commission's Deputy Chief Commissioner position would be eliminated; review cycles under the Tobacco and Vaping Products Act would move from every two years to every five; mandatory re-evaluation of registered pesticides would be replaced with a risk-triggered process; and the Territorial Lands Act would let cabinet, on national-interest grounds, cancel or block mineral claims, leases and prospecting licences on certain Nunavut lands, with compensation determined by the Minister of Northern Affairs. Division 16 creates a new Defence Investment Agency and broadens the Defence Production Act to cover national security, giving the responsible minister exclusive authority over most defence and security purchasing plus new investment and stockpiling powers. (The published summary of Division 17, concerning the Canada Trade... Act, is cut off in the available text.)

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Individual taxpayers are touched through automatic benefit delivery for lower-income people, the Canada Carbon Rebate filing deadline, and higher dollar limits for informal Tax Court appeals. Businesses are affected by the manufacturing building write-off, the hydrogen credit expansion, tighter anti-avoidance rules, and new obligations for crypto-asset reporting. Large multinational corporations face the global minimum tax backstop. Financial institutions, credit unions, insurers and investment plans face numerous technical GST/HST and banking-law changes.

Workers in federally regulated sectors would be affected by the non-compete ban. Defence and security suppliers would deal with a new agency and centralized procurement authority. Mineral rights holders in parts of Nunavut could see claims or licences cancelled by cabinet order. Home buyers and lenders are indirectly affected through the higher CMHC guarantee and insured-loan limits.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Budget implementation bills are routine after each federal budget, and it is common for governments to split them into two acts, with a second bill later in the cycle. This one is unusually broad, bundling technical tax fixes with substantive policy shifts in labour, pesticide regulation, northern land management and defence procurement — a structure that often draws debate about whether omnibus budget bills allow adequate scrutiny of each measure.

The bill is currently at committee stage in the House of Commons. It must still complete committee study, report stage and third reading in the House, then pass the Senate and receive royal assent before taking effect. Provisions may be amended or dropped along the way, and many measures have their own coming-into-force dates.

C-35.overview: Bill C-35 would create a stand-alone federal law banning the importation into Canada of goods made, in whole or in part, with forced labour. It gives Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) officers explicit authority to decide whether imported goods were produced with forced labour and to hold those goods for up to 90 days while they investigate. It also lets the Minister of Foreign Affairs publish a regulated list of goods suspected of being made with forced labour — identifying the producer, the country or region, or both — and requires importers of listed goods to hand over specified information to the CBSA on request; if they don't, the goods are automatically treated as banned. Importers and owners could be billed for the cost of detaining, storing, moving or disposing of prohibited goods. The bill matters because it shifts Canada's forced-labour import ban out of the customs tariff schedule and into its own act with new listing powers, new information demands on importers, and a narrower route for challenging border decisions.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill enacts the Ban on Importing Goods Made with Forced Labour Act, which states plainly that goods produced wholly or in part by forced labour are prohibited from importation. "Forced labour" is defined by reference to the International Labour Organization's Forced Labour Convention, 1930 (No. 29), and "produced" is defined broadly to include goods that are grown, assembled, manufactured or mined. The Act binds the federal and provincial Crowns, meaning governments themselves are also covered.

At the same time, the bill removes the existing wording about goods made with forced labour or child labour from tariff item No. 9897.00.00 in the Customs Tariff, and repeals a related provision in section 132 of that Act. In effect, the import ban on forced-labour goods moves from the customs tariff schedule into this new dedicated statute.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Enforcement runs through the existing customs system: the Customs Act applies with any necessary modifications, and breaking the new Act counts as breaking the Customs Act. A customs officer designated by the President of the CBSA may determine whether goods were produced with forced labour, and may detain goods for up to 90 days (or longer if regulations allow) to make that determination.

The Minister of Foreign Affairs may make regulations establishing a list of goods there are "reasonable grounds to suspect" were produced with forced labour, and must identify the producer, the country or region of production, or both. Several federal ministers and CBSA officials — Public Safety, Labour, Transport, Agriculture and Agri-Food, Industry, plus anyone else named in regulations — may share information with the Minister to help build the list. Importers of listed goods must provide prescribed information to the CBSA when asked; failing to do so means the goods are deemed prohibited. Importers and owners of prohibited goods are jointly liable for the government's detention, storage, transportation and disposal costs, which become a debt owed to the Crown. Most of the details — including what information must be provided and what can or cannot be shared between ministers — are left to future regulations made by the Governor in Council.

deepDive.heading: How decisions can be challenged
deepDive.body:
The bill removes the usual Customs Act ladder of appeals, reviews and re-determinations for decisions made under this Act. Instead, the only avenue is judicial review in the Federal Court under section 18.1 of the Federal Courts Act.

Transitional rules apply the same approach to cases already in the system when the Act receives royal assent. Existing forced-labour or child-labour classifications under tariff item 9897.00.00 that have not yet produced a decision can no longer be appealed or re-determined under the Customs Act, and pending re-determination requests become void — though judicial review remains available, and recent determinations or decisions (within 90 days before royal assent) are treated as if communicated on the day the Act takes effect for timing purposes. Appeals already filed with a notice of appeal before that day continue under the old rules.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected groups are importers and the owners of imported goods, who face the possibility of detention at the border, demands for supply-chain information if their goods appear on the Minister's list, financial liability for detention and disposal costs, and a narrower set of options to contest CBSA decisions. Businesses whose products come from producers, countries or regions named on the list would face the heaviest new paperwork obligations.

On the government side, the CBSA and the Minister of Foreign Affairs take on central roles, supported by information sharing among several other federal departments. Because the Act binds the Crown, federal and provincial government purchasers are also subject to the import ban.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-35 is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Anita Anand as Minister of Foreign Affairs, and it is at second reading in the House of Commons — an early stage, meaning it has not yet been studied in committee, amended, passed by both chambers or given royal assent. Its contents could change before becoming law.

Most of the Act would come into force on royal assent, but sections 8 and 9 — the importer information requirement for listed goods and the rule deeming non-compliant shipments prohibited — would come into force only on a day or days set by order of the Governor in Council, allowing time for the necessary regulations to be developed. Readers should note that the bill deletes the reference to goods made with "forced labour or child labour" from tariff item 9897.00.00, while the new Act as written addresses forced labour; the text above does not contain a separate child-labour import prohibition.

C-37.overview: Bill C-37, the First Nations Clean Water Act, is a government bill that would set out federal rules and commitments for drinking water, wastewater and water infrastructure on First Nation lands. It affirms that First Nations' inherent right to self-government under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 includes law-making authority over water, source water, drinking water, wastewater and related infrastructure on their lands, and it creates a framework of principles, minimum national standards and funding obligations for the federal government. The bill also declares it to be Government of Canada policy to further the 'progressive realization' of the human right to safe drinking water for people on First Nation lands. It responds to long-standing problems the preamble describes as regulatory gaps, policy gaps and underfunding that have contributed to long-term drinking water advisories and health inequities. As of this summary the bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning MPs are debating it in principle and it could still change.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has two main pillars. First, it affirms First Nations jurisdiction: section 6 confirms that the inherent right of self-government includes the authority to make and enforce laws about water, source water, drinking water, wastewater and related infrastructure on, in and under First Nation lands, with accompanying provisions on how that jurisdiction applies, its limits, publication of laws, and delegation.

Second, it creates a federal backstop: the bill sets out minimum standards for drinking water quality, water quantity and wastewater effluent (sections 14–16), and allows the Governor in Council and the Minister of Indigenous Services to make regulations, including on 'protection zones' for source water and on enforcement. Provisions address what happens if a First Nation has not made a choice about which standards apply, and rules for resolving conflicts between First Nation laws, federal regulations, and modern treaties or self-government agreements.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Principles: decision-making under the Act is to be guided by stated principles, including substantive equality and reliable access to water services. The preamble also emphasizes First Nations' traditional knowledge, the role of First Nation women as water protectors and Elders as knowledge keepers, and First Nations control over their own water-related data.

Money and machinery: the bill sets out federal funding obligations — funding based on need, funding to support services comparable to those elsewhere, and funding for a First Nations Water Commission — and requires consultation on how funding is allocated. It ties in obligations under the 2021 Settlement Agreement from the class action on long-term drinking water advisories. It provides for the Minister to use best efforts on access to drinking water, to enter agreements supporting the exercise of First Nations jurisdiction and the administration and enforcement of First Nation laws, and to make agreements on source water protection with other governments. It also includes grant authority, immunity for employees and hired persons, tabling of Water Commission reports, an annual report, and a five-year review conducted in collaboration with First Nations. The Act would come into force one year after royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to 'First Nation lands' as defined in the Act — lands referred to in Class 24 of section 91 of the Constitution Act, 1867, including water and source water on, in and under them. It expressly does not cover lands over which Aboriginal title is claimed or has been confirmed by a court.

The most directly affected parties are First Nations and their governing bodies, residents of First Nation lands, and the federal government, particularly the Minister of Indigenous Services. Because source water often crosses boundaries, the bill also contemplates collaboration with provincial, territorial and municipal governments, including through transboundary source water protection planning and agreements. Signatories to modern treaties and self-government agreements are addressed through a specific conflict provision.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The preamble frames the bill as a response to inadequate infrastructure and long-term drinking water advisories on First Nation lands, and links it to Canada's commitments under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, citing specific UNDRIP articles, as well as UN resolutions recognizing safe drinking water and sanitation as a human right. It also references the September 15, 2021 Settlement Agreement in the class action on long-term drinking water advisories.

The bill is sponsored by Hon. Mandy Gull-Masty as a government bill and is at second reading in the House of Commons. This summary is based on the text as introduced; provisions can be amended at committee and later stages, and much of the detail — such as standards and protection zones — would be filled in later through regulations, with consultation requirements attached.

C-36.overview: Bill C-36 would replace Canada's main private-sector privacy law with a new statute called the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act. That new Act would set out the rules businesses must follow when they collect, use or share personal information in the course of commercial activities — including when they need your consent, how long they can keep your data, how they must secure it, and what rights you have to see, correct or have your information deleted. Enforcement would sit with a Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada, a new Privacy and Consumer Data Commissioner and a dedicated tribunal-style Division, with powers to investigate complaints, order changes and impose monetary penalties. The existing Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) would lose its privacy portion (Part 1) and be renamed the Electronic Documents Act. The bill is sponsored by Hon. Evan Solomon, the Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation, and is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet been passed or amended by committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has four parts. Part 1 enacts the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, a full replacement framework for private-sector privacy in Canada. Its stated purpose is to support and promote digital commerce while protecting personal information collected, used or disclosed in commercial activities — in other words, it tries to balance individual privacy with organizations' business needs.

Part 2 amends PIPEDA by repealing its privacy portion (Part 1) and changing its short title to the Electronic Documents Act, leaving behind only the electronic-documents and signature rules. Part 3 deals with the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada, amending the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and the Digital Safety Act, along with consequential changes to the Access to Information Act, Financial Administration Act, Privacy Act and Public Service Superannuation Act. Part 4 makes further consequential and related amendments to a long list of statutes, including the Competition Act, Telecommunications Act, Broadcasting Act, Canada Evidence Act, Canada Business Corporations Act, Aeronautics Act, Railway Safety Act, CRTC Act and Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act. Most provisions would come into force on a date set by order in council rather than immediately on royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Key obligations for organizations
deepDive.body:
Businesses would have to be accountable for personal information under their control, designate an individual responsible for privacy, and maintain a written privacy management program that the regulator can request. Collection would have to be limited to what is appropriate, consent would generally be required (and consent obtained by deception would be invalid), and individuals could withdraw consent. The Act sets out a long list of situations where consent is not required — for example certain routine business activities, transfers to service providers, de-identified or anonymized data, research and development, prospective business transactions, fraud prevention, debt collection, emergencies, financial abuse, journalistic or artistic purposes, and specified disclosures to government institutions or as required by law.

Other duties include setting retention periods and disposing of information when it is no longer needed, honouring an individual's request to have their data disposed of, keeping information accurate, maintaining security safeguards, reporting breaches of security safeguards to the Commission and keeping breach records, being transparent about policies and practices, and providing plain-language access to personal information within set time limits. The Act also creates rules for de-identification (including a prohibition on re-identifying data in some circumstances) and provides for a future "data mobility framework" that would let individuals move their data between organizations. Definitions worth noting: a "child" means anyone under 18, "personal information" expressly includes information inferred about a person, and "automated decision system" covers machine learning, neural networks and similar technologies.

deepDive.heading: Oversight, penalties and remedies
deepDive.body:
Enforcement would be shared among three bodies: the Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission of Canada, a Privacy and Consumer Data Commissioner designated under the Act, and a Privacy and Consumer Data Division. Individuals could file complaints; the Commissioner could investigate, use dispute-resolution mechanisms, enter into compliance agreements, conduct audits, issue interim orders and, at the conclusion of an investigation, issue notices of contravention. The Division would handle applications for review and set penalties, subject to specified maximums, with an explicit statement that the purpose of a penalty is compliance rather than punishment.

The bill also provides a right of appeal (in some cases with leave), a mechanism to file orders with the Federal Court for enforcement, and a private right of action allowing individuals to seek damages for contraventions. There are whistleblower protections, offence and punishment provisions, rules for handling national-security information under the Canada Evidence Act, and a requirement that a parliamentary committee review the Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The Act applies to "organizations" — defined broadly to include businesses, associations, partnerships, individuals and trade unions — that handle personal information in the course of commercial activity, which expressly includes selling or trading donor, membership and fundraising lists. Employee information is also addressed for federal works, undertakings and businesses, a category that covers banks, airlines, railways, telecommunications and broadcasting, interprovincial shipping and similar federally regulated sectors.

For ordinary consumers, the practical effects would be clearer consent rules, a right to request deletion of their data, access and correction rights, breach notification, and the ability to complain to a regulator or sue for damages. Organizations that certify under approved codes of practice or certification programs would have a route to demonstrate compliance. The Act also contemplates consultation with provinces, since several provinces have their own private-sector privacy laws.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-36 is a government bill introduced in the 45th Parliament and sponsored by the Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation. PIPEDA, the law it would largely replace for privacy purposes, dates from 2000 and has been the subject of repeated modernization efforts; this bill would retire its privacy provisions entirely and rename the remaining statute the Electronic Documents Act.

The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons. That means MPs are debating the principle of the bill; it has not been studied in committee, amended, passed by the House or Senate, or received royal assent. Many operational details — including the data mobility framework, publicly available information, codes of conduct and certification programs — would be filled in later through regulations, and the timing of coming into force would be set by order in council.

S-2.overview: Bill S-2 amends the Indian Act to expand who can be registered as a Status Indian and who can be added to a band list. It responds to a court challenge, Nicholas v. Canada (Attorney General), in which parts of the Act's registration rules were argued to violate the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The bill's centrepiece is the removal of the so-called "second-generation cut-off" structure in section 6: it repeals subsection 6(2) and replaces the main entitlement rule so that anyone with at least one parent entitled to registration can themselves be registered. It also creates new entitlements for descendants of certain people historically removed from the register, adds a formal process for people who wish to have their names removed from the Indian Register, and modernizes outdated language by replacing the term "mentally incompetent Indian" with "dependent person." The bill is a government bill sponsored in the Senate by Marc Gold and is currently being studied by a House of Commons committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill rewrites parts of the Indian Act's registration rules (section 6) and band membership rules (section 11). The most significant change is to paragraph 6(1)(f), which would say a person is entitled to be registered if at least one parent is entitled to be registered — or, if that parent has died, was or would have been entitled at the time of death. At the same time, subsections 6(2) and 6(2.1) are repealed, along with paragraphs 6(1)(d) and (e).

Under the existing structure, people registered under subsection 6(2) generally could not pass status to their own children unless the other parent also had status — the arrangement commonly called the second-generation cut-off. By folding those people into a single entitlement category under paragraph 6(1)(f), the bill changes how status flows between generations. Transitional provisions in sections 10 and 11 of the bill make clear that anyone already registered or entitled under subsection 6(2) is deemed registered under paragraph 6(1)(f), and that the Registrar must recognize entitlements that existed under 6(2) before the change takes effect.

deepDive.heading: New and expanded entitlements
deepDive.body:
The bill broadens paragraph 6(1)(a.1), which covers people whose names were removed from the Indian Register or an early band list under historic provisions — including the old section 12 rules, section 13 (as it read before September 4, 1951), section 111 (as it read before July 1, 1920) and section 112 (as it read before April 17, 1985). Paragraph 6(1)(a.3) is broadened so that any direct descendant of a person who is, was, or would have been entitled under paragraphs (a), (a.1) or (a.2) is entitled to registration.

A new subsection 11(3.2) creates additional band membership rights for people who lost membership under the former section 14 of the Act — a provision that historically applied to married women — and for their registered direct descendants. Related changes to section 11 tie band list entry to the new paragraph 6(1)(f) test, so that a person qualifies if a parent is (or was at death) entitled to be on that band's list.

deepDive.heading: Removal from the register and other changes
deepDive.body:
A new subsection 5(8) lets a person who wishes to be taken off the Indian Register apply in writing to the Registrar, who must then remove the name from both the Register and the band list maintained in the Department. Section 9 of the bill clarifies that a person's own entitlement to be registered is not lost if they, a parent, grandparent or other ancestor has been removed under this new process.

The bill also replaces the Indian Act's definition of "mentally incompetent Indian" with "dependent person," defined as an Indian who, under provincial law, has been found unable to manage their estate because of an illness or impairment affecting cognitive capacity. Section 51 is rewritten with the new terminology, keeping the Minister's authority over such a person's estate, including appointing an administrator, ordering property dealt with to pay debts or maintenance costs, and directing that off-reserve property be handled under provincial law.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and when it takes effect
deepDive.body:
The changes primarily affect First Nations individuals and families whose registration or band membership was limited by the previous rules — particularly descendants of people removed from the register under historic provisions, descendants of women who lost band membership on marriage, and people registered under subsection 6(2) who could not pass status to their children. Band lists maintained by the Department of Indigenous Services would grow accordingly, since newly entitled people also gain the right to have their names entered on those lists.

Most of the core registration changes — including the new paragraph 6(1)(f), the repeal of subsection 6(2), and the related band list amendments — come into force 12 months after the bill receives royal assent, rather than immediately. Section 7 makes a consequential update to section 64.1 to reflect the repeal of paragraphs 6(1)(d) and (e), and section 4.1 is updated so that references to "Indian" in a list of Act provisions also cover people entitled to be on a band list.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
According to the bill's own summary, the new registration entitlements respond to a Charter challenge to certain provisions of the Indian Act in Nicholas v. Canada (Attorney General). The bill continues a series of amendments to the Act's registration provisions, several of which date from 2017 legislation and earlier reforms tied to the April 17, 1985 changes referenced throughout the text.

Bill S-2 is a government bill introduced in the Senate and sponsored there by Marc Gold. It has passed the Senate stage and is at consideration in committee in the House of Commons, meaning the text described here could still be amended before becoming law.

S-4.overview: Bill S-4 is a government bill that would update the Energy Efficiency Act, the 1992 law that sets minimum energy-performance standards and labelling rules for products like appliances, heating equipment and lighting sold or shipped across provincial or international borders. The bill broadens the law's reach to cover digital labels, online advertising and new kinds of sellers and commercial users; adds a purpose statement covering things like the low-carbon transition, innovation, and collaboration with Indigenous peoples and provinces; and bans false or misleading energy-efficiency claims. It also gives the Minister of Natural Resources new tools, including the ability to grant exemptions from the Act, order corrective measures, and impose administrative monetary penalties, and it modernizes inspection powers to include remote access by telecommunication. For ordinary readers, it mainly matters because it aims to make energy-efficiency ratings on products more reliable and enforceable. The bill has passed the Senate and is at second reading in the House of Commons, so it is not yet law and could still change.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Energy Efficiency Act (originally passed in 1992) rather than replacing it. According to the bill's own summary, it has three main goals: to let the Minister of Natural Resources create exemptions from the Act and its regulations in order to design a regulatory regime that supports innovation, competitiveness and economic growth; to strengthen enforcement, including through administrative monetary penalties, updated fines and a new ministerial power to order corrective measures; and to widen the Act's scope so it accounts for modern technologies, new market participants, misleading claims and the 'responsible use of energy.'

The Act's long title would be changed to 'An Act respecting the energy efficiency of energy-using products and the responsible use of energy and energy sources' — signalling a shift from a focus purely on product efficiency toward energy use more broadly.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
A new purpose section (2.2) would state that the Act exists to promote energy efficiency and responsible energy use, encourage the transition to a low-carbon economy, stimulate innovation and competitiveness, foster collaboration with Indigenous peoples and provincial governments, and support international and interprovincial trade in energy-efficient products. The definition of an 'energy efficiency standard' is expanded well beyond simple energy consumption to include durability, interoperability, energy demand, water conservation, system design, the type of energy used, and a product's 'technological composition and capabilities.'

Other notable changes: 'label' is redefined to include digital as well as physical labels, marks, stamps and tags; 'dealer' is expanded to cover those who advertise or offer products for sale or lease; and a new category, 'commercial entity,' captures businesses that use energy-using products commercially. A new section 5.1 prohibits dealers from labelling or advertising products in a way that is false, misleading or deceptive about energy efficiency, or that is likely to create an erroneous impression. Businesses must keep supporting documents and records for six years.

deepDive.heading: Enforcement and inspection powers
deepDive.body:
The Minister could require dealers and commercial entities to make products available for testing, hand over test data and calculations, and provide information about — or access to — computer software, digital modelling or simulation tools used to test products. Such requests must be complied with 'without delay.' The Minister may dismantle and test products, and inspectors may seize and detain them.

Inspection powers are updated for a digital era: inspectors, designated by the Minister, may enter places where regulated activities occur, examine products, packages, documents and computer systems, make copies, and conduct tests. Importantly, an inspector is considered to have 'entered' a place when accessing it remotely by telecommunication; for places not open to the public, remote access must occur with the knowledge of the owner or person in charge and last no longer than necessary. Entry into a private dwelling still requires consent or a warrant, and warrants may now be applied for and issued electronically. The threshold for many powers is broadened from verifying compliance to also 'preventing non-compliance.'
