deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The rules apply chiefly to manufacturers, importers, retailers and now advertisers of energy-using products that cross provincial or international borders, as well as to businesses that use such products commercially. These parties face reporting obligations to the Minister, record-keeping duties, testing requirements, and potential penalties, forfeiture of goods, or orders to take corrective measures.

For consumers, the practical effect would largely be indirect: clearer and potentially more trustworthy energy-efficiency labels and advertising claims, including online, and standards that may address more than just how much electricity a product uses. The bill also preserves and adjusts a process allowing third parties who claim an interest in forfeited goods to apply to a court within 30 days.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill S-4 is a government bill sponsored by Hon. Pierre Moreau that began in the Senate (indicated by the 'S' in its number) and is now at second reading in the House of Commons. It must still be studied, possibly amended, and passed by the House and receive Royal Assent before taking effect.

Many of the details — such as which products are exempt, the size of administrative monetary penalties, and specific standards — would be set through regulations made under the Act rather than spelled out in the bill itself. The text provided here is partial, so some provisions (including the penalty and fine provisions referenced in the bill's summary) are not reproduced in full above.

S-3.overview: Bill S-3 is a government bill that updates two older federal laws governing measurement accuracy in Canada: the Weights and Measures Act (which covers scales, fuel pumps and other trade measuring devices) and the Electricity and Gas Inspection Act (which covers electricity and natural gas meters). The bill modernizes the powers of the Minister of Industry and of federal inspectors — clarifying what they can do, allowing devices to be checked by testing samples rather than every single unit, and letting inspectors order businesses to fix or prevent problems. It also broadens the definition of "meter," lets the Minister grant temporary or time-limited permissions and exemptions, and repeals some existing regulatory provisions. In practical terms, it affects the rules that ensure consumers get the amount of gasoline, groceries, electricity or natural gas they pay for. The bill originated in the Senate and is currently at second reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends four instruments at once: the Weights and Measures Act, the Electricity and Gas Inspection Act, and the regulations made under each. According to the bill's own summary, its main goals are to clarify existing powers, duties and functions of the Minister of Industry and of inspectors, to give the Minister new powers (including over sampling during device examinations and over corrective and preventive measures), and to give inspectors additional powers.

On the electricity and gas side, it also broadens the definition of "meter," gives the president (of Measurement Canada, the body administering that Act) authority to grant certain exemptions, and clarifies the steps required before a device can be put into service. The bill repeals certain provisions in both sets of regulations and includes transitional provisions to bridge the old rules and the new ones.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: testing, permissions and exemptions
deepDive.body:
A significant change is the introduction of examination by sampling. New section 15.2 allows a device to be examined "using any means, including by sampling devices of the same class, type or design," and permits the results to be applied to other devices of that same class, type or design when issuing certificates or attaching seals and tags. The Minister may issue written directions about how examinations and sampling are done; those directions must be made public but are exempt from the Statutory Instruments Act, meaning they do not go through the normal regulation-making process.

The bill also creates flexibility mechanisms. New section 8.1 lets the Minister give a trader temporary permission to use a device in trade without prior approval or examination, for a specified period and under specified conditions. That permission can be suspended or revoked, but only after written notice, an opportunity for interested persons to object and make representations, and consideration of those representations. Separately, the Minister may exempt local standards from the usual recalibration timelines, and may authorize outside entities — not just the National Research Council of Canada — to calibrate and certify reference standards.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: inspection and enforcement powers
deepDive.body:
The bill rewrites the inspection provisions of the Weights and Measures Act. Inspectors may enter any place, including a vehicle (newly defined to include vessels, aircraft, trains, motor vehicles, trailers and cargo containers), where they have reasonable grounds to believe a regulated activity occurs or regulated things are located. Once there, they may examine and test things, seize and detain items, use computers and copying equipment on site, reproduce data, take photographs, require people to identify themselves, order equipment started or stopped, and limit access to the site. Notably, an inspector is considered to have "entered" a place if they access it remotely by telecommunication. Entry to non-public places must occur at a reasonable time, with the knowledge of the owner or person in charge, and only for as long as necessary; entry to a dwelling-house still requires a warrant, which may now be applied for and issued by telecommunication. Owners and employees have a duty to give reasonable assistance.

On enforcement, new sections create "remedial and preventive measures." An inspector who has reasonable grounds to believe someone has contravened or is likely to contravene the Act may order that person to take measures to remedy or prevent it. The Minister may issue public written directions about plans, procedures or processes for compliance, and the Minister or an inspector may order a regulated person to develop or implement such a plan; where a ministerial order and an inspector's order conflict, the Minister's prevails. Inspectors must attach prescribed tags and seals to devices that fail to meet requirements, and tampering with seized items without permission remains an offence. Police may, at an inspector's request and in their company, stop and detain a vehicle for examination.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected groups are businesses that use measuring devices in trade — retailers with scales, gas stations with fuel pumps, and similar traders — as well as electricity and natural gas utilities whose meters determine customer bills, and manufacturers, importers and servicers of such devices. These parties would face the clarified inspection powers, possible orders to take corrective or preventive action, and new duties to assist inspectors, while also gaining access to temporary permissions and exemptions.

Consumers are affected indirectly: the framework exists so that the quantity shown on a pump, scale or meter matches what is actually delivered. The bill also addresses fees and charges, providing that fees for an examination or service performed by an inspector are payable after the work is done and are recoverable as a debt to the Crown, and consolidating the regulation-making authority over such fees. Where a dispute arises between a trader and another person about a device's accuracy, the Minister may make regulations about the examinations, rules and criteria used to settle it, and an inspector may calculate what would have been payable had an inaccurate device been accurate.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Pierre Moreau. It began in the Senate — indicated by the "S" in S-3 — and has since moved to the House of Commons, where it is at second reading. That means it has not yet been studied by a Commons committee and could still be amended before any final vote.

Both statutes being amended are long-standing federal laws (the Weights and Measures Act dates to the Revised Statutes of Canada), and much of the bill is housekeeping: replacing outdated wording, repealing superseded subsections, and adding transitional rules. Several of the new tools — public ministerial directions that are exempt from the Statutory Instruments Act, remote access by telecommunication, and warrants obtained electronically — reflect approaches used in other modernized federal inspection regimes. This summary is based on the text provided, which appears to be truncated; provisions later in the bill, including the full set of Electricity and Gas Inspection Act amendments and the transitional provisions, are not detailed here.

S-5.overview: Bill S-5, the Connected Care for Canadians Act, targets the companies that sell or license the software and hardware used to store and share Canadians' health records. It would require that this technology be "interoperable" — meaning users can easily, completely and securely access health information and exchange it with other systems — and it would prohibit "data blocking," any practice that prevents, discourages or interferes with access to or the sharing of electronic health information. The stated goal is to make it easier for patients and their health care providers to get complete health information when they need it, which the bill's preamble links to patient safety, better health outcomes, and support for virtual care and mobility across the country. Because health care delivery is largely a provincial and territorial responsibility, the Act would only apply in a province or territory if the federal Cabinet issues an order saying that jurisdiction does not already have rules that are substantially similar to, or stronger than, the federal ones. Most of the operational detail — the technical standards, what counts as data blocking, enforcement and penalties — would be set later through regulations.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act creates two core obligations for "health information technology vendors" — any individual, company, partnership or organization that licenses, sells, or supplies as a service the hardware, software or integrated technology used to create, maintain, access, use or exchange electronic health information.

First, section 5 requires that the technology be interoperable. Under the bill, technology is interoperable if it lets users easily, completely and securely access and use all electronic health information and exchange it with other health information technologies — except where a federal, provincial or territorial privacy law prohibits that — and if it meets standards and specifications to be set out in regulations. Second, section 6 prohibits data blocking by vendors, subject to whatever exceptions regulations may create. Data blocking is defined broadly as any practice or act that prevents, discourages or interferes with access to, or the use or exchange of, electronic health information, plus any additional practices listed in future regulations.

deepDive.heading: How it would apply across provinces and territories
deepDive.body:
The Act does not apply automatically everywhere. Section 4 states it applies in a province or territory only if that jurisdiction is named in an order made by the Governor in Council (the federal Cabinet).

Under section 7, Cabinet may make such an order only if it is satisfied — after applying criteria and a process to be set out in regulations — that the province or territory does not already have requirements that are substantially similar to or exceed those in the Act. Cabinet can also later repeal or amend such an order using the same criteria and process. In effect, the federal rules are designed as a backstop that fills gaps where provincial or territorial rules are weaker or absent. The preamble also states Parliament's intent to promote cooperation and consultation with provincial and territorial governments, First Nations, Inuit and Métis Peoples and stakeholders on common standards, and affirms that data governance relating to Indigenous Peoples under the Act must respect Indigenous data sovereignty.

deepDive.heading: Regulations and enforcement
deepDive.body:
Much of the substance of this bill would be filled in later by regulation. Section 8 gives Cabinet broad regulation-making powers, including to set the technical standards for interoperability, specify what practices count as data blocking, define exceptions to the prohibition, and set the criteria and process for the province-and-territory orders. Notably, it also allows regulations to amend the definitions found in section 2 of the Act itself.

On enforcement, regulations could authorize the Minister of Health to verify a vendor's compliance, including by requiring vendors to hand over information or documents the Minister considers necessary; create a complaints process; establish a system of administrative monetary penalties for vendors that contravene the interoperability requirement, the data-blocking prohibition, or the regulations; and set out how those decisions, notices of violation or penalties can be reviewed. Section 10 states that section 126 of the Criminal Code — the general offence of disobeying a federal statute — does not apply to contraventions of this Act, indicating an administrative rather than criminal enforcement approach. Section 9 removes the usual requirement that documents incorporated by reference into interoperability standards be fixed as of a particular date, which allows technical standards to be referenced as they change over time.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The direct legal obligations fall on health information technology vendors — the companies that supply electronic medical record systems, health data platforms and related tools — rather than on hospitals, clinics or individual clinicians. Vendors operating in jurisdictions covered by a Cabinet order would need to meet the interoperability standards and refrain from data blocking, and could face verification requests and monetary penalties under future regulations.

Indirectly, the bill is aimed at patients and health care professionals, who the preamble says currently cannot easily access health information. Provincial and territorial governments are also affected, since their existing rules determine whether the federal Act applies in their jurisdiction. The bill's definition of electronic health information covers personal health information whether or not it has been de-identified, and personal health information is defined broadly to include information about a person's physical or mental health, health services received, organ or tissue donation and test results, and information collected in or incidental to the provision of health services — for both living and deceased individuals.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
Bill S-5 is a government bill sponsored by the Hon. Pierre Moreau. As a Senate bill (bills beginning with "S" originate in the Senate), it has already moved through the Senate and is now at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it is still under debate and not yet law.

Even if passed, the Act would come into force only on a date fixed by order of the Governor in Council (section 11), and its practical effect would depend on regulations being made and on Cabinet orders designating specific provinces or territories. The preamble frames the bill against the backdrop of increased mobility of Canadians and health professionals, growing use of virtual care, e-prescribing and e-consultation including in rural and remote areas, and the value of connected data for evidence-based decisions by governments, administrators and researchers.

C-201.overview: Bill C-201 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would amend the Canada Health Act — the federal law that sets the conditions provinces must meet to receive full federal health transfer payments — so that mental health, addictions and substance use services are explicitly counted as "insured health services." Right now the Act's definition covers hospital services, physician services and surgical-dental services; the bill would add mental, addictions and substance use health services to that list, and would specify that these include services delivered in community settings rather than only in hospitals or doctors' offices. It would also rewrite the Act's "comprehensiveness" criterion so that a provincial health insurance plan must cover insured services including those provided in community settings. In practical terms, the bill aims to put mental health and addictions care on the same statutory footing as physical health care under the national framework. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is at a very early stage.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes two targeted changes to the Canada Health Act. First, it expands the definition of "insured health services" in section 2 to include "mental, addictions and substance use health services" alongside the existing categories of hospital, physician and surgical-dental services. Second, it adds a new definition clarifying that this new category includes services provided in community settings.

It also replaces section 9 of the Act, the provision setting out the "comprehensiveness" criterion that provincial insurance plans must satisfy. The revised wording keeps the existing requirement that plans insure all insured health services provided by hospitals, medical practitioners or dentists — and, where provincial law permits, similar or additional services from other health care practitioners — while adding the words "including those provided in community settings."

deepDive.heading: Key provisions in plain terms
deepDive.body:
The Canada Health Act does not itself deliver health care; it sets criteria (such as comprehensiveness, universality and accessibility) that provinces and territories must meet to receive their full federal health transfer. Changing what counts as an "insured health service" therefore changes what provincial plans are expected to cover under that federal framework.

The bill also preserves an existing carve-out in the definition: services a person is entitled to under another Act of Parliament, or under provincial workers' compensation legislation, are still excluded from "insured health services." The bill text does not set out funding amounts, timelines, lists of specific covered treatments, or enforcement details beyond what already exists in the Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it could affect
deepDive.body:
The most direct effect would be on provincial and territorial governments, which administer health insurance plans and would face an expanded expectation of what their plans cover in order to satisfy the Act's comprehensiveness criterion. Providers working outside hospitals and physicians' offices — in community-based mental health, addictions and substance use settings — are specifically named through the reference to "community settings."

For individuals, the bill speaks to people seeking mental health, addictions or substance use care, whose services in many cases fall outside the categories currently listed in the Act. The bill itself does not specify how or when any change in coverage would reach patients.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-201 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual Member of Parliament rather than by the government. It is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not yet in the queue for House of Commons debate time. Private members' bills face long odds and lengthy timelines, and most do not become law.

The bill was introduced in 2025 in the 45th Parliament. Because it amends federal legislation that operates through conditions on transfer payments to provinces, any practical change would depend on how provinces respond and on federal-provincial arrangements — matters the bill text does not address.

C-202.overview: Bill C-202 is a short private member's bill, sponsored by Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet, that adds one new rule to the law governing Canada's foreign affairs department. It says the Minister of Foreign Affairs cannot agree, in any international trade treaty or agreement, to let in more foreign dairy, poultry or egg products at low tariff rates, or to lower the high tariffs that apply to imports above those set limits. In practical terms, it removes two specific bargaining chips from Canada's negotiators when they sit down at trade talks — the concessions that have historically been made on supply-managed farm products. The bill received royal assent in 2025, meaning it is now law. It matters because it converts a long-standing federal policy position on protecting supply management into a binding statutory restriction.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends section 10 of the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development Act — the statute that sets out the Minister of Foreign Affairs' powers and responsibilities, including conducting Canada's international trade negotiations. It inserts a new subsection 10(2.1) that places a limit on what the Minister may commit to on Canada's behalf.

Specifically, when carrying out the duties listed in subsection 10(2), the Minister must not make any commitment, through an international trade treaty or agreement, that would either increase the 'tariff rate quota' for dairy products, poultry or eggs, or reduce the tariff that applies to those goods when they are imported beyond that quota.

deepDive.heading: Key terms explained
deepDive.body:
A 'tariff rate quota' (a term the bill borrows from subsection 2(1) of the Customs Tariff) is the volume of a product that can be imported at a low or zero tariff. Once imports exceed that volume, a much higher tariff applies. Together, the quota and the over-quota tariff are the border controls that underpin Canada's supply management system for dairy, poultry and eggs.

The bill blocks movement on both levers at once: negotiators cannot enlarge the low-tariff quota, and they cannot soften the high tariff charged on anything above it. The restriction is written as an absolute prohibition in the text provided — the bill as set out contains no listed exceptions, sunset date, or override mechanism.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Canada's trade negotiators, whose mandate in future treaty talks is narrowed by statute. Farmers and processors in the dairy, poultry and egg sectors, which operate under supply management, are the intended beneficiaries of the protection.

It also has implications for trading partners seeking greater access to the Canadian market for these products, and potentially for other Canadian export sectors, since concessions on supply-managed goods have historically been part of broader trade packages. The bill itself does not address those trade-offs; it simply sets the limit on what the Minister may agree to.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — sponsored by Yves-François Blanchet. Protecting supply management has been a recurring theme in Canadian trade debates, particularly following agreements that granted foreign producers additional access to the Canadian dairy, poultry and egg markets.

According to the information provided, the bill has received royal assent, the final stage in the legislative process, meaning the new subsection is now part of the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development Act. It is a single-clause amendment; it does not change tariff levels or quotas as they currently exist, only what the Minister may commit to going forward.

C-203.overview: Bill C-203 is a short private member's bill that would formally designate September as "Ukrainian Heritage Month" across Canada. It contains no funding, no new programs and no legal obligations for anyone — it is a symbolic recognition, similar to other heritage-month designations Parliament has passed. The bill's preamble explains the reasoning: the first official Ukrainian immigrants arrived in Canada in September 1891, more than 1.3 million Canadians are of Ukrainian descent, and Parliament wishes to recognize their contributions and educate Canadians about them. Sponsored by Liberal MP Yvan Baker, the bill is currently "outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate. If passed, its practical effect would be to give governments, schools, community groups and others an officially recognized month for commemorative events.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The operative part of the bill is a single sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each year, the month of September is to be known as 'Ukrainian Heritage Month.'" A second clause simply gives the law its short name, the Ukrainian Heritage Month Act.

That is the entire substance of the legislation. It does not create a statutory holiday, does not require any level of government to hold events, and does not allocate money or create any new rights, duties or penalties.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
There are only two sections. Section 1 sets the short title. Section 2 makes the annual designation of September.

Everything else in the bill is a preamble — the "whereas" statements that explain Parliament's reasoning. Preambles help interpret a law's purpose but do not themselves impose requirements.

deepDive.heading: The reasoning set out in the preamble
deepDive.body:
The preamble cites the arrival of the first official Ukrainian immigrants, Vasyl Eleniak and Ivan Pylypiw, on September 7, 1891 — which explains the choice of September — followed by larger waves of Ukrainian immigration. It notes that Canada is now home to more than 1.3 million Ukrainian Canadians and that Canada was the first Western nation to recognize Ukraine's independence in 1991.

It also references Canada's recognition of the Holodomor of 1932–33 as a genocide carried out under Joseph Stalin's Soviet regime, and Canada's opposition to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and support for Ukrainian sovereignty. Finally, it states Parliament's wish to recognize the contributions of Ukrainian Canadians to Canada's economic, political, social and cultural life and to educate Canadians about that role.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
No individual, business or government body would face new legal requirements. The most direct effect would be on Ukrainian Canadian community organizations, schools, municipalities and cultural institutions, which would have a federally recognized month to anchor commemorative and educational programming.

Designation bills of this kind are often used to give official standing to observances that some communities already mark informally, and to signal parliamentary recognition of a group's place in Canadian history.

deepDive.heading: Status and what happens next
deepDive.body:
C-203 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — sponsored by Yvan Baker. Its listed status, "Outside the Order of Precedence," means it has been introduced in the House of Commons but has not yet reached the queue of private members' business scheduled for debate.

Most private members' bills never become law, largely because limited House time is available for them. Symbolic designation bills, however, have historically had a comparatively better chance of passing when they attract support across party lines.

S-6.overview: Bill S-6 is a technical housekeeping bill that updates the wording of 51 federal statutes so they work properly in both of Canada's legal systems: the common law used in nine provinces and three territories, and the civil law used in Quebec. Because federal laws apply across the whole country and exist in both English and French, terms borrowed from only one legal tradition (such as "real property" or "executor") can create confusion in the other. The bill adds or substitutes matching civil-law terms — for example pairing "real property" with "immovable," "agent" with "mandatary," and "void" with "null" in Quebec — and fixes definitions in laws governing banks, insurance companies, trust and loan companies and credit associations, plus many other Acts including the Access to Information Act, the Financial Administration Act, the Interpretation Act and the Official Languages Act. It is the fourth in a series of harmonization bills the Department of Justice began after the Civil Code of Québec came into force in 1994 and changed civil-law concepts and terminology. The bill is described as ensuring each language version takes both legal traditions into account, rather than as a change to substantive policy; it has passed through the Senate and awaits first reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's short title is the Federal Law–Civil Law Harmonization Act, No. 4. Its purpose, as stated in its long title and summary, is to harmonize federal statutes with the civil law of Quebec and to make sure that both the English and French versions of federal laws account for common law and civil law concepts alike.

In practice, this means combing through existing federal statutes and adjusting definitions and phrasing so that legal terms are understood correctly in both systems. Examples visible in the text include amendments to the Bank Act that add "immovable" alongside "real property," replace references to "agent" with "agent or mandatary," broaden "personal representative" to include a "liquidator of a succession" and "tutor," and clarify that a document that becomes "void" is "null" in Quebec. It amends 51 statutes in total.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Part 1 deals with financial institutions. It amends the four main statutes in this area — the Bank Act, the Cooperative Credit Associations Act, the Insurance Companies Act and the Trust and Loan Companies Act — along with related changes to the Canada Business Corporations Act, the Canada Cooperatives Act, the Canada Not-for-profit Corporations Act and the Budget Implementation Act, 2018, No. 1, plus coordinating amendments. Illustrative changes include revised definitions of "fiduciary," "personal representative," "proxy," "residential property" and "security interest" (the latter now referring to "mortgage or hypothec"), and updated rules on transmitting securities after a death that recognize Quebec instruments such as letters of verification, notarial wills and probate by a notary.

Part 2 makes similar adjustments across a long list of other statutes, including the Access to Information Act, the Privacy Act, the Canada Evidence Act, the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, the Financial Administration Act, the Interpretation Act, the Official Languages Act, the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Food and Drugs Act, the Museums Act, the Lobbying Act, the Conflict of Interest Act, the Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act and several agriculture, heritage and defence-related Acts.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most direct audiences are lawyers, notaries, judges, drafters and compliance staff who apply federal statutes in Quebec, where the Civil Code governs private-law matters such as property, contracts, successions and security over assets. Banks, credit unions, insurers, and trust and loan companies are singled out by Part 1, since their governing statutes contain a great deal of property, corporate and estate-related language.

For ordinary Canadians, the effects are largely indirect. The bill is presented as a terminology and drafting exercise rather than a change to rights, benefits or obligations, though clearer wording can reduce ambiguity in areas such as transferring shares after a shareholder dies, or determining what counts as a security interest.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
Canada is a bijural country: federal legislation must operate alongside both the common law and Quebec's civil law. When the Civil Code of Québec came into force in 1994, it substantially changed civil-law concepts, institutions and terminology, leaving many federal statutes using outdated or common-law-only language. The Department of Justice responded with an ongoing harmonization program, of which this bill is the fourth instalment.

Bill S-6 is a government bill sponsored in the Senate by the Hon. Pierre Moreau. Its listed status is a Senate bill awaiting first reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has completed the Senate stage of the process and must still be considered by MPs before it could become law.

deepDive.heading: What to watch for
deepDive.body:
Because the bill amends 51 statutes across hundreds of clauses, most parliamentary scrutiny of harmonization bills typically focuses on whether any individual wording change unintentionally alters the substance of a law rather than just its terminology. The text also includes coordinating amendments (referencing 2018, c. 12 and Bill C-15) to manage overlaps with other legislation.

This summary is based on the bill's summary, table of provisions and the portion of the text provided, which is truncated; the full text contains many further amendments not detailed here.

C-204.overview: Bill C-204 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would change the Income Tax Act to make two existing tax credits more generous: the volunteer firefighter tax credit and the search and rescue volunteer tax credit. Right now, each credit is calculated using a base amount of $6,000; the bill would raise that base amount to $10,000. Because these are non-refundable credits calculated by multiplying the base amount by the lowest federal tax rate (the "appropriate percentage"), the change would increase the amount of federal tax a qualifying volunteer can subtract from their bill, rather than handing out $10,000. The bill also rewrites the definition of "eligible volunteer firefighting services" to spell out that it covers being available or on call for firefighting, emergency and non-emergency duties, and that a volunteer may receive nominal pay that does not amount to a liveable wage. If passed, the changes would apply starting with the 2026 tax year.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends two sections of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 118.06(2) sets out the volunteer firefighter tax credit and subsection 118.07(2) sets out the search and rescue volunteer tax credit. In both, the dollar figure used to calculate the credit would rise from $6,000 to $10,000.

It also replaces subsection 118.06(1), the provision that defines "eligible volunteer firefighting services" for both credits. Section 3 of the bill states that these changes apply to the 2026 and subsequent taxation years.

deepDive.heading: How the credit actually works
deepDive.body:
These are non-refundable tax credits, not payments. The Act calculates the credit by multiplying the base amount by "the appropriate percentage for the taxation year" — the lowest federal personal income tax rate. So raising the base from $6,000 to $10,000 raises the maximum amount that can be deducted from federal tax payable, but the benefit is a fraction of $10,000, not the full amount.

The bill does not change the other conditions in the Act that an individual must meet to claim either credit; it only changes the dollar figure in the calculation and the definition of eligible firefighting services.

deepDive.heading: The new definition of eligible services
deepDive.body:
Under the bill, "eligible volunteer firefighting services" would mean services provided by someone acting as a volunteer firefighter for a fire department, consisting of being available or on call to perform firefighting services, emergency services and non-emergency duties for that department as needed.

The new wording adds that, in return for their time, the individual may receive "nominal remuneration that does not constitute a liveable wage." This addresses the status of volunteers who receive small stipends or per-call payments. This definition applies to both section 118.06 (firefighters) and section 118.07 (search and rescue volunteers).

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill is aimed at volunteer firefighters and search and rescue volunteers across Canada who claim these federal credits when filing their income tax returns. Volunteers who owe federal income tax would see a larger credit; because the credits are non-refundable, the size of the benefit depends on an individual's tax situation.

Because the changes would take effect for the 2026 and later taxation years, they would not apply retroactively to earlier returns.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-204 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual Member of Parliament rather than the government. Its listed status is "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not currently scheduled for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law.

The bill builds on credits that already exist in the Income Tax Act rather than creating new programs. Beyond the dollar increase and the revised definition, it makes no other changes to the tax treatment of volunteers.

C-205.overview: Bill C-205 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Jenny Kwan that would amend the National Housing Strategy Act — the 2019 law in which Ottawa recognized adequate housing as a fundamental human right. The bill would require Canada's National Housing Strategy to include measures aimed at preventing the removal (often called 'clearing' or 'dismantling') of homeless encampments located on federal land, and to identify alternatives to encampments after meaningful engagement with the people living in them. It would also add explicit references to Indigenous peoples throughout the Act, requiring that they be actively involved and supported in developing culturally appropriate housing programs and that responses to encampments respect their rights. Finally, it would require the federal government's triennial report on the Strategy to include success metrics developed with Indigenous organizations and longitudinal data broken down by group. As a private member's bill currently 'outside the Order of Precedence,' it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is a long way from becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The National Housing Strategy Act requires the federal government to maintain a national housing strategy and to report on it. Bill C-205 would add new content requirements to that strategy and to the reporting that follows it.

Specifically, the strategy would have to establish measures to prevent the removal of homeless encampments on federal land, and to identify alternatives to encampments following meaningful engagement with encampment residents. The bill also adds new definitions to the Act for 'federal land' (land belonging to the Crown in right of Canada, including waters on it and airspace above it), 'homeless encampment' (an outdoor settlement of one or more temporary structures such as tents or vehicles used as a residence by people experiencing homelessness), and 'Indigenous peoples' (using the definition in section 35(2) of the Constitution Act, 1982).

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Indigenous involvement: The bill would add a new objective to the Act committing the government to implement the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples with respect to the active involvement of Indigenous peoples in determining and developing housing programs that affect them. It would require the strategy to provide processes ensuring Indigenous peoples are actively involved and supported in developing culturally appropriate housing programs, and that responses to encampments respect their rights. Indigenous peoples would also be added by name to several existing lists in the Act, including participatory processes, the groups whose impacts must be monitored, and two other provisions (subsections 8(3) and 16.2(2)).

Consultation: Before setting the encampment measures and the Indigenous-involvement processes, the Minister would have to consult provincial governments responsible for housing, and consult and collaborate with a variety of organizations representing Indigenous interests.

Reporting: The triennial report on the strategy would have to include success metrics developed in consultation and collaboration with Indigenous organizations, plus longitudinal data disaggregated as far as possible by group — including vulnerable groups, Indigenous peoples, people with lived experience of housing need, and people with lived experience of homelessness.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most direct effect would be on people living in encampments on federal land, since the strategy would need to include measures directed at preventing their removal and at identifying alternatives developed through engagement with residents. The bill's text limits the encampment-removal measures to federal land; it does not address encampments on provincial, municipal or private land.

Indigenous peoples and organizations representing their interests would gain named roles in consultation, program development, monitoring and the design of success metrics. Federal officials responsible for the National Housing Strategy would carry new consultation and reporting obligations, and provincial housing ministries would be consulted parties.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble points to the federal government's existing declaration that housing policy recognizes the right to adequate housing as a fundamental human right, and states that a human-rights-based approach is needed to address the systemic causes of homelessness and the situation of encampment residents. The amendments build on the framework created when the National Housing Strategy Act was enacted in 2019.

This is a private member's bill rather than a government bill, and it is listed as being outside the Order of Precedence — meaning it has not yet reached the stage where it is scheduled for House of Commons debate. Most private members' bills do not become law. The bill sets requirements for what the strategy and reports must contain; it does not itself create housing programs or allocate funding.

C-206.overview: Bill C-206 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would require the federal Minister of Health to create a national strategy on brain injuries. The strategy would have to be developed in consultation with provincial health authorities, Indigenous groups and other stakeholders, and would cover prevention, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and recovery, as well as related issues such as mental health, addiction, homelessness and involvement with the criminal justice system. The Minister would have to table a report setting out the strategy in Parliament within 18 months of the bill becoming law, publish it online, and report back on how well it is working within five years. The bill does not itself create programs or medical services; it sets out a planning and reporting process, since health care delivery is largely a provincial responsibility. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet reached the stage of being debated and voted on in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally titled the National Strategy on Brain Injuries Act, directs the Minister of Health to develop a national strategy aimed at improving brain injury awareness, prevention and treatment, and at supporting the rehabilitation and recovery of people living with a brain injury.

The Minister must build the strategy in consultation with representatives of provincial governments responsible for health, Indigenous groups and relevant stakeholders. The legislation sets out what the strategy must address but leaves the specific policies and funding decisions to be worked out through that process.

deepDive.heading: What the strategy must include
deepDive.body:
The bill lists eleven required elements. Among them: promoting preventive measures; identifying training and education needs for health care and other professionals; supporting research and better data collection; sharing information on prevention, diagnosis and treatment; and creating national guidelines and recommended standards of care reflecting best medical and psychosocial practices.

The strategy must also promote public awareness and protect the rights of people living with brain injuries; foster collaboration with and provide financial support to national, provincial and local brain injury associations and service providers for integrated mental health resources; encourage consultation with mental health professionals in schools, sports organizations and workplaces; identify challenges linked to brain injury such as mental health problems, addiction, housing and homelessness, and criminality including intimate partner violence; maintain online resources with current facts and best practices; and establish a task force including policy makers, community agencies, brain injury associations, Indigenous groups, and people with lived experience of brain injury and their families.

deepDive.heading: Timelines and accountability
deepDive.body:
Two reporting requirements build in accountability. First, within 18 months of the Act coming into force, the Minister of Health must prepare a report setting out the strategy and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed. That report must then be published on Health Canada's website within 10 days of tabling.

Second, within five years after the strategy report is tabled, the Minister must — again in consultation with provinces, Indigenous groups and stakeholders — evaluate how effective the strategy has been and assess the overall situation regarding brain injury prevention, treatment and recovery. The resulting report, with conclusions and recommendations, must also be tabled in both Houses.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill's stated focus is people living with brain injuries and their families, along with the organizations that serve them. Its provisions touch health care and allied professionals (through training and guidelines), researchers (through data collection and research promotion), and brain injury associations and service providers, which the strategy is directed to collaborate with and financially support.

Because the bill highlights settings such as educational institutions, sports organizations and workplaces, and issues such as addiction, housing and homelessness, and criminality including intimate partner violence, its scope extends beyond clinical care into broader social supports. Provincial and territorial health authorities and Indigenous groups are named as required consultation partners, reflecting that much of the actual delivery of health services falls outside federal jurisdiction.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP — Gord Johns — rather than by the government. Its status is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate time in the House of Commons. Many private members' bills never advance to a vote.

The bill follows a common template in Canadian legislation: rather than creating new federal programs directly, it requires a minister to develop, publish and report on a strategy within set deadlines. Whether any particular measure listed in the bill is ultimately funded or implemented would depend on the strategy that is developed and on subsequent government decisions.

C-207.overview: Bill C-207 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Heather McPherson that would change the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) to make it harder for a province to leave the CPP and set up its own pension plan. Right now, a province can be recognized as running its own "comprehensive pension plan" (as Quebec does with the Quebec Pension Plan) through federal regulations. Under this bill, those regulations could only be made if at least two-thirds of the provinces still in the CPP — representing at least two-thirds of their combined population — formally agree. The stated reason, set out in the bill's preamble, is that when one province withdraws, the pension benefits of Canadians in the remaining provinces could be affected, and Parliament wants to protect the benefits people have paid into. The bill is a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not yet reached the stage of being debated and voted on.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a single new requirement to section 3 of the Canada Pension Plan. Section 3 currently allows the federal government to make regulations recognizing that a province provides its own "comprehensive pension plan" instead of participating in the CPP. Bill C-207 would add a condition: before such regulations can be made, other provinces must consent.

Specifically, the lieutenant governor in council (essentially the provincial cabinet) of at least two-thirds of the provinces that do not already run their own comprehensive pension plan would have to signify consent, and those consenting provinces would together have to represent at least two-thirds of the population of all such provinces. This is a double threshold — both a count of provinces and a population share must be met.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
There are only two operative elements. First, the new subsection 3(2.1) imposes the two-thirds provinces / two-thirds population consent test on regulations recognizing a provincial plan. Second, the bill would come into force on the 180th day after it receives royal assent, giving a six-month lead time before the new requirement applies.

The bill does not change contribution rates, benefit amounts, or eligibility rules. It does not explicitly prohibit a province from creating its own plan; it changes the federal process by which such a plan is formally recognized under the Canada Pension Plan.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The immediate effect would be on provinces considering withdrawal from the CPP, since they would need the agreement of a supermajority of the remaining CPP provinces before federal recognition could be granted. It would also give provinces that stay in the CPP a formal say in another province's departure, which they do not currently have under this section.

Indirectly, it concerns the roughly all working Canadians outside Quebec who contribute to the CPP. The preamble frames the bill around the concern that a province's withdrawal could change the pension benefits of people living and working in the provinces that remain.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Quebec already operates its own comprehensive plan, the Quebec Pension Plan, and would be an example of a province not counted among those whose consent is required. The bill's framing reflects broader public discussion in recent years about whether a province could exit the CPP and establish a provincial alternative.

As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, C-207 has not been scheduled for debate. Private members' bills face limited House time and most do not become law; this one would need to advance through the Order of Precedence, committee study, and votes in both the House of Commons and the Senate before receiving royal assent.

C-208.overview: Bill C-208 is a short private member's bill that would formally recognize a specific livestock brand — the design shown in a schedule attached to the bill — as the official "national livestock brand of Canada." It is a symbolic measure: it does not create rules for branding animals, change agricultural regulations, or impose obligations on anyone. The bill's preamble frames livestock brands as part of Canada's western and frontier heritage, as heraldic-style symbols for livestock owners, and as a history shared with Indigenous peoples. If passed, it would add a symbol drawn from ranching and pioneer culture to Canada's list of official national symbols. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it is not yet scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally titled the National Livestock Brand of Canada Act, contains only two operative sections. Section 1 gives the Act its short title. Section 2 states that the livestock brand illustrated in the schedule attached to the bill "is hereby recognized and declared to be the national livestock brand of Canada."

That is the entirety of the bill's legal effect. It is a declaratory statute — the kind of law Parliament uses to designate national symbols — rather than a regulatory one. Nothing in the text creates penalties, funding, programs, or restrictions on the use of the brand.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Short title (section 1): the Act may be cited as the National Livestock Brand of Canada Act.

Recognition (section 2): the brand depicted in the schedule becomes Canada's national livestock brand. The schedule itself is where the actual design appears, presented bilingually as "National Livestock Brand — Marque de bétail nationale." The bill text as reproduced here does not describe the design in words; readers would need to consult the published schedule to see it.

deepDive.heading: The reasoning set out in the preamble
deepDive.body:
The preamble — the "whereas" clauses that explain Parliament's rationale — makes several points. It states that livestock brands have been part of Canada's western and frontier heritage since before Confederation; that brands serve both to identify livestock and as heraldic symbols for their owners; and that the history of branding in western Canada is shared with Indigenous peoples.

It further says that recognizing western and frontier heritage, pioneer culture, farming, ranching and agriculture can promote national unity, and that Parliament sees value in including an element of western and frontier culture among Canada's official national symbols. Preambles are interpretive context and do not themselves create legal obligations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the bill is purely symbolic, it does not directly regulate ranchers, farmers, livestock producers, or provincial brand-registration systems, which handle the actual assignment and enforcement of individual brands. No one gains or loses a legal right under the text as written.

The practical impact would be cultural and representational: an official national symbol associated with ranching, agriculture and western Canadian history would exist alongside Canada's other recognized symbols.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-208 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP, in this case Steven Bonk, rather than by the government. It is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but has not yet reached a position in the queue that would guarantee House time for debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and many never receive substantive debate.

The bill fits a familiar category of Canadian legislation that designates national symbols or commemorative days. Assessing it mainly involves the question of whether Parliament should adopt this particular symbol, rather than any change to policy or regulation.

C-210.overview: Bill C-210 is a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Xavier Barsalou-Duval that would change the swearing-in requirement for federal parliamentarians. Right now, section 128 of the Constitution Act, 1867 requires every senator and MP to swear an oath of allegiance to the monarch before taking their seat. This bill would let each parliamentarian choose instead to swear a new "oath of office" — a promise to faithfully carry out the duties of the job — or to swear both oaths. It matters because the oath of allegiance to the King has long been a point of contention for some members, particularly Quebec sovereigntists and others who object to the monarchy, and this bill would make that oath optional rather than mandatory. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it is at a very early stage and has not been debated or voted on.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends section 128 of the Constitution Act, 1867, which sets out the oath every senator and member of the House of Commons must take before sitting in Parliament. Under the current text, that oath is the oath of allegiance to the monarch, found in the Fifth Schedule of the Act.

The bill would keep the existing requirement in place as subsection 128(1), but add a new subsection 128(2) saying that, notwithstanding the existing rule, any senator or MP may take the new oath of office instead of the oath of allegiance — or may take both.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 renumbers the current section 128 as subsection 128(1) and adds the new subsection 128(2) creating the choice of oath. Clause 2 adds the text of the new "Oath of Office" to the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution Act, 1867, immediately after the existing oath of allegiance.

The wording of the new oath is: "I, A.B., do solemnly and sincerely promise and declare that I will truly and faithfully and to the best of my skill and knowledge execute the powers and trusts reposed in me as a member of the Senate [or House of Commons (as the case may be)] of Canada." Clause 3 is a technical interpretation provision stating that any reference to the Constitution Acts, 1867 to 1982 is deemed to include this Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to every member of the Senate and every member of the House of Commons at the point when they are about to take their seat. It would not remove the oath requirement entirely — a parliamentarian would still have to swear something before sitting — but it would give each individual a choice among three options: the oath of allegiance, the new oath of office, or both.

The bill does not address oaths taken by other officials, and it does not change the wording of the existing oath of allegiance itself.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. It was introduced on June 16, 2025, in the 45th Parliament, and is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence" — the queue that determines when private members' business is debated. Bills in that position have not yet been scheduled for second-reading debate, and most private members' bills do not become law.

Because the bill would alter the text of the Constitution Act, 1867, questions about the appropriate amending procedure — that is, whether Parliament can make this change on its own or whether provincial consent is required — are typically raised with proposals of this kind. The bill text itself is drafted as an ordinary enactment of the Senate and House of Commons and does not address that question.

C-209.overview: Bill C-209 is a short private member's bill that would officially designate November of each year as "Albanian Heritage Month" across Canada. Sponsored by MP Yvan Baker, the bill contains just two operative clauses: one giving the law its short title, and one declaring the November designation. It creates no new programs, funding, holidays or legal obligations — it is a symbolic recognition intended to highlight the contributions of Albanian Canadians and to help other Canadians learn about them. The bill's preamble explains that November was chosen because it includes both Albania's Declaration of Independence (November 28, 1912) and its Liberation Day (November 29, 1944). As of this writing the bill sits "outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has not yet been scheduled for debate in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The entire substance of the bill is one sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each year, the month of November is to be known as 'Albanian Heritage Month.'" A separate clause gives the legislation its short title, the Albanian Heritage Month Act.

That is the whole of it. The bill does not create a statutory holiday, does not require any level of government or any employer to do anything, and does not attach spending, tax measures or penalties. Heritage-month bills of this kind are declaratory: they put a formal recognition into federal law that communities, schools, governments and organizations can then reference when marking the month.

deepDive.heading: Why November
deepDive.body:
The preamble — the introductory section that explains Parliament's reasoning — points to two dates that fall in November and are significant to Albanians and Albanian Canadians. The first is Albania's Declaration of Independence on November 28, 1912, which established Albania as an independent sovereign nation. The second is Liberation Day on November 29, 1944, commemorating Albania's liberation from Nazi forces following Albanian resistance.

The preamble also states that Canada's strength is reflected in the diversity of its population, that Canada is home to many Albanian Canadians, and that Albanian Canadians have contributed to the country's economic, political, social and cultural life. Preambles help explain intent but do not themselves impose requirements.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The designation applies throughout Canada, but because the bill imposes no duties, no individual, business or government body would be legally required to change anything. In practical terms, the people most directly affected would be members of Albanian Canadian communities and the organizations, schools, municipalities and cultural groups that choose to hold commemorative or educational events during November.

The bill's stated purpose includes informing Canadians more broadly about Albanian Canadian contributions, so any wider effect would come through public awareness and voluntary participation rather than through legal obligation.

deepDive.heading: Status and process
deepDive.body:
C-209 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP — Yvan Baker — rather than by the government. Its listed status is "outside the Order of Precedence." The Order of Precedence is the list, set by a random draw at the start of a Parliament, that determines which private members' items get House time; bills outside that list have been introduced and given first reading but are waiting for their sponsor's turn to come up.

Most private members' bills never become law, either because time runs out or because they are not adopted. To take effect, C-209 would still need to pass second reading, committee study and third reading in the House of Commons, then go through the Senate, and finally receive royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
Parliament has passed a number of similar heritage-month statutes and motions recognizing particular communities. These measures are generally uncontroversial in substance because they carry no cost or compulsion; debate around them, when it occurs, tends to focus on how many such designations should exist and whether they are best made by statute or by motion or proclamation.

Nothing in the text of C-209 addresses those broader questions. This explainer describes only what is in the bill as introduced; it does not predict whether it will advance.

C-211.overview: Bill C-211 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would let people who already qualify for a provincial disability benefit be automatically treated as qualifying for two federal ones: the federal disability tax credit under the Income Tax Act, and disability benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. The bill's preamble argues that requiring people to apply twice — once provincially, once federally — for the same impairment creates "undue hardship." Under the bill, provincial eligibility would be "deemed" to satisfy the federal test, though the responsible Minister could still decide otherwise in a given case. The income tax change would apply starting with the 2026 tax year. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is at a very early stage.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes two parallel changes. First, it adds a new subsection to section 118.3 of the Income Tax Act — the section that governs the federal disability tax credit for mental or physical impairment. Second, it rewrites part of paragraph 42(2)(a) of the Canada Pension Plan, the provision that defines when a person is considered "disabled" for CPP disability purposes.

In both cases the mechanism is the same: a "deeming provision." Rather than changing the underlying federal criteria, the bill says that a person who already meets a provincial standard is treated as having met the federal one, without having to prove it again from scratch.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
On the tax side, new subsection 118.3(1.01) would provide that an individual who can claim an amount for mental or physical impairment under the laws of the province where they live is deemed to meet the federal requirements for the disability tax credit — "unless the Minister determines otherwise." This change would apply to the 2026 and subsequent taxation years.

On the CPP side, the existing definition of disability (a "severe and prolonged" mental or physical disability, where "severe" means the person is incapable regularly of pursuing any substantially gainful occupation and "prolonged" means likely to be long continued and of indefinite duration or likely to result in death) is kept, but a second route is added: a person is also considered disabled if they are "in receipt of a provincial pension or benefit by reason of disability." This paragraph is likewise prefaced with "unless the Minister determines otherwise."

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill is aimed at people with disabilities who have already been approved for a provincial disability tax credit, pension or benefit and who also seek the federal disability tax credit or CPP disability benefits. For those individuals, provincial approval would serve as the basis for federal eligibility.

It would also affect the federal departments that administer these programs — the Canada Revenue Agency for the disability tax credit and the CPP disability administration — since both retain a discretionary power for the Minister to determine otherwise, rather than being bound in every case.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out Parliament's stated rationale: that applicants sometimes must apply at both the provincial and federal levels for the same impairment, that doing so twice causes undue hardship, and that it is desirable for provincial eligibility to carry over to the federal level.

Bill C-211 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. Its status is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not yet in the queue for debate and votes. Most private members' bills at this stage do not become law; the text above describes what the bill proposes, not current law.

C-212.overview: Bill C-212 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Jenny Kwan that would create a new independent watchdog — an "Ombud" — for the federal Department of Citizenship and Immigration (IRCC). The Ombud's job would be to examine whether the department's practices are fair, equitable and free of bias, racism and discrimination, including systemic racism, and to investigate complaints from people who believe they were treated unfairly in immigration, refugee or citizenship matters. The Ombud would be appointed for a seven-year term by the government after consulting party leaders in both chambers and receiving approval from the Senate and House of Commons, and would have investigative powers such as summoning witnesses and compelling documents. Findings would go to the Minister, who would have to respond and explain any recommendation not followed. As a private member's bill "outside the Order of Precedence," it has not yet reached the stage of scheduled debate, and most such bills do not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would establish an Office of the Ombud for the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, headquartered in the National Capital Region, with staff hired under the Public Service Employment Act and the ability to bring in outside technical experts on a temporary basis. The Ombud would hold the rank and powers of a deputy head of a department and serve as the office's chief executive.

The Ombud's mandate is to examine departmental practices to ensure they are "fair, equitable, unbiased, non-racist and non-discriminatory," and to investigate where there are reasonable grounds to believe someone has been the victim of unfairness, bias, racism or discrimination — including systemic racism and systemic discrimination — in the department's decision-making. Specific duties include reviewing IRCC policies, programs, training and processing standards under the Citizenship Act and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act; receiving and investigating complaints; tracking trends and patterns in complaints; and recommending fixes to the Minister.

deepDive.heading: How the Ombud would be appointed
deepDive.body:
The Governor in Council (effectively the federal Cabinet) would appoint the Ombud, but only after consulting the leaders of recognized parties and groups in both the Senate and the House of Commons, and only after the appointment is approved by resolution of both chambers. The appointee must be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident.

The term is seven years, held "during good behaviour," with removal for cause possible only on address of both the Senate and House of Commons. One reappointment is allowed. If the position is vacant or the Ombud is absent or incapacitated, Cabinet can name an interim office-holder for up to six months. The Ombud must work exclusively in the role and hold no other paid employment.

deepDive.heading: Complaints, investigations and powers
deepDive.body:
Any person could complain to the Ombud if they believe a decision, act or omission relating to the department's affairs treated them unfairly or with bias or discrimination. The Ombud could also investigate on their own initiative or at the Minister's request, and would normally have to notify the department in writing before starting — unless doing so could hinder the investigation. The Ombud could decline or stop an investigation in certain circumstances, such as complaints that are frivolous, vexatious or in bad faith, where the complainant hasn't used other available avenues, where another process under federal law is better suited, or where the matter is already being handled or has already been reported on. Refusals must be explained in writing to the complainant.

Investigative powers include summoning witnesses and compelling testimony under oath, requiring production of documents or other items, and making copies (documents must be returned within 10 days of a request, though they can be required again). Limits apply: the Ombud cannot access Cabinet confidences protected under section 39 of the Canada Evidence Act, and cannot review matters that occurred before the office was established unless the Minister asks. The Ombud and staff are shielded from criminal and civil liability and defamation actions for good-faith actions, and are generally not compellable witnesses in other proceedings. Knowingly obstructing the Ombud or making false or misleading statements would be a summary conviction offence with a fine of up to $2,000.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and ministerial response
deepDive.body:
After investigating a complaint, the Ombud must send a report to both the Minister and the complainant summarizing the complaint and setting out findings, conclusions, reasons and any recommendations. For investigations or examinations started by the Ombud or requested by the Minister, the report goes to the Minister.

Importantly, the Minister must then tell the Ombud, within a timeframe the Ombud can set, what measures have been or will be taken in response — and give reasons for any recommendation not followed. The recommendations themselves are not binding; the obligation is to respond and explain. Cabinet could make regulations on matters such as time limits for complaints, investigations and reports.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The bill would most directly affect people dealing with IRCC — applicants for visas, permanent residence, citizenship and refugee protection, and their families and representatives — by creating a dedicated channel to raise fairness and discrimination concerns outside the existing appeal and review routes. It would also affect the department itself, which would be subject to external review of its policies, programs, training and processing standards, and department employees and others who could be compelled to testify or produce documents.

Beyond the main act, the bill makes a related amendment to the Languages Skills Act and consequential amendments to certain other statutes (the provided text is truncated before those details and before the section on reports to Parliament, so their specifics are not described here). Procedurally, this is a private member's bill listed as "outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not currently scheduled for debate time in the House; bills at this stage have not been voted on and frequently do not advance.

C-213.overview: Bill C-213 is a private member's bill from MP Jenny Kwan that would make two small but significant deletions from Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. It would repeal section 40.1, which makes a person inadmissible to Canada when their refugee protection has been found to have 'ceased,' and paragraph 46(1)(c.1), which causes a permanent resident to automatically lose that status when a cessation finding is made. In practical terms, the bill targets the rules that allow former refugees who have already become permanent residents to lose their status — and face removal from Canada — if the government successfully applies to have their refugee protection declared at an end, for example after they travel back to their country of origin or renew a passport from that country. The bill does not create any new program or process; it simply removes these two provisions from the law. As of its introduction on June 18, 2025, it sits outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is unlikely to advance unless that changes.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is extremely short — two operative clauses. Clause 1 repeals section 40.1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, and clause 2 repeals paragraph 46(1)(c.1) of the same Act. Nothing is added in their place.

The summary attached to the bill describes its purpose as repealing 'provisions related to inadmissibility and loss of status resulting from the cessation of refugee protection for permanent residents.'

deepDive.heading: What 'cessation' means in current law
deepDive.body:
Under the Act, the government can ask the Refugee Protection Division to declare that a person's refugee protection has 'ceased' — for instance because the person has voluntarily re-availed themselves of the protection of the country they fled, reacquired or acquired a nationality, or re-established themselves in that country. Cessation is separate from a finding that a claim was fraudulent.

The two provisions this bill would repeal are the consequences attached to such a finding for people who are already permanent residents: paragraph 46(1)(c.1) causes permanent resident status to be lost automatically, and section 40.1 renders the person inadmissible to Canada. Repealing them would remove those automatic consequences from the statute, though the bill does not address the cessation process itself.

deepDive.heading: Who it would affect
deepDive.body:
The people most directly affected are former refugees who were granted protection in Canada and later became permanent residents. Under the current rules, a cessation finding can strip them of permanent residence years after it was granted, even if they have lived and worked in Canada for a long time.

Because the bill removes the automatic loss-of-status and inadmissibility consequences, it would primarily change outcomes for this group. The bill text does not mention refugee claimants who have not yet obtained permanent residence, citizens, or other immigration categories.

deepDive.heading: Status and next steps
deepDive.body:
C-213 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual Member of Parliament rather than by the government. It was introduced on June 18, 2025, in the 45th Parliament.

Its listed status is 'Outside the Order of Precedence.' In the House of Commons, private members' bills are debated according to a randomized list; bills outside that list have been tabled but have no scheduled debate time, and only a first reading has occurred. Most private members' bills in this position do not become law, and the bill would still need to pass three readings in the House, clear the Senate, and receive royal assent.

deepDive.heading: How to read this bill
deepDive.body:
Because the text works by repealing existing sections rather than spelling out new rules, its full effect can only be understood by reading it alongside the current Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The bill itself contains no new definitions, no transitional rules, and no coming-into-force provision in the text as published above.

This explainer describes only what is in the bill and the sections it references; it does not assess how many people would be affected or predict the practical results of the change.
