C-214.overview: Bill C-214 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Don Davies that would require the federal Minister of Natural Resources to create and carry out a national strategy so that, by December 31, 2030, all electricity generated in Canada comes from renewable sources. The Minister would have to build the strategy in consultation with provincial energy ministers and Indigenous governing bodies, and would also have to work with the Minister of Finance to set up financial incentives for renewable projects and for home and business retrofits. The bill sets deadlines for tabling the strategy in Parliament and for regular follow-up reports on how well it is working. It matters because electricity generation is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, and the bill would put a specific national target and reporting schedule into law. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, however, it is not currently scheduled for debate and is unlikely to become law in its present form.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would create the National Renewable Energy Strategy Act. Its core requirement is that the Minister of Natural Resources develop and implement a national strategy aimed at having 100% of electricity generated in Canada come from renewable energy sources by December 31, 2030. The bill defines renewable energy broadly as energy from a source that can be naturally replenished or renewed within a human lifespan.

The strategy would have to be developed in consultation with the provincial government representatives responsible for energy and with Indigenous governing bodies, defined as councils, governments or entities authorized to act for Indigenous groups holding rights recognized under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The strategy must include measures designed to meet four objectives: starting twice as many renewable energy production projects as non-renewable ones each calendar year; increasing investment in research and development of renewable technologies; federal-provincial cooperation on establishing new large-scale public electric utilities; and building a renewable energy economy and renewable energy jobs.

Separately, within one year of the Act coming into force, the Minister of Natural Resources and the Minister of Finance would have to design and implement incentives for solar, wind, tidal and biomass electricity projects, and for homeowners and businesses retrofitting their properties with new or more efficient renewable energy technology. The bill specifies that these incentives would apply only to a project's start-up costs, not to ongoing costs.

deepDive.heading: Reporting to Parliament
deepDive.body:
The Minister would have to prepare a report setting out the national strategy within two years of the Act coming into force, and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is finished. The report must then be published on the Natural Resources Canada website within 10 days of being tabled in both chambers.

After that, the Minister would have to produce a report on the effectiveness of the strategy — including conclusions and recommendations — three years after the initial tabling and every three years thereafter, again in consultation with provinces and Indigenous governing bodies.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and jurisdictional context
deepDive.body:
Electricity generation in Canada is largely under provincial jurisdiction, and the bill reflects this by framing the federal role as developing a strategy in consultation with provincial energy officials rather than directly regulating provincial utilities. Provinces, Indigenous governing bodies, electricity producers, homeowners and businesses considering retrofits would all be touched by the strategy and the proposed incentives.

The bill's preamble points to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's findings on the emissions cuts needed by 2030 and 2050, to projections that clean energy jobs will grow nearly four times faster than the average sector to 2030, and to the federal target of cutting greenhouse gas emissions 40% to 45% below 2005 levels by 2030.

deepDive.heading: Status
deepDive.body: C-214 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is currently listed as outside the Order of Precedence, so it has not been scheduled for second reading debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one would need to advance through both the House of Commons and the Senate before taking effect.

C-215.overview: Bill C-215 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would amend the Marine Liability Act to require the federal government to create and carry out a national strategy for dealing with pollution caused when shipping containers fall off vessels into Canadian waters. Before writing the strategy, the Minister would have to commission an independent study looking at gaps in current rules, salvage and clean-up capacity, container tracking, ship manifest requirements, and whether a dedicated compensation and clean-up fund would be worthwhile. The strategy itself would have to include prevention measures, better communication with coastal communities, a joint spill response task force, debris monitoring and removal, and funding for research on plastics and microplastics in the water. Indigenous organizations would have to be given a meaningful opportunity to help develop the strategy, and the Minister would report to Parliament on the strategy and then annually on progress. The bill sets out a planning and reporting process rather than creating new penalties or liability rules; as a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new Part 7.1 to the Marine Liability Act, the federal law governing liability and compensation for damage related to shipping. The new part would obligate the Minister to "develop and implement a national strategy to address pollution caused by shipping container spills" — that is, the environmental mess created when cargo containers are lost overboard and their contents, along with materials such as polystyrene and other plastics, wash into the ocean and onto shorelines.

Importantly, the bill does not itself set new fines, liability rules or clean-up standards. It creates a legal requirement for the government to study the problem, produce a strategy with specified elements, and report publicly on its progress.

deepDive.heading: The independent study
deepDive.body:
Before the strategy is finalized, the Minister must have an independent study conducted. The study must identify gaps in the current regime for container-spill pollution, review Canada's salvage capabilities, and assess how adequate existing measures are for preventing, repairing or minimizing pollution damage and for tracking containers lost at sea.

The study must also examine whether the rules on ship manifests (the documents listing what a vessel is carrying) are adequate, and evaluate the potential benefits of creating a fund to pay for compensation and clean-up when containers are lost. The findings and recommendations must be tabled in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after the study is complete.

deepDive.heading: What the strategy must contain
deepDive.body:
The strategy has to respond to the study's findings and must include six specific types of measures: preventing container spills; improving communication among responders, stakeholders and coastal communities; establishing a joint spill response task force; monitoring and removing debris from lost containers; closing any gaps identified in the current regime; and funding research on polystyrene, microplastics and other plastics in the water, including removal techniques.

The proposed task force is notable for its composition: it would bring together representatives of the federal and provincial governments, local authorities, Indigenous organizations, commercial fishing organizations and non-governmental organizations.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and timelines
deepDive.body:
Within one year of the provision coming into force, the Minister would have to prepare a report setting out the strategy and a schedule for implementing it, table it in both Houses within 15 sitting days, and publish it on the Transport Canada website within 30 days of tabling.

Starting in the year of the second anniversary of the Act coming into force, and every year afterward, the Minister would have to prepare an annual progress report describing implementation and any changes to the strategy, table it in Parliament and publish it online on the same timelines. These recurring reports are the bill's main accountability mechanism.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The bill defines "Indigenous governing body" and "Indigenous organization" and requires that Indigenous organizations be given a meaningful opportunity to collaborate on developing the strategy. Beyond that, the parties most directly touched would be coastal communities, commercial fishing organizations, provincial and local governments, non-governmental organizations, and the shipping industry — the latter chiefly through any future measures on prevention, container tracking and manifest requirements that could flow from the strategy.

Procedurally, C-215 is a private member's bill sponsored by Gord Johns and is currently listed as outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has been introduced but is not yet in line for debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the details described here reflect the bill as introduced, which could change if it advances.

C-217.overview: Bill C-217 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Don Davies that would have the federal government pay the tuition fees of post-secondary students who qualify for the disability tax credit. It would amend the Canada Student Financial Assistance Act so that, for eligible students enrolled at a designated educational institution, the Minister pays their tuition directly to the school, and it would amend the Income Tax Act so that this benefit is not counted as taxable income. The bill's preamble points to figures suggesting about one in four Canadians aged 15 and over has a disability, and that youth with disabilities are more likely to be out of school and out of work. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been debated and would need to work its way through the House and Senate before it could become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section (9.21) to the Canada Student Financial Assistance Act creating a tuition-payment program for students with disabilities. If a person qualifies for the disability tax credit under section 118.3 of the Income Tax Act and is enrolled at a "designated educational institution," the Minister would be required to pay that person's tuition fees directly to the institution.

The payment is legally treated as a grant to the student — meaning it does not have to be repaid, unlike a student loan. A companion amendment to the Income Tax Act (a new paragraph 81(1)(h.2)) excludes the amount from the student's income, so the tuition payment would not be taxed.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
There are three operative pieces. First, the new tuition-payment obligation on the Minister. Second, an amendment to subsection 15(1) of the Canada Student Financial Assistance Act giving the government authority to make regulations setting out the conditions that must be met before a payment can be made — so the practical details, eligibility checks and administration would be filled in later through regulations rather than in the bill itself. Third, the income-tax exclusion.

The bill also gives itself an alternative short title: the Post-Secondary Education Financial Assistance for Persons with Disabilities Act. Notably, the bill text as written covers tuition fees only; it does not, on its face, address other education costs.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The eligibility gate is the federal disability tax credit. Only individuals for whom an amount is deductible under section 118.3 of the Income Tax Act — the credit that requires certification of a severe and prolonged impairment — would qualify. Students with disabilities who have not obtained that certification would not be covered as the bill is drafted.

Designated educational institutions would also be affected, since they would receive tuition payments directly from the federal government rather than from the student. The federal government would bear the cost, though the bill itself does not attach a dollar figure or estimate.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out the rationale Parliament is asked to accept: an estimated one in four Canadians aged 15 and over has one or more disabilities limiting daily activities, and the 2022 Canadian Survey on Disability found youth with disabilities face a higher risk of being neither in school nor employed, with that risk rising as disability severity increases.

The bill is a private member's bill introduced in the 45th Parliament and is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one would require passage by both the House and the Senate, plus royal assent, before taking effect. Because it proposes federal spending, questions of whether it requires a royal recommendation could also arise in the parliamentary process.

C-216.overview: Bill C-216, the Promotion of Safety in the Digital Age Act, is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner that bundles together three sets of online-safety measures. Part 1 creates a new law requiring online platforms — social media, apps, video games and similar services likely to be used by young people — to design their products with children's safety in mind, turn on protective settings and parental controls by default, and stop using kids' personal data in ways that could harm them. Part 2 updates Canada's existing law requiring internet service providers to report child sexual abuse material, streamlining how reports are made and giving police more time and information to act. Part 3 amends the Criminal Code to ban sexually explicit "deepfake" images of real people, create a distinct offence of online criminal harassment, and let courts impose peace bonds and identity-revealing production orders on people who harass anonymously. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and would need to clear that hurdle before it could advance.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has three parts. Part 1 enacts a brand-new statute, the Protection of Minors in the Digital Age Act, aimed at making online spaces safer for people under 18. Part 2 amends the existing Act respecting the mandatory reporting of Internet child pornography by persons who provide an Internet service (which the bill would rename to refer to "child sexual abuse and exploitation material"). Part 3 amends the Criminal Code to add new offences and tools related to sexual deepfakes and online harassment.

Part 1 would come into force 18 months after royal assent, giving platforms a transition period. The bill designates the Minister of Industry and references the CRTC in the new Act's definitions.

deepDive.heading: Part 1: A duty of care for platforms serving minors
deepDive.body:
The new Act defines a "minor" as anyone under 18 and a "child" as anyone under 16, and applies to any "operator" — the owner or operator of an online service, app, social media service or online video gaming service that a minor is using or could reasonably be expected to use. Operators would owe a duty of care to act in the best interests of users they know or should know are minors, taking reasonable steps in design and operation to prevent or reduce harms including physical harm, online sexual violence, sexually exploitative imagery (altered or not), marketing of age-restricted products such as alcohol, cannabis, tobacco, gambling and pornography, content promoting eating disorders, self-harm or suicide, addiction-like usage patterns, and predatory or deceptive marketing. The bill clarifies that operators are not required to stop a minor from deliberately searching for specific content, and are not prevented from offering prevention resources and clinical information.

Practically, platforms would have to offer clear safety settings for children and their parents — controls over who can contact a child, limits on public access to their personal data, reduction of engagement-maximizing features like autoplay and streak-style rewards, the ability to opt out of personalized recommendation algorithms in favour of chronological feeds, and restrictions and notifications around geolocation tracking. All of these would have to default to the most protective option. Operators would also need privacy-preserving age verification, options to delete a child's account and data and cap screen time, parental controls (defaults for under-16s, with an opt-out for parents and notice to the minor), and a dedicated reporting channel with an internal process for responding. Prohibitions bar operators from using design features or personal data to market age-restricted products, from using "dark pattern" interfaces that undermine the required safety settings, and from requiring or requesting a digital identifier representing a user's identity and right to access services online. The Act also sets out disclosure, advertising, record-keeping, independent review and annual reporting obligations, offences and penalties, a due diligence defence, a private right of action, standards or codes of practice, and regulation-making powers.

deepDive.heading: Part 2: Mandatory reporting of child sexual abuse material
deepDive.body:
This part updates the existing law that requires internet service providers to report child sexual abuse material. According to the bill's summary, it would clarify which types of internet services are covered, simplify notification by directing all reports to a single law enforcement body designated in regulations, and require that transmission data accompany the notice when the content is manifestly child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

It would also extend how long data related to an offence must be preserved, extend the limitation period for prosecuting offences under that Act, and add new regulation-making powers.

deepDive.heading: Part 3: Criminal Code changes on deepfakes and online harassment
deepDive.body:
The bill would make it an offence to publish a computer-generated or computer-edited image that falsely depicts a real person — in a way intended to look authentic — as nude, exposing their genitals, anal region or breasts, or engaged in explicit sexual activity. This targets so-called sexual "deepfakes."

It would also create a separate offence of criminal harassment carried out through the internet, a social media service or another digital network, and require sentencing courts to treat anonymous or false-identity communication as an aggravating factor. Finally, it sets out when someone who poses a risk of committing online harassment can be required to enter a recognizance (a peace bond), and when a court may issue a production order to identify a person who has communicated anonymously or under a false identity.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and where it stands
deepDive.body:
The main obligations fall on companies that operate online services, apps, social media platforms and online games accessible to Canadian minors, as well as on internet service providers subject to the mandatory reporting law. Parents and young users would gain new default protections, settings and reporting tools, and the private right of action would allow individuals to pursue certain claims directly. The Criminal Code changes could apply to any individual who publishes sexualized fake imagery of another person or who harasses someone online.

This is a private member's bill rather than a government bill, and it is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has not yet been slotted for House debate. Private members' bills face long odds and can be amended substantially if they do advance; nothing in the bill takes effect unless it passes both the House and Senate and receives royal assent, with Part 1 then waiting a further 18 months. Note also that the full text above is truncated, so some details of Parts 1 through 3 — including specific penalty amounts and the precise wording of the Criminal Code amendments — are not reflected here.

C-218.overview: Bill C-218 is a private member's bill from MP Tamara Jansen that would change the Criminal Code so that a mental illness, on its own, can never qualify a person for medical assistance in dying (MAID). Under Canada's current law, a person must have a "grievous and irremediable medical condition" to be eligible for MAID; this bill would state plainly that a mental disorder does not count as such a condition. In practice, that would make the current temporary exclusion of mental illness as a sole basis for MAID permanent, rather than allowing it to expire on a set date. The bill matters because it addresses one of the most contested questions in Canadian health and criminal law: whether people whose only underlying condition is a mental illness should be able to seek an assisted death. As a private member's bill at second reading, it has not been passed and would need to clear several more stages in both the House of Commons and the Senate to become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The operative part of the bill is a single sentence. It replaces subsection 241.2(2.1) of the Criminal Code with wording stating that, for the purposes of the MAID eligibility test, "a mental disorder is not a grievous and irremediable medical condition."

Because having a grievous and irremediable medical condition is a core eligibility requirement for MAID, this change would mean that a person whose only medical condition is a mental disorder could not lawfully receive medical assistance in dying. The bill does not change any other MAID eligibility criteria, safeguards, or procedures set out in the Criminal Code.

deepDive.heading: The preamble and stated rationale
deepDive.body:
The bill includes a preamble — an introductory statement of Parliament's reasoning that is not itself an enforceable rule. It says Parliament considers it a priority to ensure adequate mental health supports are in place for Canadians, that vulnerable Canadians should receive suicide prevention counselling rather than access to MAID, and that Canada's MAID regime risks normalizing assisted dying as a solution for those suffering from a mental disorder.

The preamble sets out the sponsor's stated reasons for the bill. It does not create any funding, programs, or services for mental health or suicide prevention; the bill's only legal effect is the Criminal Code amendment described above.

deepDive.heading: Coordinating amendments explained
deepDive.body:
Section 2 of the bill deals with timing. It refers to an earlier law — the 2021 Act to amend the Criminal Code (medical assistance in dying) — which set out a time-limited exclusion of mental illness as a sole basis for MAID. Because that existing exclusion is scheduled to change on its own timeline, this bill includes rules to avoid a legal conflict.

In short: if this bill takes effect first, the corresponding provision in the 2021 Act is repealed. If the 2021 Act's provision takes effect first, the new exclusion is instead added to section 241.2 of the Criminal Code. If both happen the same day, the 2021 Act is treated as coming first. These are technical drafting rules; the practical outcome in every scenario is that the exclusion of mental disorders would be written into the Criminal Code without an expiry date.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would most directly affect people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental disorder and who might otherwise seek MAID, as well as the physicians and nurse practitioners who assess MAID requests and who face criminal liability if eligibility rules are not met. Provincial health systems, MAID assessors, and mental health and disability organizations would also be affected by the certainty (or the restriction, depending on one's view) the change would create.

People seeking MAID for physical conditions would not be affected by this bill, since the change is limited to how mental disorders are classified under the eligibility test.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-218 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. It was introduced in 2025 and is at second reading in the House of Commons — the stage where MPs debate the bill's general principle before deciding whether to send it to committee. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the bill has no legal effect unless and until it passes both chambers and receives royal assent.

The bill fits into an ongoing parliamentary debate over the scope of MAID in Canada, including whether and when eligibility should extend to people whose only condition is a mental illness. This summary describes what the bill says; it does not assess whether the change would be constitutional or advisable.

C-219.overview: Bill C-219 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP James Bezan that would update Canada's two main sanctions laws — the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (the "Magnitsky" law) and the Special Economic Measures Act — plus the law governing the Department of Foreign Affairs. Its central changes are to make "transnational repression" (foreign states intimidating, surveilling, harassing or harming people abroad, including in Canada) an explicit ground for sanctions, to raise the maximum penalties for summary-conviction sanctions offences, to require that sanctions orders be tabled in Parliament, and to require the Minister of Foreign Affairs to publish an annual report on Canada's international human rights work, including prisoners of conscience and human rights defenders. It also renames the Special Economic Measures Act as the "Global Sanctions and Special Economic Measures Act (Sergei Magnitsky Law No. 2)" and updates that name in dozens of other statutes and regulations. The bill matters because it would broaden the circumstances in which Canada can freeze assets and impose economic measures on foreign individuals, and add reporting requirements meant to increase transparency about how sanctions are used. As of the version shown, the bill is at report stage in the House of Commons after being amended in committee, and several originally proposed clauses have been deleted.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends three statutes (the version reprinted after committee no longer lists the Broadcasting Act in its own title, though the bill's official long title still mentions it). It adds a new definition of "transnational repression" to both the Magnitsky Act and the Special Economic Measures Act, defined as tactics used by a foreign state to intimidate, harass, surveil, threaten or physically harm people or groups outside its borders — including elected officials, dissidents, human rights defenders, exiled journalists, diaspora communities, activists and refugees — in order to silence dissent and stifle activism.

Under the Magnitsky Act, sanctions could be imposed where a foreign national has committed transnational repression as an agent of or on behalf of a foreign state, or has engaged in activities that undermine (or are likely to undermine) international peace, security or stability. Parallel language is added to the Special Economic Measures Act, whose stated purpose is expanded to cover situations where international peace, security or stability "has been undermined or is likely to be undermined."

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Penalties: the maximum punishment on summary conviction under both Acts would rise to a fine of up to $100,000, imprisonment of up to three years, or both.

Parliamentary transparency: copies of sanctions orders and regulations made under the Magnitsky Act would have to be tabled in both Houses within 15 days (or sent to the Clerk if the House is not sitting), and orders under the Special Economic Measures Act would have to be laid before each House within five sitting days.

Seized property: where private property has been seized or restrained, the Minister would have to apply for forfeiture within 24 months and dispose of forfeited property within 30 days — except where legal proceedings are ongoing.

Renaming: the Special Economic Measures Act would become the "Global Sanctions and Special Economic Measures Act (Sergei Magnitsky Law No. 2)," with consequential name changes in statutes such as the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the Seized Property Management Act and the Online News Act, and in numerous country-specific sanctions regulations.

deepDive.heading: New human rights reporting duty
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a requirement to the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development Act: the Minister of Foreign Affairs must publish, at least once a year, a report outlining the measures Canada has taken to advance human rights internationally and to support prisoners of conscience and human rights defenders. The first report would be due within 12 months of that provision coming into force.

The bill defines "prisoner of conscience" as someone detained or physically restricted, contrary to international human rights standards, solely because of their identity or conscientiously held beliefs, including religious or political beliefs.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Directly, the bill targets foreign nationals, entities and foreign states that Canada may sanction — expanding the grounds to include transnational repression and conduct undermining international peace and security. Indirectly, it affects people in Canada who could be targets of foreign interference or intimidation, such as diaspora communities, exiled journalists and activists, by creating an explicit sanctions tool for that conduct.

It also affects the federal government: the Minister of Foreign Affairs gains an annual reporting obligation, ministers face deadlines for tabling sanctions instruments in Parliament and for handling forfeited property, and businesses or individuals who breach sanctions face higher maximum penalties on summary conviction.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble states that Parliament supports aligning Canada's sanctions regime more closely with allied countries, and that it is desirable for Canada to keep working with allies toward establishing an International Anti-Corruption Court. The bill builds on the existing 2017 Magnitsky law, named after Sergei Magnitsky, and positions itself as "Sergei Magnitsky Law No. 3."

This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. The text shown is a working copy reprinted as amended by the Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development and reported to the House on June 18, 2026; it is at report stage. Several clauses in the original bill are marked "[Deleted]," meaning committee members removed them, so the bill is narrower than first introduced. Like all bills, it would still need to pass the House and Senate and receive royal assent before taking effect.

C-220.overview: Bill C-220 was a short private member's bill from Conservative MP Michelle Rempel Garner that would have added one new rule to the Criminal Code's sentencing provisions. It said that when a judge sentences someone who is not a Canadian citizen, the judge must not take into account how the sentence might affect that person's immigration status in Canada — or the immigration status of a family member. In practice, this would have stopped judges from adjusting a sentence (for example, shortening it) to help an offender avoid consequences such as deportation or the loss of an immigration appeal. The bill mattered because Canadian courts have long been permitted to weigh these so-called "collateral consequences" as one factor among many when crafting a fit sentence, and the bill would have removed immigration consequences from that list. The bill was defeated and did not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill contains a single substantive change: it would insert a new section 718.202 into the Criminal Code, immediately after section 718.201, within the part of the Code that sets out sentencing principles.

The new section reads that a court sentencing an offender who is not a Canadian citizen "shall not take into consideration any potential impact the sentence could have on the offender's immigration status in Canada, or on that of a member of their family." The word "shall not" makes this a mandatory prohibition rather than a guideline — judges would have no discretion to consider immigration effects.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
There is only one operative clause. It applies to offenders who are not Canadian citizens, which would include permanent residents, foreign nationals, temporary residents and people without status. It does not create any new offence, change any penalty ranges, or alter immigration law itself.

Notably, the prohibition extends beyond the offender: a judge would also be barred from considering the effect a sentence might have on the immigration status of the offender's family members. The bill says nothing about other factors judges normally weigh at sentencing — such as the seriousness of the offence, an offender's record, rehabilitation prospects, or other personal circumstances — so those would have continued to apply as usual.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would have affected non-citizens convicted of criminal offences in Canada, their families, and the judges who sentence them. Under Canada's immigration law, certain criminal sentences can trigger removal from Canada or eliminate the right to appeal a removal order, so the exact length of a sentence can carry immigration consequences well beyond the punishment itself.

Because the bill removed immigration effects from the sentencing calculus, its practical impact would have been felt most in borderline cases — situations where a judge might otherwise have imposed a sentence just below a threshold that carries immigration consequences. Canadian citizens would have been unaffected.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-220 was introduced on September 17, 2025 in the 45th Parliament as a private member's bill — legislation brought forward by an individual MP rather than by the government. Private members' bills face limited debate time and a low success rate, and this one was defeated, meaning it will not become law unless reintroduced and passed in some future session.

The bill responds to a long-standing feature of Canadian sentencing practice in which courts may consider the "collateral consequences" of a sentence, including immigration consequences, as part of arriving at a proportionate sentence. Supporters of measures like this argue sentences should be identical regardless of citizenship; critics argue judges should retain flexibility to consider an offender's full circumstances. The bill text itself takes no position on these arguments — it simply states the prohibition.

C-221.overview: Bill C-221 is a short private member's bill from MP Mel Arnold that would make one targeted change to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the law governing federal prisons and parole. Under current law, registered victims of an offence can be told certain dates about the offender — such as when the offender becomes eligible for temporary absences or parole, when their case will be reviewed, and when they are set to be released. This bill would require that, whenever those dates are given to a victim, the disclosure also include an explanation of how the dates were calculated. It does not change who is eligible for release, when they become eligible, or how those decisions are made — it only adds a requirement to explain the reasoning behind the dates that are already shared. Supporters of this kind of change generally frame it as helping victims understand a complex system, though the bill itself simply sets out the new disclosure requirement.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends four subparagraphs of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act. Each of the amended provisions currently allows information about an offender's eligibility dates, review dates, or scheduled release dates to be disclosed to a victim. In each case, the bill adds the words requiring 'an explanation of how those dates have been determined' (or, for a single date, 'how that date has been determined').

The practical effect is that a victim who receives a date would also receive information about the calculation or reasoning behind it, rather than the date on its own. Nothing else in the release or parole framework is altered by the bill.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 1 amends section 26 of the Act, which deals with information the Correctional Service of Canada may share with victims. Subparagraph 26(1)(a)(iv) covers eligibility and review dates for temporary absences or parole; subparagraph 26(1)(c)(i) covers the date, if any, on which an offender is to be released on temporary absence, work release, parole or statutory release. Both would now also require an explanation of how the date was determined.

Section 2 makes the parallel changes to section 142 of the Act, which governs information the Parole Board of Canada may share with victims — covering eligibility and review dates for unescorted temporary absences or parole, and the date of release on unescorted temporary absence, certain escorted temporary absences approved by the Board under subsection 746.1(2) of the Criminal Code, parole or statutory release.

deepDive.heading: Coordinating amendments
deepDive.body:
Section 3 is a technical 'coordinating' provision. It addresses the possibility that another law — An Act to Bring Fairness for the Victims of Violent Offenders (2015, c. 11) — may renumber or replace parts of section 142 before or after this bill takes effect. The section sets out which version of the text applies depending on the order in which the two laws come into force.

This is standard legislative housekeeping to prevent conflicting or duplicated wording in the statute book. It does not create any new obligations beyond the explanation requirement described above.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill primarily affects registered victims of offences who request information about an offender under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act. It also affects the Correctional Service of Canada and the Parole Board of Canada, which would be responsible for preparing and providing the explanations along with the dates they already disclose.

Offenders are not directly affected in terms of their eligibility or release timing; the bill changes only what information victims receive about how those dates are set.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-221 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — sponsored by Mel Arnold and introduced on September 17, 2025, in the 45th Parliament. As of this summary, it is at the committee consideration stage in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading in principle and is being studied in detail before any further votes.

Private members' bills must still clear committee, report stage and third reading in the House, then pass the Senate and receive Royal Assent before becoming law. The bill's text does not specify a separate coming-into-force date apart from the coordinating rules in section 3.

C-222.overview: Bill C-222, known as Evan's Law, would change two federal laws to reduce the paperwork and financial disruption parents face when a child dies. Under the Employment Insurance Act, a parent receiving EI maternity/parental or adoption-related benefits would keep those benefits for the rest of the benefit period even if the child dies, and would not have to file a new claim or submit reports to prove eligibility. Under the Canada Labour Code, it would extend bereavement leave for the death of a child to up to 10 weeks, taken within a defined window after the funeral or memorial service. The bill is a private member's bill sponsored by Hon. Terry Beech, has been amended by a House committee, and is currently at report stage in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has two parts. First, it amends the Employment Insurance Act so that a parent already receiving benefits to care for a newborn or a child placed for adoption is legally 'deemed' to still be caring for that child if the child dies during the benefit period — meaning the benefits continue until the period would normally end. It applies the same rule to self-employed people who have opted into EI special benefits.

Second, it amends the Canada Labour Code, which governs federally regulated workplaces, to set bereavement leave in the case of the death of a child at up to 10 weeks.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions — Employment Insurance
deepDive.body:
New subsections added to sections 23 and 152.05 of the Employment Insurance Act state that if the child or children die during the benefit period, the claimant is treated as continuing to care for the child until that period expires. Importantly, the bill specifies that the claimant does not need to make a new claim or file a report to prove ongoing eligibility — this is the 'administrative burden' referred to in the short title.

There is one exception: the continued-benefits rule does not apply if the child died as the result of an offence and the claimant is convicted of that offence.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions — bereavement leave
deepDive.body:
Subsection 210(1.01) of the Canada Labour Code would be replaced so that an employee is entitled to up to 10 weeks of leave when a child of the employee, or a child of their spouse or common-law partner, dies. The leave can be taken starting the day of the death and ending 12 weeks after the last funeral, burial or memorial service.

A new subsection covers the situation where the child dies while the parent is on (or entitled to be on) maternity/parental leave under section 206. In that case, the 10-week leave window ends at the later of 12 weeks after the last funeral or memorial service, or 12 weeks after the end of the section 206 leave. Two clauses of the original bill (sections 4 and 5) were deleted at committee.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The EI changes would affect parents — employees and self-employed EI participants — who are receiving maternity, parental or adoption-related benefits when their child dies. The Canada Labour Code changes apply only to federally regulated workplaces (sectors such as banking, telecommunications, interprovincial transportation and federal Crown corporations), not to jobs covered by provincial labour law.

Transitional rules mean the new leave provisions would also reach employees whose existing leave period has not yet ended when the changes take effect, or who are on (or entitled to be on) section 206 leave at that time. An employee who had already taken two periods of leave under the old rules could take one additional period.

deepDive.heading: Status and coming into force
deepDive.body:
C-222 is a private member's bill sponsored by Hon. Terry Beech. It was reviewed and amended by the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities, reported back to the House on April 22, 2026, and is at report stage — meaning it still requires further House debate, a third reading vote, Senate passage and royal assent before becoming law.

If passed, the Act would come into force on the first Sunday after the day that is six months after royal assent, or earlier if the Governor in Council (cabinet) sets an earlier date by order.

C-223.overview: Bill C-223, the Keeping Children Safe Act, is a private member's bill from MP Lisa Hepfner that would amend the federal Divorce Act to change how family violence is handled in divorce and parenting cases. It would require a divorcing spouse's lawyer to check for signs of family violence and, where there is a risk, help put a safety plan in place; it would bar courts from considering allegations that one parent has deliberately turned a child against the other parent (sometimes called "parental alienation" claims), except in narrow circumstances; and it would list a series of assumptions judges may not make when weighing family violence, such as concluding abuse has stopped simply because the couple has separated. The bill also lets a court, under strict conditions, hear directly from a child about their views, and it rewrites the rules for when a parent wants to move away with a child. Because the Divorce Act governs parenting arrangements for married couples across Canada, these changes would affect how judges, lawyers and parents approach custody disputes where abuse is alleged. The bill is currently at committee stage in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading but is not yet law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Divorce Act, the federal law that governs divorce and related parenting and support decisions for married couples. Its stated purpose, set out in a preamble, is to put the safety and well-being of children and survivors of family violence at the centre of family law, and to have courts rely on evidence-based understandings of trauma and coercive control rather than "myths and stereotypes." The preamble also cites Canada's obligations under the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women and the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

The preamble states a concern that claims one parent has undermined a child's relationship with the other parent are being used in family court to justify changing parenting time, and that such claims may be used in abuse cases to support an accused parent's continued access to their children. The operative sections of the bill translate that concern into specific rules for lawyers and judges.

deepDive.heading: New duties for lawyers
deepDive.body:
Under the bill, any legal adviser acting for a spouse in a divorce proceeding would have a duty to consider whether there are reasonable grounds to believe there is a risk of family violence toward the spouse or another family member — either a risk to safety, or a risk to the spouse's ability to negotiate a fair agreement. If such a risk exists, the lawyer must take steps to implement an appropriate plan, ensure the family has a safety plan, and tell the spouse about support services the lawyer knows of.

The bill also adds "evidence of a risk of family violence" to the circumstances in which a lawyer is not required to encourage reconciliation or to push the parties toward a family dispute resolution process such as mediation. Separately, it removes the court's existing duty (subsection 10(1)) to satisfy itself about the possibility of reconciliation, and limits reconciliation adjournments to cases where both spouses request them.

deepDive.heading: Parenting decisions and family violence
deepDive.body:
The most substantial changes are to section 16, the "best interests of the child" test. New subsection 16(3.1) says courts must not consider allegations that a spouse has, or is likely to, deliberately manipulate a child into becoming estranged from or resisting contact with the other parent. A narrow exception allows evidence of deliberate, repeated interference with a child's relationship with the other parent only where the spouse accused of interfering has engaged in family violence, the evidence is relevant to the child's best interests, and it is not being used to support the type of allegation just prohibited.

The bill also sets out grounds on which a court may not infer that family violence has stopped, no longer has an impact, or was exaggerated: separation or the start of divorce proceedings; the absence of earlier or later reports to police or child welfare; no criminal charges, withdrawn allegations, no child welfare intervention, or an acquittal; late or previously unmade allegations; inconsistent statements or conflicting evidence; a spouse continuing to live with or maintain a relationship with the other spouse or resuming cohabitation; and the absence of visible injuries or outward signs of fear. A new provision states that leaving a violent household for a shelter or temporary housing — or leaving the province with the children, with or without notice — is not by itself contrary to the child's best interests. Courts would also be barred from presuming that equal or shared parenting time, or ongoing contact with each parent, is in a child's best interests. Finally, parenting orders could not restrict the parenting time of a parent the child is close to in order to improve the child's relationship with the other parent, and could not require a child to attend "reunification therapy" or allow one parent to consent to it without the other's consent.

deepDive.heading: Hearing from the child, and relocation rules
deepDive.body:
The bill would let a court obtain information directly from a child — in writing or through an in-camera (private) interview with an amicus curiae, a neutral lawyer appointed to assist the court — to determine the child's views and preferences. This is permitted only if it is in the child's best interests, both spouses agree, and the court believes the child's safety and privacy would not be compromised and there is no other appropriate way to get the information. What the child says may be disclosed to the parents only if the court thinks disclosure is in the child's best interests.

On relocation (a parent moving with a child), the bill adds family violence to the list of factors a court weighs, requires the court to consider the impact on the child of blocking the move, and directs the court to presume the relocating parent will move regardless of whether the child's relocation is allowed. Courts could not take into account the existing parenting arrangement in the parties' current locations. The burden of proof rules are rewritten: where the child spends most of their time with the parent who wants to move, the court must authorize the move unless the objecting parent proves both that the move is not in the child's best interests and that the child should primarily live with them.

deepDive.heading: Status, scope and transition
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner rather than by the government, and it is at consideration in committee in the House of Commons. It would still need to clear committee, report stage and third reading in the House, then pass the Senate and receive royal assent before becoming law; private members' bills often do not complete that path.

Because it amends the Divorce Act, the bill applies to married spouses who divorce; provincial and territorial family law governs unmarried couples. Two transitional rules are included: proceedings already underway when the Act comes into force would be dealt with under the new version of the Divorce Act, and where a past decision relied on an allegation that a parent deliberately turned a child against the other parent, the new rule is deemed to be a "change in circumstances" — the legal trigger that allows a party to apply to vary an existing order.

C-225.overview: Bill C-225 is a private member's bill from MP Frank Caputo that amends the Criminal Code to toughen how the justice system treats violence against intimate partners, particularly where there is a pattern of coercive or controlling behaviour. It automatically classifies a killing as first-degree murder — even without planning and deliberation — when the victim is the accused's intimate partner and the death occurs during or after a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct; in manslaughter cases with the same background, judges must at least consider a life sentence, with parole ineligibility set between 10 and 25 years for adults. The bill also creates a new stand-alone offence that raises the maximum penalty for any existing offence involving violence used, threatened or attempted against an intimate partner, and tightens bail rules for repeat intimate-partner violence. Finally, it extends the time police may hold seized property from three months to 180 days. The bill has received Royal Assent, though several of its provisions may be replaced by overlapping measures in a separate government bill, C-16 (the Protecting Victims Act).

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes targeted changes to the Criminal Code focused on intimate-partner violence. Its four stated goals are: creating a specific first-degree murder rule for the killing of an intimate partner in the context of coercive or controlling conduct; requiring courts to consider a life sentence for manslaughter in similar circumstances; creating new offences that escalate penalties when violence is used, threatened or attempted against an intimate partner; and extending the period police may detain seized items from three months to 180 days.

Most of the remaining sections are technical consequences of these changes — updating appeal rights, parole-eligibility rules, youth sentencing provisions and rules about how juries and judges record convictions so that the new manslaughter and intimate-partner-violence offences fit into the existing structure of the Code.

deepDive.heading: Murder and manslaughter provisions
deepDive.body:
New subsection 231(3.1) says that murder is first-degree murder — regardless of whether it was planned and deliberate — when the victim is the accused's intimate partner and the accused caused the death while engaging in, or after having engaged in, a pattern of coercive or controlling conduct intended to make the victim believe their physical or psychological safety was threatened. First-degree murder carries the Code's most serious consequences, including a 25-year parole ineligibility period for adults.

For manslaughter in those same circumstances, new subsection 236(2) requires the sentencing court to consider imposing life imprisonment. If life is imposed, new section 745.52 lets the trial judge set parole ineligibility at 10 years, or substitute a longer period up to 25 years, based on the offender's character, the nature of the offence and the circumstances. Offenders who were under 18 are treated separately, with parole ineligibility of five to seven years. Both offenders and the Crown gain the ability to appeal these parole-ineligibility periods. The manslaughter rules do not apply to offences committed before the 30th day after Royal Assent.

deepDive.heading: The new intimate-partner violence offence and bail changes
deepDive.body:
New section 263.1 creates an offence layered on top of existing crimes: if someone commits any offence in which violence is used, threatened or attempted against their intimate partner (called the "included offence"), they can be charged under this new provision, which carries higher maximum penalties. For example, an included offence with a maximum of 5 to 10 years becomes punishable by up to 10 years; one with a maximum of 14 years or more can carry life imprisonment. The bill preserves the existing procedural route — a summary-only offence cannot be prosecuted by indictment and vice versa — and if the evidence proves only the underlying offence, the accused can still be convicted of that offence. Judges must note on the charging document which included offence was proved.

The bill also amends the bail provisions in section 515 so that a reverse-onus applies more broadly: an accused charged with intimate-partner violence must justify their release if they have a prior conviction or discharge for violence against any intimate partner, or were subject to a listed peace bond taken out on behalf of any intimate partner at the time of the alleged offence.

deepDive.heading: Seized property and other technical changes
deepDive.body:
Section 490 of the Criminal Code limits how long items seized by police can be held without a court extension. The bill changes that limit from "three months" to "180 days" — roughly doubling the baseline detention period. This change applies to any matter or proceeding ongoing as of the 30th day after Royal Assent.

The bill also repeals subsection 718.3(8) and updates the definition of "sentence" for appeal purposes, along with a series of cross-references in the parole and appeal sections so the new manslaughter sentencing scheme operates consistently.

deepDive.heading: Context and overlap with Bill C-16
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill (a bill introduced by an individual MP rather than the government) sponsored by Frank Caputo, and it has received Royal Assent. It responds to concerns about coercive and controlling behaviour as a precursor to lethal intimate-partner violence, an area the Criminal Code has historically addressed mainly through general assault, harassment and homicide provisions.

A notable feature is the lengthy set of "coordinating amendments" dealing with Bill C-16, the government's Protecting Victims Act. Because both bills would amend some of the same sections, C-225 sets out rules for which version prevails: in several cases, if the equivalent Bill C-16 provision comes into force first or on the same day, the corresponding C-225 section is repealed or deemed never to have come into force. In practice, this means some of C-225's provisions — including the first-degree murder rule in section 1 — may ultimately be superseded by the government bill's wording rather than operating on their own.

C-224.overview: Bill C-224 is a private member's bill from MP Blaine Calkins that would change how natural health products — things like vitamins, minerals, herbal remedies and probiotics — are treated under Canada's Food and Drugs Act. Since changes made through the Budget Implementation Act, 2023, No. 1, natural health products have fallen within the Act's definition of "therapeutic product," which subjects them to the same oversight and enforcement tools used for prescription drugs and medical devices. C-224 would rewrite that definition so natural health products are explicitly excluded, with one exception: nicotine-containing products used in nicotine replacement therapy would stay covered. The bill also repeals two related provisions of the Act and includes a transitional rule blocking prosecutions for certain offences involving natural health products committed during the period the 2023 rules were in effect. The bill has passed second reading and is currently being studied by a House of Commons committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The core of Bill C-224 is a single change to a definition. Section 2 of the Food and Drugs Act defines "therapeutic product," and that definition determines which products are caught by a set of stronger monitoring and enforcement powers in the Act. The bill replaces the definition so that it still covers drugs, devices and combinations of the two, but expressly excludes any "natural health product" as defined in the Natural Health Products Regulations.

There is one carve-out from the exclusion: a natural health product that contains nicotine or its salts and is used in nicotine replacement therapy would continue to be treated as a therapeutic product, and so would remain subject to the stricter regime.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 rewrites the definition of "therapeutic product" as described above. Clauses 2 and 3 repeal section 21.321 and subsection 21.8(2) of the Act — provisions tied to the therapeutic-product framework that the bill's sponsor treats as consequential to the definitional change. The bill text itself does not describe the content of those provisions.

Clause 4 is a transitional rule about past conduct. It says no prosecution may be started or continued for an offence under section 31.2 or 31.4 of the Food and Drugs Act involving a natural health product, if the offence occurred on or after the day section 500 of the Budget Implementation Act, 2023, No. 1 came into force and before the day Bill C-224 would come into force. In effect, it would close off enforcement action for that in-between period.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The bill is a direct response to section 500 of the Budget Implementation Act, 2023, No. 1, which brought natural health products within the "therapeutic product" definition. That change extended to natural health products the oversight tools in the Act that apply to drugs and devices — the regime the bill's summary describes as "the same monitoring regime as other drugs." Bill C-224 would reverse that inclusion.

The bill's own summary states its purpose plainly: to provide that natural health products are not therapeutic products under the Act and therefore are not subject to that regime. It does not repeal the Natural Health Products Regulations, which would continue to define what counts as a natural health product.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are manufacturers, importers, distributors and retailers of natural health products, who would no longer be subject to the therapeutic-product oversight and enforcement provisions of the Food and Drugs Act. Health Canada, as the regulator, would lose the ability to apply those particular tools to natural health products. Companies that make nicotine replacement therapy products would be unaffected by the exclusion, since those products are specifically kept within the definition.

Consumers of natural health products would be affected indirectly, through the change in the federal oversight framework that applies to the products they buy. The bill does not itself set out any replacement monitoring requirements.

deepDive.heading: Status and next steps
deepDive.body:
C-224 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — sponsored by Blaine Calkins and introduced on September 18, 2025, in the 45th Parliament. Private members' bills face limited debate time and a lower likelihood of passage than government bills.

The bill is currently at the committee stage in the House of Commons, meaning MPs on a committee are studying it, may hear from witnesses, and can propose amendments before it returns to the House for report stage and third reading. If passed there, it would still need to go through the Senate and receive royal assent to become law.

C-226.overview: Bill C-226 is a private member's bill that would require the federal Minister of Industry to create a "national framework" aimed at making grocery prices easier for shoppers to understand. Working with provincial officials responsible for consumer affairs, the Minister would have to develop national standards for how grocery stores display unit prices (for example, the price per 100 grams or per litre) and for how price increases and fluctuations are communicated, plus measures to teach Canadians what unit prices are and how to use them. The Minister would then have to write up the framework in a report to Parliament within 18 months, publish it online, and review how well it is working within five years. The bill itself does not set prices, cap prices, or create penalties — it directs the government to build a plan and report back publicly. It matters because it responds to widespread concern about grocery costs by focusing on the information shoppers see on the shelf when comparing products.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally the National Framework for Food Price Transparency Act, instructs the Minister of Industry to develop a national framework on grocery pricing and unit price display practices. The stated purpose is to help consumers make informed decisions when buying food and other household goods.

The framework must be developed in consultation with representatives of provincial governments responsible for consumer affairs. This reflects the fact that retail and consumer protection rules often fall under provincial jurisdiction, so the bill relies on collaboration rather than directly regulating stores.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 sets out what the framework must contain. It must include measures to establish national standards for the grocery retail sector covering two things: unit pricing for food and household goods — including the accuracy, usability and accessibility of unit price displays — and transparency about price increases, adjustments and fluctuations. It must also include measures to promote consumer education about what unit prices are and how to use them.

Sections 4 and 5 create the reporting requirements. Within 18 months of the Act coming into force, the Minister must prepare a report setting out the framework, table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed, and publish it on the Department of Industry's website within 10 days of tabling. Within five years of that tabling, the Minister must review how the framework has been implemented and how effective it has been, again in consultation with the provinces, and table and publish a second report with conclusions and recommendations following the same timelines.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does not do
deepDive.body:
As written, the bill is a framework-and-reporting statute. It does not set or limit grocery prices, does not create offences, fines or enforcement powers, and does not itself impose legal obligations on retailers. The "national standards" it refers to are to be developed through the framework process rather than spelled out in the legislation.

The only binding duties in the bill fall on the Minister of Industry: to consult, to develop the framework, and to report and publish on schedule.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Consumers are the intended beneficiaries: the framework is meant to make shelf labels — particularly unit prices that allow comparison between different package sizes and brands — more accurate, usable and accessible, and to help shoppers understand them.

Grocery retailers are the sector the proposed national standards would address. Provincial governments are directly involved as required consultation partners, and Parliament is the recipient of the two required reports, giving MPs and senators a scheduled opportunity to scrutinize the framework and its results.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-226 is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Gurbux Saini, introduced in 2025 in the 45th Parliament. It has passed second reading in the House of Commons and is currently at consideration in committee, meaning it may still be amended before any further votes; it would also need to pass the Senate and receive royal assent to become law.

The bill's subject matter — grocery price transparency and unit pricing — sits within ongoing public and parliamentary attention to food costs in Canada. Because it assigns responsibility to the Minister of Industry and requires provincial consultation, its practical effect would depend heavily on what the eventual framework contains and on cooperation between levels of government.

C-227.overview: Bill C-227 is a private member's bill from MP Braedon Clark that would require the federal government to create a national strategy aimed at making housing more affordable and secure for Canadians aged 17 to 34. It does not itself build housing, spend money or change housing rules; instead, it directs a designated federal minister to consult provinces, territories, municipalities, housing organizations, young people and others, hold at least one conference, and produce a written plan. That plan would have to assess how young people are faring in the rental, student housing and first-time-buyer markets, and set out measures to improve access. The strategy would have to be tabled in Parliament within 18 months of the law taking effect and posted online, with a follow-up report on how well it is working four years later. The bill is currently being studied by a House of Commons committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates a legal obligation for the federal government to develop and publish a national housing strategy focused specifically on young Canadians, defined in the bill as anyone in Canada who is at least 17 but under 35 years old. The Governor in Council (effectively the federal Cabinet) would designate which minister is responsible for carrying out the Act.

The strategy must be developed in consultation with provincial and territorial housing officials, municipalities, organizations and communities that provide housing services, young Canadians themselves, youth-serving organizations and other relevant stakeholders. The minister must hold at least one conference with these groups as part of the process.

deepDive.heading: What the strategy must contain
deepDive.body:
The strategy must include an assessment of the current state of housing affordability and availability for young people, covering rental housing, student housing and entry-level home ownership. Beyond that assessment, it must include measures to improve access to affordable and secure rental housing, support young people buying a first home, promote construction of rental, student, co-operative and first-time-buyer-affordable housing, encourage knowledge-sharing and coordination among federal, provincial and municipal partners, and identify further ways to reduce barriers young Canadians face.

In drafting the strategy, the minister must take into account existing federal housing frameworks and strategies as well as relevant provincial, territorial and municipal housing initiatives.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and timelines
deepDive.body:
Within 18 months of the Act coming into force, the minister must prepare a report setting out the strategy and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed. The report must then be published on a public website within 10 days of being tabled in both chambers.

Four years after that first tabling, the minister must prepare a second report evaluating how effective the strategy has been, including the minister's conclusions and recommendations. The same tabling and online publication rules apply to this follow-up report.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and what it does not do
deepDive.body:
The bill's stated focus is people in Canada between 17 and 34 years old, including renters, students and prospective first-time homebuyers. It would also involve provincial, territorial and municipal governments, housing service providers and youth organizations as consultation partners, though the bill does not compel those other governments to take any action — housing policy is largely shared or provincial jurisdiction, and the bill's obligations fall on the designated federal minister.

As written, the bill is a planning-and-reporting measure. It does not create funding programs, set housing targets, change tax or mortgage rules, or alter existing housing legislation. Its practical effect would depend on the content of the strategy that is eventually produced and on whatever separate decisions governments make in response.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-227 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. It has passed second reading and is at the committee stage in the House of Commons, where members can study it, hear witnesses and propose amendments. It would still need to clear the remaining House stages, pass the Senate and receive Royal Assent before becoming law.

The bill itself acknowledges that federal housing frameworks already exist, and requires the new strategy to build on them rather than replace them. This explainer is based solely on the text of the bill as provided.

C-228.overview: Bill C-228 was a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Mario Simard that would have changed the rules for how the federal government brings international treaties before Parliament. Under the bill, the Minister of Foreign Affairs would have had to table the text of a treaty, along with a detailed explanatory memorandum, in the House of Commons at least 21 sitting days before ratifying it — and for a defined category of "major treaties," the Minister would have had to seek the advice of the House, with a committee reviewing the treaty and reporting back. The bill also set out publication deadlines so treaties would appear in the Canada Gazette, on the department's website and in the Canada Treaty Series after being finalized. This matters because, in Canada, the power to negotiate and ratify treaties belongs to the executive branch; the bill was an attempt to give MPs a formal look at treaties before Canada is bound by them. The bill was defeated, so none of these changes became law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would have amended the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development Act by adding new sections (12.1 to 12.5) dealing with treaties. Its core requirement was advance transparency: before ratifying a treaty, the Minister of Foreign Affairs would have to table the treaty in the House of Commons, together with an explanatory memorandum, at least 21 sitting days before ratification. Similar advance-tabling rules applied when Canada wanted to "modify" a treaty it had already ratified — in that case the original treaty, a memorandum about it, and the proposed modification with an explanatory letter would all have to be tabled 21 sitting days ahead.

The bill defined its terms carefully. A "treaty" meant a written international agreement between Canada and a state that is governed by international law, whatever its title or format. An "amendment" meant an official change affecting all parties to a treaty, while a "modification" meant a change negotiated by only some parties, including Canada, that applies only between them.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the explanatory memorandum
deepDive.body:
Rather than simply tabling treaty text, the bill listed eleven items that the explanatory memorandum would have to contain. These included the treaty's title and a summary; the ministers responsible for drafting and implementing it; a statement of its implications for Canada and of Canada's obligations; an estimate of what it would cost Canada; the text of any reservations Canada has made or plans to make; whether parties can withdraw from, denounce or suspend the treaty; a record of consultations Canada held with interested parties other than foreign governments; and a summary or list of any federal laws that would have to be passed or amended to implement it.

For modifications, a shorter "explanatory letter" would be required, covering a summary of the modification, the responsible ministers, its implications for Canada and the resulting obligations.

deepDive.heading: "Major treaties" and parliamentary review
deepDive.body:
The bill created a special category called "major treaties," which would trigger an extra step: before ratifying one, the Minister would have to obtain the advice of the House of Commons, and a designated or newly established House committee would review the treaty and report back to the House as soon as feasible. The bill did not state that the House's advice would be binding.

A treaty counted as "major" if it required an Act of Parliament, new Crown powers or a new tax to implement it; imposed a significant direct or conditional financial obligation on Canada; involved transferring part of Canada's territory or changing its boundaries; required Canada to impose economic or military sanctions; concerned Canada's territorial jurisdiction, including maritime areas or airspace; concerned international trade or investment or Canada's place in the global economy; or concerned Canada's participation in international institutions, including transferring jurisdiction to them.

deepDive.heading: Exceptions and publication requirements
deepDive.body:
The bill included an escape valve: the Governor in Council (effectively cabinet) could, by order, exempt the Minister from the tabling requirements if it considered that exceptional circumstances warranted it. In that case, the Minister would have to table the documents that would otherwise have been required as soon as feasible after ratification or modification, along with written reasons for the order — unless the documents had already been tabled.

The bill also set out after-the-fact publication deadlines. Within seven days of a treaty being ratified or modified, the treaty and an explanation of any changes made between tabling and ratification would have to be posted on the department's website; within 21 days, the same material would have to appear in the Canada Gazette; and within three months, the treaty would have to be published in the Canada Treaty Series.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-228 was a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government — sponsored by Mario Simard and introduced in September 2025 during the 45th Parliament. Private members' bills face a harder path to passage than government bills, and this one was defeated, meaning the Department of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Development Act remains unchanged by it.

The bill spoke to a long-running debate about the executive branch's authority over treaty-making. Because the power to negotiate, sign and ratify treaties rests with the government rather than Parliament, MPs have historically had a limited formal role before Canada commits internationally. C-228 would have written a minimum notice period, disclosure standards and a committee review step into statute for the first time in that Act.

C-229.overview: Bill C-229 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Heather McPherson that would require the federal Minister of Health to create a national framework on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
