The framework would be developed in consultation with provincial governments, Indigenous governing bodies responsible for health and education, and other stakeholders, and would focus on five areas: better public resources for families, training for teachers, improved training for medical and mental health professionals, access to that training, and fairer access to trained practitioners. The bill sets deadlines — the framework must be tabled in Parliament within two years of the law taking effect, and a follow-up report on how well it is working must come five years after that. Notably, the bill does not itself change health services, create funding programs, or set diagnostic or treatment rules; it directs the government to plan, report and publish. The bill is currently outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not yet been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally titled "An Act to establish a national framework respecting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder," would obligate the Minister of Health to develop a single, coordinated national framework on ADHD. Health care and education are largely provincial responsibilities, so the bill requires the Minister to build the framework in consultation with provincial government representatives responsible for health and education, Indigenous governing bodies, and other relevant stakeholders.

This is a common structure for private members' bills: rather than creating new programs or spending directly, it requires the federal government to produce a strategy document and then report publicly on its progress and effectiveness.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 lists what the framework must contain. It must include measures to: develop resources helping people with ADHD and their families recognize, understand and manage the disorder; ensure educators have the knowledge, training and resources to support students with ADHD and related learning comorbidities; improve training for medical and mental health practitioners; ensure those practitioners can access training and support on evidence-based ADHD assessment and treatment; and facilitate equitable access to practitioners who have that training.

Sections 4 and 5 set the reporting timeline. Within two years of the Act coming into force, the Minister must table a report setting out the framework in both the House of Commons and the Senate, and publish it on the Health Canada website within 10 days of tabling. Within five years after that first tabling, the Minister must produce a second report assessing the framework's effectiveness, including conclusions and recommendations, subject to the same tabling and publication rules.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble states that ADHD is a chronic neurodevelopmental disorder affecting more than one million Canadians, both children and adults, across ethnic origins and socio-economic backgrounds. Beyond individuals with ADHD and their families, the framework's measures are aimed at educators, physicians and mental health practitioners, who would be the intended recipients of new training and resources.

Because the framework must be developed jointly with provinces and Indigenous governing bodies, those governments would also be directly involved. The Act does not compel provinces to adopt anything; it requires federal consultation and a federal plan.

deepDive.heading: Context and rationale
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out the reasoning Parliament would be endorsing: that many students with ADHD do not graduate high school, that many people with the disorder have at least one comorbid psychiatric condition such as anxiety, depression or substance use disorder, and that they are believed to have a shorter life expectancy as a result of these and other comorbidities.

As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, C-229 has not yet been assigned a slot for debate in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the bill would need to pass both the House and the Senate and receive royal assent before any of its deadlines would begin to run.

C-230.overview: Bill C-230 would require the federal government to publish an online, searchable registry of large debts owed to the Crown by businesses that have been forgiven, written off, waived or remitted. Whenever $2 million or more owed by a corporation, trust company or partnership is cancelled, the President of the Treasury Board would have to post the company's name, the amount, the fiscal year, and the legal basis for both the debt and its cancellation. The registry would have to be up and running within 18 months and updated within 90 days of each year's Public Accounts being tabled in Parliament. Because some of this information is currently protected by tax confidentiality rules, the bill also amends the Income Tax Act and several other tax statutes so the information can be shared for registry purposes, while allowing the Treasury Board President to withhold details that are confidential, personal or sensitive. The bill is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Adam Chambers and has passed the House of Commons; it is currently being studied in committee in the Senate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 25.1 to the Financial Administration Act, the law that governs how the federal government manages public money. It obliges the President of the Treasury Board to create and maintain a public registry — specifically an online, searchable database — listing debts, obligations and claims of $2 million or more owed to His Majesty (the Crown) by a corporation, trust company or partnership that have been remitted, forgiven, written off or waived, in whole or in part, under any Act of Parliament.

The stated purpose is transparency: currently such write-offs may appear in aggregate government accounting, but the bill would make the individual entities and amounts publicly searchable in one place.

deepDive.heading: What the registry must contain
deepDive.body:
For each entry, the registry must list: the name (and any business name) of the company, trust company or partnership; the amount cancelled; whether it was remitted, forgiven, written off or waived; the fiscal year involved; the Act, contract or other instrument under which the debt arose; the Act under which it was cancelled; and any other information the President of the Treasury Board considers appropriate.

There is a built-in exception. The President of the Treasury Board may leave out information they consider inappropriate to publish for reasons of confidential, personal or sensitive information — but if something is left out, the registry must state which of those three reasons applied.

deepDive.heading: Timelines and scope limits
deepDive.body:
The registry must be established within 18 months of the provision coming into force. At launch, it must cover qualifying write-offs that occurred after the section came into force, during the fiscal year covered by the most recently tabled Public Accounts. After that, the registry must be updated within 90 days of each tabling of the Public Accounts in the House of Commons.

The bill sets two important boundaries on scope. First, only amounts of $2 million or more are captured. Second, the bill states explicitly that debts owed to, or claims by, a Crown corporation are not treated as debts owed to or claims by His Majesty — so Crown corporation write-offs fall outside the registry.

deepDive.heading: Changes to tax confidentiality laws
deepDive.body:
Tax laws normally prohibit officials from disclosing taxpayer information. To make the registry workable, the bill makes consequential amendments to six statutes — the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act, the Excise Act, 2001, the Softwood Lumber Products Export Charge Act, 2006, the Digital Services Tax Act and the Global Minimum Tax Act — so that confidential taxpayer information may be provided for the purposes of the new section 25.1 as well as the existing debt-remission sections 23 to 25 of the Financial Administration Act.

The bill also includes a technical coordinating clause: if a related provision in Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, comes into force first or on the same day, the bill's amendment to the Digital Services Tax Act is repealed to avoid duplication or conflict.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and current status
deepDive.body:
The measure applies to corporations, trust companies and partnerships whose federal debts or obligations of $2 million or more are cancelled — these entities would be named publicly. It also creates a new ongoing administrative obligation for the Treasury Board Secretariat and, indirectly, for departments and agencies (including tax authorities) that hold the underlying information. Individuals who owe money to the Crown are not covered, since the registry applies only to the three listed types of business entities.

Bill C-230 is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Adam Chambers rather than a government bill. It has moved through the House of Commons and is at the committee consideration stage in the Senate, meaning it is not yet law and could still be amended or fail to complete the legislative process.

C-231.overview: Bill C-231 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Luc Berthold that would amend the Youth Criminal Justice Act — the law that governs how people aged 12 to 17 are dealt with in the criminal justice system — to make drug and other treatment programs a more explicit option at several stages of a youth's case. It would require police (and, if a related government bill passes, prosecutors) to consider referring a young person accused of simple drug or cannabis possession to a treatment program instead of laying a charge, and it would let judges pause sentencing so a young person can complete treatment first. It would also spell out that treatment attendance can be a condition of extrajudicial sanctions, non-residential program orders, probation-style orders and conditional supervision after custody. The bill uses the phrase "problematic substance use treatment program or any other treatment program," so it covers addiction treatment but is not limited to it. As of the version shown here, the bill has been studied and amended by the House Justice Committee and is at report stage in the House of Commons — it is not yet law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes a series of targeted additions to the Youth Criminal Justice Act (YCJA) so that treatment programs are formally recognized as a tool at multiple points in a youth's journey through the justice system: before charges are laid, as part of out-of-court measures, at sentencing, and while a young person is being supervised in the community.

According to the bill's own summary, it (a) clarifies the rules around problematic substance use treatment programs for young persons; (b) allows a youth justice court that has found a young person guilty to delay sentencing so the youth can take part in a treatment program; (c) allows the court to attach treatment attendance as a condition of certain orders; and (d) allows treatment attendance to be a condition of conditional supervision.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Police screening (s. 6): Where a young person is alleged to have committed simple possession under subsection 4(1) of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act or subsection 8(1) of the Cannabis Act, a police officer must consider whether referring the youth to a problematic substance use treatment program — with the youth's consent — would be enough, rather than proceeding further. A coordinating provision would extend the same duty to prosecutors under section 6.1 of the YCJA if Bill C-16, the Protecting Victims Act, becomes law.

Out-of-court measures (s. 10): Extrajudicial sanctions — measures used instead of going to court — could expressly include a requirement to attend a substance use or other treatment program.

Delayed sentencing (new s. 41.1): After a finding of guilt for any offence, a youth justice court could postpone sentencing so the young person can attend treatment. This requires the consent of both the Attorney General and the young person, and the court must weigh the YCJA's existing principles, including those in subparagraphs 3(1)(b)(iv) and (v) and the sentencing purpose and principles in section 38.

Sentencing and supervision (ss. 42, 55, 105): A judge must consider any participation in a section 41.1 treatment program when deciding on a sentence. Non-residential program orders (up to 240 hours over six months, with the provincial director's agreement) are clarified to include treatment programs. Treatment attendance is added to the list of conditions that can be imposed under subsection 55(2) and to conditions of conditional supervision under subsection 105(3).

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to young persons — those aged 12 to 17 — dealt with under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, particularly those whose offending is connected to substance use. It is not limited to drug charges: the delayed-sentencing option in section 41.1 is available after a finding of guilt for any offence, and the treatment conditions apply to a range of orders.

It also affects the actors in the system. Police officers gain a new duty to consider treatment referrals in simple possession cases, and prosecutors would too if Bill C-16 passes. Judges gain discretion to pause sentencing and to attach treatment conditions. Provincial directors remain involved, since non-residential programs require their approval and agreement. Participation depends on the young person's consent in the police-referral and delayed-sentencing provisions.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The Youth Criminal Justice Act, enacted in 2002, already emphasizes rehabilitation and reintegration and provides for extrajudicial measures that divert young people away from formal court proceedings. This bill does not replace that framework; it inserts explicit references to substance use and other treatment programs into existing sections of the Act.

The version reproduced here is a working copy reprinted as amended by the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights and reported to the House on June 1, 2026. One clause (clause 3) was deleted in committee, and several were renumbered, indicating the text changed during study. As a private member's bill it is at report stage in the House of Commons and would still need to pass the House and the Senate and receive royal assent. Most of the Act would come into force 30 days after royal assent; the prosecutor-related coordinating amendment depends on Bill C-16 also becoming law.

C-232.overview: Bill C-232 was a private member's bill from Conservative MP Tony Baldinelli that would have changed how Canada's federal prison system classifies certain offenders. Under the bill, any inmate declared a "dangerous offender" by a court, or convicted of more than one count of first-degree murder, would automatically be given a "maximum" security classification and would have to be held in a maximum-security penitentiary or a maximum-security area within a penitentiary. It would also bar those inmates from unescorted temporary absences from prison. Currently, Correctional Service Canada assigns security levels case by case using regulations, and can move inmates to lower-security institutions over time — a practice that has drawn public attention after high-profile transfers. The bill was defeated, so these changes did not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would have amended the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the law that governs federal prisons and parole. Its central change was to remove Correctional Service Canada's discretion for two specific groups of inmates: those found to be dangerous offenders under Part XXIV of the Criminal Code, and those convicted of more than one first-degree murder as defined in section 231 of the Criminal Code.

For those inmates, a new subsection 30(1.1) would require the Service to assign a security classification of "maximum," rather than assessing the appropriate level under the existing regulations. A companion provision would require that anyone classified this way actually be confined in a penitentiary — or an area of a penitentiary — designated as maximum security.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 28 of the Act, which sets out how the Service chooses where to place an inmate, would be reworded so the placement must provide "only the necessary restrictions," and a new subsection would tie maximum-classified inmates to maximum-security facilities. Section 29, which allows the Commissioner to authorize transfers between institutions, would be made subject to the new mandatory classification rule — meaning transfers could not be used to move these inmates to lower-security settings.

The bill also amended subsection 115(3) so that offenders classified as maximum security under the new mandatory rule, like those classified as maximum under the existing rules, would not be eligible for unescorted temporary absences (short, supervised-free releases granted for reasons such as medical care, family contact or rehabilitation programs).

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill targeted a narrow group: federal inmates who have received a dangerous offender designation from a court, and those convicted of more than one first-degree murder. It would not have changed classification rules for other inmates, who would continue to be assessed as maximum, medium or minimum under the existing regulations.

It would also affect Correctional Service Canada's operational discretion, since staff could no longer reclassify or transfer these offenders to medium- or minimum-security institutions based on individual assessments of risk or behaviour.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble frames the measure as consistent with "the spirit and intent of the Canadian Victims Bill of Rights," tying secure confinement of high-risk offenders to victims' interests. Debates over inmate transfers to lower-security prisons have been a recurring public and parliamentary issue in Canada.

As a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — C-232 faced the usual limited time and lower odds of passage. It was introduced in 2025 and has been defeated, so the Corrections and Conditional Release Act remains unchanged by it.

C-234.overview: Bill C-234 would create a new national honour called the Living Donor Recognition Medal, to be awarded to people who have donated an organ while alive and did not profit from the donation. The bill defines "organ" broadly to include human tissue such as blood and bone marrow, lets the Governor General award the medal, and allows recipients to use the letters "L.D.M." after their name. Much of the detail — including who exactly qualifies and what the medal looks like — would be filled in later by the federal Cabinet through regulations. The stated purpose is to publicly honour living donors and encourage more Canadians to consider donating, at a time when thousands of people are waiting for transplants. It is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Ziad Aboultaif and has passed the House of Commons stage; it is currently being studied by a Senate committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill establishes a new federal medal, the Living Donor Recognition Medal, to recognize people who donated one of their organs during their lifetime without profiting from it. The preamble explains Parliament's reasoning: thousands of Canadians await life-saving transplants, living donors act with compassion and courage at personal risk and without expectation of reward, and such donations save lives while easing pressure on the health care system.

The medal is a symbolic honour. The bill does not create any financial benefit, tax measure, health program, or change to how organ donation itself is regulated or carried out — those matters are largely handled by provinces and territories and are not addressed here.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 4 creates the medal, and section 5 lets the Governor in Council (Cabinet) decide its design and ribbon. Under section 6, the Governor General may award it to a person who donated an organ without profiting and who meets eligibility rules set out in regulations; no one may receive the medal more than once. Section 7.1 entitles recipients to use the post-nominal letters "L.D.M."

Section 7 says that, whenever possible, the medal should be presented at a public ceremony by a representative of the Crown, a territorial commissioner, a senator, an MP, or another entity named in regulations. A public servant designated by the Office of the Governor General's Secretary decides whether the ceremony is public and who presents the medal. Section 3 allows Cabinet to designate a minister responsible for the Act, and section 9 confirms the Act does not limit the Governor General's existing powers over the medal.

deepDive.heading: What is left to regulations
deepDive.body:
Several important details are not settled in the bill itself. Section 8 gives Cabinet the power to make regulations setting the eligibility criteria for the medal, naming the organizations that will assess or help assess eligibility, and naming the organizations whose representatives may present the medal at ceremonies.

This means the practical scope of the honour — for example, exactly which donations qualify, and how a donor's eligibility would be verified — would be determined after the bill becomes law rather than by Parliament in the text of the bill.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected group is living organ donors in Canada. Because the bill defines "organ" to include any form of human tissue, expressly including blood and bone marrow, the potential pool of eligible donors is defined broadly in the legislation, though eligibility regulations would set the actual criteria.

Also involved would be the Governor General's office, the designated federal minister, and whatever entities are prescribed to assess eligibility or present the medals. Parliamentarians, territorial commissioners and Crown representatives are identified in the bill as possible presenters at public ceremonies.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government — sponsored by Ziad Aboultaif. According to the status listed, it has moved beyond the House of Commons and is at the committee consideration stage in the Senate, meaning senators are studying it before any further votes.

As with any bill, it is not law unless and until it completes all remaining stages in the Senate and receives royal assent. Even then, the medal's design and eligibility rules would need to be set by Cabinet through regulations before awards could be made in practice.

C-233.overview: Bill C-233 was a private member's bill from NDP MP Jenny Kwan that would have tightened Canada's rules for exporting weapons and military equipment. It proposed changes to the Export and Import Permits Act to bring Canadian law more closely in line with the Arms Trade Treaty — an international agreement meant to keep weapons out of the hands of those who would use them to commit war crimes or human rights abuses. In practice, the bill would have ended the long-standing special treatment given to exports to the United States, required a case-by-case permit for every shipment of military goods, expanded what counts as a "weapon" to include parts and technology, and forced the government to publish a detailed annual report on arms exports. The bill was defeated, so none of these changes became law. It matters as a marker of an ongoing debate over how much scrutiny Canada applies to its arms exports and how transparent that process should be.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Export and Import Permits Act is the law that lets the federal government control what goods can leave or enter Canada, including weapons and military equipment. Exporters generally need a permit from the Minister before shipping controlled items abroad.

Bill C-233 would have amended that Act in several ways, all aimed at aligning it more fully with the Arms Trade Treaty, a UN treaty Canada joined that sets standards for the international arms trade. The bill's core approach was to remove shortcuts and exemptions in the current permit system so that every export of military goods would receive individual review against human rights and international humanitarian law criteria.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Broader definition: The bill stated that "arms, ammunition, implements or munitions of war" includes any parts, components or technology needed to assemble or use those items — closing what supporters saw as a gap where components could escape scrutiny.

No country-based exemptions and no general permits: The Export Control List could no longer exempt military goods from control based on where they were headed, and the Minister would be barred from issuing "general permits" (blanket authorizations covering many shipments) for either exporting or brokering military goods. Each shipment would instead need its own permit.

Stronger assessment criteria: Section 3 of the Act would be rewritten to explicitly bar exports where there is a substantial risk they would be used to commit or facilitate genocide, crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, attacks on civilians or civilian objects, or other war crimes. The Minister's risk assessment would have to consider misuse in the destination country or the country of end use, and whether the receiving country is a party to the Arms Trade Treaty.

End-use certificates: Where the Minister judged that there was a substantial risk of misuse, and that a written guarantee from the receiving government about how the goods would be used would sufficiently reduce that risk, the Minister would be required to demand such a certificate before issuing the permit.

Annual reporting: By May 31 each year, the Minister would have to table in Parliament a detailed report listing export permits issued, the types, quantities, values and destinations of exported military goods, summaries of how the risk factors were weighed for each permit, summaries of permit denials, and steps taken to comply with the Arms Trade Treaty.

deepDive.heading: Transition rules and the U.S. exemption
deepDive.body:
The bill included transitional provisions that would have given the arms industry and government time to adjust. All existing export and brokering permits would expire 180 days after royal assent; if goods hadn't yet shipped, a new application would be automatically deemed filed and the Minister would have to review it on an expedited basis under the new rules. Applications already submitted but not yet decided would be assessed under the new rules.

The bill specifically addressed General Export Permit No. 47, which currently allows Arms Trade Treaty–controlled items to be shipped to the United States without individual permits. That permit would remain valid for 180 days after royal assent and then cease to apply — meaning U.S.-bound military exports would move to case-by-case permitting like any other destination.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties would have been Canadian defence and aerospace manufacturers and arms brokers, who would face individual permit applications for shipments currently covered by blanket or exemption arrangements, along with possible requirements to obtain end-use certificates from foreign governments. Global Affairs Canada and the responsible Minister would carry a heavier administrative and reporting burden.

Parliament and the public would gain access to significantly more detailed information about what Canada exports, to whom, in what quantities, and on what reasoning. Foreign governments buying Canadian military goods — including the United States, Canada's largest defence trading partner — would face additional documentation and review.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This was a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP (Jenny Kwan) rather than by the government. Private members' bills face long odds: they get limited debate time and, without government support, rarely pass.

Bill C-233 was defeated, so the Export and Import Permits Act remains unchanged. The proposals reflect a continuing policy debate in Canada about whether existing arms export controls adequately reflect the country's Arms Trade Treaty obligations, and about the treatment of components and U.S.-bound shipments in particular. This summary describes what the bill proposed; it does not assess whether those proposals were desirable or whether current law is adequate.

C-235.overview: Bill C-235, the Respecting Families of Murdered and Brutalized Persons Act, is a private member's bill that would change the Criminal Code so that offenders convicted of kidnapping/abduction, sexual assault and murder against the same victim in the same incident (or connected series of incidents) could be kept ineligible for parole for longer than usual. Today, a life sentence for murder generally carries parole ineligibility of up to 25 years; under this bill, a judge could set that period anywhere from 25 up to 40 years. Before the jury is dismissed, the judge would have to ask jurors whether they wish to recommend a number of years, though a recommendation would be optional and not binding. The bill also creates appeal rights: the convicted person could appeal the longer ineligibility order, and the Crown could appeal an order of less than 40 years or a decision not to make an order at all. As of the version reprinted here, the bill has been studied and amended by the House justice committee and is at report stage in the House of Commons \u2014 meaning it has not yet become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body: The bill amends the Criminal Code to create a special sentencing rule for one narrow category of case: where the same offender is convicted, in relation to the same victim and the same event or series of events, of three things together \u2014 a sexual offence (sections 151 to 153.1 or 271 to 273, which cover offences such as sexual interference and sexual assault), an abduction or kidnapping/forcible confinement offence (sections 279 or 280 to 283), and murder.\n\nIn those cases, the sentence remains life imprisonment, but the point at which the offender can first apply for parole changes. The default stays at 25 years, and a new section 745.31 would let the sentencing judge substitute a longer period of more than 25 years and up to a maximum of 40 years. The judge must give reasons, orally or in writing, whether or not they impose the longer period.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body: New section 745.22 requires the trial judge, before discharging the jury, to read jurors a set question asking whether they wish to recommend how many years the offender should serve before becoming parole-eligible. The bill is explicit that the jury is not required to make a recommendation; if one is made, the judge \"considers\" it alongside other factors.\n\nWhen setting the period, the judge must have regard to the character of the accused, the nature of the offences, the circumstances surrounding their commission, and any jury recommendation. Two new appeal routes are added: under section 675(1.2) the offender may appeal an order made under section 745.31, and under section 676(3.1) the Crown may appeal either an order setting a period of less than 40 years or a decision not to make an order at all. A consequential change to section 746 ensures time already spent in custody counts toward the new, longer ineligibility periods in the same way it does for existing ones.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body: The bill applies only to offenders convicted of the full combination of abduction, sexual assault and murder involving the same victim in the same event or connected series of events \u2014 a small subset of homicide cases. It would not change parole eligibility for murder convictions generally.\n\nIt also affects trial participants: juries in these cases would be asked a formal question about parole ineligibility, judges would gain discretion (and a duty to give reasons), and both defence and Crown would gain new grounds of appeal. The short title signals that the sponsor frames the measure around the experience of victims' families, who under a longer ineligibility period would face parole proceedings less frequently or later.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body: This is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Jeff Kibble, introduced in the 1st session of the 45th Parliament. The text reproduced here is a working copy reprinted as amended by the Standing Committee on Justice and Human Rights and reported to the House on June 8, 2026; the bill is at report stage, meaning the full House has yet to complete debate and vote at third reading, and the Senate stage and royal assent would still follow before it could become law.\n\nThe bill includes coordinating amendments dealing with Bill C-16, the Protecting Victims Act, also before the 45th Parliament. These technical clauses simply ensure the two bills' changes to the same Criminal Code provisions fit together correctly depending on which comes into force first.

C-236.overview: Bill C-236 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Dane Lloyd that targets offenders who know where a homicide victim's body is but refuse to tell police. It would require sentencing judges to treat that refusal as an "aggravating circumstance" (a factor that pushes a sentence higher), and would generally require the court to delay the offender's eligibility for full parole to half the sentence or ten years, whichever is less. It would also let the Parole Board of Canada and provincial parole boards refuse parole or temporary absences from prison on the same basis. The stated goal, set out in the bill's preamble, is to reduce the ongoing suffering of families who cannot recover or bury their loved ones, and to deter offenders from withholding that information. The bill has passed second reading and is currently being studied by a House of Commons committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends three federal laws — the Criminal Code, the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, and the Prisons and Reformatories Act — so that a single fact carries consequences at multiple stages of the justice system: that an offender convicted of an offence relating to a person's death has information about where the body or remains are, but refuses to give it to authorities.

That refusal would count against the offender at sentencing, when the court sets parole eligibility, and later when parole boards and prison authorities decide on release or temporary absences. In each case, the decision-maker must be satisfied that the offender actually has the information and is refusing to share it.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
New section 718.05 of the Criminal Code would require a court, when sentencing for an offence related to a person's death, to treat a refusal to disclose the location of the body or remains as an aggravating circumstance, in order to denounce and deter that behaviour. If the judge is satisfied the refusal occurred but chooses not to apply it in sentencing, the judge must explain why in writing.

A new subsection 743.6(1.3) would direct courts, for sentences of two years or more (including life sentences), to order that full parole cannot be granted until half the sentence or ten years has been served, whichever is less. A judge can decline to make that order if satisfied that denunciation and deterrence would be adequately served by the normal parole eligibility rules. The order must be revoked if the circumstances that led to it no longer exist — for example, if the offender later provides the information.

Under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, any such court order becomes part of the information the correctional system and parole boards must consider. Parole boards would be explicitly permitted (not required) to refuse parole and to refuse unescorted temporary absences in these cases. A parallel amendment to the Prisons and Reformatories Act allows designated authorities to refuse temporary absences for prisoners serving provincial sentences.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to people convicted of offences "in relation to the death of a person" — a category that includes homicide offences but is defined in the bill by that phrase rather than by a specific list. It affects them at sentencing and throughout the period they are serving their sentence, in both federal and provincial custody.

It also affects sentencing judges, who gain a mandatory factor to weigh and a reasons requirement, and the Parole Board of Canada, provincial parole boards, and prison authorities, who gain explicit discretion to consider withheld information about remains. The intended beneficiaries, according to the preamble, are surviving family members of victims whose remains have not been located.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble states Parliament's view that families are "avoidably further victimized" when remains are not found, that offender refusal is the primary reason remains cannot be located, and that negative consequences at sentencing and during a sentence could deter such refusals consistent with the sentencing principles of denunciation and deterrence. It also states Parliament's opinion that the approach is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms — an assertion in the bill's text, not a judicial finding.

As a private member's bill, C-236 was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government, and such bills face a longer path to becoming law. It is currently at the committee stage in the House of Commons, where MPs can hear witnesses and propose amendments before it returns to the House for further votes; it would then still need to pass the Senate and receive royal assent.

C-237.overview: Bill C-237 was a private member's bill from MP Jonathan Rowe that would have amended the federal Fisheries Act to change how recreational groundfish fishing (species such as cod, caught near the ocean floor) is managed in Atlantic Canada. Its central idea was to make the rules more consistent and predictable: the seasons when recreational groundfish fishing is closed would have to be the same across the Atlantic provinces, could only be based on when a species spawns, and would have to be posted online at least two months before taking effect. The bill also would have required the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to report to Parliament each year on enforcement of the Act, allowed regulators to require anglers to report their daily and seasonal catch counts, and directed the Minister to build a monitoring system tracking what fish are caught, when and where. Supporters of such measures generally point to the difficulty recreational fishers and tourism operators face when season dates shift or are announced late. The bill was defeated, so none of these changes became law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill proposed a series of targeted amendments to the Fisheries Act, the main federal law governing fishing in Canada, focused specifically on recreational groundfish fishing in Atlantic waters. It would have added "the importance of stability and predictability for those who engage in recreational fishing for groundfish" to the list of considerations the Act already directs decision-makers to weigh.

The most concrete change was a requirement that federal regulations harmonize "close times" — the periods when fishing is not permitted — across the Atlantic provinces for recreational groundfish, and that those closures be set only in relation to a species' spawning period. It also required that any close time or fishing quota, including those set by variation orders, be published on the Department of Fisheries and Oceans website at least two months before coming into force.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Beyond harmonized seasons and advance publication, the bill made three other changes. First, it rewrote the Act's annual reporting rule so the Minister must prepare and table in both houses of Parliament a report on the administration and enforcement of the Act "as soon as feasible" after each fiscal year. Second, it added to the list of information that certain people can be required to provide or record: the number of fish a person catches each day they fish, and their total catch over an open season.

Third, within one year of the Act coming into force, the Minister would have had to consult key stakeholders and develop a monitoring system recording, by species, the number of fish caught and the time and place of each catch. In designing it, the Minister was directed to look at existing models and best practices across Canada, examine whether fees and penalties collected under the Fisheries Act could cover the system's administrative costs, and identify ways to encourage timely reporting by fishers — for example, by reducing certain fees.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill was aimed primarily at recreational groundfish anglers in the Atlantic provinces, who would gain more uniform and earlier-announced season dates but could also face new catch-reporting obligations. Fisheries and Oceans Canada would carry the administrative work: harmonizing closure regulations, publishing dates at least two months in advance, tabling an annual enforcement report in Parliament, and building the new monitoring system in consultation with stakeholders.

Parliament would also be affected in a modest way, since the annual report on administration and enforcement would be laid before both the House of Commons and the Senate.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This was a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. Such bills face long odds, and this one was defeated, meaning the Fisheries Act remains unchanged by it.

It is worth noting what the bill did not do: it dealt with recreational (not commercial) groundfish fishing, and it did not itself set any specific season dates or quotas. Instead, it set rules about how those decisions must be made, coordinated across provinces, and communicated to the public.

C-238.overview: Bill C-238 is a private member's bill from MP Viviane Lapointe that would amend the Criminal Code's restitution rules. Restitution is money a sentencing judge can order an offender to pay to compensate for losses caused by their crime. Right now, restitution generally goes to victims and certain other specified people; this bill would add a new category so that organizations providing front-line services to a community — such as emergency services and victim support groups — could be ordered compensation for specific costs they incur because of human trafficking or certain drug offences. The listed costs include emergency shelter and medical supplies (such as overdose-reversal kits), harm reduction programs, security upgrades, mental health support for staff who experience workplace trauma, and the cost of handling increased demand for services. The bill has passed second reading and is currently being studied by a House of Commons committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new paragraph (f) to subsection 738(1) of the Criminal Code, the provision that lists the types of losses a court may order an offender to repay when sentencing. The new paragraph applies only to convictions for certain offences: trafficking in persons–related offences under sections 279.01 to 279.02 of the Criminal Code, and offences under sections 5, 6 or 7.1 of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (drug-related offences).

For those offences, a court could order the offender to pay an organization that provides front-line services to a community — explicitly including emergency services and victim support services — for expenses that organization incurred as a result of the offence. This amount would be ordered independently of any other restitution amount under the same section, meaning it does not come out of or reduce what a victim would otherwise receive.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: which expenses qualify
deepDive.body:
The bill lists five categories of recoverable expenses: (1) emergency shelter and medical services, including emergency medical supplies such as those needed to reverse overdoses; (2) harm reduction programs, including overdose and infectious disease prevention programs; (3) implementing or strengthening security measures, including security services and equipment; (4) counselling or other mental health supports for the organization's workers who experience workplace trauma as a result of the offence; and (5) responding to increased demand for the organization's services, including increased operational costs such as hiring additional or specialized personnel or providing specialized training.

Three limits apply to any such order. The amount cannot exceed the actual expenses, the expenses must be reasonable, and the amount must be "readily ascertainable" — a standard already used in the restitution provisions, meaning the figure has to be clear enough that the sentencing court can determine it without a lengthy inquiry. As with restitution generally, the section says a court "may" make such an order, so it is discretionary rather than automatic.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The new provision is aimed at entities rather than individuals: it applies to "a person, other than an individual," which covers organizations such as non-profits, community groups, shelters and other service providers. Individual people harmed by an offence continue to be covered by the existing restitution rules.

Offenders convicted of the specified human trafficking or drug offences could face an additional restitution obligation at sentencing. Sentencing courts would gain a new head of restitution to consider, and would have to assess whether claimed organizational expenses are reasonable and readily ascertainable.

deepDive.heading: Context and stated rationale
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble sets out Parliament's reasoning: that drug and human trafficking crimes have far-reaching impacts on communities, that community organizations providing front-line services bear many resulting costs, and that acknowledging harm to communities and providing reparations are already recognized objectives of sentencing under the Criminal Code. On that basis, the preamble states it is important that community organizations be able to obtain proper restitution from offenders.

As a private member's bill, C-238 was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is at the committee stage in the House of Commons, where members study the text, may hear witnesses and can propose amendments. To become law it would still need to complete House proceedings, pass the Senate and receive Royal Assent.

C-239.overview: Bill C-239 is a private member's bill from Liberal MP Sukh Dhaliwal that would amend the Canada Health Act — the federal law that sets the conditions provinces must meet to receive their full share of federal health funding (the Canada Health Transfer). The bill would add a new requirement: each province would have to create and put in place an "accountability framework" setting standards for reasonable access to health services, including benchmarks for how quickly people can get primary care, elective procedures and emergency care. Provinces would have to publish that framework online, along with an annual report showing how well they met the benchmarks and how efficiently they spent health dollars. If a province failed to do this, the federal Cabinet could reduce or withhold its cash contribution, the same enforcement tool that already applies to the Act's existing rules. The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not been passed and is still early in the legislative process.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Canada Health Act currently sets out criteria (such as public administration, comprehensiveness, universality, portability and accessibility) and conditions that a province's health insurance plan must satisfy before Ottawa pays out its full cash transfer. Bill C-239 adds a new category of requirement focused on accountability and transparency.

Under a new section 13.1, a province would have to develop and implement an accountability framework that sets standards for reasonable access to health services under its provincial health insurance plan. Meeting this requirement would become a precondition for receiving the full federal cash contribution. The bill also updates the Act's stated purpose in section 4 to reflect that these new requirements exist alongside the existing criteria and conditions.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The accountability framework would have to include two things: benchmarks for assessing timely access to primary care, elective procedures and emergency care; and transparent reporting requirements covering both whether those benchmarks are met and the efficiency of provincial health spending.

Provinces would have to publish the framework itself on a publicly available website, and — as soon as feasible after each fiscal year ends — post a report on how far the benchmarks were achieved that year plus information on spending efficiency. Provinces would also have to periodically review and update their benchmarks based on emerging evidence and best practices, and provide the federal Minister with information on the steps taken to ensure transparent reporting. In developing the framework, a provincial health minister "may" consult the federal Minister or counterparts in other provinces — this is optional, not required.

deepDive.heading: How it would be enforced
deepDive.body:
The bill plugs the new requirement into the Canada Health Act's existing penalty machinery. Section 14 (which governs when a matter is referred for review) would be expanded so that a province's failure to implement an accountability framework can trigger the process.

Section 15 would then allow the Governor in Council (the federal Cabinet) to make an order reducing or withholding a province's cash contribution if it concludes the province has not complied with the new accountability requirements. Section 16 would allow those reductions or withholdings to be reimposed each year that the non-compliance continues, provided the federal Minister is satisfied — after consulting the provincial health minister — that the default persists.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The direct legal obligations fall on provincial governments, which would need to design, publish and report against access benchmarks in order to keep their full Canada Health Transfer payments. Provincial health ministries and the federal Health Minister would carry the administrative work of developing frameworks and exchanging information.

For the public, the practical effect described in the bill is the publication of provincial access benchmarks and annual results on public websites, which would make wait-time and spending-efficiency information available to residents. The bill does not itself set national benchmark numbers or specify wait-time targets; it leaves the content of the benchmarks to each province, subject to the required subject areas.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-239 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. Private members' bills face limited debate time and comparatively few become law. The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, the stage where MPs debate the general principle before any committee study.

Because health care delivery is a provincial responsibility, the Canada Health Act works indirectly — through funding conditions rather than direct regulation of hospitals or clinics — and this bill follows that same approach. If passed, the changes would come into force on a day or days set by order of the Governor in Council, so the timing of implementation would be determined later by Cabinet rather than fixed in the bill itself.

C-241.overview: Bill C-241 is a private member's bill that would require the federal Minister of the Environment to create a national strategy for forecasting floods and droughts in Canada. Right now, according to the bill's preamble, flood and drought forecasting is done separately by each province, without coordination among them and with limited federal technical support. The bill would have the Environment Minister work with four other ministers, and consult provinces, municipalities, Indigenous governing bodies, universities, industry (including insurers) and civil society, to assess what a coordinated national forecasting system would require and what benefits it could bring. The strategy would have to be tabled in Parliament within two years and published online, with a follow-up report on how well it is working five years later. Notably, the bill does not itself create a forecasting service or commit money — it requires study, consultation, reporting and a possible proposal for such a service.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally the National Strategy on Flood and Drought Forecasting Act, directs the Minister of the Environment to develop a national strategy aimed at giving "key stakeholders" the information they need to forecast floods and droughts. The Minister must do this in collaboration with the Ministers of Agriculture and Agri-Food, Infrastructure and Communities, Natural Resources, and Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness.

It is a framework or "strategy" bill rather than an operational one: it sets out a process (consult, assess, report) rather than establishing a new agency, granting new powers, or allocating funding. The most concrete outcome it contemplates is the possible preparation of a proposal for a national forecasting service.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The strategy must include: an assessment of the need for and benefits of national coordination, new investment and new technologies in flood and drought forecasting; an assessment of the need for modelling to support that forecasting; and an assessment of opportunities to build national forecasting capacity that meets the short- and long-term information needs of provinces, municipalities, industry (including insurers) and Indigenous communities — including mapping current and future floodplains.

The strategy must also set out measures the federal government could take in response, which may include preparing a proposal to establish a cooperative national hydrological and water resources forecasting service and system, modelled on the shared federal-provincial approach used by the existing National Hydrometric Program.

On timelines: the strategy report must be tabled in both houses of Parliament within two years of the Act coming into force (within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed) and posted on a Government of Canada website within 10 business days of tabling. Five years after that, the Minister must table and publish a further report, prepared in consultation with the same partners, assessing the strategy's effectiveness and offering conclusions and recommendations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill directly obliges federal ministers, chiefly the Minister of the Environment. Its consultation requirements bring in provincial and municipal governments, Indigenous governing bodies (defined by reference to section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982), Canadian universities, civil society organizations and industry, with the insurance industry specifically named.

Indirectly, the intended beneficiaries described in the bill are communities and industries exposed to flooding and drought. The preamble singles out farming as a sector that is "inordinately impacted," and the strategy is meant to address the forecasting information needs of provinces, municipalities, industry and Indigenous communities.

deepDive.heading: Context and rationale
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble states that flood and drought damages in Canada have risen dramatically and are expected to rise further because of extreme weather and water events linked to climate change, with floodplains expanding and droughts intensifying. It argues that modern forecasting requires sophisticated integration of hydrological and water-resource models running on supercomputers, drawing on multiple weather forecasts plus on-the-ground observations of rainfall, soil moisture, snowpack, glaciers, lake levels, ice jams and streamflow.

The preamble also notes that Canadian universities have developed water-forecasting models sought after internationally, including by the United States, and that most technologically advanced countries have a national flood forecasting service. These statements are the bill's stated justification, not independently verified findings.

deepDive.heading: Status and what happens next
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Tatiana Auguste, meaning it was introduced by an individual member rather than by the government. It has been studied by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Environment and Sustainable Development, which amended it, and the version reprinted here is the working copy for report stage, reported to the House on June 17, 2026.

To become law, the bill would still need to clear report stage and third reading in the House of Commons, pass through the Senate, and receive royal assent. Its two-year clock for tabling the strategy would begin only once the Act comes into force.

C-240.overview: Bill C-240, the Offender Rehabilitation Act, is a private member's bill that would let sentencing judges attach specific rehabilitation-related requirements to a prison sentence — such as job training, an apprenticeship, an approved treatment program, or a letter acknowledging the harm done to a victim — to be carried out while the offender is in custody. Corrections officials would have to build those court-ordered measures into an offender's correctional plan and into decisions about what programs to offer, and parole boards would have to consider how much progress the offender made on them when deciding on release. The bill also amends drug law so that trafficking fentanyl in quantities indicating large-scale trafficking must be treated as an aggravating factor at sentencing, which generally points toward a harsher sentence. The bill's preamble frames these changes as a response to Canada's addiction and overdose crisis and states that 'safe supply' programs have perpetuated dependency rather than fostered recovery. The bill is currently at committee stage in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 729.2 to the Criminal Code allowing a court, on top of any prison term it imposes, to order an offender to take one or more specified measures during the custodial part of their sentence (or another period the court specifies). The stated purposes are protecting society and helping the offender reintegrate into the community.

The permitted measures are: participating in training, apprenticeship or other employment-related programs; where appropriate, writing to the victim or others affected to acknowledge the harm and impact of the offence; participating in a provincially approved treatment program; and any other measure the court considers desirable. The offender must make 'all reasonable efforts' to complete the measures within the time the court sets. Two of the options come with limits: the training and treatment programs are subject to the program actually being available and the program director accepting the offender, and treatment programs also require the offender's agreement.

deepDive.heading: How it would work inside the corrections system
deepDive.body:
A new Criminal Code provision would require the sentencing court to send information about any ordered measures to the Correctional Service of Canada. Amendments to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act would then fold those measures into the correctional planning process: an offender's court-ordered obligations in their correctional plan would expressly include measures ordered under the new section, alongside things like restitution and child support.

The Correctional Service would also have to take these court-ordered programs into account when deciding what programs to provide, and the availability of such programs — plus the offender's willingness to participate — would factor into placement decisions. Finally, parole boards would be required to consider reports on the offender's progress with the ordered measures as part of the information they weigh when deciding on conditional release.

deepDive.heading: Fentanyl trafficking sentencing
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act to add a new aggravating factor that a sentencing court must consider: that the person trafficked, or possessed for the purpose of trafficking, a substance listed in item 16 of Schedule I (fentanyl and related substances) in quantities indicating large-scale trafficking.

Aggravating factors do not create a new offence or a mandatory minimum; they are circumstances a judge must weigh that generally push a sentence toward the higher end of the available range. This provision would sit alongside the existing aggravating factors already listed in that part of the Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would most directly affect people convicted of criminal offences who receive custodial sentences, particularly those a court identifies as candidates for training or addiction treatment while incarcerated, and people convicted of large-scale fentanyl trafficking. It would also affect sentencing judges, who gain a new ordering power; the Correctional Service of Canada, which would have to reflect court-ordered measures in correctional plans, placement and program planning; and the Parole Board, which would have new information to weigh in release decisions.

Victims are addressed indirectly through the option of an acknowledgement letter, which the court may order only 'if appropriate.'

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble situates the bill in the substance addiction and overdose crisis, citing loss of life, community breakdown and public safety concerns, and states that people with addictions need supports to recover and reintegrate. It expressly states that 'safe supply' services — the prescribing of medications such as opioids and stimulants to people with addictions — have perpetuated dependency rather than fostered recovery, and calls for a framework of 'compassionate intervention' in which the justice system directs offenders with addictions into structured, in-custody treatment. It also states that those who profit from trafficking strong opioids should face more stringent penalties.

C-240 is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Kelly DeRidder, introduced in 2025 and currently at committee consideration in the House of Commons. Private members' bills must still clear committee, third reading in the House, and the full Senate process before they can become law, and they may be amended along the way.

C-242.overview: Bill C-242, the "Jail Not Bail Act," was a private member's bill from Conservative MP Arpan Khanna that would have rewritten large parts of the Criminal Code's bail rules to make it harder for people accused of violent crimes to be released while awaiting trial. It would have replaced the current "principle of restraint" (which directs officials to favour release at the earliest opportunity on the least onerous conditions) with a principle that public safety comes first, expanded the list of charges where the accused must prove they should be released rather than the Crown proving they should be detained, and created a new category of "major offences" carrying stricter rules. The bill also added special requirements for accused people who are neither citizens nor permanent residents, barred people with recent indictable convictions from acting as sureties, and required the federal Justice Minister to table an annual report on bail in Canada. Because bail is set by judges and justices of the peace under nationally applicable Criminal Code rules, changes like these would have affected courts across the country. The bill was defeated and did not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's central move is to change the guiding principle for bail decisions. Section 493.1 of the Criminal Code currently sets out a "principle of restraint"; the bill would have replaced it with a direction that a peace officer, justice or judge "shall give primary consideration to the protection and safety of the public" when making any bail-related decision. Public protection would also be added as a factor police can consider when deciding whether to hold someone after arrest, and as a permitted basis for imposing conditions on release.

The bill also tightened the legal test for detention. Under the current "secondary ground" for keeping someone in custody, a court asks whether there is a "substantial likelihood" the accused would commit an offence or interfere with justice if released. The bill would lower that threshold to whether such conduct is "reasonably foreseeable," and would expressly require courts to weigh the accused's criminal history, including past major-offence convictions, past breaches of release conditions, and any history of reoffending while on release.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: "major offences" and reverse onus
deepDive.body:
Normally the Crown must justify keeping an accused in jail before trial. For certain listed offences, that burden is reversed and the accused must show why detention is not justified. Bill C-242 would have added a number of violent indictable offences to that reverse-onus list, including discharging a firearm with intent and drive-by shootings, administering a noxious substance, sexual assault with a weapon and aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping and abduction offences involving violence, motor vehicle theft in association with organized crime, robbery and extortion, break-and-enter into a dwelling involving violence against occupants, arson offences, and offences alleged to involve violence against a peace officer or a "first responder." The bill defines first responders as firefighters, paramedics, emergency medical technicians (paid or volunteer) and any other group added by regulation.

These reverse-onus offences would be grouped into a new category called "major offences," which triggers several stricter rules: police could not release someone arrested for a major offence (the matter would have to go before a justice); repeat cases would face mandatory detention, with release decided only by a superior court judge, where the accused was allegedly committing a major offence while already out on release for another major offence and had been convicted of a major offence in the previous ten years.

deepDive.heading: Other changes: sureties, sentencing gaps, and non-citizens
deepDive.body:
The bill would prohibit naming anyone as a surety (a person who vouches for an accused and pledges money) if they had been convicted of an indictable offence in the previous ten years. It would also change what happens between a finding of guilt and sentencing: where an accused pleads guilty to or is found guilty of an indictable offence, detention would become the default until sentencing unless the accused shows why continued custody is not justified. For summary (less serious) offences, release pending sentence would remain available.

For immigration status, the bill required a justice deciding on bail to consider whether the accused is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident and, if not, whether it is reasonably foreseeable they might try to leave the country. Anyone who is not a citizen or permanent resident would have to deposit all their passports as a mandatory condition of release, whether released by police after arrest or by a court in a reverse-onus case.

deepDive.heading: Reporting requirement
deepDive.body: Beyond the Criminal Code, the bill amended the Department of Justice Act to require the Minister of Justice to prepare an annual report on "the state of judicial interim release" (bail) in Canada and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate. The excerpt of the bill text provided is cut off before the details of what that report must contain.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-242 was a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than the government — sponsored by Arpan Khanna and introduced in the 45th Parliament in 2025. It has been defeated, meaning none of these changes take effect and the existing Criminal Code bail rules, including the principle of restraint and the "substantial likelihood" standard, remain in place.

The bill sits within an ongoing national debate about pre-trial release, repeat violent offending and the balance courts must strike between the presumption of innocence and public safety. Any such reform also interacts with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees the right not to be denied reasonable bail without just cause; this summary describes only what the bill proposed and does not assess whether the proposals would have been upheld or would have achieved their stated goals.

C-243.overview: Bill C-243 was a private member's bill from MP Kerry Diotte that would have changed how people serving sentences for first- or second-degree murder get their parole reconsidered. Under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the Parole Board both reviews cases on a set schedule and can consider new applications made by offenders themselves. This bill would have removed the ability of offenders convicted of murder to file further parole applications after the Board had already refused day or full parole, or had cancelled or terminated their parole — leaving only the Board's regular, legally scheduled reviews. In practical terms, it aimed to reduce the number of parole hearings for murder convictions, which supporters of such measures often connect to the burden repeated hearings place on victims' families. The bill was defeated, so the law is unchanged.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill proposed two narrow amendments to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the federal law that governs prisons and parole in Canada. It targeted offenders serving a sentence for first-degree or second-degree murder, as those terms are defined in section 231 of the Criminal Code.

For that group, once the Parole Board of Canada had reviewed a case and decided not to grant parole — or had cancelled or terminated parole already granted — the offender could not submit any further application for parole. Instead, as the bill's own summary explains, parole would continue to be looked at only "in accordance with the statutory time frames," meaning the reviews the Board is already required by law to conduct on its own schedule, rather than reviews triggered by the offender.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 would add a new subsection 122(4.1) to the Act. Section 122 deals with day parole (a form of release that allows an offender to participate in community activities while returning nightly to an institution or halfway house). The new subsection would state that, despite the existing rule in subsection 122(4), an offender serving a murder sentence could make no further day parole application after a refusal, cancellation or termination.

Clause 2 would add a parallel new subsection 123(6.1) covering full parole, which is governed by section 123. The wording mirrors clause 1: despite the existing subsection 123(6), no further full parole application could be made by a murder offender following a Board decision not to grant full parole, or a decision to cancel or terminate parole.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The changes would apply only to federal offenders serving sentences for first-degree or second-degree murder. People convicted of manslaughter or any other offence would be unaffected, and the bill did not change parole eligibility dates, sentence lengths, or the criteria the Board uses to decide whether to release someone.

The bill also does not remove parole review altogether for this group. The text preserves the Board's scheduled statutory reviews; what it removes is the separate pathway of the offender applying again after an unfavourable decision. Victims and their families, who may attend or make statements at parole hearings, would be indirectly affected by any resulting change in how often hearings occur.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This was a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual Member of Parliament rather than by the government. Private members' bills face limited debate time and rarely become law.

Bill C-243 was defeated, meaning none of its provisions came into force. The existing rules in sections 122 and 123 of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, including the current ability of offenders to reapply for parole, remain as they were.

C-244.overview: Bill C-244, the Clean Coasts Act, is a private member's bill from Liberal MP Patrick Weiler that makes two targeted changes to existing federal laws in order to better protect Canada's oceans and coastlines. First, it adjusts the wording of the dumping-at-sea rules in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 so the prohibition on disposing of substances in Canadian marine waters explicitly applies to ships as well as persons. Second, it adds a new offence to the Wrecked, Abandoned or Hazardous Vessels Act that bans selling or giving away a boat to someone the owner knows — or is reckless about whether — cannot or will not properly look after or dispose of it. The aim, as the bill's own summary puts it, is to increase liability for damage to marine areas, which matters because abandoned and derelict vessels can leak fuel and debris and often leave cleanup costs to governments and communities. The bill is currently at the committee stage in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading but is not yet law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is short — four clauses, including the one that gives it its short title, the Clean Coasts Act. It does not create a new law of its own; it amends two existing statutes: the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999 (CEPA) and the Wrecked, Abandoned or Hazardous Vessels Act (WAHVA), which was enacted in 2019.

According to the bill's official summary, the purpose of both amendments is to enhance the protection of marine areas by providing for increased liability for damage to those areas. In practical terms, that means widening who can be held responsible when marine pollution or vessel abandonment occurs.

deepDive.heading: Key provision 1: Dumping at sea under CEPA
deepDive.body:
Section 125(1) of CEPA prohibits the disposal of substances in certain areas of the sea under Canadian jurisdiction unless specified conditions (such as holding a permit) are met. The bill rewrites the opening words of that subsection so it reads: "No person or ship shall dispose or allow the disposal of a substance..."

The change is a wording change rather than a new prohibition — it makes clear that the ban applies to ships as well as persons, and covers both disposing of a substance and allowing its disposal. The areas of the sea covered are those already listed in paragraphs 122(2)(a) to (e) of CEPA.

deepDive.heading: Key provision 2: A new rule on transferring vessel ownership
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 34.1 to the Wrecked, Abandoned or Hazardous Vessels Act. It prohibits a vessel owner from transferring ownership to another person if the owner knows — or is reckless as to whether — that person lacks the ability, resources or intent to maintain, operate or dispose of the vessel in a way that prevents it from becoming wrecked, abandoned or hazardous.

The bill also amends paragraph 90(1)(a) of the Act to add section 34.1 to the list of provisions whose contravention triggers the Act's existing offence and penalty regime, alongside subsections 30(1), 32(1), section 33 and subsection 34(1). In other words, breaking the new transfer rule would be treated as an offence under the same framework that already applies to other core duties in that Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected group is boat owners — particularly anyone selling, gifting or otherwise handing off a vessel that may be near the end of its useful life. Under the new rule, an owner could face liability for who they pass a boat on to, not just for how they themselves handle it. Buyers and recipients of vessels may also feel indirect effects, since sellers would have reason to consider whether a purchaser can realistically care for or dispose of a boat.

The CEPA amendment is relevant to shipowners and operators in waters under Canadian jurisdiction, by confirming that ships themselves — and not only individuals — fall within the dumping prohibition. Coastal communities and the federal departments that respond to derelict vessels and marine pollution are the intended beneficiaries of the added liability.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-244 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP (Patrick Weiler) rather than by the government. Private members' bills follow a more limited legislative timetable and a smaller share of them become law than government bills.

The bill was introduced in 2025 in the 45th Parliament and is currently at consideration in committee in the House of Commons. Committee study can result in amendments; after that, the bill would still need to complete report stage and third reading in the House, pass through the Senate, and receive Royal Assent before taking effect. Nothing in the text above sets out penalty amounts, enforcement resources or a coming-into-force date beyond the existing framework in the Wrecked, Abandoned or Hazardous Vessels Act.
