C-245.overview: Bill C-245 was a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Xavier Barsalou-Duval that would have added a single line to the Canadian Multiculturalism Act stating that the Act "does not apply in Quebec." The Canadian Multiculturalism Act is the federal law that sets out Ottawa's official policy of promoting and preserving Canada's cultural and racial diversity; the bill would have exempted Quebec from that policy framework without repealing or changing the Act for the rest of the country. The bill's preamble justified the change by stating that Quebecers form a nation and already have the tools to define their own identity and protect their common values, citing the French language, the separation of state and religion, and gender equality. The bill was introduced on September 23, 2025, and has since been defeated, so it will not become law. It matters mainly as a marker of a long-running debate over how federal multiculturalism policy interacts with Quebec's own approach to integrating newcomers and defining collective identity.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill is very short. It amends the Canadian Multiculturalism Act by inserting a new section 2.1 immediately after section 2, reading: "This Act does not apply in Quebec."

That is the entirety of the operative change. The bill does not repeal the Act, does not alter its stated objectives for the rest of Canada, and does not propose any replacement policy or program. It simply carves Quebec out of the Act's application.

deepDive.heading: The reasoning set out in the bill
deepDive.body:
Bills sometimes include a preamble — an introductory statement explaining the rationale. This bill's preamble states that Quebecers form a nation and "therefore possess all the tools needed to define their identity and protect their common values," specifically naming the protection of the French language, the separation of state and religion, and gender equality.

A preamble is not itself an enforceable rule; it explains the purpose behind the change and can help with interpreting the law. Beyond this statement, the bill offers no further detail or conditions.

deepDive.heading: Who it would affect
deepDive.body:
The direct target is federal multiculturalism policy as it applies within Quebec. The Canadian Multiculturalism Act directs federal institutions to take diversity into account in their policies and programs and declares multiculturalism as official federal policy; exempting Quebec would mean that statutory framework no longer applied there.

The bill text as provided does not spell out practical consequences — for example, it does not list specific programs, funding streams, or federal institutions that would be affected. Readers should note that the bill was defeated, so no change to the law occurred.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This was a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. Private members' bills face long odds: they get limited debate time and rarely pass without broader support in the House of Commons.

The sponsor, Xavier Barsalou-Duval, is a Bloc Québécois MP, and the bill reflects a recurring position in Quebec politics that the province's own model for integrating newcomers and managing cultural diversity should take precedence over the federal multiculturalism framework. The bill was introduced in 2025 and has been defeated, meaning the Canadian Multiculturalism Act continues to apply across Canada, including Quebec.

C-246.overview: Bill C-246 was a private member's bill from Conservative MP Rachael Thomas that would have changed one sentencing rule in the Criminal Code: when someone is convicted of more than one sexual offence, the prison terms would have to be served one after the other (consecutively) rather than at the same time (concurrently). Under current practice, courts often order sentences to run concurrently, which can mean a person convicted of several offences serves less total time than the sum of the individual sentences. The bill's preamble argued that sexual offences cause lasting harm, often involve repeated conduct, and that sentences should reflect the distinct harm done to each victim. Because it was a private member's bill, it needed support beyond its sponsor's party to advance; it was defeated in the House of Commons and does not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill contains a single operative change. It would replace subsection 718.3(7) of the Criminal Code with a new rule stating that when a court sentences someone for a sexual offence, it "shall" order that prison term to be served consecutively to any other sexual-offence prison sentence imposed at the same time, and to any other sexual-offence prison sentence the person is already subject to at the time of sentencing.

The word "shall" matters: it means the court would be directed to stack the sentences rather than having discretion to decide whether they run at the same time. In plain terms, a person sentenced for three sexual offences would serve the three terms end to end instead of overlapping.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Two situations are covered. First, multiple sexual offences sentenced together in the same proceeding — each sentence would follow the others. Second, a sexual-offence sentence imposed on someone who is already serving (or already subject to) a sentence for a sexual offence — the new sentence would be added on top.

The bill's preamble sets out Parliament's stated reasoning: denouncing sexual violence, deterring it, protecting vulnerable people, and maintaining public confidence in the justice system, "while respecting the principle of proportionality." A preamble explains intent and does not itself create legal obligations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The change would apply to people being sentenced for more than one sexual offence, or for a sexual offence while already under sentence for one. For those offenders, total time in custody could be longer than under current sentencing practice.

It would also affect judges, who would lose discretion in these specific cases to order concurrent sentences. Victims and their families are the group the preamble identifies as the intended beneficiaries, on the reasoning that each offence and each victim should be reflected separately in the total sentence.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-246 was introduced on September 23, 2025, in the 45th Parliament as a private member's bill — a bill brought forward by an individual MP rather than by the government. Private members' bills face limited debate time and rarely become law without broad support.

The bill has been defeated, so subsection 718.3(7) of the Criminal Code remains as it currently stands and the consecutive-sentencing rule described above is not in force. The material above does not include the reasons given by MPs for or against the bill, so this summary does not attempt to characterize the debate.

C-247.overview: Bill C-247 is a short private member's bill from NDP MP Leah Gazan that would repeal a single provision of the Canada Labour Code — section 107. That section gives the federal Minister of Labour broad authority to take steps the Minister considers necessary to encourage a settlement in an industrial dispute, including referring questions to the Canada Industrial Relations Board or directing the Board to take specific measures. Removing it would eliminate that ministerial power from the Code. The bill matters because section 107 has been used as a tool for federal intervention in labour disputes in federally regulated industries such as rail, ports, airlines, telecommunications and banking; the bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not been passed into law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill contains one operative clause: "Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code is repealed." There are no other amendments, exceptions or transitional rules in the text as published.

According to the bill's own summary, section 107 is the provision that authorizes the Minister of Labour "to take measures to promote conditions favourable to the settlement of an industrial dispute or difference," including referring any question to the Canada Industrial Relations Board (CIRB) or directing the Board to take any measure the Minister considers necessary. Repealing it would remove that authority from the statute.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
There is effectively only one provision. The bill amends the Canada Labour Code (R.S., c. L-2) by deleting section 107 in its entirety. Nothing in the text replaces section 107 with an alternative mechanism, sets conditions on ministerial intervention, or changes any other part of the Code.

The text also does not specify a coming-into-force date, and it does not address disputes or Board proceedings that might be underway if the repeal took effect — the published text is limited to the single repealing clause.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The Canada Labour Code governs labour relations in federally regulated workplaces — sectors such as interprovincial rail and trucking, ports and marine shipping, airlines, telecommunications and broadcasting, banking, and federal Crown corporations. Unions, employers and workers in those sectors would be the parties most directly affected.

The repeal would also affect the Minister of Labour, by removing a specific power the Minister currently holds, and the Canada Industrial Relations Board, which under section 107 can be directed by the Minister or asked to consider questions referred by the Minister.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-247 is a private member's bill, introduced by Winnipeg Centre MP Leah Gazan in October 2025 during the 45th Parliament. Private members' bills are sponsored by individual MPs rather than the government, and most do not become law; they must clear second reading, committee study, third reading and the Senate before receiving Royal Assent.

As of the information provided, the bill is at second reading in the House of Commons — the stage where MPs debate the bill's general principle. No changes to the Canada Labour Code take effect unless and until the bill is passed and receives Royal Assent.

C-248.overview: Bill C-248, the Time Change Act, is a private member's bill from MP Marie-France Lalonde that would require the federal government to convene a single national conference about seasonal time changes — the twice-yearly clock shift most Canadians know as daylight saving time. The conference would have to be held within one year of the law taking effect, and would bring together federal and provincial officials, Indigenous governing bodies, and other interested groups such as health scientists, municipalities, farmers, educators and public safety representatives. Within six months of the meeting, the designated minister would have to write up a report on what was discussed, including any recommendations, and post it online. Importantly, the bill does not itself abolish, keep or change the time change anywhere in Canada — setting local time remains a provincial and territorial matter, so this is a coordination-and-discussion measure rather than a change to the clocks. It matters because it would create a formal, public federal venue for a question that provinces have so far handled individually.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill obliges a federal minister — designated by the Governor in Council (essentially, cabinet) by order — to organize a "pan-Canadian conference on time change" within one year of the Act coming into force. The stated purpose is to promote cooperation between the federal and provincial governments on the issue.

The only concrete outputs required are the conference itself and a follow-up report. The bill contains no provision that would end, keep, or standardize seasonal time changes; it does not amend any existing law on timekeeping.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 4 sets out a mandatory agenda. The conference must cover the main issues raised by time change, including economic ones; the scientific research on how time change affects health, safety and productivity; and the possibility of adopting a more uniform approach across the country.

Section 5 requires the minister to prepare a report within six months of the conference and publish it on the department's website. The report must set out the information and recommendations that came out of the discussions. Section 2 defines "Indigenous governing body" as a council, government or other entity authorized to act for an Indigenous group holding rights recognized under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

deepDive.heading: Who would be involved and affected
deepDive.body:
The minister must invite provincial government representatives responsible for time-related matters, Indigenous governing bodies, and "any other relevant stakeholders." The bill names examples: health scientists and representatives from municipal governments and from the public safety, agriculture, education, early childhood care and eldercare sectors — sectors whose schedules and operations are directly touched by clock changes.

For ordinary Canadians, the immediate practical effect would be limited: clocks would continue to be governed by provincial and territorial rules. The potential longer-term significance lies in whatever recommendations emerge from the conference and the published report, which governments would be free to act on or not.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-248 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is currently listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law, and those outside the order of precedence face particularly long odds of advancing.

The bill responds to an ongoing national patchwork: because setting local time falls under provincial and territorial jurisdiction, some jurisdictions and regions have moved away from seasonal clock changes while others have not, and several provinces have linked any change to what neighbouring jurisdictions do. The bill's approach — a conference plus a public report — is a way for Parliament to encourage coordination without legislating on an area outside clear federal control.

C-250.overview: Bill C-250, the Flight Attendants' Remuneration Act, is a private member's bill from NDP MP Don Davies that would amend the Canada Labour Code to change how flight attendants' paid working time is counted. Under the bill, employers would have to count time spent on pre-flight and post-flight duties, mandatory training, and time spent at the workplace on call and at the employer's disposal — including during flight delays — as hours worked. It would also require that this time be paid at no less than the employee's regular wage rate. The bill responds to a long-standing feature of airline pay practices in which flight attendants have often been compensated based mainly on time when the aircraft is in motion or in the air. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is at a very early stage.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would add a new section (177.01) to the Canada Labour Code, the federal law that sets employment standards for federally regulated workplaces such as airlines. The new section creates a specific rule for flight attendants about how their hours of work are calculated for pay purposes.

It directs that, when an employer calculates the time worked in a day, a week or a pay period under section 169 of the Code, certain categories of time must be included. It also sets a floor on what that time must be paid at.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Three categories of time would have to be counted as work time: (1) all pre-flight and post-flight duties relating to aircraft security and passenger service — the bill specifically names assisting with boarding and deplaning and pre-flight cabin and passenger safety checks; (2) time spent completing mandatory training programs; and (3) time spent in the workplace (as defined in section 122 of the Code) at the call of and at the disposal of the employer, which the bill says expressly includes flight delays, whether or not the delay is within the employer's control.

A second subsection requires that the employer pay at least the employee's regular rate of wages for all of the work described above. In other words, the bill sets a minimum — it does not cap what an employer may pay or prevent a higher rate being negotiated.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to employees who are flight attendants and to their employers. Because the Canada Labour Code governs federally regulated industries, this means airlines operating under federal jurisdiction and the cabin crew they employ.

The practical effect would be on how airlines track and compensate ground-based and non-flying duty time. The bill text does not address other airline employee groups, nor does it specify a coming-into-force date or transitional rules in the material provided.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-250 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government — sponsored by Don Davies (Vancouver Kingsway) and introduced on October 21, 2025. Its status is listed as "outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but has not yet been drawn into the queue for House of Commons debate time. Most private members' bills do not become law, and those that advance typically do so slowly.

The subject matter connects to public discussion in recent years about "unpaid work" in the airline sector, where compensation has commonly been tied to flight or block time rather than to the full span of a duty day. This explainer describes only what the bill's text says; it does not assess how many workers would be affected or what the cost or operational implications would be, as the bill itself does not address those questions.

C-251.overview: Bill C-251 is a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay that aims to make it harder to bring goods made with forced labour or child labour into Canada. Canadian law already bans importing such goods, but this bill would flip the burden of proof for shipments coming from places or companies the federal government has flagged as high-risk: those goods would be automatically presumed to be tainted, and the importer would have to prove otherwise. It would also require border officers to hold onto flagged goods until they are satisfied the goods are legal to import. The Governor in Council (the federal cabinet) would be given the power to designate "countries or areas of concern" and to maintain a public list of specific companies or organizations believed to use forced or child labour. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends two federal laws: the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff. Canada's Customs Tariff already prohibits importing goods mined, manufactured or produced wholly or in part by forced labour or child labour (tariff item No. 9897.00.00). In practice, stopping such goods requires establishing that the labour abuse occurred — often difficult across complex international supply chains.

C-251 addresses this by creating a legal presumption. If goods come, even partly, from a country or area the federal cabinet has designated as a "subject of concern," or from a company or organization on a government list of suspected users of forced or child labour, those goods are automatically deemed to fall under the existing import ban. The importer, rather than the government, would then have to show the goods are clean.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Detention at the border: A new subsection added to section 101 of the Customs Act would require — not merely allow — a customs officer to detain goods covered by the presumption until the officer is satisfied they are not prohibited imports.

Rebutting the presumption: An importer can overcome the presumption only by meeting four conditions together: demonstrating they carried out the prescribed supply chain monitoring and supply management measures; providing any required certification or information; showing they exercised all prescribed due diligence; and satisfying the officer that the goods were not made with forced or child labour. The bill also expands the government's regulation-making powers so it can set the rules for supply chain tracing, certification procedures and deadlines, the level of diligence required of importers, and what information must be filed and when.

Designations and listings: Cabinet could designate a country or area as a subject of concern on the recommendation of the Minister of Public Safety, after consultation with the Minister of Labour, where there are reasonable grounds to believe goods there are made with forced or child labour. Cabinet could also establish a list of named entities on the Public Safety Minister's recommendation using the same "reasonable grounds" standard. The Minister could update names or aliases on the list and remove an entity that no longer uses forced or child labour, and must review each listing every five years and recommend whether it should stay.

deepDive.heading: Definitions and how it fits with existing law
deepDive.body: The bill does not create new definitions of "forced labour" and "child labour" — it borrows them from the Fighting Against Forced Labour and Child Labour in Supply Chains Act, the federal supply-chain reporting law. "Entity" takes its meaning from the Special Economic Measures Act, the statute used for sanctions. Building on existing definitions is intended to keep the new border rules aligned with laws already on the books.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Importers and Canadian businesses sourcing from abroad would face the most direct impact: any shipment linked to a designated country or area, or to a listed entity, could be held at the border until the importer produces documentation and evidence of supply chain due diligence. The specific paperwork and timelines would be set later through regulations, not by the bill itself.

The Canada Border Services Agency and its officers would carry a new mandatory detention duty, while the Minister of Public Safety, the Minister of Labour and cabinet would decide which countries, areas and companies are flagged. Workers abroad in industries associated with forced or child labour are the intended beneficiaries of the tighter import controls.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-251 was introduced on October 21, 2025, in the 45th Parliament. It is a private member's bill, meaning it comes from an individual MP rather than the government, and it is currently "outside the Order of Precedence" — it has not yet reached a position in the queue for House debate. Most private members' bills do not become law.

The bill responds to a long-standing gap noted by critics of the current system: although importing forced-labour goods is already banned in Canada, very few shipments have been stopped under that prohibition. The presumption-and-list approach resembles measures adopted in some other jurisdictions, though the bill text itself makes no reference to foreign legislation.

C-252.overview: Bill C-252 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would designate October 22 of each year as "Peacetime Service and Sacrifice Memorial Day" across Canada. The day would honour Canadian Armed Forces members who have died in the line of duty on Canadian soil during peacetime — including those killed in non-combat incidents, in attacks at home, and by suicide. The only concrete government action the bill requires is that the national flag on the Peace Tower be lowered to half-mast on that day; it does not create a statutory holiday, new benefits or new spending. The date is symbolic: October 22, 2014 is the day Corporal Nathan Cirillo was shot and killed while standing guard at the National War Memorial in Ottawa. The bill is currently outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not yet been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has four short operative parts: a short title, a statement of purpose, the designation of the day, and a flag provision. Section 3 states that throughout Canada, in each year, October 22 is to be known as "Peacetime Service and Sacrifice Memorial Day." Section 2 sets out the purpose: to encourage all Canadians to remember and honour Canadian Armed Forces members who have lost their lives on Canadian soil during peacetime.

Section 4 is the one requirement placed on government: on that day, the national flag of Canada on the Peace Tower is to be lowered to half-mast. Beyond that, the bill imposes no obligations on employers, governments or individuals.

deepDive.heading: What it does not do
deepDive.body: Like most "national day" bills, C-252 is commemorative rather than regulatory. Nothing in the text creates a statutory or public holiday, closes workplaces or schools, provides funding for ceremonies, or changes veterans' benefits, compensation or mental-health programs. It also does not alter Remembrance Day on November 11, which the preamble explicitly references as the existing occasion for honouring those who served in war and conflict.

deepDive.heading: Why October 22, and the reasons given
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out the rationale. It cites two October 2014 attacks: Warrant Officer Patrice Vincent, killed in a deliberate vehicular attack at Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu on October 20, 2014, and Corporal Nathan Cirillo, shot and killed while on ceremonial guard at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on October 22, 2014 — the date the bill selects.

The preamble also points to broader figures: since 1914, approximately 2,000 Canadian Armed Forces members have died in non-combat roles on Canadian soil, and between 2013 and 2024, 177 Regular Force members and at least 36 Reserve Force members died by suicide. It contrasts this with the more than 118,000 members who died in war and are remembered each November 11, framing peacetime deaths at home as a category that currently lacks its own day of remembrance.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body: The direct practical effect is narrow — it changes flag protocol on the Peace Tower for one day a year. The symbolic reach is broader, aimed at serving members, veterans, and the families of Canadian Armed Forces personnel who died in training accidents, other non-combat incidents on Canadian soil, attacks at home, or by suicide. Commemorative days of this kind typically prompt voluntary ceremonies, moments of silence and public awareness activities, but the bill does not mandate any.

deepDive.heading: Status and what happens next
deepDive.body: C-252 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced and given first reading but has not yet been drawn into the queue for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills in this position never reach a vote; the bill would still need to pass the House of Commons and the Senate and receive Royal Assent to take effect.

C-249.overview: Bill C-249 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Alexandre Boulerice that would make three changes to Employment Insurance (EI). First, it would carve maternity (pregnancy) and parental benefits out of the rule that caps the total number of weeks a person can collect when they combine regular EI with special benefits in the same claim. Second, it would let a claimant's benefit period — the window of time in which benefits can be drawn — be extended when the person is receiving maternity or parental benefits. Third, it would raise the maximum number of weeks of benefits for someone caring for a critically ill adult from 15 to 26, for both employees and self-employed claimants. The practical effect would be to give some new parents, and people caring for seriously ill adults, access to more weeks of EI than the current rules allow. The bill is currently "outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Employment Insurance Act sets separate maximums for different kinds of benefits (regular benefits for job loss, plus "special" benefits such as sickness, maternity, parental, compassionate care, and care for a critically ill child or adult). It also sets an overall cap when a claimant combines more than one type in a single claim. Bill C-249 adjusts these caps and time limits in three ways.

It (1) exempts certain benefits from the combined-weeks cap, (2) adds receiving maternity or parental benefits to the list of circumstances that can extend a claimant's benefit period, and (3) lengthens the maximum benefits available for caring for a critically ill adult. It does not change eligibility rules, benefit amounts, or premium rates.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Combined weeks: Section 12(6) of the Act currently says that when a claimant combines regular benefits with special benefits, the total cannot exceed 50 weeks. The bill would keep that 50-week cap but add an exception for benefits paid under paragraphs 12(3)(a), (b) and (f) — that is, pregnancy (maternity) benefits, parental benefits, and benefits for caring for a critically ill adult. The bill also repeals subsection 12(7) and Schedule IV, related provisions that set out combined maximums.

Benefit period extension: A new paragraph 10(10)(c.1) adds being "in receipt of benefits paid because of pregnancy under section 22 or parental benefits under section 23" to the list of grounds on which a benefit period may be extended. Related wording in subsections 10(13.02) and 23(3.22), dealing with extensions of up to 26 weeks where regular and parental benefits are combined, is restated.

Critically ill adults: The maximum goes from 15 to 26 weeks in the provisions for employees (sections 12(3)(f), 12(4.5), 23.3(6) and (7)) and, in parallel, for self-employed claimants (sections 152.062(6) and (7) and 152.14). Where two or more people share care for the same critically ill adult, the pool of weeks they can divide between them would likewise rise to 26 weeks within a 52-week period.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The main groups are new parents who claim EI maternity or parental benefits — particularly those who also draw regular benefits or other special benefits in the same benefit period and currently bump up against the 50-week combined ceiling — and people who take time away from work to care for or support a critically ill adult family member.

Because the critically ill adult provisions are amended in both the regular EI sections and the self-employed sections of the Act, the increase from 15 to 26 weeks would apply to self-employed people registered for EI special benefits as well as to employees.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It was introduced on October 21, 2025, in the 45th Parliament by Alexandre Boulerice.

Its status is listed as "outside the Order of Precedence." In the House of Commons, only a limited number of private members' items are placed in the Order of Precedence for debate and votes at any given time; a bill outside that list has been introduced and given first reading but has no scheduled debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one would need to be taken up for debate, pass the House and Senate, and receive Royal Assent before any of the changes described above took effect.

C-253.overview: Bill C-253 would require the federal Minister of Finance to design a national plan — a "framework" — for a guaranteed livable basic income available to everyone in Canada over the age of 17, including temporary workers, permanent residents and refugee claimants. Importantly, the bill does not itself create a basic income program or send anyone money; it directs the Minister to consult widely, produce a plan, table it in Parliament within one year, and report back regularly on how well it is working. The framework would have to set income levels that reflect the cost of living in different regions, establish national standards for accompanying health and social supports, and make clear that people would not have to work, train or study to qualify. It would also have to ensure that existing benefits for health or disability-related needs are not cut back. As a private member's bill currently "outside the Order of Precedence," it has not yet reached the stage where it would be debated and voted on in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's central requirement is procedural: it obliges the Minister of Finance to develop a national framework for implementing a guaranteed livable basic income program across Canada for any person over 17. The bill's preamble states that such a program would help eradicate poverty, improve income equality, health conditions and educational outcomes, and support the transition to an economy responding to the climate crisis.

The legislation itself does not set a dollar amount, create an application process, or allocate funding. Those details would be worked out through the framework the Minister is directed to produce and report on.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The framework must include four specific elements. First, it must determine what counts as a "livable" basic income in each region of Canada, based on the goods and services needed for a dignified and healthy life and what those cost in accessible markets. Second, it must create national standards for health and social supports that complement the income program and guide how provinces implement it. Third, it must ensure that participation in education, training or the labour market is not a condition of qualifying. Fourth, it must ensure the program does not reduce services or benefits meant to address exceptional needs related to health or disability.

In developing the framework, the Minister must consult the Minister of Health, ministers responsible for employment, social development and disability, provincial representatives in health, disability, education and social development, Indigenous elders, Indigenous governing bodies, and other stakeholders including policy experts and specialists in existing basic income programs.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and timelines
deepDive.body:
The Minister would have one year after the Act comes into force to prepare a report setting out the framework — including social, health and economic conclusions and recommendations — and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed. The report must then be published on the Department of Finance website within 10 days of tabling.

Two years after that first report is tabled, and every year afterward, the Minister must review how effective the framework has been, again in consultation with the same groups, and table a further report with findings and recommendations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The framework is aimed at all persons in Canada over the age of 17, and the bill explicitly names temporary workers, permanent residents and refugee claimants as included. Because income support, health care, education and social services are areas where federal and provincial responsibilities overlap, the bill builds in mandatory consultation with provincial representatives and with Indigenous elders and Indigenous governing bodies — defined as entities authorized to act for Indigenous groups holding rights recognized under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

People receiving disability- or health-related benefits are addressed directly through the requirement that the framework not reduce supports tied to exceptional needs.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
C-253 is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Lori Idlout, introduced in 2025. Private members' bills are put forward by individual MPs rather than the government, and they compete for limited debate time. This bill is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has not been drawn into the queue for House debate and second reading; bills in that position often do not advance.

The bill also reflects a broader pattern in Canadian legislation of "national framework" bills, which direct a minister to consult, plan and report rather than directly creating or funding a program. Any actual guaranteed basic income would require separate decisions on funding and design, and would involve provincial governments given their role in social assistance and health services.

C-254.overview: Bill C-254 is a private member's bill from MP Leah Gazan that would add a new hate-propaganda offence to the Criminal Code. It would make it a crime to wilfully promote hatred against Indigenous peoples by condoning, denying, downplaying or justifying Canada's Indian residential school system, or by misrepresenting facts about it, when those statements are made outside of private conversation. The offence would carry a maximum of two years in prison if prosecuted as an indictable offence, or lesser penalties as a summary conviction offence, and prosecutions could only proceed with the Attorney General's consent. The bill also sets out four defences, including truth, good-faith religious opinion, and statements on matters of public interest reasonably believed to be true. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is a long way from becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends section 319 of the Criminal Code, the section that already deals with publicly inciting or wilfully promoting hatred against identifiable groups. It inserts a new subsection 319(2.01) creating a specific offence: wilfully promoting hatred against Indigenous peoples by condoning, denying, downplaying or justifying the Indian residential school system in Canada, or by misrepresenting facts relating to it, through statements communicated other than in private conversation.

The offence is a 'hybrid' one, meaning the Crown can choose how to proceed. If prosecuted as an indictable offence, the maximum penalty is two years' imprisonment; it can alternatively be prosecuted as a summary conviction offence, which carries lower penalties. 'Indigenous peoples' would be defined using the existing constitutional definition of 'aboriginal peoples of Canada' in subsection 35(2) of the Constitution Act, 1982.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and defences
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new subsection 319(3.11) listing four defences that mirror those already available for existing hate-promotion offences. A person cannot be convicted if: the statements they communicated were true; they were, in good faith, expressing or arguing an opinion on a religious subject or based on a religious text; the statements were relevant to a subject of public interest whose discussion was for the public benefit and they had reasonable grounds to believe them true; or they were, in good faith, pointing out matters that produce hatred toward Indigenous peoples for the purpose of having those matters removed.

Two further safeguards and procedural rules apply. First, no prosecution can be started without the consent of the Attorney General — the same gatekeeping requirement that applies to other hate-propaganda charges. Second, the bill updates the Criminal Code's forfeiture provision (allowing items used to commit the offence to be forfeited to the Crown) and the exemption from seizure of communication facilities so that these existing rules also cover the new offence.

deepDive.heading: Who it would affect
deepDive.body:
The offence targets public communication rather than private speech: statements made 'other than in private conversation' — which in practice would cover things like public speeches, broadcasts, publications and online posts. Because the offence requires that hatred be promoted 'wilfully,' the Crown would have to prove intent, not merely that a person made an inaccurate or unpopular statement about residential schools.

The protected group is Indigenous peoples as defined in section 35(2) of the Constitution Act, 1982, which covers the Indian, Inuit and Métis peoples of Canada. The Attorney General consent requirement means the number of prosecutions would depend on prosecutorial discretion.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Section 319 of the Criminal Code already prohibits inciting hatred in a public place likely to lead to a breach of the peace, and wilfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group. This bill does not replace those provisions; it adds a distinct offence aimed specifically at speech that denies or minimizes the residential school system.

The bill includes a coordinating amendment addressing what happens if Bill C-9, the Combatting Hate Act, also becomes law. If both pass, the forfeiture, seizure-exemption and Attorney General consent provisions would be rewritten to cover the new offences created by each bill so the sections work together.

As of its introduction on October 31, 2025, Bill C-254 is listed as a private member's bill 'Outside the Order of Precedence,' meaning it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for second reading debate. Most private members' bills do not become law.

C-255.overview: Bill C-255 is a private member's bill from MP Kelly Block that would add a new offence provision to section 430 of the Criminal Code, the section dealing with "mischief" — that is, damaging, destroying, defacing or interfering with property. The new provision would create a specific offence for mischief committed against religious property: buildings used primarily for worship (the bill names churches, mosques, synagogues and temples), objects associated with worship inside or on the grounds of such buildings, and cemeteries. Anyone convicted would face a mandatory minimum penalty of at least $1,000 in compensation to the property owner, with escalating mandatory jail time for repeat convictions (at least 14 days for a second offence and at least 30 days for each subsequent one). Maximum penalties would be up to 10 years in prison if the Crown proceeds by indictment, or up to two years less a day on summary conviction. The bill was introduced on November 6, 2025 and is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning MPs have not yet voted to send it to committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes a single change: it inserts a new subsection (4.12) into section 430 of the Criminal Code, immediately after the existing subsection (4.11). Section 430 is the general mischief provision, which covers destroying, damaging, defacing or obstructing the lawful use of property.

The new subsection singles out mischief against religious property and sets out its own penalty structure, including minimum punishments that a judge would have to impose on conviction.

deepDive.heading: What property is covered
deepDive.body:
The offence would apply to three categories: (1) a building or structure, or part of one, that is primarily used for religious worship — the bill gives churches, mosques, synagogues and temples as examples; (2) an object associated with religious worship located in or on the grounds of such a building; and (3) cemeteries.

The listed places of worship are given as examples rather than an exhaustive list, so the test is whether a building or structure is "primarily used for religious worship."

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the penalties
deepDive.body:
The offence is a "hybrid" offence, meaning the Crown could choose to prosecute it either as an indictable offence (more serious process) or by summary conviction (less serious process). The maximum penalty would be up to 10 years' imprisonment by indictment, or up to two years less a day on summary conviction.

What is distinctive is the mandatory minimum punishment, which would apply no matter which route the Crown chooses. A first offence would require the offender to compensate the property owner at least $1,000. A second offence would require at least $1,000 in compensation plus at least 14 days in jail. Each subsequent offence would require at least $1,000 in compensation plus at least 30 days in jail. Mandatory minimums remove a judge's discretion to impose a lighter sentence than the floor set out in the law.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would affect anyone charged with damaging or defacing a place of worship, religious objects on those premises, or a cemetery — and, on the other side, the owners of that property, who would be entitled to court-ordered compensation of at least $1,000 on conviction.

It would also affect prosecutors and judges, who would have less flexibility in sentencing for this category of offence than they have under the general mischief rules, because of the mandatory minimums.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The fact that the new provision is added after subsection (4.11) indicates that section 430 already contains several specialized mischief provisions; this bill layers an additional, religious-property-specific offence on top of the existing framework. As drafted, the text of the new subsection does not refer to the offender's motive — it turns on the type of property damaged rather than on why the damage was done.

C-255 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. It is at second reading, the stage where the House debates the bill in principle and decides whether to send it to committee for study. Private members' bills face limited debate time and many do not become law; no changes take effect unless the bill passes both the House of Commons and the Senate and receives royal assent.

C-256.overview: Bill C-256 is a private member's bill from MP Gord Johns that would end what is often called the "gold-digger clause" in several federal pension laws. Under current rules, if a member of the Canadian Forces, the RCMP, the federal public service, the judiciary or Parliament marries or begins living common-law after turning 60 or after retiring, their spouse or partner is generally not entitled to a survivor pension when they die. The bill would repeal those age- and retirement-based restrictions in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Judges Act, the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, the Public Service Superannuation Act and the RCMP Superannuation Act, and make related changes to the Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985 and the Pooled Registered Pension Plans Act. It would also cancel the existing "optional survivor benefit" arrangements, under which affected pensioners could buy coverage for a late-life spouse by permanently reducing their own pension. The bill is at an early stage: it was introduced on November 7, 2025 and sits outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not yet been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's stated purpose is to allow the survivor of an eligible person to receive pension benefits after that person's death "even if the person and the survivor married or began cohabiting in a conjugal relationship after the person attained the age of 60 years or retired." It does this by repealing the specific provisions in each federal pension statute that currently exclude such spouses and partners.

In the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, for example, the bill rewrites the definition of "survivor" so it simply covers a person who was married to the member immediately before death, or who was living with them in a conjugal relationship for at least one year immediately before death — with no reference to when the relationship began. A parallel change is made to the definition that applies to the spouse or partner of a Prime Minister or former Prime Minister.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The bill repeals the sections that create the post-60 or post-retirement bar on survivor benefits: section 31(1) of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, subsection 44(4) of the Judges Act, sections 25 and 45 of the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act, subsection 26(1) of the Public Service Superannuation Act and subsection 19(1) of the RCMP Superannuation Act, along with related regulation-making powers.

It also repeals the "optional survivor benefit" provisions (such as section 25.1 of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, section 44.2 of the Judges Act, section 13.1 of the Public Service Superannuation Act and section 14.1 of the RCMP Superannuation Act), which let pensioners in this situation elect to take a smaller pension in exchange for coverage for their spouse. Transitional provisions state that anyone who had made such an election is deemed to have revoked it on the day the bill comes into force. Because these late-life spouses would now count as survivors, the bill also adjusts the children's allowance formulas in several of the Acts, which pay a larger amount to children when there is no eligible surviving spouse.

deepDive.heading: Private-sector and pooled plans
deepDive.body:
Beyond the federal public-sector plans, the bill amends two laws governing federally regulated private-sector pensions. Under the Pension Benefits Standards Act, 1985, it rewrites the survivor's entitlement to variable benefits from a defined contribution account, and changes the joint-and-survivor pension rule so that it applies where a member has a spouse or common-law partner at the time the pension starts "or at any time after it commences to be paid."

A similar change is made to the Pooled Registered Pension Plans Act, restating a survivor's entitlement to variable payments from a deceased member's account. These entitlements remain subject to the applicable regulations and to the Income Tax Act.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would primarily affect the spouses and common-law partners of retired Canadian Forces members, RCMP members, federal public servants, federally appointed judges and MPs (including former Prime Ministers) — specifically those whose relationship began after the pensioner turned 60 or retired. It would also affect pensioners who had already elected to reduce their own pension to buy optional survivor coverage, since those elections would be treated as revoked.

Members and survivors under federally regulated private-sector plans and pooled registered pension plans would be affected by the changes to the joint-and-survivor and variable-benefit rules.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It was introduced on November 7, 2025 and is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," so it has not been scheduled for second reading debate and has not been voted on. Most private members' bills do not become law.

The restrictions the bill targets are long-standing features of federal pension legislation and have been the subject of ongoing public discussion, particularly among veterans' organizations, which commonly refer to the rule as the "marriage after 60" or "gold-digger" clause. The bill text itself does not include a costing estimate or a statement of rationale beyond its summary.

C-257.overview: Bill C-257 is a private member's bill from MP Roman Baber that would add a new criminal offence to Canada's Criminal Code: wilfully promoting a terrorist activity, a terrorist group, or any activity of a terrorist group by communicating statements. The maximum penalty would be five years in prison, and the offence would be indictable (the more serious category of criminal charge). Notably, the bill says a person could be convicted even if their statements were general rather than specific, and even if no one was actually persuaded to take part in terrorism. It also builds in several defences — including truth, good-faith religious opinion, and statements on subjects of public interest — modelled on the existing defences for hate-speech offences. Because the bill sits outside the Order of Precedence, it has not been scheduled for debate and is unlikely to advance without that changing.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates a new section 83.171 in the Criminal Code, placed among the existing terrorism offences dealing with participating in, facilitating, instructing and harbouring terrorism. The new offence covers anyone who, "by communicating statements, wilfully promotes any terrorist activity or terrorist group, or any activity of a terrorist group." It is an indictable offence carrying a maximum of five years' imprisonment.

The word "wilfully" means the promotion must be intentional rather than accidental. The terms "communicating" and "statements" are borrowed from subsection 319(7) of the Criminal Code, the provision used for the existing hate-propaganda offences.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Subsection (2) clarifies how far the offence reaches: a person can be convicted whether their statements relate specifically or only generally to a terrorist activity or group, and whether or not the statements actually encouraged or instigated anyone to take part in terrorism. In other words, no proven real-world effect would be required.

Subsection (3) sets out four defences. A person cannot be convicted if: the statements were true; they were made in good faith while expressing or arguing an opinion on a religious subject or based on a religious text; the statements were relevant to a subject of public interest whose discussion was for the public benefit and the person reasonably believed them to be true; or the person, in good faith, intended to point out material promoting terrorism so that it could be removed.

deepDive.heading: Related technical amendments
deepDive.body:
Three other changes make the new offence fit into the existing Criminal Code framework. First, the definition of "terrorism offence" in section 2 is updated so the new offence counts as one, which triggers other terrorism-related consequences elsewhere in the Code. Second, section 83.26 is amended so that a sentence for the new offence (other than life imprisonment) must be served consecutively to — that is, on top of — certain other sentences.

Third, the offence is added to the list in section 183, which is the list of offences for which police may seek judicial authorization for wiretaps and other interception of private communications. The heading before section 83.18 is also reworded to add "Promoting" to the list of conduct covered by that part of the Code.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The offence would apply to anyone in Canada who communicates statements promoting terrorist activity or a listed terrorist group. Because it targets speech rather than conduct, it would potentially affect online posts, public speeches, published material and other communications. The built-in defences are aimed at protecting truthful statements, religious discussion, good-faith public-interest debate, and people flagging extremist content for removal.

Police and prosecutors would gain a new charge to lay in cases involving pro-terrorism speech, along with access to interception powers for investigating it.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, introduced on November 17, 2025, meaning it comes from an individual MP rather than the government. Its status is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has not been drawn into the queue of private members' business scheduled for House debate. Bills in this position typically do not proceed to a vote unless and until they enter that queue.

The bill's structure closely mirrors Canada's existing hate-propaganda provisions (section 319), borrowing both their definitions of "communicating" and "statements" and a similar list of defences. As with any new speech-related offence, the interaction between the offence and the Charter's guarantee of freedom of expression would be a central question in any parliamentary study or subsequent litigation, though the bill text itself does not address that issue.

C-258.overview: Bill C-258 is a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Rhéal Éloi Fortin that would write the Supreme Court of Canada's 2016 R. v. Jordan rules on trial delay directly into the Criminal Code. Under Jordan, criminal charges can be thrown out ("stayed") if a case takes longer than 30 months in superior court or 18 months in provincial court, unless the Crown can point to exceptional circumstances. The bill would put those same time limits in the law, along with the rule that delays caused or accepted by the defence don't count. Its most significant change is an exception: the time limits would not apply at all to "primary designated offences" — a category of serious crimes already defined in the Criminal Code. To make that exception stick, the bill invokes section 33 of the Charter — the notwithstanding clause — so that the exception operates despite the Charter right to be tried within a reasonable time. As of the material provided, the bill is outside the Order of Precedence, meaning it has not been scheduled for debate.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new part to the Criminal Code (Part XVI.1, following section 529.5) titled "Reasonable Time for Trial Before Superior or Provincial Court." Its stated purpose is to codify — that is, put into written statute — the analytical framework the Supreme Court set out in R. v. Jordan, and to create exceptions to that framework.

Currently these rules exist as judge-made law flowing from paragraph 11(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees anyone charged with an offence the right to be tried within a reasonable time. The bill would place equivalent rules in legislation and then carve out a category of offences from them.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the time ceilings
deepDive.body:
New section 529.6 would require a superior court judge to stay proceedings if more than 30 months pass between the day a charge is laid and the actual or expected end of trial. For provincial court, the ceiling is 18 months. In both cases, the stay is avoided if the prosecutor establishes that the delay is reasonable by showing that exceptional circumstances exist.

Subsection (3) provides that any delay caused solely or directly by the defence's own conduct, or that the defence waives, does not count toward the ceilings. These figures and rules mirror the framework the Supreme Court laid out in Jordan.

deepDive.heading: The exception and the notwithstanding clause
deepDive.body:
Subsection (4) states that the 30-month and 18-month ceilings do not apply to a "primary designated offence" as defined in section 487.04 of the Criminal Code — an existing list used elsewhere in the Code (in the DNA data bank provisions) that covers a range of serious offences. In practice, this means accused persons facing those charges would not be able to rely on the statutory ceilings to have proceedings stayed.

Subsection (5) then invokes subsection 33(1) of the Charter — the "notwithstanding clause" — declaring that the exception operates despite paragraph 11(b) of the Charter, the right to be tried within a reasonable time. Section 33 allows Parliament or a provincial legislature to shield legislation from certain Charter challenges; such declarations expire after five years unless re-enacted.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would affect people charged with criminal offences, prosecutors, defence counsel and the courts. For most offences, the practical rules would remain similar to what courts already apply under Jordan, but they would be found in statute rather than case law. For those charged with primary designated offences, the statutory ceilings would not be available, and the bill's notwithstanding declaration is intended to prevent the Charter's trial-within-a-reasonable-time guarantee from being used to obtain a stay in those cases.

Provincial and superior courts across the country would apply the new provisions, since criminal law is federal and applies nationally.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
R. v. Jordan is a 2016 Supreme Court decision that set presumptive ceilings on how long criminal cases may take before delay is considered unreasonable, and it has led to stays of proceedings in some cases, including serious ones. Bills of this kind respond to that ongoing debate about court delays; this one does so by putting the ceilings in the Criminal Code while removing a set of serious offences from their reach.

This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but is not currently scheduled for debate or votes. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the text described here is the bill as introduced, not law.

C-260.overview: Bill C-260 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Garnett Genuis that would add a new offence to the Criminal Code relating to medical assistance in dying (MAID). Under the bill, a federal or provincial government officer or employee who is in a position of trust or authority over someone because of their job would commit a crime if they brought up MAID with that person without being asked. The offence would not apply to doctors, registered nurses or nurse practitioners, and it applies only when the official knows the person has not specifically requested such a discussion. The stated aim, reflected in the bill's short title, is to protect people who are not seeking MAID from feeling pressured toward it by officials they rely on. The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not been passed and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Criminal Code by inserting a new section, 241.301, immediately after the existing section 241.3. It creates a new criminal offence of initiating an unsolicited discussion about the availability of medical assistance in dying with a person, when that discussion is started by certain government officials.

The offence is punishable on summary conviction, which in Canadian criminal law is the category used for less serious offences. The bill text provided does not set out a specific penalty amount or term, so the general summary conviction rules of the Criminal Code would apply.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and conditions
deepDive.body:
For the offence to apply, several conditions must all be met. First, the person raising MAID must be an officer or employee of the Government of Canada or of a province. Second, they must, by virtue of their profession, be in a position of trust or authority towards the person they are speaking with. Third, they must know that the person has not specifically requested to have that discussion with them.

The bill also carves out an explicit exception: it does not apply to medical practitioners or registered nurses, including nurse practitioners. In other words, health-care providers in those categories could still raise the topic of MAID without committing this offence.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill targets public servants and other government officers or employees who deal with the public in roles of trust or authority — a category that could include a wide range of federal and provincial staff, though the bill itself does not list specific job titles beyond excluding doctors and registered and nurse practitioners.

Indirectly, it affects people who interact with government officials and who may be eligible for, or perceived as eligible for, MAID. The bill frames the concern as protecting people who have not asked about MAID from having it raised with them by someone in a position of authority over them.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
Bill C-260 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. Private members' bills face a more limited path through Parliament than government bills and many do not become law. The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, the stage where MPs debate the general principle of the bill before any committee study or votes at later stages.

The bill builds on the existing MAID provisions already in the Criminal Code, which include section 241.3 and related sections. It does not change who is eligible for MAID or how MAID is provided; it only addresses who may initiate a conversation about it and under what circumstances doing so would be a criminal offence.

C-259.overview: Bill C-259, the Fair Representation Act, is a private member's bill from NDP MP Heather McPherson that would amend the Canada Labour Code — the law governing labour relations in federally regulated workplaces such as banks, airlines, railways, telecommunications and interprovincial trucking. Its goal is to make sure unions are genuinely independent of the employers they bargain with. The bill spells out, for the first time in the Code's text, what counts as an employer "dominating or influencing" a union: taking part in or interfering with a union's formation, administration or representation of employees, or giving a union financial or other support. Any union found to be dominated or influenced could not be certified as a bargaining agent, and an existing certification would have to be revoked; employers who break the rule could face fines of up to $100,000 on summary conviction. The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not been passed and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill rewrites parts of the Canada Labour Code dealing with the certification of unions. Under the current system, the Canada Industrial Relations Board (the "Board") certifies a union as the exclusive bargaining agent for a group of workers. This bill adds an explicit definition of employer domination or influence and makes the absence of such domination a condition of certification.

Specifically, new subsection 94(1.1) states that an employer, or someone acting for an employer, dominates or influences a union if they directly or indirectly (a) participate in or interfere with the formation or administration of a union or with its representation of employees, or (b) contribute financial or other support to a union. Section 94(1) is reworded as a flat prohibition: no employer or person acting on an employer's behalf shall dominate or influence a trade union.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Certification: The Board could not certify a union it is satisfied is dominated or influenced, and any collective agreement between that union and the employer would be treated as not being a collective agreement under the Code. A new certification requirement (section 28(d)) also requires the Board to be satisfied that the union is not dominated or influenced and that it is governed by members elected by the employees in the proposed bargaining unit.

Revoking certification: A new section 40.1 lets any group of employees apply at any time to have a union's certification revoked on domination grounds. The Board may launch an inquiry on its own, and must do so if at least 25% of employees in the bargaining unit apply in writing. If the Board concludes the union is dominated or influenced, it must revoke the certification. Applications generally cannot be made during a lawful strike or lockout without the Board's consent.

Penalties: A new section 100.01 makes contravening the prohibition an offence punishable on summary conviction by a fine of up to $100,000. The bill also extends the existing administrative monetary penalty regulation-making power so it can cover subsection 94(1). Related sections (41 and 42) are updated so the new revocation route fits with existing rules, including for councils of trade unions.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The Canada Labour Code applies to federally regulated employers and their employees — sectors such as banking, air and rail transport, shipping, telecommunications, broadcasting, and federal Crown corporations. Provincially regulated workplaces, which make up most of the Canadian workforce, are governed by provincial labour laws and would not be directly affected.

Within that federal sector, the bill would affect employers (who face new explicit prohibitions and potential fines), unions seeking or holding certification (who must show independence and member-elected governance), and employees, who gain a new mechanism to challenge a union they believe is controlled by their employer.

deepDive.heading: Context and stated rationale
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble sets out Parliament's stated reasoning: that collective bargaining is a cornerstone of fair labour relations; that workers have the right to freely choose representatives independent of their employer; that employer domination undermines that right, suppresses wages and erodes trust in bargaining; and that every certified bargaining agent should be independent, democratic and accountable to its members.

The Code already contained a provision (section 25) barring certification of employer-dominated unions; the bill's contribution is to define what domination and influence mean, add an explicit revocation process, and attach financial penalties.

deepDive.heading: Timing, review and status
deepDive.body:
If passed, the Act would come into force 30 days after receiving royal assent. The Minister of Labour would be required to review the new provisions and how they are working within five years, and to table a report in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed.

As a private member's bill at second reading, C-259 is at an early stage. It would still need to pass second reading, committee study, third reading in the House, and the full Senate process before becoming law; private members' bills historically face longer odds than government bills.

C-262.overview: Bill C-262 is a private member's bill from MP Dan Albas that would change the Canada Post Corporation Act to deal with shipping alcohol across provincial borders directly to consumers. It would require Canada Post to stop refusing to ship beer, wine and spirits between provinces to individual customers, and it would give Canada Post an exclusive legal privilege over that kind of interprovincial direct-to-consumer alcohol delivery — similar to the monopoly it already holds on letter mail. At the same time, the bill creates an exception so that private couriers officially designated as "trusted carriers" could also make those deliveries, with the federal Cabinet able to set rules such as age-verification and secure-handling standards. A public list of trusted carriers would have to be posted and kept current on the responsible minister's departmental website. The bill matters because it touches on a long-standing practical question for consumers and small wineries, breweries and distilleries: whether and how alcohol ordered from another province can actually be shipped to your door.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Canada Post Corporation Act in three connected ways. First, it adds a new section 5.1 stating that Canada Post "shall not refuse" to provide postal service within Canada for collecting, transmitting and delivering beer, wine or spirits interprovincially, direct to consumers. Second, it expands Canada Post's "exclusive privilege" — the legal monopoly that currently covers letters — to also cover interprovincial direct-to-consumer shipments of beer, wine and spirits. Third, it carves out an exception to that monopoly for carriers designated as "trusted carriers," and gives the Governor in Council (the federal Cabinet) authority to make regulations about how such carriers are designated and supervised.

The bill also adds definitions of "beer," "wine" and "spirits" to the Act, borrowing the meanings already used in the Excise Act and the Excise Act, 2001, so the terms line up with existing federal alcohol tax law.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 20.1 is the operational heart of the trusted-carrier system. It allows Cabinet to make regulations establishing the process and criteria for designating trusted carriers — the bill specifically mentions age-verification protocols and secure handling and delivery procedures as examples — to designate individual common carriers or entire classes of carriers, and to set oversight mechanisms for how those carriers handle interprovincial direct-to-consumer alcohol shipments.

Two transparency and transition features are notable. The Minister must publish a list of designated trusted carriers on the departmental website and update it within 30 days of any carrier gaining or losing its designation. And, if no regulations have been made yet, the Minister may designate a carrier or class of carriers as trusted on their own. The provisions come into force in stages: the definitions, the duty to serve, the initial monopoly provision and the regulation-making power take effect three months after royal assent, while the trusted-carrier exception and related amendments take effect one year after royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Consumers who want to order beer, wine or spirits from a producer in another province would be the most directly affected, as would wineries, breweries and distilleries that sell directly to customers by mail or courier. Canada Post would face a new obligation not to refuse this type of shipment, along with a new exclusive privilege in that market.

Private courier and delivery companies are also affected: under the bill, they could not carry interprovincial direct-to-consumer alcohol shipments unless they are designated as trusted carriers. Federal regulators — Cabinet and the responsible Minister — would gain new powers and duties to set standards, designate carriers, and maintain the public list.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual Member of Parliament rather than by the government. Its status is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not currently scheduled for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the text can change if the bill advances through committee study.

The bill's subject sits at the intersection of federal and provincial responsibilities: the federal government controls Canada Post and interprovincial matters, while provinces regulate liquor sales and distribution within their own borders. The bill itself does not address provincial liquor rules; it speaks only to postal service obligations, Canada Post's exclusive privilege, and the trusted-carrier framework described above.

C-263.overview: Bill C-263, the Silver Alert National Framework Act, is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Raquel Dancho that would require the federal Minister of Public Safety to create a national framework for "silver alerts" — emergency public notifications, similar in concept to Amber Alerts, issued when a vulnerable older person such as someone living with dementia goes missing. The bill does not itself create an alert system; instead, it directs the Minister to develop a coordinated national approach, in consultation with provinces, territories, police, alerting organizations and care providers, using the public alerting infrastructure that already exists in Canada. The framework would have to address issues such as when an alert should be issued, how alerts can cross provincial boundaries, privacy protections, and public education. The Minister would have to table the framework in Parliament within one year and review how well it is working within two years after that. The bill's preamble points to Canada's aging population and rising dementia rates, noting that a missing person with dementia who is not found within 12 hours faces a high risk of death.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill requires the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness to develop a national framework supporting a dedicated, coordinated silver alert system across Canada, aimed at the rapid and safe recovery of missing vulnerable older persons. It defines a "silver alert" as an emergency notification telling the public that a vulnerable older person, including a person with dementia, has gone missing, issued to help locate them as quickly as possible.

In developing the framework, the Minister must consult representatives of provincial and territorial governments responsible for public safety, as well as other interested parties including police forces, organizations that issue alerts, and care providers who serve vulnerable older people. This reflects the fact that emergency alerting and policing are largely provincial and territorial responsibilities, so a national approach depends on cooperation.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The framework must include measures to: make better and more consistent use of Canada's existing public alerting infrastructure, including wireless alerts sent to cellphones; harmonize the risk thresholds and criteria police must meet before issuing an alert (such as whether there are reasonable grounds to believe the person's health or safety is at risk and whether telling the public would help find them); improve the chances of locating a missing person no matter where in Canada they disappear; reduce the risk of alerts being issued inappropriately; allow for both geographically targeted alerts and alerts that cross provincial borders; set privacy guidelines on what personal information can be released and how long an alert lasts; and support public education and awareness so people know how to respond.

The bill also allows — but does not require — the Minister to enter into agreements with individual provinces or territories on the standards, guidelines and codes of practice for running a silver alert system.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and review
deepDive.body:
