Within one year of the Act coming into force, the Minister must prepare a report setting out the national framework and table it in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed. The report must then be published on a public website within 10 days of being tabled in both chambers.

Within two years after the report is tabled, the Minister must review how effective the framework has been and prepare a further report setting out conclusions and recommendations, including any updates or revisions the Minister thinks are appropriate.

deepDive.heading: Context and who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble cites Alzheimer Society of Canada projections that nearly one million Canadians will be living with dementia by 2030 and more than 1.7 million by 2050, and states that a person with dementia who is not found within 12 hours has a 50% probability of being found dead from drowning, severe hypothermia or dehydration. It notes that Canada currently has no nationally coordinated, centralized emergency alert framework for missing vulnerable older persons, and points to the existing National Alert Aggregation and Dissemination System — the technical backbone of Canada's National Public Alerting System — as the infrastructure a national approach would use.

Those most directly affected would be older Canadians at risk of going missing and their families and caregivers, along with police services, provincial and territorial public safety agencies, and broadcasters and telecommunications providers that carry public alerts. Members of the public would also be affected, since silver alerts would reach them through channels such as cellphone broadcasts.

deepDive.heading: Status
deepDive.body: C-263 is a private member's bill — legislation introduced by an individual MP rather than by the government. It is currently at the committee consideration stage in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading in the House and is being studied in detail by a committee, which may propose amendments. It would still need to complete the remaining stages in the House of Commons and pass the Senate before receiving Royal Assent and becoming law.

C-261.overview: Bill C-261 is a private member's bill from Bloc Québécois MP Claude DeBellefeuille that would raise Old Age Security (OAS) payments for all seniors aged 65 and over by about 10%, setting the basic full monthly pension at $808.45 (before the regular quarterly inflation adjustments). It would also make it easier for low-income seniors who still work to keep their Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS): the amount of employment or self-employment income that is ignored when calculating GIS would rise from $5,000 to $6,500, with half of the next $13,000 also exempt. In practice, the bill would extend to all pensioners the kind of 10% boost that currently applies only to those aged 75 and over, and it repeals the separate provisions that created that age-based top-up. The bill matters because OAS is a baseline income for nearly all Canadian seniors, and because the current two-tier structure (65–74 versus 75+) has been a recurring point of debate. As a private member's bill at second reading, it is still early in the legislative process and has not been adopted.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Old Age Security Act in two main ways. First, it sets the basic amount of the full monthly OAS pension at $808.45 for the payment quarter beginning July 1, 2025 — roughly a 10% increase over the base amount then payable to pensioners aged 65 to 74. Second, it increases the earnings exemption used in calculating the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the additional benefit paid to low-income OAS recipients.

The bill's own summary describes these two changes as its purpose: increasing the full pension for all pensioners aged 65 or older by 10%, and raising the GIS employment-income exemption from $5,000 to $6,500.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 2 replaces subsection 7(1) of the Act with the new base pension figure of $808.45 per month, and repeals subsection 7(5) — the provision that provides the existing 10% increase for pensioners aged 75 and over. Because the higher amount is written into the general base figure, the effect is to apply the increase to all pensioners rather than only to those 75 and older. Related provisions on voluntary deferral (subsection 7.1(2)) are restated to keep the 0.6% per-month increase for people who delay taking their pension, while subsections 7.1(5) and (6), which dealt with the 75+ top-up in deferral cases, are repealed.

Section 1 rewrites the GIS earnings exemption: for benefits payable for months after June 2025, the first $6,500 of combined employment and self-employment income would be fully excluded from the income calculation, plus half of the next $13,000 (the text caps the second deduction at $6,500). Sections 4 and 5 make consequential changes so that the allowance calculation in section 12 and the definition of "pension equivalent" in section 22 refer to the revised full pension amount.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The pension increase would apply to everyone receiving OAS, but the practical change is largest for pensioners aged 65 to 74, who currently receive the lower base amount. Pensioners 75 and over already receive a 10% top-up under the provision the bill repeals; the bill folds that higher level into the base pension for everyone.

The GIS change targets low-income seniors who continue to work or are self-employed. A larger exemption means more of their earnings are set aside before GIS is calculated, so the supplement is clawed back more slowly. Because the definition of the full pension is also used in calculating the Allowance under section 12 and the "pension equivalent" under section 22, other benefits tied to the OAS amount would reflect the higher figure as well.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, the stage where MPs debate the principle of the legislation before any committee study. It is a private member's bill rather than a government bill, which means it is not part of the government's legislative agenda; historically, only a small share of private members' bills become law, and measures that would require new federal spending face additional procedural requirements in Parliament.

A few technical features are worth noting for readers looking at the text: the dates in the bill refer to benefits payable after June 2025 and to the quarter beginning July 1, 2025, even though the bill was introduced later, and the text contains a spelling variant ("fourty-five") in the dollar amount. Amounts set in the Act are normally adjusted quarterly for inflation under other provisions that the bill does not change, so the $808.45 figure would serve as the starting point rather than a permanent fixed amount. This explainer describes only what the bill text provides and does not assess its cost or likelihood of passage.

C-264.overview: Bill C-264 is a very short private member's bill that would repeal the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, the 2019 federal law that restricts large oil tankers from stopping or unloading along British Columbia's northern coast. The bill contains a single operative clause: it simply erases that law from the statute books, with no replacement rules or transition measures included in the text. If passed, the current federal ban on certain oil tanker traffic in that region would end, and shipping there would fall back on other general marine and environmental laws that remain in force. The bill is sponsored by MP David McKenzie and is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it is still at an early stage and has not become law. It matters because the tanker moratorium sits at the centre of long-running debates over oil exports, coastal shipping, marine protection and Indigenous and coastal community interests in northern B.C.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The entire substance of Bill C-264 is one sentence: "The Oil Tanker Moratorium Act, chapter 26 of the Statutes of Canada, 2019, is repealed." A repeal means the law is cancelled outright and no longer has legal effect.

The bill adds nothing new. It does not create replacement restrictions, set conditions, phase in the change over time, or amend any other statute. Its only legal effect, as written, is to remove the 2019 Act.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 is the only clause. The bill's official summary confirms the same thing in a single line: "This enactment repeals the Oil Tanker Moratorium Act."

Because the text is limited to the repeal, any questions about what rules would govern tanker traffic afterwards are not answered by this bill itself — those would depend on other existing federal laws and regulations that the bill does not touch.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties would be those connected to marine shipping of oil on the coast covered by the 2019 Act: shipping operators, oil and pipeline proponents, ports and terminals, and the coastal and Indigenous communities, and environmental and marine interests along that coastline.

The bill's text does not itself describe these effects or single out any group; this description reflects the subject matter of the law being repealed rather than provisions written into Bill C-264.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-264 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP (David McKenzie) rather than by the government. Private members' bills follow a more limited timetable and a smaller share of them become law compared with government bills.

The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons — the stage where MPs debate the bill's general principle and vote on whether to send it to committee for study. It would still need to clear committee, report stage and third reading in the House, pass the Senate, and receive Royal Assent before taking effect.

C-266.overview: Bill C-266 is a private member's bill from Liberal MP Parm Bains that would require the federal Minister of Employment and Social Development to build a "national framework" aimed at making it easier for skilled trades workers — electricians, welders, plumbers and the like — to work in any province or territory. Because training, certification and licensing of trades are handled separately by each province, a worker certified in one place can face extra paperwork, testing or delays when moving to another. The bill would require at least nine months of consultation with provinces, trades regulators, unions, employers, Indigenous organizations and colleges, and would have the Minister catalogue every skilled trade in Canada, map how provincial credentials compare, and propose ways to harmonize and streamline them. The Minister would have to table the finished framework in Parliament within a year and report on progress every year after that, with a parliamentary committee review after five years. The bill is a planning-and-reporting measure: it explicitly respects provincial jurisdiction and does not itself change any licensing rules.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill directs the Minister of Employment and Social Development to develop a national framework on skilled trades and labour mobility, with the stated goal of reducing barriers that stop certified tradespeople from working across provincial borders. It defines a "skilled trade" broadly as any trade that a province recognizes as certified or regulated, including trades covered by the Interprovincial Standards Red Seal Program or the Blue Seal business-competency certification.

Importantly, the bill creates a process, not new national licensing rules. The preamble states that Parliament intends to modernize and harmonize credential recognition "while respecting provincial and territorial jurisdiction over training, certification and labour market regulation." Any actual changes to how trades are certified would still have to be made by the provinces and territories.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Consultation: Before finalizing the framework, the Minister must consult for at least nine months with provincial governments, trades regulatory bodies, industry and employer associations, unions and apprenticeship organizations, Indigenous governing bodies and organizations, and training institutions such as colleges.

Contents of the framework: It must include a complete list of skilled trades across Canada, compare and map equivalencies between provincial standards and credentials, and set out measures to harmonize standards, cut duplication and red tape in getting credentials recognized between provinces, modernize certification to reflect new technologies and emerging trades, support ongoing collaboration with partners, and promote public awareness of the trades.

Reporting and review: The framework must be tabled in both houses of Parliament within one year of the Act coming into force and posted on the department's website within 30 days. Annual progress reports follow, covering implementation, mobility and harmonization progress, results of work with the provinces, and the Minister's assessment of what should be changed. A Senate, House or joint committee must conduct a comprehensive review within five years and report back with any recommended changes.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most direct interest lies with certified tradespeople and apprentices who want to move between provinces for work, and with the employers, contractors and project owners who hire them — particularly in sectors the preamble singles out, such as housing construction, transportation infrastructure and energy projects.

Provincial and territorial governments and trades regulators would be consulted partners rather than parties bound by the framework. Unions, apprenticeship organizations, Indigenous governing bodies and organizations, and colleges and training institutions are also named as required participants in the consultation process. Federally, the obligations fall on the Minister of Employment and Social Development and the department's staff.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill C-266 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is at second reading in the House of Commons, an early stage; most private members' bills do not become law, and the text can change if it advances to committee.

The bill builds on existing mechanisms rather than replacing them — it references the Red Seal Program, the long-standing interprovincial standards system for trades, and Blue Seal business-competency certification. Its approach of mandating consultations, a tabled framework and recurring progress reports follows a template used by a number of other recent "national framework" private members' bills in Parliament. Because it imposes reporting and consultation duties rather than regulatory changes, the practical effect would depend heavily on how much provincial cooperation the process attracts.

C-265.overview: Bill C-265 is a private member's bill from MP Marcus Powlowski that would amend the federal Food and Drugs Act to create a new "List of Therapeutic Products Pre-approved for Special Access." Canada already has a Special Access Programme that lets doctors request drugs or devices that aren't sold here, but each request is handled case by case; this bill would let the Minister of Health pre-approve certain non-marketed drugs, devices or natural health products for specific uses, so doctors could order them directly from a manufacturer without a separate approval each time. The list would target serious or life-threatening conditions, including rare diseases, where no comparable product is available on the Canadian market. The bill also adds reporting duties for doctors, manufacturers and importers, requires an annual public report, and includes safeguards so companies cannot use the list to avoid seeking normal regulatory approval. The bill is currently at committee stage in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading but is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill inserts a new part into the Food and Drugs Act requiring the Minister of Health to establish and maintain a published list of "non-marketed" therapeutic products — products that either never received Canadian authorization or are no longer sold here — that are pre-approved for special access. The list must be posted on the Health Canada website and, for each product, set out its name, the uses it is approved for, and any limits on which practitioners may use it or in what settings.

The purpose is streamlined access: products may be listed for treating or preventing the progression of serious or life-threatening conditions, including rare diseases, and for situations where no comparable product is sold in Canada. The bill specifies that two products are not "comparable" if they differ significantly in cost, formulation, effectiveness, contraindications, or rates of adverse reactions or device incidents in particular populations.

deepDive.heading: How products get on and off the list
deepDive.body:
The Minister may add a product if it meets appropriate quality and safety standards and one of two conditions is met: for a new drug, it has already been the subject of a special-access letter of authorization under the Food and Drug Regulations for that use; for other products, it was previously authorized in Canada (and that authorization was not cancelled for safety reasons) or it is authorized by a foreign regulator the Minister considers comparable to Canada. Notably, for foreign-authorized products, the listed use does not have to match the foreign approval, but must be supported by generally accepted guidelines or clinical evidence. The Minister may restrict use to practitioners with specified training or to specified clinical settings, or attach conditions.

Products or uses can be removed if new safety concerns emerge, if the product gains full Canadian approval or starts being marketed here, if the manufacturer withdraws it internationally or stops production, or if it leads to misuse, diversion or public health risks. Removals must be published with reasons. Before creating or changing the list, the Minister must consult a non-partisan expert committee of medical researchers and clinicians — including specialists likely to use the products, such as those working with children — whose members serve without pay or expense reimbursement.

deepDive.heading: How access would work in practice
deepDive.body:
Doctors and other qualified practitioners could ask a manufacturer directly to sell them a specified quantity of a listed product for a patient in their care, using a form set by the Minister, provided the intended use matches the listed use. Importantly, the practitioner does not need to know the identity of the patient when making the request, which would allow stocking in advance. Manufacturers may sell, and licensed importers may import and distribute, listed products either in response to such a request or in anticipation of one, subject to any ministerial limits.

These sales, imports and distributions would be exempt from most of the Food and Drugs Act and its regulations, other than the new part itself. The Minister may, however, order that specific regulatory rules still apply to imports for storage, transportation, quality control, tracking and record keeping.

deepDive.heading: Oversight, reporting and safeguards
deepDive.body:
Practitioners who make a request must report to the Minister within 90 days, must supply further information if the Minister orders it, and can be barred from using a product — or limited in how they use it — if the Minister finds a significant risk to health or safety. Manufacturers must notify the Minister of each sale within 90 days, including the requesting practitioner's name, the shipping recipient's name and address, the product and its intended use, and the quantity supplied. Importers must similarly report imports within 90 days.

To prevent the list from becoming a substitute for full drug approval, the Minister may demand that a manufacturer explain why it has not submitted a product for regular regulatory approval; if the explanation is inadequate, the Minister may either keep the product listed until approval is obtained or remove it. The bill also requires the Minister to decide on outside submissions to add a product or use within 120 days, and to prepare and publish an annual report in the first three months of each year — developed with the expert committee, practitioners, pharmacists, hospitals and medical non-profits — on how well the list is working and how to improve it.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects, and context
deepDive.body:
The bill would most directly affect patients with serious, life-threatening or rare conditions who cannot obtain a suitable treatment in Canada, along with the physicians, pharmacists, hospitals and medical non-profit organizations that can nominate products for the list. Manufacturers and licensed importers would gain a clearer route to supply such products, but with new notification duties. Health Canada would take on the work of building the list, consulting the expert committee, ruling on submissions within 120 days, and reporting annually.

A separate clause states, "for greater certainty," that nothing in the Act prevents a licensed physician, in an emergency, from temporarily giving a patient in their care any therapeutic product lawfully made in or imported into Canada and available to them, if that is the best available treatment in their clinical judgment. The bill also adds regulation-making authority so the government can set rules about establishing, maintaining and publishing the list. As a private member's bill at committee stage, it may still be amended, and it must clear the remaining stages in both the House of Commons and the Senate before it could become law.

C-267.overview: Bill C-267 is a private member's bill that would require the federal Minister of Industry to develop a national framework aimed at making electronic products and essential home appliances — things like fridges, stoves, washing machines, heaters and communication devices — last longer and be easier to repair. The framework would have to be built in consultation with provincial consumer-protection officials and, where appropriate, consumer advocacy groups, and would cover topics such as minimum useful life, labelling, availability of replacement parts, access to repair tools and information, technical documentation, and how long software support lasts. Importantly, the bill itself does not impose rules on manufacturers or set penalties; it directs the Minister to design a framework and to discuss with the provinces what legislation might later be proposed. The Minister would have to table a report setting out the framework within 18 months, and review how well it is working within five years after that. The stated rationale is that Canadian households lose money when products fail or become unrepairable sooner than expected, and that clearer information about product lifespan supports a fairer, more competitive market.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates the National Framework on the Durability of Electronic Products and Essential Home Appliances Act. Its central requirement is that the Minister of Industry develop a national framework on the durability and repairability of electronic products and essential home appliances that are offered for sale, distributed or sold in Canada — whether made in Canada or imported.

This is a framework-and-reporting bill rather than a regulatory one. It obliges the government to consult, plan and report, but it does not itself create binding obligations for companies, inspection powers or fines. Any such rules would have to come later through separate legislation or regulation.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 lists what the framework must contain: measures to promote durability; measures to improve transparency about a product's useful life and about how to maintain and repair it; and national standards covering minimum useful life and the labelling of that information, maintenance and repair (including reasonably accessible parts, tools and information), how long replacement parts must remain available, technical documentation, and the duration of or conditions for software support. The framework must also include ways to inform consumers across Canada about these standards and must determine the responsibilities that manufacturers, importers and distributors owe to consumers.

Section 3(3) requires the Minister, during the provincial consultations, to discuss possible future legislative measures — including obligations on manufacturers, importers and distributors, inspection mechanisms, and penalties for non-compliance. Sections 4 and 5 set the timelines: a report setting out the framework within 18 months of the Act coming into force, tabled in both Houses within 15 sitting days and published on the Department of Industry website within 10 days of tabling; then a review of the framework's implementation and effectiveness within five years of that first tabling, with the same tabling and publication rules.

deepDive.heading: Key definitions
deepDive.body:
The bill defines an "essential home appliance" as a device intended for regular household use, including for food preservation, cooking, washing, heating or communication. "Useful life" is defined as the period during which a product may be used in a safe and functional manner under normal conditions of use. "Minister" means the Minister of Industry.

The bill does not separately define "electronic products," leaving the scope of that term to be worked out as the framework is developed.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Consumers are the stated focus: the preamble points to the costs households bear when devices and appliances have to be replaced prematurely, and to consumers' growing reliance on these products. If the framework leads to standards and labelling, buyers would get more information about expected lifespan, repair options and software support.

Manufacturers, importers and distributors are the businesses the framework would address, since it must determine their responsibilities to consumers and since the consultations must cover possible obligations, inspections and penalties for them. Provincial governments are also directly involved: consumer protection is largely a provincial responsibility, and the bill requires the Minister to consult provincial representatives responsible for consumer protection, and where appropriate consumer advocacy groups, in both developing and later reviewing the framework.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-267 is a private member's bill sponsored by MP Abdelhaq Sari, and is at the committee consideration stage in the House of Commons. Like all private members' bills, it must still clear committee, remaining House stages and the Senate before it could become law, and its text may be amended along the way.

The bill sits within the broader "right to repair" and product-durability policy discussion, and the preamble frames durability and repairability as ways to protect consumers, reduce household expenses, and support a competitive market. Because the bill sets out a consultation-and-reporting process rather than enforceable standards, its practical effect would depend on what the resulting framework contains and whether governments act on it.

C-268.overview: Bill C-268 is a private member's bill that aims to improve cellphone coverage in Canada, especially in rural, remote and Indigenous communities and along highways. It would require the CRTC to set up a process, within six months, to verify that the mobile coverage maps and data submitted by phone companies are actually accurate. It would also require the Minister of Industry to conduct a full review of the Spectrum Policy Framework for Canada — the federal document guiding how airwaves used by wireless networks are managed, last updated in 2007 — within 18 months, after consulting carriers, rural and Indigenous representatives, first responders and experts, and to report the results to Parliament. After that, the Minister would have to report to Parliament every five years on how well the Framework is working. The bill matters because coverage gaps affect everyday connectivity and emergency access, and because it would create a legal duty to keep the Framework current rather than leaving updates to government discretion.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has three main components. First, it directs the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to establish, within six months of the Act coming into force, a process for ensuring the accuracy of mobile network coverage data that Canadian carriers provide to it — including data on areas served and on deployment requirements. The bill specifies that this does not limit any of the CRTC's other existing powers or duties.

Second, it obliges the Minister of Industry to carry out a comprehensive review of the Spectrum Policy Framework for Canada within 18 months and to keep the Framework maintained and updated. Third, it sets ongoing reporting requirements, including a recurring five-year report to Parliament on how the Framework is being implemented and how effective it is.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the review and reporting rules
deepDive.body:
For the initial review, the Minister must consult telecommunications providers and spectrum licence holders, representatives of rural and remote municipalities and Indigenous communities, public safety agencies and first responders, telecom and spectrum researchers, the CRTC, and any other stakeholders the Minister considers appropriate. The resulting report must state the results of those consultations with particular attention to competition issues such as deployment requirements and the licensing of unused spectrum; assess connectivity in rural and remote areas and along numbered roads with a focus on public safety; take coverage data into account; and set out any changes the Minister thinks are needed to the Framework.

The bill also tells the Minister what to prioritize when proposing changes: connectivity — including for rural and remote areas and numbered roads — while taking into account that competition and market forces have so far not delivered coverage everywhere, and using the coverage data verified through the new CRTC process. Reports must be tabled in both the House of Commons and the Senate within the first 15 sitting days after completion, and published on the Department of Industry's website within 30 days of tabling.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Directly, the bill imposes duties on two federal bodies: the CRTC (to build a data-verification process) and the Minister of Industry (to review, update and report on the Framework). Canadian carriers, as defined in the Telecommunications Act, would have the coverage data they submit subject to a verification process.

Indirectly, the bill is aimed at residents of rural, remote and Indigenous communities and travellers on numbered highways, whose service the preamble describes as poor. Municipal representatives, Indigenous communities, emergency services and academic experts are given a formal role through the mandatory consultations.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The Spectrum Policy Framework for Canada is the federal government's guiding policy document for managing radio spectrum — the airwaves that wireless networks rely on. The bill's preamble notes that it was last updated in 2007, and argues that existing tools tied to conditions attached to spectrum licences have not been enough to close cellular coverage gaps, particularly in rural areas. The preamble also states that a lack of competition in the wireless sector may leave providers without sufficient incentive to build out networks in under-served areas.

The bill's stated purpose is to create, by statute, an ongoing legal obligation to maintain and update the Framework, rather than relying on periodic administrative decisions. As a private member's bill sponsored by MP Marianne Dandurand, it is currently at committee consideration in the House of Commons, meaning it has passed second reading but still requires further approval in both the House and the Senate before it could become law, and its text could be amended along the way.

C-269.overview: Bill C-269 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Greg McLean that would change the Income Tax Act to create a new "heat recovery tax credit." It would let Canadian corporations deduct 30% of the cost of new equipment they buy to capture waste heat from industrial processes and turn it into usable energy. Many industrial operations — refineries, manufacturing plants, processing facilities — release large amounts of heat as a by-product, and the credit is designed to make investment in equipment that recaptures that heat more financially attractive. The bill would slot the new credit alongside existing clean-economy tax credits (such as those for carbon capture, clean technology, clean hydrogen and clean electricity), and much of its text consists of technical cross-references adding the new credit to lists where those other credits already appear. As a private member's bill at second reading, it has not yet been debated to a conclusion or passed, and it is a long way from becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 127.431 to the Income Tax Act creating a "heat recovery tax credit." A taxable Canadian corporation that buys qualifying heat recovery equipment could deduct an amount equal to 30% of the equipment's capital cost from the tax it would otherwise owe for that year. To claim it, the corporation must file a prescribed form with prescribed information by its tax filing deadline.

The credit is described as non-refundable. That means it reduces tax payable rather than producing a cash payment to a company that owes no tax.

deepDive.heading: What counts as "qualifying heat recovery equipment"
deepDive.body:
The bill defines this as equipment acquired by a taxable Canadian corporation after December 31, 2025, used all or substantially all to recover heat produced by industrial processes and convert it in order to generate energy. Equipment whose primary function is generating energy in the first place is specifically excluded.

Two further conditions apply: the equipment must be intended for use exclusively in Canada, and it must be new — it cannot have been used, or acquired for use or lease, in Canada for any purpose before the corporation bought it. The credit is also unavailable for a taxation year if the equipment has been exported, sold or leased by the corporation before the end of that year.

deepDive.heading: Key technical rules
deepDive.body:
The bill includes safeguards against double-counting. The capital cost used to calculate the credit must be reduced by any non-government assistance the company received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably expect to receive in relation to the equipment. If that assistance is later repaid or never materializes, the amount is added back to the capital cost. Amounts deducted through the credit are also brought into existing rules that reduce a property's cost base and undepreciated capital cost, and are included in income under paragraph 12(1)(t) in later years — the same treatment applied to other investment tax credits.

Separate rules cover partnerships. A corporate partner can claim its reasonable share of a credit the partnership would have earned, but shares allocated in unreasonable proportions can be reset to a reasonable amount, and a limited partner's share cannot exceed its "at-risk amount" in the partnership. Assistance received by a partner in respect of partnership equipment is treated as having been received by the partnership.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The credit is limited to taxable Canadian corporations, including those operating through partnerships. It would not be available to individuals, and by its terms it targets businesses with industrial processes that produce recoverable waste heat.

Because the equipment must be new, intended for exclusive use in Canada, and acquired after December 31, 2025, the measure is aimed at future capital purchases rather than equipment already in service. Rules on amalgamations and wind-ups treat a successor corporation as a continuation of its predecessor for the purposes of the credit.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Much of the bill's length comes from housekeeping: adding references to the new section 127.431 into provisions that already list Canada's other investment tax credits — the CCUS (carbon capture, utilization and storage) credit, the clean technology credit, the clean hydrogen credit, the clean technology manufacturing credit and the clean electricity credit. This ensures the new credit interacts with the rest of the tax system the same way those credits do.

This is a private member's bill, not a government bill, and it is at second reading in the House of Commons. Private members' bills that would reduce federal revenue face additional procedural questions in Parliament, and the bill would still need to pass the House, the Senate and receive Royal Assent before taking effect.

C-270.overview: Bill C-270, titled the Stand on Guard Act, is a private member's bill from MP Sandra Cobena that would amend the Criminal Code's self-defence provisions (section 34). It would spell out that a person lawfully inside a home may use force — including lethal force — that they consider reasonably necessary to protect themselves or someone else from an intruder who has entered without legal right. It would also create two legal presumptions: that an intruder who knowingly entered unlawfully did so intending to use force against people inside, and that the legal conditions for a valid self-defence claim are met when force is used against such an intruder. In practical terms, the bill would shift the starting point in court so that a homeowner's use of force against an intruder is presumed justified unless evidence shows otherwise. The bill is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet been debated to a conclusion or become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes three targeted changes to section 34 of the Criminal Code, the provision that governs the defence of person (self-defence and defence of others). It does not repeal or replace existing self-defence law; it adds clarifying language and presumptions on top of it.

The changes apply specifically to situations involving a "dwelling-house" — a home — where the person using force is lawfully present and the other person has entered without being entitled by law to do so.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
New subsection 34(1.1) states "for greater certainty" that the act constituting the offence may involve force, including lethal force, that the person deems reasonably necessary to defend or protect themselves or another person against someone who has unlawfully entered a dwelling-house in which they are lawfully present.

New subsection 34(2.1) creates a presumption about intent: if the intruder knowingly entered without legal entitlement, that fact is treated as proof — in the absence of evidence to the contrary — that they entered intending to use force against a person lawfully in the home. New subsection 34(2.2) creates a presumption that the conditions for the self-defence provision in subsection 34(1) are met when force, including lethal force, is used against such an intruder. Both presumptions are rebuttable in the sense that subsection (2.1) is expressly subject to "evidence to the contrary."

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The provisions are aimed at people who are lawfully present in a home — such as residents, guests or others with a right to be there — and who use force against someone who has entered unlawfully. It would also affect people accused of an offence in those circumstances, since the presumptions change what must be established in a self-defence claim.

It would likewise affect police, prosecutors and courts, who apply section 34 when deciding whether charges are warranted and whether a self-defence claim succeeds. The bill's text does not address situations outside a dwelling-house.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, not a government bill. Private members' bills are introduced by individual MPs and, historically, relatively few become law; they must still pass all stages in the House of Commons and the Senate and receive Royal Assent.

The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, the stage where MPs debate the general principle of the legislation before deciding whether to send it to committee for detailed study. Nothing in the bill takes effect unless and until it completes the full legislative process.

C-272.overview: Bill C-272 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Dan Mazier that would change the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act — the federal law that governs illegal drugs — to create a minimum distance rule for supervised drug consumption sites. Under the bill, the federal government could not use regulations or exemptions to permit a site where people consume illegally obtained drugs under supervision if that site is within 500 metres of an elementary or secondary school, a daycare centre, or a playground. Existing permissions for sites inside that 500-metre zone would be cancelled when the law takes effect, and mobile sites would be barred from offering those services while inside the zone. The bill would come into force 180 days after receiving royal assent, giving affected sites and health authorities a transition period. It matters because supervised consumption sites currently operate only through special federal exemptions, and this bill would place a hard geographic limit on where those exemptions can apply.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
Supervised consumption sites can only operate legally because the federal government grants them an exemption from the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, which otherwise makes possessing certain drugs illegal. Bill C-272 would add a new section (54.2) to that Act stating that, despite anything else in the law, no regulation or exemption may have the effect of allowing such a site to be located within 500 metres of an elementary or secondary school, a daycare centre, or a playground.

The restriction is written to apply to sites providing services related to the consumption of any controlled substance or precursor that was obtained in a way not authorized under the Act — in other words, drugs from illegal sources rather than prescribed or otherwise lawful supplies.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Three elements make up the bill. First, the permanent restriction: federal regulations and exemptions cannot authorize a qualifying site within 500 metres of the listed locations. Second, a transitional rule: any exemption or authorization already in force on the day the law takes effect is revoked to the extent it covers a site inside the 500-metre zone. Third, a special rule for mobile sites: rather than being revoked outright, their exemptions are treated as automatically including a condition that services cannot be provided while the mobile site is within 500 metres of a school, daycare, or playground.

The bill would take effect 180 days after royal assent, meaning roughly six months would pass between final approval and enforcement.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties would be existing and proposed supervised consumption sites — both fixed locations and mobile services — along with the provincial health authorities, municipalities, and community organizations that operate them. Sites currently operating within 500 metres of a school, daycare, or playground would lose their federal exemption once the law came into force, unless they relocated.

The federal Minister of Health and Health Canada, which process exemption applications, would also be affected, since the bill removes their discretion to approve sites in the restricted zones. Schools, daycares, and neighbourhoods near existing or proposed sites are the communities the distance rule is framed around.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. Its status is listed as "outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has not yet been drawn for debate time in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills in this position do not advance unless they are selected through the lottery system that determines which ones get House consideration.

The bill does not change whether supervised consumption sites are legal in general, nor does it alter the criteria the Minister uses to assess applications beyond the location rule. It addresses only where such sites may be located relative to schools, daycares, and playgrounds.

C-271.overview: Bill C-271 is a private member's bill that would amend the Criminal Code to create new criminal offences aimed at metal theft — particularly copper and other metals stripped from power lines, rail lines, pipelines and similar infrastructure. It would make it a crime to traffic in (or possess for trafficking) scrap metal that a person knows was obtained through crime, with fines up to $25,000 and up to 10 years in prison, and it would create a separate, lesser offence for scrap metal dealers who are reckless or wilfully blind about where their metal came from. The bill would also add a new form of the offence of 'mischief' for damaging a physical component of essential infrastructure, and would require judges to treat certain factors — such as an interruption of essential services or danger to public safety — as aggravating circumstances at sentencing. The stated aim is to target not just the thieves but the resale market that makes metal theft profitable, and to respond more directly to damage that knocks out services people rely on. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, titled the Protecting Canada's Essential Infrastructure Metals Act, makes two main changes to the Criminal Code. First, it adds a set of new offences dealing with scrap metal that was obtained through crime — covering both people who traffic in it and scrap metal dealers who handle it without asking questions. Second, it adds a new offence of mischief (damage or interference) in relation to the physical components of 'essential infrastructure'.

It also updates the Criminal Code's existing definition of 'traffic' (in section 355.1) so that it applies to the new scrap metal offences. Under that definition, trafficking means selling, giving, transferring, transporting, importing, exporting, sending, delivering or otherwise dealing with something — or offering to do any of those things.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: scrap metal offences
deepDive.body:
A new section 355.6 would make it an offence to traffic in, or possess for the purpose of trafficking, scrap metal knowing that all or part of it came from a crime. Penalties depend on how the Crown proceeds: as an indictable offence, a first conviction could bring a fine up to $10,000 and/or up to 10 years' imprisonment, rising to a $25,000 fine for repeat offences; on summary conviction, the maximums are a $5,000 fine (or $15,000 for repeat offences) and/or up to two years less a day.

A separate offence (section 355.9) targets scrap metal dealers specifically. A dealer who trades in or holds scrap metal while being 'reckless or wilfully blind' as to whether it was obtained through crime could face a fine of up to $10,000 and/or up to two years less a day. The bill defines 'scrap metal' as copper, aluminum, brass, bronze, steel or iron — or alloys and derivatives of those metals — that has been dismantled, altered or prepared for recycling or resale.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: infrastructure damage and sentencing
deepDive.body:
The bill adds subsection 430(4.3) to the mischief section of the Criminal Code. It would be an offence to commit mischief against a physical component of essential infrastructure — as that term is already defined in subsection 52.1(2) of the Criminal Code — while knowing, or being reckless as to whether, the infrastructure cannot function without that component. Penalties run up to a $10,000 fine and/or 10 years' imprisonment if prosecuted by indictment, or up to $5,000 and/or two years less a day on summary conviction.

The bill also directs judges to treat certain facts as aggravating circumstances, which generally means a tougher sentence. For scrap metal trafficking, an aggravating factor is that the metal was taken from public or private infrastructure — the bill lists electrical systems, telecommunications, railways, pipelines, water and wastewater systems, and transportation signage or safety equipment as examples. For the new mischief offence, aggravating factors include interrupting essential services, endangering public life, health or safety, or acting to commit or facilitate another offence such as theft or trafficking.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected groups are people who steal or resell metal taken from infrastructure, and businesses in the scrap metal and recycling trade. The dealer offence sets a lower threshold than the trafficking offence: a dealer does not need to know the metal was stolen, only to have been reckless or wilfully blind about its origin, which places a practical onus on dealers to make inquiries about the metal they buy.

Utilities, telecommunications companies, railways, pipeline operators and municipal water systems are the infrastructure owners the bill references. More broadly, the aggravating factors are framed around the public consequences of infrastructure damage, such as service outages and risks to safety.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill sponsored by Mrs. Connie Cody, not a government bill. Its status is listed as 'outside the Order of Precedence', meaning it has been introduced but is not currently in the queue for House of Commons debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one would need to pass the House of Commons, the Senate and receive Royal Assent before taking effect.

The bill builds on existing Criminal Code structures rather than creating a standalone regime: it extends the property-obtained-by-crime trafficking provisions (sections 355.1 to 355.5) to scrap metal, and adds to the existing mischief provisions in section 430, relying on the definition of 'essential infrastructure' already found in subsection 52.1(2). It does not create licensing or record-keeping rules for scrap dealers — those matters are generally handled by provincial and municipal law — and it sets maximum penalties rather than mandatory minimums.

C-273.overview: Bill C-273 is a private member's bill that would speed up how Canada approves farm inputs — animal feeds, fertilizers, seeds, pesticides and veterinary drugs — by leaning on approvals already granted in other countries. Under the bill, if a feed, fertilizer, seed variety or pest control product has already been approved in at least two foreign jurisdictions that Canada designates as "trusted," Canadian regulators would generally have to grant it a provisional (temporary) registration within 90 days of a complete application, while the full Canadian review continues in the background. It also lets regulators formally rely on the evidence, reviews and evaluations produced by those foreign authorities when doing their own assessments, and expands an existing Food and Drugs Act power so the Health Minister can deem certain requirements met for veterinary drugs based on a foreign regulator's decision. The stated aim is faster market access for products farmers already use abroad. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is not close to becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill, formally the Facilitating Agricultural Regulatory Modernization Act, amends five existing federal laws: the Feeds Act, the Fertilizers Act, the Seeds Act, the Pest Control Products Act and the Food and Drugs Act. Its core idea is a new two-step approval system — "provisional" and "final" — for agricultural inputs.

It introduces a new legal term, "trusted jurisdiction," meaning a foreign country or part of a foreign country (for example, a state or province) that the federal government designates by regulation. The bill itself does not name any countries; that would be decided later through regulations made under the new authorities the bill creates.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: the 90-day provisional approval
deepDive.body:
For feeds, fertilizers and supplements, if a product is already approved for manufacture, sale or import in at least two trusted jurisdictions, the Minister "must" approve or register it provisionally within 90 days of a complete application — unless within that window the product is found not to comply with Canadian law. Final approval or registration follows once the full evaluation is done and the product is found compliant. The same 90-day structure applies to seed varieties, with the Canadian Food Inspection Agency's Registrar required to register a variety provisionally if it is approved for sale in two or more trusted jurisdictions, unless the prescribed requirements are found not to be met.

For pesticides, applicants could apply for provisional registration by submitting information from reviews or evaluations done by trusted-jurisdiction authorities. If, within 90 days of a complete application, the Minister has not determined that the health and environmental risks and the product's value are unacceptable, the Minister must register it provisionally — assigning a registration number and setting conditions on things like composition, handling, labelling and use. Provisional pesticide registration would remain valid until the product is either fully registered or the application is withdrawn or denied. The bill specifically requires that safety information, including a material safety data sheet, be provided to workplaces where a provisionally registered pesticide is used or made.

deepDive.heading: Relying on foreign evidence and veterinary drugs
deepDive.body:
Beyond the fast track, the bill adds regulation-making powers letting Ottawa spell out how much weight Canadian evaluators may place on evidence and information generated during a product's approval in a trusted jurisdiction. For pesticides, the Minister could expressly consider information from a trusted jurisdiction's review when judging whether risks and value are acceptable.

The bill also amends section 30.06 of the Food and Drugs Act. That provision currently lets the Health Minister issue an order deeming certain requirements met for therapeutic products and food based on a foreign regulator's decision, information or documents; the bill adds "veterinary drugs" to that list, subject to existing limits and regulations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected groups are farmers and livestock producers, who would potentially gain earlier access to feeds, fertilizers, seed varieties, pesticides and veterinary drugs already on the market abroad, and the companies that manufacture, import and sell those products, who would face a shorter wait for at least a provisional market entry. Regulators at the Canadian Food Inspection Agency and Health Canada's Pest Management Regulatory Agency would take on new statutory deadlines and new authorities to use foreign review material.

Because the bill affects pesticide and veterinary drug approvals, it also touches health, environmental and worker-safety interests — which is why it preserves the Minister's ability to refuse or halt provisional registration where compliance or acceptability is not established, keeps consultation requirements for full registration of products with unregistered active ingredients, and mandates workplace safety information for provisionally registered pesticides.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a private member's bill sponsored by MP David Bexte, not a government bill. Its status is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," meaning it has been introduced but has not yet reached the queue for House of Commons debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one has not been studied or amended by a committee.

Much of how the system would actually work is left to future regulations: which jurisdictions count as "trusted," the rules governing the duration and cancellation of provisional approvals, fees, and how heavily foreign evidence may be relied upon would all be set by the Governor in Council under the new regulation-making powers the bill creates, rather than in the bill text itself.

C-274.overview: Bill C-274 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Jenny Kwan that would create a new route to Canadian citizenship for people who spent time in child welfare care — foster homes, group homes, guardianship arrangements or certain institutions — but who never became citizens before aging out of that care. Under the bill, someone who meets set conditions (such as at least a year in care and three years of physical presence in Canada) could apply, and the Minister would be required to grant citizenship. It also changes immigration law so that a deportation order cannot be carried out while such an application is pending, and the order becomes void if citizenship is granted. The bill's preamble frames the issue as a gap in protection for immigrant, refugee and asylum-seeking children, noting that the state acts in the place of a parent for children in its care. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is not close to becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends two federal laws. In the Citizenship Act, it adds a new section 5.3 creating a citizenship grant for certain people who were in government or agency care as children and were not citizens when that care ended. In the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, it adds a pause on removal (deportation) while such an application is being decided.

Importantly, the wording says the Minister "shall" grant citizenship to a person who meets the requirements — meaning that if the criteria are met, the grant is mandatory rather than discretionary.

deepDive.heading: Who would qualify
deepDive.body:
The bill covers people who, while in Canada, lived in or were maintained by: an institution (including a psychiatric or addiction treatment facility), a group foster home, or the private home of a foster parent, guardian or tutor under a court order, funded by a federal or provincial child protection body; an institution licensed under provincial law to have custody or care of children; or who received services from a provincial child protection agency to improve their living conditions. The person must have been ordinarily resident in Canada on the day those circumstances ended.

Four additional requirements apply: the person must not have been returned to a parent's custody when the care arrangement ended (unless that happened within 365 days of turning 18); must have been in care for at least 365 days in total; must have been physically present in Canada at least 1,095 days (three years) before applying; and must not have lived outside Canada for more than 10 years since turning 18. The Minister may waive any of these requirements on compassionate grounds after reviewing a person's circumstances.

deepDive.heading: Proof and process
deepDive.body:
To ease the burden of documenting a childhood spent in care, the bill says an applicant's own written statement that they were in one of the listed situations counts as proof — unless the Minister determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the circumstances did not exist. In other words, the applicant's account is accepted by default and the onus shifts to the government to rebut it.

The bill also makes technical updates so the new pathway fits into the existing Citizenship Act: adding it to the list of ways citizenship can be acquired, requiring the Minister to provide proof of citizenship after a successful application, and extending existing regulation-making powers to cover the new section 5.3 (including factors to be considered, when requirements are deemed met, when a review is suspended, and how to request a ministerial waiver).

deepDive.heading: Effect on removal orders
deepDive.body:
Two changes to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act protect applicants while their file is pending. Section 50 would be amended so a removal order cannot be enforced against a foreign national who has applied under the new section 5.3 until a final decision is made on that application. Section 51 would be amended so that an unenforced removal order becomes void if the person is granted citizenship under section 5.3.

Together, these provisions are meant to prevent someone from being deported while their citizenship claim is still being assessed.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out the reasoning: Canada is a party to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child; the best interests of the child are a primary legal consideration; gaps remain for children who arrive as immigrants, refugees or asylum seekers; the state acts in place of a parent for children in care; and citizenship affects access to health care, education and employment, as well as the risk of removal to a country a person may have no connection to.

Bill C-274 is a private member's bill, not a government bill, and is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence." That means it has been introduced but has not been drawn into the queue for House debate. Most private members' bills do not become law, and the text described here is the bill as introduced — it could be amended or not proceed at all.

C-275.overview: Bill C-275 is a private member's bill that would add a new section to the Criminal Code creating offences related to "sexual assault material" — visual recordings (photos, film or video) that depict, in an explicit and realistic way, non-consensual sexual intercourse or other sexual activity that violates a person's sexual integrity. The bill would make it a crime to produce, publish, distribute, sell, advertise, import or export such material, as well as to simply possess it or knowingly access it, with penalties ranging from summary-conviction sentences up to 14 years' imprisonment and fines of up to $100,000. It also sets out a mandatory aggravating factor when the offence is committed for profit, limits the defence of believing the activity was consensual, and exempts conduct with a legitimate purpose related to justice, science, medicine, education or art. In effect, the bill would create a framework for recordings of non-consensual sexual activity involving adults that resembles the existing structure of Canada's child pornography offences. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is at a very early stage.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Criminal Code by inserting a new section 163.01, immediately after the existing obscenity provisions in section 163. It defines a new category of illegal material called "sexual assault material": any visual recording made by any means — photographic, film or video — that depicts in an explicit and realistic way non-consensual sexual intercourse, or any other sexual activity that violates a person's sexual integrity.

Around that definition, the bill builds four separate offences covering the full chain of creation and consumption: making it, distributing it, possessing it, and accessing it. This mirrors the way the Criminal Code already structures offences for child pornography, but applies the approach to recordings of non-consensual sexual activity generally.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and penalties
deepDive.body:
Making, printing, publishing or possessing for the purpose of publication is an indictable offence carrying up to 14 years in prison, a fine of up to $100,000, or both. The same maximum penalties apply to transmitting, making available, distributing, selling, advertising, importing, exporting, or possessing the material for any of those purposes.

Simple possession is a hybrid offence: up to five years in prison and/or a $50,000 fine if prosecuted by indictment, or up to two years less a day and/or a $20,000 fine on summary conviction. Accessing the material — defined as knowingly causing it to be viewed by or transmitted to oneself — carries up to 10 years and/or a $50,000 fine by indictment, or the same summary-conviction penalties. If a person is convicted under any of these provisions, the sentencing court must treat an intent to make a profit as an aggravating factor.

deepDive.heading: Defences and limits
deepDive.body:
The bill restricts one defence and creates another. For the offence of making, printing or publishing the material, an accused cannot simply claim they believed the depicted activity was consensual. That belief only counts as a defence if the accused took all reasonable steps to confirm consent and, where the activity was in fact consensual, took all reasonable steps to ensure the material did not portray it as non-consensual — a provision that appears aimed at staged or simulated content that is presented as real assault.

A broader exemption states that no one may be convicted under the section if the conduct in question serves a legitimate purpose related to the administration of justice, or to science, medicine, education or art. This would cover, for example, evidence handling in criminal investigations, or research and educational uses.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The offences are drafted broadly and would apply to individuals who create or share such recordings, to people who commercially distribute or advertise them, and to anyone who knowingly possesses or views them. Because the distribution offence includes "transmits," "makes available," "imports" and "exports," it reaches online sharing and cross-border transfers.

Several of the offences turn on knowledge — the making, distribution and possession offences all use the word "knowingly," and the access offence is defined in terms of knowingly causing the material to be viewed or transmitted to oneself. The provisions do not specify the age of the persons depicted, so the definition is not limited to adults, and the bill does not address how it would interact with existing Criminal Code offences such as voyeurism, child pornography, or the non-consensual distribution of intimate images.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-275 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual Member of Parliament — Mr. Bailey — rather than by the government. Its listed status is "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but has not yet reached a place on the list of private members' business scheduled for debate in the House of Commons.

Most private members' bills do not become law, and those that advance are typically subject to amendment at committee. Readers should treat the text above as the bill as introduced; nothing in it takes effect unless and until it passes both the House of Commons and the Senate and receives Royal Assent.

C-276.overview: Bill C-276 is a private member's bill from Conservative MP Ted Falk that aims to make sure Canadians can keep getting and using physical cash — coins and bank notes — no matter how popular digital payments become. It would require the Minister of Finance to review existing rules about cash availability at financial institutions and then build a national "framework" covering things like access to ATMs and branches, protecting people's and businesses' ability to pay with cash, easing barriers to cash donations to charities, and keeping Canada's cash-handling infrastructure running. It also makes two notable legal changes: it removes the federal Cabinet's existing power to "call in" (withdraw from circulation) coins and bank notes, and it bars the Bank of Canada from ever issuing a digital version of the Canadian dollar. The bill matters because cash use has declined sharply in favour of cards and apps, and the bill's preamble argues that seniors, Indigenous peoples, newcomers, and low-income Canadians rely on cash most, and that cash offers more privacy than digital payments. As a private member's bill currently outside the Order of Precedence, it has not yet been scheduled for debate and is a long way from becoming law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates the Framework on the Access to and Use of Cash Act. Within 90 days of the Act coming into force, the Minister of Finance would have to conduct a comprehensive review of the laws, regulations and policies that govern how available cash is within financial institutions.

The Minister would then have to develop and implement a framework to ensure continued access to cash across Canada, table a report on that framework in both the House of Commons and the Senate within 18 months, and publish it on the Department of Finance website within 10 days of tabling. Three years after that report is tabled, the Minister must review how the framework has been implemented, how effective it has been, and what its social and economic impacts are, and report those findings to Parliament as well.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions of the framework
deepDive.body:
The bill spells out four things the framework must address. First, ensuring everyone in Canada can access cash, including making sure the physical infrastructure for withdrawals and deposits exists nationwide and setting what counts as a "reasonable distance" someone should have to travel to withdraw or deposit cash. Second, protecting the ability of people and businesses to keep using cash even as digital currencies and cryptocurrencies spread.

Third, removing barriers and disincentives to cash donations to non-profit and community organizations — while not undermining efforts against money laundering, fraud and other financial crimes. Fourth, ensuring the long-term viability of Canada's cash infrastructure, meaning the equipment and facilities used to sort, store and distribute cash.

deepDive.heading: Changes to existing laws
deepDive.body:
Beyond the framework, the bill amends two statutes. It repeals subsection 9(1) of the Currency Act, which is the provision giving the Governor in Council (effectively the federal Cabinet) the power to call in coins and notes — that is, to order them withdrawn from circulation. A related housekeeping change updates a cross-reference in the Bank of Canada Act.

The bill also adds a new subsection to section 23 of the Bank of Canada Act stating plainly that the Bank "shall not issue a digital form of the dollar." This would legally block the creation of a central bank digital currency (CBDC) in Canada.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and why
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble points to groups it says depend disproportionately on cash: seniors, Indigenous peoples, newcomers to Canada, and people with low incomes, including those living in poverty or relying on income assistance. It also cites charities and community organizations that raise money through cash donations.

A third rationale in the preamble is privacy: the bill states that cash payments offer more privacy than digital alternatives, and links this to privacy protections in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the federal Privacy Act, and provincial privacy laws. In practical terms, banks and other financial institutions would be affected by any framework requirements around maintaining cash access points, and the Bank of Canada would be prohibited from pursuing a digital dollar.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-276 is a private member's bill, not a government bill, and it is currently "outside the Order of Precedence." That means it has not yet been drawn into the queue of private members' business scheduled for debate in the House of Commons. Most private members' bills do not become law, and this one has not yet had first-stage debate.

It is worth noting what the bill does and does not do. It does not require any business to accept cash directly; instead, it directs the Minister to build a framework that includes measures to protect the ability to use cash. The specific content of that framework — including what counts as a "reasonable distance" to a cash machine — would be worked out by the government, not set out in the bill itself.

C-277.overview: Bill C-277 is a private member's bill from MP Michael Coteau that would create a new law, the Regulating the Online Use of Deepfakes Act, aimed at AI-generated fake images, video and audio of real people. It would place four main duties on online platforms and services: set up a way to detect and report deepfakes, clearly label deepfakes shared on their services, take reasonable steps to prevent and remove deepfakes that could seriously harm someone, and keep records showing they are complying. To back this up, the bill lets the federal Cabinet create a system of administrative monetary penalties — financial penalties, not criminal charges — that could apply to platforms and, in some cases, to their directors and officers. The bill's preamble argues that deepfakes are increasingly used for fraud, identity theft, harassment and intimidation, and that existing laws do not adequately protect people from these harms. As a private member's bill sitting outside the Order of Precedence, it is at a very early stage and has not been debated or voted on.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill would enact a stand-alone statute, the Regulating the Online Use of Deepfakes Act, whose stated purpose is to protect individuals from the significant harm deepfakes can cause by regulating how they are used and spread online, including through greater transparency about their use.

Rather than banning deepfakes outright or creating new criminal offences, the bill takes a regulatory approach: it imposes obligations on the companies that host or distribute online content and creates a penalty system to encourage compliance.

deepDive.heading: Key definitions
deepDive.body:
A "deepfake" is defined as a photo, video or audio recording of an individual that is meant to look or sound authentic and that either (a) has been edited using an artificial intelligence system to replace the person's appearance or voice, or (b) was created using an AI system using a person's identifiable characteristics such as their appearance or voice.

"Significant harm" is defined broadly to include psychological harm such as humiliation and damage to reputation or relationships, as well as economic losses such as lost business, professional or employment opportunities, and identity theft. An "operator" means the owner or operator of an online undertaking under the Broadcasting Act, or of any internet-connected platform, online service or application, including social media services. The Minister responsible would be the Minister of Industry.

deepDive.heading: Duties placed on online platforms
deepDive.body:
Section 4 requires every operator to establish a process for identifying deepfakes shared through its products or services, including reporting mechanisms so users can flag them. Section 5 adds a transparency duty: operators must take reasonable steps in the design and operation of their services to ensure any deepfake shared on them is clearly identified as a deepfake.

Section 6 sets out a duty of care — operators must take reasonable steps to prevent the sharing of deepfakes that may cause significant harm to a person or their interests, and must remove such content as soon as feasible once it has been identified. Section 7 requires operators to keep the records needed to show whether they are meeting these duties, with the details of record-keeping to be set out later in regulations made by the Governor in Council (Cabinet).

deepDive.heading: Enforcement: administrative monetary penalties
deepDive.body:
The bill does not itself set penalty amounts. Instead, it authorizes Cabinet to create an administrative monetary penalties scheme by regulation, covering which provisions count as violations (including whether an ongoing violation counts as a separate violation each day), how proceedings work, available defences, penalty amounts and the factors used to set them, payment and collection of unpaid penalties, reviews and appeals, compliance agreements, and who administers the system.

Directors or officers who directed, authorized, assented to, acquiesced in or participated in a violation can also be held liable, whether or not the company itself is proceeded against. The bill states that the purpose of penalties is to promote compliance rather than to punish, and section 9 clarifies that a violation is not a criminal offence, so section 126 of the Criminal Code does not apply.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
C-277 is a private member's bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual MP rather than the government. It is listed as "Outside the Order of Precedence," which means it has been introduced but is not yet scheduled for debate; most bills in this position do not proceed further unless the sponsor's name is drawn or the bill advances in the parliamentary lottery system.

The preamble frames the bill as a response to gaps in existing law, stating that current legal frameworks do not adequately protect against deepfake-related harms to personal autonomy, dignity, privacy and trust in authentic communication. Because many operational details — including penalty amounts, defences and record-keeping requirements — would be left to future regulations, the bill's practical effect would depend heavily on how Cabinet chose to fill in those details.

C-278.overview: Bill C-278 is a private member's bill from NDP MP Don Davies (Vancouver Kingsway) that would change the Parliament of Canada Act to address what is commonly called "floor-crossing."
