S-204 is a Senate public bill — introduced by a senator rather than the government — sponsored by Senator Yonah Martin and dated May 2025. It is currently at consideration in committee in the Senate.

To become law it would still need to complete the Senate stages and then pass through all stages in the House of Commons before receiving royal assent. Until then, none of its deadlines or requirements are in effect.

S-203.overview: Bill S-203 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Patrick Brazeau that would broadly ban the advertising and promotion of alcoholic beverages in Canada, modelled closely on the kind of restrictions already used for tobacco. It would prohibit most alcohol ads, sponsorships, contests, free samples and "two-for-one"-style inducements, and would bar alcohol brand names from appearing on sports and cultural venues — while carving out narrow exceptions for factual information about price and availability, promotions aimed only at industry, and unpaid mentions in news, art or entertainment. The bill also creates a system of federal inspectors with powers to enter premises and seize materials, plus regulation-making powers and offences with penalties. The stated rationale, set out in the bill's preamble, is that alcohol's health and social costs exceed the tax revenue governments collect from it, and that limiting promotion — especially promotion appealing to young people — is an effective way to reduce consumption. The bill is at second reading in the Senate, an early stage, and would come into force one year after receiving royal assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Alcoholic Beverage Promotion Prohibition Act would make it illegal, with limited exceptions, to promote any beverage containing 1.1 per cent or more alcohol by volume. "Promote" is defined broadly as making a representation about a product, for the purpose of selling it, that is likely to influence attitudes, beliefs or behaviours.

The stated purpose is to protect young persons (defined as anyone under 18) and others from inducements to drink, in order to protect public health and reduce alcohol-related social costs. The preamble argues that health-care, lost-productivity and criminal-justice costs create an "alcohol deficit" that is not covered by government alcohol revenues. The Governor in Council would designate a Cabinet minister to administer the Act, and the law would take effect on the first anniversary of royal assent.

deepDive.heading: Key prohibitions
deepDive.body:
Section 6 bans promotion generally, and specifically calls out advertising that communicates price or distribution information, that could appeal to young people, that uses testimonials or endorsements, that depicts a person, character or animal (real or fictional), or that links a brand to a lifestyle involving glamour, recreation, excitement, vitality, risk or daring. Other sections prohibit false or misleading promotion (including claims that create an erroneous impression about health effects or risks), the use of specific terms, logos or symbols to be listed in future regulations, and any sponsorship of people, entities, events, activities or facilities using an alcohol brand element or producer's name. Section 10 would bar alcohol brands and producer names from appearing on sports or cultural venues, including in the venue's name.

Section 12 targets sales inducements: sellers could not give away free alcohol, bundle it with other purchases, or offer prizes, contests, draws or services as an incentive to buy alcohol. Section 11 also makes it an offence to publish, broadcast or otherwise disseminate a prohibited promotion on someone else's behalf.

deepDive.heading: Exceptions and carve-outs
deepDive.body:
The bill is not an absolute ban. Part 1 does not apply to literary, dramatic, musical, film, scientific, educational or artistic works that depict alcohol, or to reports, commentary or opinion about alcohol — provided no one was paid for the mention (in other words, unpaid references and journalism are exempt, but paid product placement is not). Business-to-business promotion among producers, distributors and sellers that is not aimed at consumers is also exempt.

"Informational" and "brand-preference" promotion would still be allowed in restricted settings: in named mail or messages to identified adults 18 or over, in places where minors are not legally permitted, or online where reasonable steps have been taken to block access by young people. At the point of sale, a promotion may state only availability and/or price. Brand elements could appear on non-alcohol items unless those items are associated with or appealing to young people, or evoke a lifestyle image. Required or permitted label information under other federal laws is unaffected. Distributors of imported publications, licensed broadcasters and online undertakings retransmitting programs (except for ads they themselves insert), and anyone who unknowingly disseminated a prohibited ad, are also shielded from the publication offence.

deepDive.heading: Enforcement, offences and who is affected
deepDive.body:
The designated Minister could appoint inspectors, who would carry certificates of designation and could enter any place — including vehicles — where they reasonably believe alcohol is being promoted or where promotional materials or related records are kept. Inspectors could examine and copy documents and electronic data, use on-site computers and copiers, take photographs and recordings, order the production of items, seize and detain things believed to be connected to a contravention, and restrict the movement of goods or conveyances. The bill also includes regulation-making powers and a Part on offences and punishment covering promotion offences, liability of corporate officers, continuing offences, responsibility for acts of employees or agents, a due diligence defence, a limitation period and venue rules. (The provided text is truncated, so the specific fines and penalty amounts are not shown here.)

The practical reach would extend to breweries, wineries and distilleries, bars, restaurants and retailers, advertising and media companies, and organizations that rely on alcohol-industry sponsorship, such as sports teams, festivals and arenas.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
S-203 is a Senate public bill — introduced by an individual senator rather than the government — and is currently at second reading in the Senate, an early stage of debate in principle. Senate public bills must pass both the Senate and the House of Commons before becoming law, and many do not advance beyond initial stages.

The bill's structure and language closely parallel Canada's existing tobacco advertising framework, applying similar concepts (brand elements, informational versus lifestyle promotion, sponsorship bans, inspector powers) to alcohol. Because alcohol sales and retailing are largely regulated by the provinces and territories, the bill approaches the issue through federal authority over promotion and advertising. Its coming-into-force clause gives industry and regulators one year to adjust after royal assent.

S-205.overview: Bill S-205, known as Tona's Law, is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Kim Pate that would amend the Corrections and Conditional Release Act — the federal law governing prisons and parole. Its central change is to require that no federal prisoner be held in a "structured intervention unit" (a form of separation from the general prison population) for more than 48 hours unless a superior court judge orders it, bringing judicial oversight to a decision now made inside the prison system. The bill would also require mental health assessments for people entering a penitentiary or a structured intervention unit, expand the ability of the Correctional Service to partner with Indigenous and other community organizations to house and support prisoners and plan their release, and create a new right for prisoners to ask the sentencing court to shorten their sentence or parole ineligibility period if their sentence was administered unfairly or unlawfully. The bill has passed the Senate and is at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, the 1992 statute that sets the rules for federal penitentiaries, prisoner treatment and release. It focuses on four areas: mandatory mental health assessments, strict time limits and court oversight for isolation-like confinement, greater use of community and Indigenous organizations in custody and release planning, and a new court remedy for prisoners who experience unfairness in how their sentence is carried out.

The bill also broadens the legal definition of a "structured intervention unit" (SIU). Currently the term applies to areas formally designated as SIUs; under the bill it would also cover any part of a penitentiary where a person is separated from the mainstream population and spends less time out of their cell or in activities than other prisoners. This matters because the bill's new safeguards would then apply to those conditions as well, not only to officially labelled units.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Mental health: The head of an institution would have to refer every person sentenced, transferred or committed to a penitentiary for a mental health assessment as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after arrival. Anyone transferred into a structured intervention unit would have to be referred for an assessment within 24 hours.

Limits on isolation: Confinement in a structured intervention unit would have to end as soon as possible and could not exceed 48 hours unless a superior court, on application by the Correctional Service, extends it because the extension is necessary for a purpose already set out in section 32(1) of the Act. Sentence remedy: A new Part III.1 would let a person apply to the court that sentenced them for a reduction in their period of incarceration or parole ineligibility if a decision, act or omission by the Commissioner or those working under them was, in the court's view, contrary to law or policy, unreasonable, unjust, oppressive or discriminatory, based on a mistake of law or fact, or an improper exercise of discretion. Applications would generally have to be filed within 60 days of the triggering event, the receipt of a related report, or being informed of certain findings by the Correctional Investigator — though a court could allow a longer period.

deepDive.heading: Community and Indigenous organizations
deepDive.body:
The bill rewrites section 81 of the Act, which currently allows agreements with Indigenous organizations for the care and custody of prisoners. Under the bill, the Minister could enter agreements not only with Indigenous organizations and governing bodies but also with community groups serving a "disadvantaged or minority population" and any other entity providing community-based support services. "Disadvantaged or minority population" is defined as any population subject to direct or indirect discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or disability.

The Commissioner would be required to take all reasonable steps to find such organizations and to seek transfers to them, and could not refuse a transfer where both the prisoner and the organization consent unless a court determines the transfer is not in the interests of justice. On release, the bill would require the Service to inform prisoners about relevant organizations, give those organizations an opportunity to propose a release and reintegration plan when a prisoner requests their support, provide notice of parole reviews or statutory release dates, and require the Parole Board of Canada to give written reasons whenever it makes a decision inconsistent with such a plan.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to people serving sentences in federal penitentiaries, and in particular to those held in structured intervention units or otherwise separated from the general population. It would also create new duties for the Correctional Service of Canada, institutional heads, the Commissioner, the Parole Board of Canada and the Minister, and would give superior courts and sentencing courts new roles in reviewing correctional decisions.

Indigenous organizations, Indigenous governing bodies and community groups serving disadvantaged or minority populations would gain expanded opportunities to enter agreements with the federal government, take custody of consenting prisoners and propose release plans.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble sets out the reasoning behind it: that correctional decisions affecting human rights are not routinely reviewed by courts, that the SIU Implementation Advisory Panel and the Office of the Correctional Investigator have documented persistent segregation-like conditions, that harm can occur after as few as 48 hours of isolation, and that Black and Indigenous people, 2SLGBTQQIA+ people and people with mental health disabilities are overrepresented in segregation. It also references section 12 of the Charter (cruel and unusual treatment or punishment), international human rights standards, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's call to eliminate the overrepresentation of Indigenous people in federal prisons.

S-205 is a Senate public bill — introduced by an individual senator rather than the government. It is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, an early stage in that chamber. It would still need to complete committee study, report stage, third reading and royal assent before taking effect, and its provisions could be amended along the way.

S-206.overview: Bill S-206 is a Senate public bill from Senator Kim Pate that would require the federal Minister of Finance to draw up a national framework for a "guaranteed livable basic income" — a regular income floor available to everyone in Canada over the age of 17. Importantly, the bill does not itself create a basic income program or set payment amounts; it directs the government to design a plan, in consultation with other ministers, provincial officials, Indigenous Elders and governing bodies, and experts, and to report that plan to Parliament within one year. The framework would have to define what counts as a "livable" income in each region, set national standards for related health and social supports, and guarantee that people are not required to work, train or study to qualify. It would also have to ensure that existing disability- and health-related benefits are not cut back as a result. The bill matters because it would put a formal, deadline-bound planning process behind a policy idea that has been widely debated in Canada, while leaving actual implementation to future decisions.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill obliges the Minister of Finance to develop a national framework for implementing a guaranteed livable basic income program across Canada for anyone over the age of 17. It is a framework-and-reporting bill: it mandates planning, consultation and public reporting rather than establishing a benefit, setting eligibility rules beyond the age threshold, or appropriating money.

The preamble states the rationale the sponsor puts forward: that a guaranteed livable basic income would help reduce poverty and income inequality, improve health, education, food and housing security, support unpaid care work and people in precarious jobs, and assist the transition to an economy responding to the climate crisis.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 requires the framework to include measures that: (a) determine what constitutes a livable basic income region by region, based on the goods and services needed for a dignified and healthy life and their local cost; (b) create national standards for health and social supports that complement a basic income and guide implementation in every province; (c) ensure that participation in education, training or the labour market is not a condition of qualifying; and (d) ensure that implementing the program does not reduce services or benefits meant to address exceptional needs related to health or disability.

Sections 4 and 5 set the reporting timeline. Within one year of the Act coming into force, the Minister must table a report setting out the framework — including social, health and economic conclusions and recommendations — in both the Senate and House of Commons, and publish it on the Department of Finance website within 10 days of tabling. Two years after that tabling, and every year afterward, the Minister must review the framework's effectiveness in consultation with the same parties and table further reports on findings and recommendations.

deepDive.heading: Consultation and jurisdiction
deepDive.body:
In developing the framework, the Minister must consult the Minister of Health; the ministers responsible for employment, social development, housing and disability; provincial representatives responsible for health, disability, education, housing and social development; Indigenous Elders; Indigenous governing bodies; and other relevant stakeholders, including policy developers, political decision-makers and experts on other guaranteed livable basic income programs.

The bill also requires the Minister to consider the jurisdictional responsibilities of federal, provincial and Indigenous governments. This reflects the fact that many income-support, health and social programs are delivered by provinces and territories, so a national approach would involve coordination rather than unilateral federal action. The bill defines "Indigenous Elder" and "Indigenous governing body" by reference to groups holding rights recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Directly, the bill affects the Minister of Finance and the federal government, which would carry the obligation to consult, design the framework and report to Parliament on a fixed schedule. Provincial governments, Indigenous governing bodies and Elders, and a range of stakeholders and experts would be drawn into the consultation process.

Indirectly, the subject matter concerns everyone in Canada over 17, and particularly people living on low incomes, people with disabilities, unpaid caregivers and workers in precarious employment. However, no individual would receive a payment under this bill as drafted — any actual program would require separate legislative and budgetary decisions.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
S-206 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator (Kim Pate) rather than by the government. It is currently at committee consideration in the Senate, which is an early stage: to become law it would still need to complete Senate study and third reading, then pass all stages in the House of Commons and receive Royal Assent.

Senate public bills often do not complete this full path, and similar basic income framework proposals have been introduced in previous parliamentary sessions. Because the bill mandates a framework rather than a program, questions about cost, benefit levels and interaction with existing income supports would be addressed through the consultation and reporting process it sets out, not by the text of the bill itself.

S-208.overview: Bill S-208 is a Senate public bill from Senator Kim Pate that would give judges the power to depart from mandatory minimum sentences in the Criminal Code and other federal laws. Right now, when Parliament sets a mandatory minimum penalty for an offence, a judge must impose at least that punishment no matter the circumstances of the case or the person being sentenced. Under this bill, the minimum would become a guide rather than a hard floor: a judge could impose a different sentence, but before imposing a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment or period of parole ineligibility, the judge would first have to consider all other options, conclude no other just and reasonable option exists, and put written reasons on the record. The bill would also let judges choose which treatment or counselling program a convicted person attends before sentencing, remove the Crown's veto over delaying sentencing for that purpose, and let juries in both first- and second-degree murder cases recommend a parole ineligibility period for the judge to consider. The bill is at second reading in the Senate, an early stage, and has not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The core change is to section 718.3 of the Criminal Code, which governs how much discretion a sentencing judge has. The current wording says the punishment is in the judge's discretion "subject to the limitations prescribed in the enactment" — meaning judges are bound by any mandatory minimum Parliament has set. The bill would change that phrase to "despite the limitations prescribed in the enactment, including a punishment declared to be a minimum punishment," making the choice of sentence a matter for the court even where a minimum exists.

The bill does not repeal any specific mandatory minimum sentence. Instead, it creates a general mechanism allowing courts to depart from them, and it applies not only to the Criminal Code but to minimum sentences and parole ineligibility periods "under a provision of this Act or any other Act of Parliament."

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 rewrites subsections 718.3(1) and (2) to place sentencing, including where a minimum is prescribed, in the discretion of the convicting court. Clause 2 adds a new section 718.4 setting out a procedure: before imposing a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment or a mandatory parole ineligibility period, a court must consider all available alternatives and determine that no alternative would be just and reasonable, and must give written reasons for imposing the minimum.

Clause 3 amends subsection 720(2), which allows a judge to delay sentencing so a person can attend a court-supervised treatment or counselling program. Currently this requires the consent of both the Attorney General and the offender, and the program must be one approved by the province. The bill removes the Attorney General's consent requirement and the provincial-approval limit, leaving the choice of program to what the court "considers appropriate in the circumstances," with the convicted person's consent still required and the interests of justice and of any victim still to be considered.

Clause 4 rewrites section 745.2. Today, a jury is asked for a recommendation on parole eligibility only after a second-degree murder conviction, and the judge may substitute a period between 10 and 25 years. The bill extends the question to first-degree murder as well (where the default is 25 years), and drops the specified upper and lower bounds, referring instead to substituting "another period of time." The jury recommendation would remain optional and non-binding, but the judge would consider it.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill would affect anyone convicted of an offence carrying a mandatory minimum penalty or a set parole ineligibility period, as well as sentencing judges, Crown prosecutors and defence counsel. Because it removes the Attorney General's consent requirement for delayed sentencing, it shifts some control over that step from prosecutors to judges.

The bill's preamble identifies groups the sponsor says are particularly affected by mandatory minimums: women, including those whose criminalization follows violent victimization and who may face pressure to plead guilty; Indigenous people, whom the preamble describes as systemically over-incarcerated; and people with mental disabilities, described as vastly overrepresented in prisons. It also references paragraph 718.2(e) of the Criminal Code, the existing provision directing courts to consider alternatives to imprisonment with particular attention to Indigenous offenders.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble frames the bill around the principle of proportionality — that a sentence should match the gravity of the offence and the offender's degree of responsibility — and argues that inflexible minimums can produce disproportionate sentences, potentially engaging equality rights under section 15 of the Charter and risking miscarriages of justice such as wrongful guilty pleas. These are the stated reasons for the bill, not neutral findings.

Procedurally, S-208 is a Senate public bill, meaning it is sponsored by an individual senator rather than the government. It is at second reading in the Senate, an early stage: to become law it would still need to complete Senate debate, committee study and third reading, then pass all stages in the House of Commons and receive royal assent. Many Senate public bills do not complete that process.

S-207.overview: Bill S-207 is a Senate public bill from Senator Kim Pate that would rewrite the Criminal Records Act so that most criminal records expire automatically after a set period, instead of people having to apply — and pay — for a "record suspension" (commonly called a pardon). Under the bill, a record would generally expire two years after the end of the sentence for a summary conviction offence and five years after the end of the sentence for an indictable offence, with no waiting period at all for offences committed while the person was a child. The Parole Board of Canada would still have a role, but mainly in cases where someone picked up a new conviction, faces outstanding charges, or is under investigation during the waiting period. The bill also repeals the regulation that sets pardon application fees and makes matching changes to other laws, including the Criminal Code, the Canadian Human Rights Act, the Income Tax Act and the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. As a Senate public bill at second reading, it is at an early stage and would have to pass both the Senate and the House of Commons to become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill changes the basic design of Canada's criminal-record relief system. Today, a person who wants relief from a criminal record must apply to the Parole Board, satisfy eligibility rules, provide supporting documents, pay a fee, and persuade the Board to grant a "record suspension." Bill S-207 would replace that application-based model with an automatic "record expiry" that happens by operation of law once the required time has passed.

The shift is signalled in the first clause, which changes the statute's long title from "An Act to provide for the suspension of the records of persons who have been convicted of offences and have subsequently rehabilitated themselves" to "An Act to provide for the expiry of criminal records." The definitions of "record suspension" and "possession" are repealed, and the sections describing the Board's role are rewritten around expiries rather than suspensions.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: timelines and how expiry works
deepDive.body:
For adults, a record would expire five years after the lawful end of the sentence for an offence prosecuted by indictment (or an equivalent serious service offence under the National Defence Act), and two years after the end of sentence for a summary conviction offence or lesser service offence. "End of sentence" includes finishing imprisonment and probation and paying any fine. A new section 4.02 specifies that, for calculating this, the sentence's expiry date is read without counting statutory release or earned remission. These periods are shorter than the current waiting times of 10 years (indictable) and five years (summary) before a person may even apply. If the offence was committed while the person was a child, there would be no waiting period — the record would expire once the sentence has been completed.

As drafted, an expired record "is evidence of the fact that the conviction... should no longer reflect adversely on the character of the person," requires the judicial record to be kept separate and apart from other criminal records, and removes any disqualification or obligation that exists under any Act of Parliament because of the conviction. Notably, the new wording does not carry forward the list of exceptions in the current law (which preserves things such as certain firearms and driving prohibitions and sex-offender registry obligations despite a record suspension). The bill also repeals the current eligibility bars, including the rules that permanently disqualify people convicted of Schedule 1 offences or of more than three serious indictable offences.

deepDive.heading: Where the Parole Board still has a role
deepDive.body:
The Board keeps "exclusive jurisdiction and absolute discretion" to order or refuse a record expiry, to revoke one, and to order that an expiry cease to have effect. Its main new function arises where the RCMP's automated criminal conviction records system shows that, during the waiting period, the person was convicted of another offence, or that at the end of the period there were outstanding charges or an ongoing investigation. In those cases the record does not expire automatically.

Instead, the Board must notify the person within 30 days after the waiting period ends that their record has not expired and that they may apply for an expiry order. On such an application, the Board must order the expiry if it is satisfied of the test set out in the bill (the provided text is cut off mid-sentence, referring to whether expiry "would sustain the applicant's rehabilitation"). Decisions on expiry applications are to be handled by employees of the Board rather than by Board-member panels, which is a change from the current one-member panel structure.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and related changes
deepDive.body:
The bill would apply to people convicted of offences under any Act of Parliament, including Canadians transferred to Canada under the International Transfer of Offenders Act, and to people convicted of service offences under military law. People who currently hold a record suspension, and those with applications still pending when the law changes, are dealt with through transitional provisions (sections 27 and 28).

Because the concept of a "record suspension" appears throughout federal law, the bill makes consequential amendments to the Criminal Code, the Canadian Human Rights Act, the National Defence Act, the Income Tax Act, the DNA Identification Act, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and the Youth Criminal Justice Act. It also repeals the Pardon Services Fees Order — the regulation that sets the fee charged for pardon/record suspension applications — consistent with a system where expiry is automatic and no application is normally required.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill S-207 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator (Kim Pate) rather than by the government. It was introduced in 2025 and is at second reading in the Senate, which is an early stage: it must still be debated and voted on there, studied in committee, and then pass all stages in the House of Commons before it could receive Royal Assent.

This explainer is based on the text of the bill as provided, which is truncated partway through the new section 4.1. Details of later clauses — including the exact wording of the Board's decision-making test, the revocation and cessation rules, the transitional provisions and each consequential amendment — are not fully reproduced in the source material and are therefore described only in general terms here.

S-209.overview: Bill S-209 would make it a criminal offence for a company or organization to make pornography available online to anyone under 18 in Canada, when it does so for commercial purposes. Fines could reach $250,000 for a first offence and $500,000 for later ones. An organization could avoid conviction if it used a government-approved age-verification or age-estimation system, if the material served a legitimate scientific, medical, educational or artistic purpose, or if it fixed the problem after being formally warned. A federal enforcement body would issue those warnings, and if a site ignored one, it could ask the Federal Court to order Internet service providers to block young people's access to the material in Canada. The bill matters because it would create Canada's first legal requirement for age checks on commercial pornography sites, including foreign ones, and it raises practical questions about how such checks work and how privacy is protected.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates a new offence: any organization that, for commercial purposes, makes pornographic material available on the Internet to a person under 18 is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction. The maximum fine is $250,000 for a first offence and $500,000 for a second or subsequent offence.

"Pornographic material" is defined as visual material (photo, film, video or other visual representation) that shows genitals or the anal region of a person engaged or depicted as engaged in explicit sexual activity and is intended to cause sexual excitement. Child sexual abuse and exploitation material, which is already covered by the Criminal Code, is excluded from this definition. The stated purpose of the Act is to protect public health and safety, including the mental health of young people, and to deter commercial pornography sites from allowing minors access.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: defences and age checks
deepDive.body:
Simply believing a user was 18 or older is not a defence. An organization can only rely on that belief if it used an age-verification or age-estimation method set out in regulations. Two other defences exist: the material had a legitimate purpose related to science, medicine, education or the arts; or the organization received an official notice and took the required corrective steps within the deadline.

The Cabinet (Governor in Council) would set the approved age-check methods by regulation, and the bill requires that any prescribed method be highly effective, run by an independent third party at arm's length from the pornography provider, protective of privacy, limited to collecting only what is strictly necessary, used only for age checking, and required to destroy personal information once the check is done. Regulations could also specify when free material is not considered "commercial," and could set up a system of administrative monetary penalties for organizations that ignore a notice.

deepDive.heading: How enforcement would work
deepDive.body:
Cabinet would designate a federal agency, division or branch as the enforcement authority. If that authority has reasonable grounds to believe an offence occurred, it may send the organization a notice identifying it, explaining the belief, listing the steps needed to comply, and giving 20 days to act. The organization may make representations in response, and must be told that failure to comply could lead to a court application and possible administrative penalties.

If the organization does not comply within 20 days, the enforcement authority has a further 20 days to apply to the Federal Court for an order requiring Internet service providers to prevent young people in Canada from accessing the material. The affected ISPs must be named as respondents alongside the organization, and the case is heard in a summary (expedited) way. The Court must issue the order if it finds reasonable grounds to believe the offence occurred, that the organization ignored the notice, and that the ISPs' services could be used in Canada to reach the material.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and who is excluded
deepDive.body:
The offence applies to "organizations" as defined in the Criminal Code — companies, firms and similar entities — rather than to individual users, and only where material is made available for commercial purposes. Internet service providers are not the targets of the offence, but they can be ordered by the Federal Court to block access, and they are defined broadly to include providers of Internet access, content hosting and email.

The bill also states explicitly that an organization that only incidentally provides a service used to search for, transmit, download, store or access content is not treated as making pornography available for commercial purposes. In plain terms, general-purpose services such as search or transmission tools are meant to fall outside the offence itself.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill S-209 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Julie Miville-Dechêne. It began in the Senate and is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, meaning it has not yet become law and could still be amended, delayed or defeated. If passed, it comes into force on a day fixed by order of the Governor in Council; the heading in the bill refers to one year after royal assent.

The preamble sets out Parliament's reasoning: that pornography, including demeaning and violent material, is easily reached online by minors; that much of it is commercial and lacks effective age checks; that youth consumption is associated with harms including addiction, reinforcement of gender stereotypes and attitudes favourable to harassment and violence, particularly against women; and that age-verification technology has advanced enough to check age without breaching privacy. The bill also requires the responsible minister to table an annual report in Parliament listing the number of notices issued, the number of court applications made, and their outcomes.

S-210.overview: Bill S-210, the Ukrainian Heritage Month Act, is a short, symbolic bill that would officially designate September of every year as "Ukrainian Heritage Month" across Canada. It contains just two operative clauses — one naming the Act and one making the designation — and creates no new programs, spending, holidays or legal obligations. The bill's preamble explains the reasoning: Canada is home to more than 1.3 million Ukrainian-Canadians, the first recorded arrival of Ukrainians in Canada happened in September more than 125 years ago, and Parliament wishes to recognize the community's contributions to Canadian life. It matters mainly as a formal act of national recognition, giving schools, community groups and governments a fixed annual occasion to mark Ukrainian-Canadian history and culture. Introduced in the Senate by Senator Stanley Kutcher, the bill has passed the Senate and is now at third reading in the House of Commons — the final stage before it could become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has one substantive effect: clause 2 states that "Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the month of September is to be known as 'Ukrainian Heritage Month'." Clause 1 simply gives the law its short title, the Ukrainian Heritage Month Act.

That is the entire operative content. The bill does not create a statutory or public holiday, does not require any level of government or employer to do anything, and does not allocate funding. Designation bills of this kind are declaratory — they place a recognition in federal law without changing anyone's rights or duties.

deepDive.heading: Why September
deepDive.body:
The preamble points to the first recorded arrival of Ukrainians in Canada, which it says took place in the month of September more than 125 years ago. That historical anchor is the stated reason for choosing September rather than another month.

The preamble is the explanatory part of a bill; it sets out Parliament's reasoning but is not itself an enforceable rule.

deepDive.heading: Reasons given in the bill
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out several grounds for the designation: that Canada is home to more than 1.3 million Ukrainian-Canadians; that the peoples of Canada and Ukraine share bonds of friendship and a commitment to human rights, democracy and respect for international law; and that Ukrainian-Canadians have made significant contributions to Canada's social, economic, political and cultural fabric, including artistic, linguistic, culinary, religious and folkloric contributions.

It also states that a designated month would provide an opportunity to "remember, celebrate and educate future generations" about the role Ukrainian-Canadians play in communities across the country.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the bill imposes no obligations, its practical effect falls on those who choose to mark the month — community organizations, cultural associations, schools, museums, municipalities and federal institutions that may organize events or educational programming in September.

For individuals and businesses, nothing changes: there is no day off, no reporting requirement and no new entitlement created by the Act.

deepDive.heading: Status and process
deepDive.body:
S-210 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator — in this case Senator Stanley Kutcher — rather than by the government. Such bills must clear all stages in the Senate and then all stages in the House of Commons before receiving Royal Assent.

The bill is currently at third reading in the House of Commons, the last debate and vote stage in that chamber. If it passes third reading and receives Royal Assent, the September designation would take effect as federal law.

S-211.overview: Bill S-211 would require the federal Minister of Canadian Heritage to create a "national framework" on sports betting advertising — a coordinated plan for how such ads should be regulated across Canada, along with national standards for preventing and treating gambling harm. It doesn't ban or restrict any advertising by itself; instead, it directs the Minister to consult widely (with other federal ministers, provinces and territories, Indigenous communities, health and research experts, gaming regulators, and the advertising and gambling industries) and to report a framework and implementation strategy to Parliament within one year, followed by a progress report five years later. The bill also requires the CRTC, Canada's broadcasting and telecom regulator, to review its own rules and report within a year on whether they adequately reduce harms from the spread of sports betting ads. The bill responds to the sharp rise in gambling advertising since single-event sports betting was legalized in Canada in 2021, and to concerns raised in its preamble about exposure among minors and people at risk of gambling harm. As a Senate public bill now at committee stage in the House of Commons, it has advanced further than most private members' legislation but is not yet law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's core requirement is in section 3: the Minister of Canadian Heritage "must develop a national framework on sports betting advertising." A framework is a plan or set of agreed approaches — it is not itself a regulation, and the bill does not directly change any advertising rules, impose fines, or amend the Criminal Code.

The framework must do three things: identify measures to regulate sports betting advertising with a view to restricting it (including limiting the number, scope or location of ads, or limiting or banning the participation of celebrities and athletes in promoting sports betting); identify measures to promote research and information-sharing between governments on preventing and diagnosing harmful gambling among minors and supporting those affected; and set out national standards for preventing and diagnosing harmful gambling and addiction and for support measures.

deepDive.heading: Consultation and reporting requirements
deepDive.body:
Before finalizing the framework, the Minister must consult a broad list of parties: other federal ministers (Industry, Justice, Health, Employment and Social Development, mental health and addictions, Indigenous Services, and any others deemed relevant); provincial and territorial governments; stakeholders including self-advocates, service providers, medical and research experts, and representatives of the advertising and gambling industries; Indigenous communities and organizations with predominantly Indigenous leadership; provincial gaming regulators; and organizations associated with sports and ethics.

Within one year of the Act coming into force, the Minister must prepare a report containing the framework and a strategy to implement it, table it in both the Senate and House of Commons within 15 sitting days, and publish it on the Canadian Heritage website within 10 days of tabling. Five years after that report is tabled, a second report must be tabled explaining which measures were actually implemented and how effective they were, and — for measures not implemented — why not and on what timeline, if any.

deepDive.heading: The CRTC review
deepDive.body: Separately from the framework, section 6 requires the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission to review its own regulations and policies to assess whether they are adequate and effective at reducing harms from the proliferation of sports betting advertising. The CRTC must give the Minister a report with its conclusions and recommendations no later than one year after the bill receives royal assent, and the Minister must table that report in both Houses of Parliament within 15 sitting days of receiving it. As with the framework, the bill requires the review and the report but does not dictate what the CRTC must conclude or change.

deepDive.heading: Context and who is affected
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble ties the proposal to the Safe and Regulated Sports Betting Act, which came into force on August 27, 2021 and made it lawful for provinces (or provincially licensed entities) to run betting on single sporting events, races other than horse races, and fights. The preamble states that gambling advertising has since become pervasive, cites research linking increased ad exposure to increased gambling participation — particularly among minors and people at heightened risk — and notes that approaches across the country are non-standardized while other countries have moved to restrict such advertising.

In practical terms, the bill directly binds federal actors: the Minister of Canadian Heritage and the CRTC. Any eventual effects on betting operators, broadcasters, advertisers, athletes and celebrity endorsers would depend on what the framework recommends and on what federal and provincial authorities choose to do with it, since gambling licensing and regulation is largely a provincial responsibility. Bill S-211 originated in the Senate, is sponsored by Senator Marty Deacon, and is currently at committee consideration in the House of Commons — meaning it must still clear remaining House stages and receive royal assent before any of these obligations take effect.

S-212.overview: Bill S-212 would require the federal government to create a single, written national strategy for children and youth in Canada. A minister designated by cabinet would have to consult widely — including with children and youth themselves, other federal ministers, provincial and municipal governments, Indigenous governing bodies and advocacy organizations — and then table a strategy in Parliament within two years, setting objectives such as eliminating child poverty, ensuring equitable access to mental health services, and complying with international agreements Canada has signed on children's rights, Indigenous rights and the rights of persons with disabilities. The bill also builds in reporting: progress updates every six months until the strategy is tabled, and a review of how well it is working every five years afterward. It matters because Canada currently has many separate programs for children but, according to the bill's preamble, no unified vision or set of measurable goals. As a Senate public bill now at second reading in the House of Commons, it is a planning and accountability measure — it directs the government to produce a plan and report on it, rather than creating new benefits or services directly.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill instructs the Governor in Council (cabinet) to designate a federal minister who must develop a national strategy for children and youth. The strategy must be tabled in both the Senate and the House of Commons within 24 months of the bill receiving royal assent, and published on a Government of Canada website within 10 days of tabling.

The bill does not itself create programs, funding or entitlements. Its legal effect is procedural: it obliges a minister to consult, write a strategy containing specified elements, and report to Parliament on schedule.

deepDive.heading: What the strategy must contain
deepDive.body:
The strategy must set out federal objectives that include the complete elimination of child poverty; equitable access to mental health services for all children and youth, with particular attention to First Nations, Inuit and Métis communities, refugee and immigrant families, people in rural or remote areas, vulnerable groups, Black and other racialized communities, and children with disabilities; a high and consistent standard of living across Canada; and full compliance with five named international instruments, including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and its two optional protocols, the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

Beyond objectives, the strategy must identify measurable indicators aligned with international standards, plus a separate set of indicators developed to reflect the realities of Indigenous children and youth. It must assess with evidence whether objectives have been met, lay out a detailed plan for unmet objectives (including immediate actions on pressing harms), estimate the resources needed, and propose mechanisms for public monitoring, ongoing consultation, updating the strategy, handling complaints from children and youth, and parliamentary oversight.

deepDive.heading: Consultation requirements
deepDive.body:
Before finalizing the strategy, the minister must consult children and youth directly; other relevant federal ministers (Health, Justice, Crown-Indigenous Relations, Indigenous Services, and Employment and Social Development are named); provincial and municipal representatives; Indigenous governing bodies and organizations serving First Nations, Inuit and Métis children and youth; organizations that serve and advocate for children and youth; and anyone else the minister considers appropriate.

Consultations with children and youth must take place in a culturally safe environment, respect participants' cultures, and give them the chance to take part in their own languages. The minister must also ensure the young people consulted reflect the diversity of children and youth in Canada. In developing the strategy, the minister must consider Canada's human rights obligations, Jordan's Principle as defined by the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal, the Inuit Child First Initiative, recommendations from the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, the distinct rights and cultures of First Nations, Inuit and Métis, and federal commitments on early learning and child care.

deepDive.heading: Reporting and review timelines
deepDive.body:
Starting six months after royal assent, and every six months thereafter until the strategy is tabled, the minister must table a progress report in both Houses of Parliament describing how development is going and listing who has been consulted (where those consulted have consented to being named).

After the strategy is tabled, the minister must prepare a review report within five years, and every five years after that, describing how much of the strategy has been implemented, assessing whether its objectives have been met, and offering any further conclusions or recommendations. Those reviews require the same consultations as the original strategy, and each report must be laid before Parliament within its first 15 sitting days after completion.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble states that Canada ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1991 but has not met its obligations under it, and that Canada lacks a clear vision or set of objectives for the well-being of all children and youth. It also references Canada's Truth and Reconciliation commitments, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, Indigenous peoples' right to free, prior and informed consent regarding the parts of the strategy affecting their children, the vulnerability of young people to racism and marginalization, and what it calls a current mental health crisis.

S-212 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Rosemary Moodie — meaning it originated with an individual senator rather than the government. It has passed the Senate and is at second reading in the House of Commons, so it is not yet law and could still be amended or fail to proceed. Because many services affecting children, such as health and education, fall largely under provincial jurisdiction, the bill relies on consultation and cross-jurisdictional collaboration rather than direct federal control over those areas.

S-213.overview: Bill S-213 is a Senate public bill from Senator Donna Dasko that would amend the Canada Elections Act to shed more light on who runs for federal office and what parties are doing to diversify their candidate pools. It would require larger registered political parties to publish, on their websites, their candidate-selection rules, any diversity programs and any targets for nominating women — or explain why they don't have them. It would also revive a repealed section of the Act to have the Chief Electoral Officer send voluntary self-identification questionnaires to candidates, nomination contestants and leadership contestants, and publish anonymized reports on the results after elections and leadership races. The bill does not set quotas or require parties to nominate any particular number of people; it focuses on disclosure and data collection. As of now it is at second reading in the Senate, meaning it is early in the legislative process and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has two main parts. First, it creates a new set of "diversity-related obligations" for registered political parties, requiring them to post specific information publicly on their websites and update it once a year. Second, it directs the Chief Electoral Officer (the head of Elections Canada) to collect voluntary demographic information from people who seek or hold nominations and party leaderships, and to publish anonymized reports on that data.

To support this, the bill adds a definition of "designated groups" to the Canada Elections Act, borrowing the meaning used in the Employment Equity Act. Demographic data collected must include variables relevant to each of those designated groups, and must be gathered in a way that allows the information to be broken down and analyzed across intersecting characteristics.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: what parties would have to publish
deepDive.body:
Parties covered by the bill would have to post their candidate-selection rules (including those of their local riding associations), any programs or policies aimed at increasing diversity among candidates, how those programs relate to each designated group, the concrete steps taken to implement them (such as whether formal search committees are required), how effectiveness will be measured, and cumulative progress made.

There is a separate list of requirements specific to women candidates: parties would have to publish any plan with targets — expressed as a number, percentage or range — for nominating women by a set date, any rules governing the nomination of women in ridings where a sitting MP is not expected to run again or has resigned, any rules for ridings the party lost by 10 percentage points or less, and progress toward those targets. Importantly, if a party has no such program, policy, plan or rules, it does not have to create one — but it must publish a statement explaining why, along with any proposed timeline for adopting one. Parties would also have to post the name and contact information of a person who can receive concerns about these obligations.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions: demographic data collection and reporting
deepDive.body:
The bill restores section 535.1 of the Act (repealed in 2014) with new content. The Chief Electoral Officer would provide a self-identification questionnaire to candidates who file nomination papers, nomination contestants named in nomination contest reports, and registered leadership contestants. Answering is explicitly voluntary, and the individual responses are confidential and may be used only for the required public report.

After a general election, the Chief Electoral Officer would have to publish a report on the collected demographic data within 90 days of the return of the writs. Reports would also be published for by-elections and leadership contests, at times and in formats the Chief Electoral Officer chooses. All published data must be anonymized. The Speaker of the House of Commons would be required to table these new reports in the House without delay, as already happens with other Elections Canada reports.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and how it would be enforced
deepDive.body:
The website-disclosure rules would not apply to every registered party. They apply only to parties whose candidates won at least 2% of all valid votes nationally in the most recent general election, or at least 5% of valid votes in the ridings where the party ran candidates — a threshold that captures the larger parties and exempts very small ones. The data-collection provisions, by contrast, reach individual candidates, nomination contestants and leadership contestants across parties, though participation is optional for each person.

On enforcement, the bill adds the new diversity obligations to the list of duties that can trigger the Chief Electoral Officer's existing non-voluntary deregistration procedure. In practice, that means if the Chief Electoral Officer has reasonable grounds to believe a party has failed to meet these obligations, the party and its named officers would receive written notice under the Act's existing process.

deepDive.heading: Status, timing and context
deepDive.body:
S-213 is a Senate public bill — introduced by an individual senator rather than the government — and it is currently at second reading in the Senate. It would still need to complete Senate study and pass the House of Commons before becoming law, and many such bills do not.

If it were enacted, the party-disclosure requirements in clause 3 would not take effect immediately: they would come into force on the second anniversary of royal assent, giving parties time to prepare. The other changes, including the demographic questionnaire and reporting provisions, are not given a delayed coming-into-force date in the bill text. The bill builds on an existing framework — section 535.1 previously existed in the Act before being repealed in 2014 — and relies on the Employment Equity Act's definition of designated groups rather than creating a new one.

S-214.overview: Bill S-214 is a Senate public bill, sponsored by Senator Donna Dasko, that would change Canada's Special Economic Measures Act — the law used to impose sanctions, including freezing and seizing property connected to foreign governments and individuals. Right now, property frozen or seized under sanctions can only be permanently taken (forfeited) by the government through an application to a court. This bill would create a separate, faster route for assets owned or controlled by a foreign state: Cabinet (the Governor in Council) could order those assets forfeited to the Crown directly, without going to a judge. At the same time, the bill would explicitly bar the existing court-based forfeiture process from being used against foreign-state property, so state assets would move exclusively through the new Cabinet route. Money raised from selling such assets would flow into the same account and be available for the same purposes as other forfeited sanctioned property.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Special Economic Measures Act (originally passed in 1992), the statute that authorizes Canada to impose economic sanctions on foreign states and people connected to them. Under the current Act, property can be frozen or seized by order, and section 5.4 allows the government to apply for a court order forfeiting that property to the Crown.

Bill S-214 adds a new section 5.41 that lets the Governor in Council — effectively the federal Cabinet — order the forfeiture of property that is owned, held or controlled, directly or indirectly, by a foreign state, where that property is already subject to a seizure or restraint order under paragraph 4(1)(b) of the Act. As the bill's own summary puts it, the goal is to allow disposal of a foreign state's seized assets when the seizure occurred without a judicial order.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Three changes work together. First, a new subsection 5.4(1.1) states that the existing court-ordered forfeiture process cannot apply to property owned, held or controlled, directly or indirectly, by a foreign state. Second, the new section 5.41 creates the Cabinet-order route for exactly that kind of foreign-state property. Third, several existing provisions are updated so that they refer to both section 5.4 and the new section 5.41 — meaning the rules that already apply to court-forfeited property extend to Cabinet-forfeited property.

Those consequential updates include: costs incurred by the Crown in seizing, restraining or disposing of the property remain a debt owed by the property's owner and recoverable in court; the Minister may, after consulting the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Foreign Affairs, pay out amounts from the Proceeds Account (as defined in the Seized Property Management Act) up to the net proceeds of the disposition, but only for the purposes already listed in section 5.6; and the RCMP Commissioner may assist the Minister in matters related to making a section 5.41 order, including collecting and disclosing information.

deepDive.heading: Who and what it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill is directed at property belonging to foreign governments — including property held or controlled indirectly on their behalf — that has already been frozen or seized under Canadian sanctions. It does not change the rules for privately owned sanctioned property, which would continue to go through the existing court-application process in section 5.4.

It also affects the decision-makers: authority over foreign-state assets would shift from the courts to Cabinet, with the responsible Minister deciding how proceeds are spent after consulting the finance and foreign affairs ministers. The RCMP is given an explicit supporting role in the new process.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
S-214 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government. According to the status information provided, it has passed the Senate and is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons. It would still need to complete all stages in the Commons and receive royal assent before becoming law, and many Senate public bills do not complete that path.

The existing forfeiture and proceeds provisions in the Special Economic Measures Act (sections 5.2 through 6.2) are relatively recent additions to Canada's sanctions toolkit; this bill builds on that framework rather than creating a new one. The materials above do not set out the sponsor's stated rationale or any specific foreign state, so no motivation beyond the text of the bill is described here.

S-215.overview: Bill S-215 is a short, symbolic bill that would officially designate November of every year as "National Immigration Month" across Canada. It does not change immigration rules, spending, or anyone's legal status — it simply creates a recognized annual period for Canadians to acknowledge and celebrate the contributions immigrants have made to the country. The bill's preamble points to immigrants' role in Canada's social, cultural and economic life, and notes that November already hosts National Francophone Immigration Week and marks the anniversary of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act receiving royal assent on November 1, 2001. Sponsored by Senator Amina Gerba, it began in the Senate and is now at second reading in the House of Commons. If passed, its main practical effect would be to encourage commemoration and public education, particularly among young people.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The operative part of Bill S-215 is a single sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the month of November is to be known as 'National Immigration Month.'" The only other section gives the law its short title, the National Immigration Month Act.

That is the entirety of the bill's legal content. There are no funding commitments, no new programs, no reporting requirements, and no obligations placed on governments, employers or individuals. November would not become a holiday, and no one is required to mark the month in any particular way.

deepDive.heading: Why November was chosen
deepDive.body:
The preamble — the introductory statement explaining the bill's rationale — gives two reasons tied to the calendar. First, Canada already celebrates National Francophone Immigration Week in November, so the designation would build on an existing observance. Second, the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the federal law that sets out Canada's core immigration and refugee rules, received royal assent on November 1, 2001.

The preamble also states that Canada has benefited from immigrants' contributions to its social and cultural development, economic prosperity and global outreach, and that it is important to educate children and future generations about immigration's role in building the country.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the bill is declaratory, it has no direct legal effect on immigrants, applicants, or anyone else. Nobody gains or loses a right, benefit or obligation as a result.

Its practical audience is broader: schools, community organizations, municipalities, cultural groups and federal institutions that may choose to organize events, educational activities or commemorations during November. Designation bills of this kind typically work by giving such activities an official national label to rally around.

deepDive.heading: Context: how commemorative bills work
deepDive.body:
The preamble itself notes that Canada has already recognized many days, weeks and months celebrating the heritage of diverse communities and ethnic groups. Bill S-215 would add one more designation to that list, this time focused on immigration as a whole rather than a single community.

S-215 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator — in this case Hon. Amina Gerba — rather than by the government. Having cleared the Senate, it is now at second reading in the House of Commons, the stage where MPs debate the bill's general principle before deciding whether to send it to committee. It would still need to complete the remaining Commons stages and receive royal assent to become law.

S-217.overview: Bill S-217 would change the Canada Revenue Agency Act to force the CRA to report more information about taxes that go unpaid. Specifically, the CRA's annual report to the Minister of National Revenue would have to include a detailed list of all tax evasion convictions, with a separate list for international tax evasion cases. Every three years, that report would also have to include statistics on Canada's "tax gap" — an estimate of how much tax should have been paid but was never assessed or collected. The bill also requires the Minister to hand the underlying tax gap data over to the Parliamentary Budget Officer so that office can do its own independent analysis. In short, the bill is about transparency and measurement: it does not create new taxes, penalties or enforcement powers, but it would give Parliament and the public a clearer, recurring picture of how much tax revenue is going uncollected.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Percy E. Downe. It amends the Canada Revenue Agency Act, which governs how the CRA operates and reports to Parliament. The bill adds three reporting obligations: a list of tax evasion convictions in the CRA's annual report, periodic tax gap statistics, and a duty to share tax gap data with the Parliamentary Budget Officer (PBO).

The bill's short alternate title is the "Fairness for All Canadian Taxpayers Act (measuring the tax gap to fight international tax evasion)." Its focus is on disclosure and measurement rather than on changing what people owe or how the CRA audits and enforces the law.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
First, section 88(2) of the Act would be amended so the CRA's annual report to the Minister must include "a detailed list of all convictions for tax evasion," plus a separate list specifically for international tax evasion.

Second, a new subsection 88(3) would require the annual report to include tax gap statistics once every three years, starting three years after the provision comes into force. Because of a built-in time lag, each report would cover the fiscal year ending three years before the report is submitted. Third, a new section 88.1 defines the tax gap and sets out what the estimate must be based on, and requires the Minister to give the resulting data to the PBO.

deepDive.heading: How the "tax gap" would be defined and measured
deepDive.body:
The bill defines the tax gap as the taxes that should have been assessed on undeclared income, plus the difference between taxes that were assessed and taxes actually collected. In other words, it captures both income that was hidden and tax bills that were issued but never paid.

The calculation must be based on, among other things: the value of reassessments resulting from audits of individuals, corporations and trusts across income sources such as employment, capital gains, dividends and interest; the likelihood that money from those reassessments can actually be collected; the rate of incorrect returns that audits show were missed before assessment; and uncollected tax linked to failures to report specified foreign property under section 233.3 of the Income Tax Act. The Minister must compile these statistics broken down by category of taxpayer — individuals, corporations segmented by size, and trusts resident in Canada.

deepDive.heading: Role of the Parliamentary Budget Officer
deepDive.body:
Under the new subsection 88.1(3), the Minister must provide the PBO with the tax gap data collected, along with any additional data the PBO considers relevant to conducting further analysis. This effectively creates a second, independent set of eyes on the CRA's numbers.

Subsection 88.1(4) applies existing confidentiality and access rules from the Parliament of Canada Act (subsection 79.4(2) and sections 79.41 to 79.5) to this data, with any necessary modifications, as if the PBO had formally requested it under that Act. Those provisions govern how the PBO obtains and handles sensitive government information.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and context
deepDive.body:
The direct obligations fall on the Canada Revenue Agency and the Minister of National Revenue, who would carry out the new reporting and data-sharing duties, and on the Parliamentary Budget Officer, who would receive the data. Parliamentarians, journalists, researchers and the general public would be the main audiences for the resulting information. Ordinary taxpayers would not face any new filing requirements or taxes under this bill.

As a Senate public bill, S-217 originated with an individual senator rather than the government. It has passed the Senate and, according to its status, is at second reading in the House of Commons — meaning it still requires further debate, committee study and votes in the House before it could become law.

S-216.overview: Bill S-216 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Jim Quinn that would formally declare the Chignecto Isthmus Dykeland System — the network of dykes, aboiteaux and breakwaters protecting the narrow strip of land connecting Nova Scotia and New Brunswick — and related works to be "for the general advantage of Canada." That declaration is a constitutional tool that brings a local work under federal jurisdiction, and the bill accordingly assigns responsibility for the system to the Minister of Infrastructure and Communities. The bill also gives federal ministers authority to sign agreements with private parties, Indigenous bodies, the two provinces and municipalities to design, build and operate the system, and lets Cabinet grant emergency exemptions from federal permitting requirements. The issue matters because the isthmus carries the only road and rail links between Nova Scotia and the rest of Canada, and existing dykes are increasingly exposed to rising sea levels and severe storms. The bill is currently at committee consideration in the Senate, meaning it has not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The core of the bill is a single declaration: section 4 states that the Chignecto Isthmus Dykeland System and related works are "works for the general advantage of Canada." In Canadian constitutional practice, this phrase is a recognized way for Parliament to bring a specific work under federal authority. The bill defines the system as the dyke systems used for water management located wholly within the Nova Scotia portion and wholly within the New Brunswick portion of the Chignecto Isthmus trade corridor.

The bill also defines the supporting infrastructure it covers. "Dyke" includes dykes, aboiteaux and breakwaters associated with the system; "related work" includes water level control structures, steel sheet pile walls, and any work useful for maintaining or operating a dyke or water level control structure. "Construction" is defined broadly enough to include demolishing existing structures.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 3 makes the Minister of Infrastructure and Communities responsible for administering the Act, with powers covering all matters relating to the dykeland system and related works. Section 5 allows the Minister of Public Works and Government Services to enter agreements with any person for the design, construction or operation of the system, and to take measures to carry out those agreements or protect the Crown's interests — including holding, releasing or realizing on security. The bill specifies that anyone contracting under this section is not an agent of the Crown. Section 6 lets the Infrastructure Minister enter agreements with any person, with the governments of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, or with municipalities or agencies of either province.

Section 7 creates an emergency mechanism: in response to an emergency, the Governor in Council (Cabinet) may exempt a person from any federal requirement to obtain a permit, licence, approval or other authorization related to construction, subject to conditions Cabinet considers to be in the interest of preventing environmental damage or protecting public health or safety. Such orders are exempt from the Statutory Instruments Act but must be published in the Canada Gazette. Once construction is complete, any authorization that would otherwise have been needed is deemed to have been issued.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are the governments of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, municipalities and agencies in the isthmus area, and the communities and farmlands the dykes protect. Federal departments — Infrastructure and Communities, and Public Works and Government Services — would take on defined roles, and contractors or other entities engaged in design, construction or operation would deal with the federal government under the agreement provisions.

The bill's definitions expressly contemplate Indigenous participation: "person" includes an Indigenous governing body or Indigenous organization, so such bodies can be parties to agreements under sections 5 and 6. The definitions of Indigenous governing body, Indigenous organization and Indigenous peoples are tied to section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982.

deepDive.heading: Context
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble sets out the rationale. It describes the Chignecto Isthmus as an interprovincial surface and rail trade corridor of national importance, and notes that the Intercolonial Railway built along the isthmus under section 145 of the Constitution Act, 1867 physically linked Nova Scotia with Ontario and Quebec. It recalls that Parliament passed the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act in 1948, under which the federal government built and rebuilt dykes, aboiteaux and breakwaters.

The preamble also states that the isthmus is of critical cultural and historical significance to the Mi'kmaq and Acadian peoples, that it is vulnerable to rising sea levels and increasingly intense severe weather, and that Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have undertaken a Chignecto Isthmus Climate Change Adaptation Comprehensive Engineering and Feasibility Study. Responsibility for funding and maintaining the dykes has been a point of discussion between the federal and provincial governments; this bill approaches the question by placing the works under federal jurisdiction through the "general advantage of Canada" declaration.

deepDive.heading: Status and what comes next
deepDive.body: S-216 is a Senate public bill — introduced by an individual senator rather than the government — and it is at consideration in committee in the Senate. To become law it would need to complete the remaining Senate stages, pass all stages in the House of Commons, and receive Royal Assent. As with any bill at committee stage, its provisions could be amended before any further votes.

S-218.overview: Bill S-218 is a Senate public bill from Senator Peter Harder that would amend the Constitution Act, 1982 to make it harder for the federal Parliament to use the "notwithstanding clause" (section 33 of the Charter). That clause lets a legislature pass a law that operates even if it violates certain Charter rights, such as freedom of expression, legal rights, and equality rights.
