The bill would not remove the clause, but would add a new section 33.1 setting out procedural hurdles that apply only to Parliament — including that the Supreme Court must first have found a Charter infringement, that the bill must be a government bill starting in the House of Commons, that a written justification must be tabled, that debate cannot be time-limited, and that third reading requires a two-thirds vote with support from more than one recognized party. It matters because the notwithstanding clause is one of the most contested features of Canada's Charter, and this bill would make federal use of it a rare and demanding step. The bill is at second reading in the Senate, an early stage, and would still need to pass both chambers.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 33.1 to the Constitution Act, 1982, immediately after the existing section 33 (the notwithstanding clause). Section 33 currently allows Parliament or a provincial legislature to declare that a law operates "notwithstanding" section 2 (fundamental freedoms such as expression, religion, and association) or sections 7 to 15 (legal rights and equality rights) of the Charter.

S-218 does not repeal or limit the substance of section 33. Instead, it sets out a series of conditions and procedural requirements that would have to be satisfied before Parliament could pass a law containing such a declaration. The bill calls a bill containing that kind of declaration an "infringing bill."

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Under the proposed section 33.1, an infringing bill would have to originate in the House of Commons and be introduced by a minister — meaning private members and senators could not initiate one. It could only be introduced after the Supreme Court of Canada has found that the bill (through a reference under section 53 of the Supreme Court Act) or the existing law being shielded actually infringes one of the listed Charter rights.

The bill would also require a preamble giving reasons for the declaration, and would require the sponsoring minister to table a statement in the House explaining the bill's potential effects on the listed rights and why the infringement cannot be justified under section 1 of the Charter. Procedurally, neither the House nor the Senate could adopt a motion limiting debate time (time allocation), and the bill could not be studied in Committee of the Whole. Finally, third reading in the House of Commons would require a two-thirds supermajority of all members — not just those present — plus support from members of at least two recognized parties, overriding the ordinary majority rule in section 49 of the Constitution Act, 1867.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The new rules would apply only to the Parliament and government of Canada, covering all matters within federal authority, including matters relating to Yukon and the Northwest Territories. The text expressly states this despite section 32 of the Charter, which otherwise defines the Charter's application to both federal and provincial governments.

Provincial legislatures would not be bound by the new conditions and could continue to invoke section 33 under the existing rules. In practical terms, the bill would affect federal ministers seeking to shield legislation from Charter challenges, parliamentarians in both chambers who would face different debate and voting rules, and the Supreme Court, which would need to have ruled on the Charter question before such a bill could be introduced.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill — a bill introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government — sponsored by Senator Peter Harder. It was introduced in 2025 and is currently at second reading in the Senate, an early stage in the legislative process. To become law it would need to be approved by the Senate and the House of Commons.

The explanatory note accompanying the bill indicates that clause 1 is entirely new text. Beyond what appears in the bill itself, the material provided does not include debate, committee study, or commentary on how the proposed amendment would interact with the constitutional amending formula, so no conclusions on those points are drawn here.

S-219.overview: Bill S-219 is a short Senate public bill that would officially designate January 11 of every year as "Judicial Independence Day" across Canada. It is a symbolic or commemorative bill: it does not create a statutory holiday, spend money, change how judges are appointed or disciplined, or impose any new legal obligations on anyone. Its stated purpose, set out in a preamble, is to draw public attention to the importance of an impartial judiciary and to the threats judicial independence faces in various countries. The date was chosen to mark the January 11, 2020 "1,000 Robes March" in Warsaw, a large demonstration by judges from across Europe against attacks on judicial independence in Poland. Sponsored by Senator Pierre Moreau, the bill has passed the Senate stage and is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The operative part of Bill S-219 is a single sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the 11th day of January is to be known as 'Judicial Independence Day.'" A second clause gives the law its short title, the Judicial Independence Day Act.

That is the entirety of the bill's legal effect. Like other federal commemorative days (for example, days recognizing particular communities, causes or historical events), the designation is symbolic. It does not create a public or statutory holiday, does not require businesses, schools or government offices to close, and does not require anyone to hold events or ceremonies.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 sets the short title. Clause 2 makes the designation of January 11 as Judicial Independence Day.

The bill also contains a preamble — introductory text explaining Parliament's reasoning. The preamble states that the rule of law is fundamental to a democratic society and to upholding human rights; that the rule of law requires judges who are impartial and independent from political pressure and interference; and that judicial independence depends on appointment and promotion processes based on merit, along with fair, impartial and transparent disciplinary mechanisms. A preamble helps explain a law's purpose and can assist in interpreting it, but it does not itself create rules or obligations.

deepDive.heading: Why January 11
deepDive.body:
The preamble ties the date to a specific international event. On January 11, 2020, tens of thousands of people — including hundreds of judges from 22 European countries — took part in the "1,000 Robes March" in Warsaw, Poland, to protest what participants described as attacks on judicial independence in that country.

The preamble further notes that the International Association of Judges formally asked the United Nations to commemorate the 1,000 Robes March, partly to recognize the judges' peaceful mobilization in defence of an independent judiciary. Parliament, the preamble says, recognizes the importance of drawing public attention to threats to judicial independence in many countries around the world.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the bill imposes no duties and grants no powers, it has no direct legal effect on individuals, employers, courts or governments. No one gains a day off, and no court procedure or judicial appointment rule changes.

Its practical significance is expressive: it gives legal recognition to a date that governments, legal organizations, law schools, bar associations, media and civil society groups could use as a focal point for public education or commemoration relating to judicial independence and the rule of law.

deepDive.heading: Status and process
deepDive.body:
S-219 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator — here, Hon. Pierre Moreau — rather than by the government as part of its legislative program. It has completed the Senate stage and is listed as awaiting first reading in the House of Commons.

To become law, the bill would still need to pass first, second and third reading in the House of Commons, including committee study, and then receive Royal Assent. Senate public bills often move slowly in the House because they compete for limited time reserved for private members' business, so passage is not guaranteed.

S-220.overview: Bill S-220 is a short Senate public bill that would officially designate March of every year as "Hellenic Heritage Month" across Canada. Sponsored by Senator Tony Loffreda, it is symbolic legislation: it creates no new programs, funding, holidays or legal obligations, and simply gives national recognition to the contributions of Canadians of Greek descent. The bill's preamble notes that more than 260,000 Canadians are of Greek heritage, that Greek Canadians have contributed to Canadian political, economic, scientific, legal, medical, cultural and social life, and that March is significant because Greece's war of independence began on March 25, 1821. The bill is currently at committee consideration in the Senate, meaning it has passed second reading there but still has several steps to go — including passage through the House of Commons — before it could become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The operative part of the bill is a single sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the month of March is to be known as 'Hellenic Heritage Month'." A second clause gives the legislation its short title, the Hellenic Heritage Month Act. That is the entirety of the bill's legal content.

Because a heritage month designation is recognitional rather than regulatory, the bill does not create a statutory holiday, does not require any level of government or any employer to do anything, and does not allocate money.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Clause 1 sets out the short title. Clause 2 makes the designation, applying nationwide and recurring annually without the need for further action or renewal.

The preamble — the "whereas" clauses at the front of the bill — explains Parliament's reasons for the designation but is not itself enforceable law. It cites the size of the Greek Canadian community, its contributions across many fields, the historical link between Canadian democracy and ancient Athens, and the significance of March 25, 1821, the Feast of the Annunciation, when Greece began its war of independence from the Ottoman Empire.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill's most direct relevance is to the Greek Canadian community, which the preamble numbers at over 260,000 people with communities across the country. A formal designation gives community organizations, schools, cultural groups and governments a recognized national occasion around which to organize events and educational programming.

For Canadians generally, the practical effect is minimal: no rights, obligations, taxes or entitlements change. The preamble frames the month as an opportunity for Greek Canadians to share their culture and traditions with other Canadians.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
S-220 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government. Bills of this kind are common vehicles for heritage month designations, and Parliament has passed a number of similar acts recognizing other communities.

The bill was introduced in 2025 and is now at consideration in committee in the Senate. To become law it would need to complete committee study and third reading in the Senate, then pass all three readings in the House of Commons and receive Royal Assent. Like all bills, it would die if Parliament is prorogued or dissolved before that process is finished.

S-221.overview: Bill S-221, the National Bird of Canada Act, is a short symbolic bill that would officially declare the Canada jay (Perisoreus canadensis) the national bird of Canada. The entire operative content is two lines: one naming the Act and one recognizing the bird. Canada currently has no official national bird, even though every province and territory — and more than 100 countries — have designated one. The bill imposes no rules, spends no money and creates no programs; it simply adds an official avian emblem alongside symbols like the maple leaf and the beaver. It is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Salma Ataullahjan, and it has passed the Senate and is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has just two clauses. Clause 1 gives the law its short title, the National Bird of Canada Act. Clause 2 states that the bird known as the Canada jay (Perisoreus canadensis) "is hereby recognized and declared to be the national bird of Canada."

That is the whole legal effect. There is nothing in the text that regulates behaviour, protects the species, creates penalties, assigns responsibilities to any government department, or authorizes spending. It is a declaratory or symbolic statute, similar in structure to other laws that recognize national emblems or commemorative days.

deepDive.heading: The reasons given in the preamble
deepDive.body:
Most of the bill is a preamble setting out why the Canada jay was chosen. It notes that Canada, unlike its provinces and territories and over 100 other countries, has no official bird; that the Canada jay lives in Canada year-round, is adapted to very cold environments, and breeds in all ten provinces and three territories; and that it has long been known to Canada's First Peoples by names including "grey jay," "camp robber" and the Cree wîskicahk, which the preamble says likely evolved into the English nickname "whiskey jack."

The preamble also states that the bird historically greeted explorers, fur trappers, loggers, prospectors, settlers and First Peoples in winter camps; that it draws visitors to Canada's boreal forest and parks; that the choice has support from naturalists, birdwatchers and ornithologists; that the species is not endangered, hunted or considered a nuisance; and that it is not already an official symbol of any country, province, territory or state. Preambles explain Parliament's reasoning and can help with interpretation, but they do not themselves create legal obligations.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
No individual, business, or level of government would face new requirements under this bill. Because it is purely declaratory, its practical effects would be symbolic and cultural — for example, use of the Canada jay in official materials, education, tourism promotion or commemorations, none of which the bill itself mandates.

Notably, the bill does not confer any legal protection on the Canada jay or its habitat. Conservation of birds and wildlife continues to be governed by existing federal and provincial laws, which this bill does not amend.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill — legislation introduced by an individual senator rather than by the federal government — sponsored by Senator Salma Ataullahjan. Its listed status is that it has cleared the Senate and is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons, meaning it must still complete the full Commons process (readings, committee study and votes) and receive Royal Assent before becoming law.

Senate public bills often face limited time on the Commons agenda, so passage is not automatic. Until then, Canada remains without an officially designated national bird, notwithstanding informal or unofficial designations that have been promoted in the past.

S-223.overview: Bill S-223 is a short Senate public bill, sponsored by Senator Mary Jane McCallum, that would amend the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act to explicitly add First Nation laws to the list of laws the RCMP is responsible for enforcing. At present, the Act says RCMP members who are peace officers must help prevent offences against the laws of Canada and the laws of the province where they work, and must execute warrants under those laws. The bill adds a definition of "First Nation law" and inserts that term into both duties, so that preventing offences against First Nation laws and executing warrants issued under them would be part of the RCMP's formal mandate. This matters because enforcement of band bylaws and other First Nation laws has long been an unsettled area, and the change would put those laws on the same explicit footing in the RCMP's governing statute as federal and provincial laws. The bill is currently at the committee consideration stage in the Senate, meaning it has not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes two changes to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. First, it adds a new definition of "First Nation law" to section 2(1), the Act's definitions section. Second, it rewrites paragraphs 18(a) and 18(b), which set out the core duties of RCMP members who are peace officers, so that those duties expressly cover First Nation laws alongside federal and provincial laws.

According to the bill's own summary, the purpose is to provide that the duties of RCMP members who are peace officers include the prevention of offences against First Nation laws and the execution of warrants that may lawfully be executed by peace officers under those laws.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
The new definition covers three categories of law: (a) bylaws made under the Indian Act; (b) a "First Nation law" as defined in the Framework Agreement on First Nation Land Management Act; and (c) a law enacted by a council, government or other entity authorized to act on behalf of a First Nation under a self-government agreement that has been implemented by an Act of Parliament.

In section 18, paragraph (a) currently requires peace officer members to work on preserving the peace and preventing crime and offences against "the laws of Canada and the laws in force in any province in which they may be employed"; the bill inserts "and First Nation laws" into that list. Paragraph (b) currently requires them to execute all warrants that may lawfully be executed by peace officers under the RCMP Act, the laws of Canada, or provincial laws; the bill adds First Nation laws to that list as well. Both duties remain, as before, "subject to the orders of the Commissioner."

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are RCMP members who serve as peace officers, whose statutory duties would be expanded to expressly include First Nation laws, and First Nations whose bylaws, land-management laws or self-government laws fall within the new definition.

The scope is defined by the three categories listed in the bill. Laws made by a First Nation that fit one of those categories — Indian Act bylaws, laws under the Framework Agreement on First Nation Land Management Act, or laws made under a federally implemented self-government agreement — would be captured. The bill text provided does not address funding, training, prosecution arrangements, or how enforcement priorities would be set beyond the existing reference to the orders of the Commissioner.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government. Senate public bills must pass both the Senate and the House of Commons and receive Royal Assent before becoming law, and many do not complete that path.

The bill is listed as being at consideration in committee in the Senate — an early-to-middle stage where senators study the bill in detail, hear from witnesses, and may propose amendments. Nothing in the bill would take effect unless and until it completes the full parliamentary process.

S-222.overview: Bill S-222, the "Vote 16 Act," was a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Marilou McPhedran that would have lowered the federal voting age in Canada from 18 to 16. It proposed changing the Canada Elections Act so that any Canadian citizen who is 16 or older on polling day would be qualified to vote, and made matching changes to the regulation that adapts election rules for national referendums. The bill also updated a series of related provisions that reference the age of 18 — such as the definition of a "future elector" on Elections Canada's register, the offence of voting while underage, and the sworn declaration voters sign at the polls. If passed, it would have come into force six months after royal assent, or earlier if the Chief Electoral Officer announced that Elections Canada was ready. The bill was defeated, so the federal voting age remains 18.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The core change is a single sentence. Section 3 of the Canada Elections Act currently says that every Canadian citizen who is 18 or older on polling day is qualified as an elector. Bill S-222 would have replaced "18" with "16," extending the right to vote in federal elections to 16- and 17-year-old citizens.

The same change was proposed for national referendums. Section 3 of the Schedule to the Regulation Adapting the Canada Elections Act for the Purposes of a Referendum would also have been amended so that citizens 16 and older could vote in a federal referendum.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Beyond the main voting-age change, the bill adjusted several provisions that cross-reference the age of 18 so the law would remain internally consistent. The definition of "future elector" — young people who can pre-register with Elections Canada before they are eligible to vote — would have been narrowed from "14 or older but under 18" to simply "14 or 15 years of age," since 16- and 17-year-olds would become full electors. Subsection 22(5), which specifically permits certain election officers to be as young as 16, would have been repealed as unnecessary.

The bill also updated the offence provision (section 281.3) that makes it illegal to vote, or to induce someone else to vote, while knowing the person is underage — the threshold would shift from 18 to 16. Political party reporting rules for fundraising events (section 384.3) would have withheld names of attendees under 16 rather than under 18, and the standard solemn declaration voters can sign at the polls (section 549.1) would state that the elector is or will be 16 or older on polling day.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected group would be Canadian citizens aged 16 and 17, who would gain the right to cast a ballot in federal elections and referendums. Those aged 14 and 15 would still be able to sign up as "future electors" in advance of eligibility.

Elections Canada would also be affected, as it would need to update the voters register, forms, and administrative systems. Political parties would see a change in their fundraising disclosure obligations, since the age threshold for withholding attendee names would drop from 18 to 16.

deepDive.heading: Timing and coming into force
deepDive.body:
The bill included a delayed start date rather than taking effect immediately on royal assent. It would have come into force six months after receiving royal assent — on the same calendar day in the sixth month, or the last day of that month if no matching date exists.

The bill allowed for an earlier start: if the Chief Electoral Officer published a notice in the Canada Gazette confirming that the necessary preparations were complete for the whole Act or any specific provision, that Act or provision would come into force on the day the notice was published. This is a common approach for election-law changes that require administrative preparation.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
S-222 was a Senate public bill — legislation introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government. Such bills must pass both the Senate and the House of Commons to become law, and relatively few do.

This bill was defeated, meaning it did not proceed to become law. The federal voting age in Canada therefore remains 18. The bill's text, as summarized in the legislation itself, was limited to extending voting eligibility to citizens aged 16 and 17 and making the consequential adjustments described above; it did not address other aspects of election law.

S-224.overview: Bill S-224 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Mary Jane McCallum that would amend the federal Director of Public Prosecutions Act. It would make the federal Director of Public Prosecutions (the head of the Public Prosecution Service of Canada) responsible for laying and conducting prosecutions of less serious offences — known as summary conviction offences — created under First Nation laws, acting on behalf of the First Nation whose law is being enforced. The duty would not apply where a First Nation has already hired or appointed its own prosecutor, or has struck a deal with a province or territory to handle those prosecutions. The bill matters because First Nation bylaws and laws have often gone unenforced when no prosecutor is available to bring cases to court; the bill would designate a default prosecutor. As of this summary, the bill is at committee consideration in the Senate, meaning it has not become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill adds a new section 3.1 to the Director of Public Prosecutions Act. Under it, the Director of Public Prosecutions "initiates and conducts" prosecutions of summary conviction offences under First Nation laws, along with any related appeals or other proceedings, on behalf of the First Nation that made or enacted the law.

This is a default duty rather than an exclusive one. Subsection 3.1(2) says the Director must not take on such a prosecution if the First Nation in question has appointed or retained its own prosecutor, or has entered into an agreement with a provincial or territorial government for the prosecution of summary conviction offences under its laws. In other words, federal prosecutors step in only where the First Nation has not already arranged for prosecution another way.

deepDive.heading: Key definitions and technical changes
deepDive.body:
The bill inserts two new definitions into section 2 of the Act. "First Nation" is defined to cover a band under the Indian Act, a First Nation as defined in the Framework Agreement on First Nation Land Management Act, and a First Nation party to a self-government agreement implemented by an Act of Parliament. "First Nation law" correspondingly covers bylaws made under the Indian Act, First Nation laws under the Framework Agreement on First Nation Land Management Act, and laws enacted by a council, government or other entity authorized to act for a First Nation under an implemented self-government agreement.

The bill also adjusts the existing definition of "prosecution" so that it carves out matters referred to in the new section 3.1, in addition to the existing carve-out for subsection 3(8). This is a drafting change that keeps the new First Nation prosecution duty separate from the Act's general definition of prosecutions falling under the jurisdiction of the federal Attorney General.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected parties are First Nations that have enacted laws or bylaws containing summary conviction offences, and individuals who could be charged under those laws. The Public Prosecution Service of Canada, headed by the Director of Public Prosecutions, would take on new responsibilities where no other prosecution arrangement exists.

Provincial and territorial governments are referenced indirectly: an existing prosecution agreement between a First Nation and a province or territory would displace the federal duty. First Nations that employ or retain their own prosecutors would likewise continue under their own arrangements, unaffected by the new default rule.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The Director of Public Prosecutions Act (S.C. 2006, c. 9, s. 121) created the office of the Director of Public Prosecutions to conduct federal prosecutions independently of the Attorney General's day-to-day direction. Bill S-224 would extend that office's mandate into a specific new area — enforcement of First Nation laws — while preserving room for First Nations to make their own prosecution arrangements.

The bill is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator rather than the government. It is currently at consideration in committee in the Senate, an early-to-middle stage; it would still need to complete Senate stages, pass through the House of Commons, and receive Royal Assent before taking effect. The text above does not specify a coming-into-force date or any funding provisions.

S-225.overview: Bill S-225 would designate February 5 of each year as "National Thanadelthur Day" across Canada. Thanadelthur was a Denesuline (Dene) woman who, in the early 1700s, worked as an interpreter, ambassador and negotiator connected to the Hudson's Bay Company, and who helped broker peace between the Denesuline and Cree peoples in what is now northern Manitoba; she died on February 5, 1717. The bill is purely commemorative: it creates a national day of recognition but does not create a statutory holiday, does not close courts or offices, and does not spend money or change anyone's legal rights or obligations. Its stated purpose is to draw attention to a little-known chapter of the northern fur trade and to the contributions of Indigenous women to Canadian history. It is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Mary Jane McCallum and, as of this writing, is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill has only three short operative sections. Section 1 gives it a short title, the National Thanadelthur Day Act. Section 2 states that throughout Canada, in each and every year, February 5 is to be known as "National Thanadelthur Day." Section 3 clarifies that the day is not a legal holiday or a "non-juridical day" — meaning workplaces, banks and government offices stay open, and courts and legal deadlines operate normally.

That is the entire substance of the bill. It does not require any government program, funding, ceremony or reporting, and it does not amend any other law.

deepDive.heading: Who Thanadelthur was, according to the preamble
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble sets out the historical account that motivates it. It describes a hostile relationship between the Denesuline and Cree peoples in what is now northern Manitoba, aggravated by the fur trade in the early 1700s. Thanadelthur, a young Denesuline woman, was captured by the Cree in 1713 and enslaved for a year before escaping to the Hudson's Bay Company's York Factory post, then governed by James Knight.

According to the preamble, she remained at York Factory and worked with Knight on a plan to make peace between the Denesuline and Cree — both to enable trade and so the two peoples could live harmoniously. In 1715–16 she guided HBC trader William Stuart and a group of Cree northwest of York Factory into Denesuline territory. The preamble credits her contribution with bringing about peace between the Cree and Denesuline, with lasting effects on both peoples and on the Hudson's Bay Company. She died on February 5, 1717 — the date the bill selects for the commemorative day.

deepDive.heading: Practical effect and who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the day is explicitly not a legal holiday, the bill has no direct effect on employment, pay, business hours or court schedules. Its practical impact is symbolic and educational: a nationally recognized date that schools, communities, governments and organizations may choose to mark, and a reference point for public awareness of Thanadelthur's story.

The bill's own preamble frames the intended audience broadly, saying her "little-known but inspirational story of bravery and determination sheds light on the early years of the northern fur trade and speaks to the important contributions of Indigenous women." Denesuline and Cree communities, particularly in northern Manitoba, and Indigenous history and education efforts more generally, are the most directly connected to the subject matter.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill — legislation introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government — sponsored by Senator Mary Jane McCallum. Commemorative-day bills of this kind are a common category of private and public members' legislation in Canada; Parliament has passed a number of similar acts establishing national days of recognition that carry no holiday status.

The bill has cleared the Senate stage and is awaiting first reading in the House of Commons. Like any bill, it must pass all stages in the House and receive Royal Assent before the designation takes legal effect. Until then, February 5 has no official federal designation under this proposal.

S-226.overview: Bill S-226 is a short, symbolic bill that would officially designate the second week of May each year as "Jury Duty Appreciation Week" across Canada. It does not create any new legal obligations, holidays, programs or funding — it simply gives the week a name in federal law. The bill's preamble explains the reasoning: thousands of Canadians serve on juries every year, juries are described as essential to the justice system and to democracy, and jurors' well-being and mental health matter to how well that system works. Supporters of the idea see a dedicated week as a way to recognize jurors' contribution and to raise awareness — among the public, organizations, the justice system and governments — about the challenges people face when they serve. Introduced in the Senate by Senator Lucie Moncion, the bill has passed that chamber and is now at second reading in the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The entire operative content of Bill S-226 fits in one sentence: "Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the second week of May shall be known as 'Jury Duty Appreciation Week'." A second clause gives the legislation its short title, the Jury Duty Appreciation Week Act.

That is the whole of the bill. It is what is sometimes called a commemorative or designation bill — legislation whose purpose is recognition rather than regulation.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does not do
deepDive.body:
Because the text contains only a designation, the bill does not create a statutory holiday, does not change jury selection rules, does not alter juror pay or compensation, and does not require any government department, court or employer to do anything. Provincial governments, which administer most jury systems, are not given any new duties.

Any activities during the week — such as public education efforts or recognition events — would be voluntary and are not specified in the legislation.

deepDive.heading: The reasoning set out in the bill
deepDive.body:
The preamble (the introductory statement of purpose, which is not itself an operative rule) lays out four points: that jury duty is a civic duty performed by thousands of Canadians each year; that it is a vital component of the justice system and of democracy; that jurors' well-being and mental health are paramount to the proper functioning of the justice system; and that a dedicated week would highlight jurors' work and help educate citizens, organizations, the justice system, and provincial and federal governments about the issues involved in serving.

This framing signals that the bill is aimed not only at thanking jurors but also at drawing attention to the practical and psychological demands of jury service.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
In practical terms, no one is subject to new requirements. The people most directly connected to the bill are current and former jurors, who would be the focus of the annual recognition, along with courts, legal organizations and advocacy groups that might choose to mark the week.

For the general public, the effect would be limited to awareness: a named week on the calendar each May that could prompt media coverage, outreach or discussion about jury service.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
S-226 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator — in this case Senator Lucie Moncion — rather than by the government. Such bills must clear the Senate first and then proceed through the House of Commons.

The bill is currently at second reading in the House of Commons, an early stage where members debate the principle of the bill before it can be sent to committee. It is not yet law, and would still require passage through the remaining Commons stages and royal assent to take effect.

S-227.overview: Bill S-227, the Arab Heritage Month Act, is a short piece of legislation that officially designates April of every year as "Arab Heritage Month" across Canada. It is a symbolic or commemorative law: it does not create new programs, spending, rights or obligations, and it does not require anyone to hold events or observe the month in any particular way. The bill's preamble explains the reasoning behind the designation, noting that the first people of Arab origin arrived in Canada in 1882, that more than one million Arab Canadians live in the country today, and that they have contributed to Canada's social, economic, political and cultural life. Introduced in the Senate by Senator Mohammad Khair Al Zaibak, the bill has received Royal Assent, meaning it is now law. Its practical significance is recognition — giving federal, formal acknowledgment to a community's history and place in Canadian society.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The Act contains just two operative sections. The first gives the law its short title, the "Arab Heritage Month Act." The second states that "throughout Canada, in each year, the month of April is to be known as 'Arab Heritage Month.'"

That is the entire legal effect. There is no funding attached, no new federal body created, no reporting requirement, and no change to any existing statute. Commemorative months of this kind establish an official name for a period of the year; participation by governments, schools, community groups or businesses remains entirely voluntary.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions and what is not included
deepDive.body:
Section 1 (short title) and section 2 (the April designation) make up the substance of the bill. A preamble sets out Parliament's reasons but, as with most preambles, it is explanatory rather than binding.

Equally important is what the bill does not do: it does not create a statutory holiday, does not affect employment or business obligations, and does not direct any department to organize activities. Designating a heritage month is distinct from declaring a public holiday.

deepDive.heading: The reasoning in the preamble
deepDive.body:
The preamble lays out four points Parliament relied on. It notes that the first persons of Arab origin arrived in Canada in 1882, in the early years after Confederation; that the Arab Canadian population has since grown to over one million, with young and dynamic communities across the country; that Arab Canadians from all walks of life have contributed to Canada's social, economic and political life; and that they have enriched Canadian culture through literature, music, food and fashion.

The closing recital states that Parliament wishes to recognize and celebrate the historic mark Arab Canadians have made and continue to make in building Canadian society.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
Because the Act imposes no duties, no one is legally required to do anything differently. Its main effect is on Arab Canadian communities and organizations, which now have a federally recognized month to anchor cultural programming, educational events and public commemorations.

More broadly, schools, museums, municipalities and federal institutions may choose to mark the occasion, but any such activity is discretionary rather than mandated by the legislation.

deepDive.heading: Process and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate Public Bill — legislation introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government — sponsored by Senator Mohammad Khair Al Zaibak. To become law, it had to pass both the Senate and the House of Commons before receiving Royal Assent.

The bill has received Royal Assent, so the April designation is now in force. It joins a number of other commemorative months and days that Parliament has established by statute over the years.

S-228.overview: Bill S-228 is a short Senate public bill, sponsored by Senator Yvonne Boyer, that adds a new section 268.1 to the Criminal Code. It states "for greater certainty" that a sterilization procedure counts as an act that "wounds or maims" a person under subsection 268(1) of the Criminal Code — the provision dealing with aggravated assault. The bill also spells out what counts as a sterilization procedure, including cutting, clipping, tying or cauterizing the Fallopian tubes, ovaries or uterus, as well as any other procedure that permanently prevents reproduction, even if it could later be surgically reversed. A preamble explains that the bill responds to the sterilization of people without their consent, which it describes as a legacy of systemic discrimination, colonization and racism that disproportionately affects Indigenous and racialized people. The bill has received Royal Assent, meaning it has completed the parliamentary process and become law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill makes a single, targeted change to the Criminal Code. It inserts a new section 268.1 immediately after section 268, the aggravated assault provision, to clarify that performing a sterilization procedure on someone is an act that "wounds or maims" that person within the meaning of subsection 268(1).

The wording "for greater certainty" signals that the intent is to remove any ambiguity about how existing law applies, rather than to create a brand-new offence. The bill does not change the penalties in section 268 or add any new offence of its own.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Subsection 268.1(1) is the operative clause: it declares that a sterilization procedure wounds or maims a person for the purposes of subsection 268(1).

Subsection 268.1(2) defines "sterilization procedure" broadly. It covers the severing, clipping, tying or cauterizing — in whole or in part — of a person's Fallopian tubes, ovaries or uterus. It also captures "any other procedure" that results in the permanent prevention of reproduction. Importantly, the definition applies whether or not the procedure could later be reversed through further surgery, so the possibility of reversal does not take a procedure outside the definition.

deepDive.heading: Context and stated purpose
deepDive.body:
The bill includes a preamble — an introductory statement of purpose that is not itself an operative rule. It says that sterilizing people without their consent is a legacy of systemic discrimination, colonization and racism, and that this practice has disproportionately, though not exclusively, affected Indigenous and racialized persons.

The preamble situates the amendment as a response to that history. It signals to courts and readers the concern the legislation is meant to address, while the legal effect of the bill comes from the new section 268.1 itself.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The change operates within the Criminal Code's assault framework, so it is most directly relevant to criminal prosecutions and to anyone who might perform a sterilization procedure. By clarifying that such a procedure falls within the "wounds or maims" language of aggravated assault, the bill affects how that existing offence is interpreted and applied.

Based on the text provided, the bill speaks only to this classification question. It does not, on its face, set out new rules about how consent to medical procedures is obtained or documented; the wording addresses the meaning of subsection 268(1) and defines the procedures covered.

deepDive.heading: Status
deepDive.body: S-228 is a Senate public bill — that is, a bill introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government. According to the information provided, it has received Royal Assent, the final step in the legislative process, and so has been enacted into law.

S-229.overview: Bill S-229, the Gatineau Park Act, is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Rosa Galvez that would amend the National Capital Act to give Gatineau Park — the large federally managed green space just north of Ottawa, in Quebec — clear legal boundaries and stronger protection. For the first time, the park's borders would be written into law in a schedule, and land could only be added, not removed (except if a court finds the Crown doesn't actually own it). The bill would require the National Capital Commission (NCC) to make "ecological integrity" its first priority in managing the park, generally ban the sale of public land inside it, and require a long-term Master Plan tabled in Parliament. It also builds in consultation and economic participation for the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation, on whose unceded traditional territory the park sits, and for neighbouring municipalities. The bill is currently at committee study in the Senate, meaning it is still early in the legislative process and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the existing National Capital Act rather than creating a stand-alone statute. It adds a definition of Gatineau Park tied to boundaries set out in a new Schedule 2, and adds definitions of "ecological integrity" and "enforcement officer." It declares the park "dedicated to the people of Canada, including the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation, for their benefit, education and enjoyment," and says it must be left unimpaired for future generations.

Centrally, new section 10.02 states that maintaining ecological integrity — protecting natural resources and natural processes — "shall be the first priority" of the National Capital Commission in all aspects of managing the park. This is a legal ranking of priorities that the NCC would have to apply when making management decisions.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Boundaries and land: The Governor in Council (Cabinet) could enlarge the park by order if the Crown holds title to the added lands, but could not shrink it, except to remove land a court has ruled the Crown does not own. Selling or granting rights in public land inside the park would be prohibited, with two exceptions: transfers to an Algonquin Anishinabeg organization or governing body for health care, social or cultural services, and transfers to a federal, provincial or municipal authority for public health facilities or public infrastructure such as utilities or transportation corridors. If the land stops being used for that purpose, it reverts to the NCC. Using or occupying public land in the park would require NCC permission.

Planning, rules and enforcement: The NCC would have to produce a Gatineau Park Master Plan within 10 years — covering a long-term ecological vision, ecological integrity objectives and indicators, resource protection and restoration, zoning, visitor use, public awareness and performance evaluation — table it in both Houses of Parliament, and review it at least every 10 years. Cabinet could make regulations restricting activities, managing ecological integrity, and setting fees, rents and charges; fees could not exceed the NCC's actual costs. Penalties for breaking those regulations would be set by regulation within the summary-conviction limits of the Criminal Code. The Minister could designate federal, provincial, municipal or Algonquin Anishinabeg law-enforcement personnel as enforcement officers, with peace-officer powers and protections for this purpose, and could designate people to enforce offences treated as contraventions under the Contraventions Act.

deepDive.heading: Indigenous and municipal consultation
deepDive.body:
The preamble notes that Gatineau Park is on the unceded traditional lands of the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation and references the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act. The bill would require the NCC to provide opportunities for public participation at national, regional and local levels — explicitly including the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation and park residents — in developing regulations, Master Plans and land use planning.

The NCC would also have to publish a report on its website demonstrating that it consulted adjacent cities and municipalities and the region's Algonquin Anishinabeg governing bodies, and that it considered their recommendations. Separately, the NCC "must also consider" using businesses and workers from the region's Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation for part of the park's maintenance and conservation work.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected body is the National Capital Commission, the federal Crown corporation that manages the park; its mandate, planning obligations and land-disposal powers would change. Municipalities bordering the park and the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation gain formal consultation rights, and Algonquin organizations gain a specific pathway to acquire park land for health, social or cultural services.

Park users, residents and businesses operating inside the boundaries could be affected by new regulations on activities and by cost-recovery fees for permits and services. The bill also preserves the existing provision allowing the NCC to pay grants to local authorities to offset municipal and school tax revenue lost when it acquires property in the park (with a French-language wording correction).

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble situates the bill within Canada's commitment under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in Montreal in December 2022, to strengthen management of protected areas, and notes the park's ecosystems and species at risk. Gatineau Park has historically lacked the statutory boundary protection that national parks receive under separate legislation; this bill would place its boundaries in law.

The bill also includes housekeeping changes: the existing schedule to the National Capital Act becomes Schedule 1, the new park boundary description becomes Schedule 2, and dozens of other federal statutes that refer to "the schedule to the National Capital Act" are updated to say "Schedule 1." As a Senate public bill at committee stage, S-229 would still need to clear the full Senate and the House of Commons before it could become law.

S-232.overview: Bill S-232, the "Can't Buy Silence Act," is a Senate public bill that would limit how federal institutions use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in harassment, violence and discrimination cases, and would require public reporting on how often such agreements are used. Under the bill, federal departments, Crown corporations, parliamentary bodies and organizations receiving federal grants could generally not use public money to settle these complaints with an NDA attached, or to sue a complainant over an NDA. Where an NDA is still used, it would have to be specifically and voluntarily requested in writing by the complainant after they have had a chance to get independent legal advice, and it could not stop them from speaking to police, lawyers, doctors, counsellors, family or other supporters. The President of the Treasury Board would have to table an annual report to Parliament counting NDAs and the dollar value of the agreements containing them, with the data anonymized. The bill is at second reading in the Senate, meaning it is early in the legislative process and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill targets the use of NDAs — confidentiality clauses that prevent someone from talking about what happened to them — in cases involving harassment, violence, or discrimination on a ground prohibited by the Canadian Human Rights Act. It does this in three main ways: by restricting the use of public money for NDA-linked settlements and for litigation against complainants, by setting conditions that must be met before a federal body can enter into an NDA at all, and by creating a new annual transparency report to Parliament.

It amends two existing laws — the Financial Administration Act and the Parliament of Canada Act — and also creates standalone reporting and review requirements. The bill defines an NDA broadly: it covers any written provision, "however called," under which a complainant agrees not to disclose material information about the alleged harassment or discrimination, how the complaint was resolved, or the dollar value of a settlement. Non-disparagement clauses are expressly included if their purpose or effect is the same.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Spending restrictions: Federal departments, departmental corporations and Crown corporations could not use public money to litigate an NDA against a complainant. Officials with authority to make grants and contributions would have to exercise that authority in a way that prevents federal money from paying for harassment or discrimination settlements that include an NDA, or from being used to litigate NDAs against complainants. Parallel restrictions would apply to the Senate's Committee on Internal Economy, the House of Commons Board of Internal Economy, the Parliamentary Librarian and the Parliamentary Protective Service.

Consent conditions and carve-outs: An NDA could only be entered into if the complainant, after having had the opportunity to obtain independent legal advice — including advice on other ways to protect their privacy — makes a specific, voluntary, written request for one beforehand. Even then, the NDA would not apply to disclosures protected or required by federal, provincial or territorial law; to artistic expression that does not identify the responsible party or the NDA's terms; or to communications with law enforcement, lawyers, elders or spiritual and culturally specific counsellors, doctors, nurse practitioners, psychologists, registered nurses, social workers, victim services workers, or a friend, family member or other personal supporter.

Reporting: Within 45 days of each fiscal year's end, the President of the Treasury Board would table a report in both Houses listing, for each entity in the Public Accounts, the number of NDAs entered into and the total dollar value of agreements containing them. The Minister must certify the information is accurate, the data must be presented so as not to identify individuals, and it must be provided even if it would normally be shielded by solicitor-client, litigation, parliamentary privilege or Cabinet confidence — with parliamentary privilege expressly waived for this purpose only.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The rules reach across the federal public sector: departments, departmental corporations, Crown corporations, and any entity whose finances appear in the Public Accounts. They also extend to Parliament's own administrative bodies — the Senate and House internal economy committees, the Library of Parliament and the Parliamentary Protective Service — which handle workplace complaints on Parliament Hill.

Importantly, the bill also reaches outside government. Any non-governmental organization receiving a federal grant or contribution would have to include, in its funding agreement, a commitment to report annually to the President of the Treasury Board on the number of NDAs it entered into and their total dollar value, again in anonymized form. That information would be folded into the Minister's report to Parliament. For complainants, the practical effect would be that confidentiality becomes something they can choose rather than something offered as a condition of settlement.

deepDive.heading: Oversight and review
deepDive.body: The bill builds in ongoing scrutiny. As soon as feasible after the second anniversary of the Act coming into force, and every two years afterward, a Senate committee, House of Commons committee, or joint committee would be required to review the Act and how it is being administered and operating in practice. Combined with the annual Treasury Board report, this creates a recurring cycle of data collection and parliamentary examination.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
Bill S-232 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Marilou McPhedran, introduced in the 45th Parliament. Senate public bills are introduced by individual senators rather than the government, and must pass all stages in the Senate and then the House of Commons before becoming law; many do not complete that path.

The bill is currently at second reading in the Senate — the stage where senators debate the general principle of the legislation before it can go to committee for detailed study. Nothing in the bill is in force at this time, and its provisions could be amended as it proceeds. Note that the text supplied above appears to be cut off partway through the Parliamentary Protective Service clause, so later provisions of the bill are not described here.

S-233.overview: Bill S-233 is a short Senate public bill that would add one new section to the Criminal Code dealing with sentencing. If a person is convicted of assault (or of uttering a threat to cause death or bodily harm) and the victim was a health care worker — including someone providing personal care services — or a first responder who was on duty at the time, the judge would be required to treat that fact as an "aggravating circumstance" when deciding the sentence. Aggravating circumstances generally push a sentence toward the harsher end of the range a judge may impose; the bill does not create a new offence or change the maximum penalties. The bill's preamble says violence against these workers is increasing, that such assaults have physical and psychological effects, and that people who care for and protect others deserve to feel protected and valued by the justice system. Sponsored by Senator Leo Housakos, the bill has passed the Senate stage and is now being studied by a committee of the House of Commons.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill amends the Criminal Code by inserting a new section 269.02, immediately after the existing section 269.01. The new section directs that when a court imposes a sentence for certain assault-related offences, it "shall" — meaning it must, not may — consider it an aggravating circumstance that the victim was a person providing health services (including personal care services) or a first responder engaged in the performance of their duty.

This is a sentencing rule only. It does not create a new criminal offence, does not set a mandatory minimum penalty, and does not raise the maximum penalties for the offences involved. It instructs judges on a factor they must weigh once someone has already been convicted.

deepDive.heading: Which offences are covered
deepDive.body:
The new rule applies to sentencing for an offence under paragraph 264.1(1)(a) of the Criminal Code — uttering a threat to cause death or bodily harm — and to any of sections 266 to 269, which cover the range of assault offences, including simple assault, assault with a weapon or causing bodily harm, aggravated assault, and unlawfully causing bodily harm.

For the aggravating factor to apply, two things must be true at the time the offence was committed: the victim was a health services provider or a first responder, and (per the wording of the section) that person was engaged in the performance of their duty.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill names two groups of potential victims: people who provide health services, expressly including personal care services, and first responders. The text does not further define these terms, so their precise scope would be interpreted by the courts. The reference to personal care services suggests coverage beyond hospital settings.

The other group affected is people convicted of assaulting or threatening those workers, who could face stiffer sentences within existing penalty ranges. Sentencing judges are also directly affected, since the provision removes discretion over whether to count this factor as aggravating, though the weight given to it in any particular case would remain a judicial decision.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble sets out the reasons offered for the bill: an increasing number of violent incidents against health workers and first responders, the physical and psychological impact of such assaults, and the view that these workers deserve to feel protected and valued by the justice system. Preambles are interpretive context rather than operative law.

S-233 is a Senate Public Bill — a bill introduced by an individual senator rather than by the government — sponsored by Hon. Leo Housakos. Its listed status is at consideration in committee in the House of Commons, meaning it has cleared the Senate and is being examined by MPs on a committee. To become law it would still need to complete the remaining House of Commons stages and receive Royal Assent.

S-230.overview: Bill S-230 would require the federal Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food to create a national strategy for protecting, conserving and improving the health of Canada's soil. The strategy would have to be built in collaboration with other federal ministers, provinces, municipalities and Indigenous governing bodies, and after public consultation that meaningfully includes farmers from different regions and types of farm operations. It would have to cover things like recognizing soil as a strategic national asset, gathering better data on soil conditions, funding research and training, sharing soil knowledge (including Indigenous stewardship practices), and recommending the appointment of a National Advocate for Soil Health along with targets and timelines. The Minister would have to table the strategy in Parliament within two years and report on progress every three years afterward. The bill matters because it is a response to concerns that Canada is losing farmland to soil degradation, contamination and development, though it directs the government to plan and report rather than imposing specific soil rules on landowners.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
Bill S-230 is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Robert Black. It does not regulate farming practices or land use directly. Instead, it creates a legal obligation for the Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food to develop a national soil health strategy and to report to Parliament on it.

The Minister must work with the Ministers of Environment, Health, Indigenous Services, Natural Resources and any other relevant ministers. Provincial agriculture ministries, municipal governments and Indigenous governing bodies must be given an opportunity to collaborate, and the Minister must also hold public consultations with stakeholders, Indigenous and non-Indigenous agricultural industry representatives, and any interested persons. The bill specifically requires that the views of farmers from different regions and different types of farm operations be taken into account in a meaningful way.

deepDive.heading: What the strategy must contain
deepDive.body:
The bill sets out four categories of required content. First, policy and legislative measures that recognize soil as a strategic national asset essential to food security, and that protect and enhance the ability of Canadian soils to produce food, fibre and fuel sustainably and profitably.

Second, measures to improve knowledge, including analysis of soil degradation, structure, compaction, nutrients, productivity, contamination, ecology and stable carbon, plus data gathering and monitoring of indicators such as carbon content and sequestration potential and water-holding capacity. Third, education and information measures: research programs, training for producers and professionals, knowledge transfer and technical assistance, incorporation of Indigenous stewardship and knowledge, public awareness efforts, and the development of a national soil information system. Fourth, recommendations on appointing a National Advocate for Soil Health and on setting targets, timelines and the resources needed.

deepDive.heading: Timelines and accountability
deepDive.body:
The Minister would have two years from the day the Act comes into force to prepare a report setting out the strategy, and must table it in both the Senate and the House of Commons within the first 15 sitting days after it is completed. The report must be posted on the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada website within 10 days of tabling.

After that, a review report is required within three years of the strategy being tabled, and every three years thereafter. Each review must say which measures were implemented and how effective they were, explain why any measures were not implemented and give a timeline for doing so, and provide any updates, conclusions or recommendations. These reviews must also be prepared in collaboration with the other ministers and levels of government, tabled in Parliament and published online.

deepDive.heading: Context and who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill's preamble points to a June 6, 2024 report by the Standing Senate Committee on Agriculture and Forestry, which made 25 recommendations to the federal government on soil health. It also cites the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's finding that 33% of the world's soils are already degraded and that over 90% could be degraded by 2050, as well as the FAO's 2015 Revised World Soil Charter, which asks national governments to act on soil conservation.

The most directly affected parties are farmers and agricultural producers, agricultural organizations, soil researchers, and Indigenous communities, all of whom are entitled to be consulted. Because agriculture and land use are areas where provinces have significant jurisdiction, the bill repeatedly frames the strategy as a collaborative exercise across levels of government rather than a unilateral federal one. As a Senate public bill currently at second reading in the House of Commons, it has not yet become law and would still need to complete the House stages and receive Royal Assent.

S-231.overview: Bill S-231 is a Senate public bill from Senator Pamela Wallin that would change the Criminal Code rules on medical assistance in dying (MAID) to allow people to make binding "advance requests." Under current law, a person can only waive the requirement to give final consent immediately before MAID is provided in limited circumstances; this bill would broaden that in two ways: by letting people whose natural death is not reasonably foreseeable arrange MAID for a specified day even if they lose capacity beforehand, and by letting anyone diagnosed with a serious and incurable illness, disease or disability sign a written declaration setting out the conditions under which MAID should be provided if they later lose the ability to consent. The declaration route would require two independent witnesses, physician certification that the listed conditions are clear and observable, and renewal at least every five years. In all cases, the person would still have to meet MAID's existing eligibility criteria and safeguards before losing capacity, and MAID could not proceed if the person shows refusal or resistance by words, sounds or gestures. The bill responds to a gap the preamble identifies between Quebec's 2023 end-of-life care law, which permits advance requests, and the federal Criminal Code, which does not.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
MAID is governed by the Criminal Code, which sets out who is eligible and what safeguards must be followed. One of those safeguards is "final consent" — the person must confirm their consent right before the substance is administered. Since 2021, a narrow exception (a written waiver of final consent) has existed, but the Criminal Code text reproduced in the bill applies it to the stream for people whose natural death is reasonably foreseeable.

Bill S-231 would rewrite that exception so it applies to both MAID streams and would add a second, broader pathway based on a written declaration made after a diagnosis. In effect, it would create a legal basis for advance requests for MAID in federal law.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Two routes to waiving final consent are set out. The first (new subsection 3.21) is an arrangement in writing with the practitioner who will provide MAID, fixing a specified day; the person must be told of the risk of losing capacity before that day and must consent in writing to MAID being provided on or before that day if capacity is lost. The bill extends this option to people whose natural death is not reasonably foreseeable.

The second (new subsection 3.22) is a written declaration made after a diagnosis of a serious and incurable illness, disease or disability. The declaration must clearly identify conditions related to that illness that a practitioner can observe, state consent to MAID if those conditions occur and the person has lost capacity, be signed and dated by two independent witnesses confirming it was voluntary and free of pressure, and be certified by a physician as clear, observable, and properly witnessed. A declaration is valid for no more than five years.

In both cases, all MAID eligibility criteria and all other applicable safeguards must have been met before the person lost capacity, and the substance must be administered according to the terms of the arrangement or declaration.

deepDive.heading: Limits and safeguards
deepDive.body:
The bill keeps and extends the existing rule that MAID cannot proceed if the person demonstrates, by words, sounds or gestures, refusal or resistance to the administration of the substance. An amended subsection 241.2(3.4) states that once such refusal or resistance is shown, MAID can no longer be provided on the basis of either the specified-day arrangement or the written declaration.

Other built-in limits include the five-year expiry on declarations, the requirement that the triggering conditions be observable rather than subjective, the two-independent-witness rule, and the physician certification step.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill is aimed at people who fear losing the capacity to consent — for example, those diagnosed with a condition that may lead to incapacity — and who want their wishes about MAID to be carried out afterward. It also affects doctors and nurse practitioners, who would be the ones entering into arrangements, certifying declarations, assessing whether the listed conditions are present, and judging whether the person is showing refusal or resistance.

Because MAID delivery is regulated provincially while the criminal law is federal, changes here would interact with provincial health systems and professional rules, which the bill itself does not address.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
The preamble points to Quebec's Bill 11, which received royal assent on June 7, 2023, and amended that province's end-of-life care law to allow people with a serious and incurable illness leading to incapacity to make an advance request for medical aid in dying. The preamble notes that no equivalent capacity to make advance requests exists in the Criminal Code, which is the gap S-231 seeks to close.

S-231 is a Senate public bill — introduced by an individual senator rather than the government — dated June 12, 2025, and is at second reading in the Senate. To become law it would need to pass all stages in the Senate, then be adopted by the House of Commons and receive royal assent; many Senate public bills do not complete that process.

S-234.overview: Bill S-234 would require the federal Minister of Health to create a national framework to prevent fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and better support people who live with it, along with their families and caregivers. FASD is described in the bill as a lifelong disability affecting the brain and body, and one of the leading causes of neurodevelopmental disability in Canada. The framework would have to cover training for health professionals, research and information-sharing between governments, national standards for prevention, diagnosis and support, and a public awareness strategy that could recommend changes to alcohol consumption and marketing rules. Before finalizing it, the Minister would consult other federal ministers, provinces and territories, Indigenous communities and organizations, and stakeholders including people with FASD themselves. The Minister would have to table the framework in Parliament within 18 months and report back five years later on what has actually been done. The bill is a Senate public bill sponsored by Senator Mohamed-Iqbal Ravalia and is currently being studied by a Senate committee.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill directs the Minister of Health to develop a "national framework on fetal alcohol spectrum disorder." A framework of this kind is a plan or strategy document rather than a program with dedicated funding — the legislation sets out what topics the plan must address and when it must be delivered, but does not itself create services, benefits or penalties.

The preamble explains the reasoning: FASD is a lifelong disability that causes varying degrees of difficulty in daily living, it occurs across all regions, ethnicities, income levels and education levels, and people and families in many parts of Canada face stigma and barriers when trying to access diagnosis and support. Parliament also recognizes the need for supports to reduce alcohol-exposed pregnancies.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 2 lists five things the framework must contain: (a) measures on training, education and guidance for health care and other professionals on preventing and diagnosing FASD and supporting those affected; (b) measures to promote research and information-sharing between governments; (c) national standards for prevention, diagnosis and support; (d) a strategy to raise awareness of the risks of drinking during pregnancy and the consequences of FASD, which can include recommending changes to laws and policies on alcohol consumption and marketing; and (e) any other measures the Minister considers appropriate to prevent FASD, ensure proper diagnosis and improve outcomes.

Sections 3 and 4 set the timelines. The Minister must table a report setting out the framework in both the Senate and the House of Commons within 18 months of the Act coming into force, and publish it on the Health Canada website within 10 days of tabling. Five years after that, the Minister must table a second report listing which measures were implemented and how effective they were, and for any measure not implemented, why not and when it might be.

deepDive.heading: Who must be consulted
deepDive.body:
The bill requires the Minister of Health to consult a broad list of parties before developing the framework: the Ministers of Justice, Employment and Social Development, and Indigenous Services, plus any other relevant federal ministers; provincial and territorial governments, including officials responsible for health, mental health and addictions; and stakeholders such as self-advocates (people with FASD), caregivers, support persons, service providers, and members of the medical and research communities.

It also specifically requires consultation with Indigenous communities and organizations with predominantly Indigenous leadership, and leaves room for the Minister to consult anyone else considered appropriate.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The most directly affected groups are people living with FASD, their families and their caregivers, who would be the intended beneficiaries of the framework's standards and support measures. Health care providers and other professionals would be affected through the training, education and diagnostic guidance components.

Because health care delivery is largely a provincial and territorial responsibility, the framework's national standards would be developed in consultation with those governments rather than imposed unilaterally. The awareness strategy could also touch the alcohol sector indirectly, since the framework may recommend — but not itself enact — changes to laws and policies on alcohol consumption and marketing.

deepDive.heading: Status and context
deepDive.body:
S-234 is a Senate public bill, meaning it was introduced by an individual senator (Mohamed-Iqbal Ravalia) rather than by the government. It is currently at committee consideration in the Senate, which is an early stage: to become law it would still need to complete the remaining stages in the Senate, pass all stages in the House of Commons, and receive Royal Assent.

The bill follows a pattern used for several other federal "national framework" statutes, which oblige a minister to consult, produce a plan within a set deadline, table it in Parliament, and report later on progress. Its practical effect depends on the content of the framework that is eventually produced and on the actions federal, provincial and territorial governments choose to take.

S-235.overview: Bill S-235 would turn Canada's existing National Strategy to Combat Human Trafficking — currently a government policy — into a legal obligation. It requires the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness to maintain and update the Strategy, spells out what the Strategy must contain (prevention, victim support, prosecution, partnerships and training), and adds fixed deadlines for reviewing it and reporting to Parliament. The bill also requires public consultation and consultation with provinces, municipalities, affected communities and survivors, and it directs that certain advisory roles be filled by people with lived experience of trafficking. It matters because it would make the Strategy harder for a future government to quietly drop or leave unchanged, and would create a regular, public record of progress. As a Senate public bill, it is still at the committee stage in the Senate and is not law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill creates the National Strategy to Combat Human Trafficking Act. Its core requirement is that the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness must "maintain and update" the National Strategy, whose stated aims are ending human trafficking, addressing the harms suffered by people who have been trafficked, and enhancing support for them.

The bill defines human trafficking by reference to existing Criminal Code offences (sections 279.01, 279.011, 279.02 and 279.03). It does not create new criminal offences or penalties; it is a planning, review and reporting law layered on top of a strategy the federal government has already developed.
