S-1001.overview: Bill S-1001 is a private-style Senate bill that gives one specific company — Gore Mutual Insurance Company, a property and casualty insurer based in Cambridge, Ontario — permission to change which level of government regulates it. Gore Mutual was created by a special Act of Parliament in 1937 and is currently a federally regulated insurer under the Insurance Companies Act. The company wants to be "continued" (essentially re-established) as a corporation under Quebec provincial law instead, but federal law contains no general mechanism allowing a federally incorporated insurance company to make that switch. This bill creates the one-time authorization the company needs, and it repeals the old federal Acts that created and renamed the company once the move is complete. The bill has received royal assent, meaning it is now law.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill authorizes Gore Mutual Insurance Company to apply to be continued as a body corporate under the laws of Quebec, as if it had originally been incorporated there. "Continuance" is a corporate law term for moving a company's legal home from one jurisdiction to another without dissolving it and starting over — the same company carries on, but under a different set of governing laws.

Importantly, the bill only grants permission to apply. The actual move depends on the company completing the process under Quebec law; the bill itself does not effect the transfer.

deepDive.heading: Key provisions
deepDive.body:
Section 1 sets aside subsection 39(5) of the federal Insurance Companies Act — the provision that would otherwise block the company from applying — and allows Gore Mutual to seek continuance under Quebec law.

Section 2 provides that on the day the continuance takes effect, the company stops being governed by the federal Insurance Companies Act. Section 3 then repeals the three historic federal statutes tied to the company: the 1937 Act that incorporated it, a 1944–45 Act respecting it, and the 1959 Act that changed its name to Gore Mutual Insurance Company. These repeals are triggered only by the continuance actually happening.

deepDive.heading: Background from the preamble
deepDive.body:
The preamble recounts the company's lineage: the Gore District Mutual Fire Insurance Company was incorporated in 1839 under the laws of Upper Canada; a federal company of the same name was created by special Act of Parliament in 1937; the federal company then acquired the provincial one, which was deemed merged into it; and the name was changed to Gore Mutual Insurance Company in 1959.

The preamble also states that policyholders entitled to vote approved the proposed move by a two-thirds majority at an annual and special meeting of the company, and that the company petitioned Parliament because no existing legislative provision allows a federally incorporated insurance company to apply for continuance under provincial law.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects
deepDive.body:
The bill applies to a single named company and its stakeholders — most directly Gore Mutual, its policyholders (who, as a mutual insurer's members, voted on the proposal) and its employees. It does not change the rules for insurers generally, and it does not create a general pathway for other federal insurance companies to move to provincial jurisdiction; each such move would still require its own authorization.

The practical consequence for the company is a change of regulator: once continued in Quebec, it would fall under Quebec's insurance and corporate law framework rather than the federal Insurance Companies Act.

deepDive.heading: Context and status
deepDive.body:
This is a Senate public bill of the type traditionally used for private matters concerning a specific corporation — reflected in the "S-1001" numbering used for such bills. It was sponsored by Senator Tony Loffreda and has received royal assent.

The bill is procedural in nature: it resolves a gap in federal law rather than setting new policy. Parliament's role here was to grant the company's petition; the substance of how the company will operate afterward will be determined by Quebec law and regulators.

C-19.overview: Bill C-19, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit Act, is a short government bill that amends the Income Tax Act to temporarily make the GST/HST credit (GSTC) bigger. It does two things: it adds a one-time top-up paid in January 2026 that raises the maximum credit for the 2025-2026 benefit year by 50%, and it raises maximum credit amounts by 25% for five years' worth of quarterly payments, from July 2026 through April 2031. The GST credit is a tax-free payment sent automatically by the Canada Revenue Agency to lower- and modest-income people who file a tax return, so the change means more money in the pockets of those households without any new application process. The bill also indexes the new higher amounts to inflation starting after 2026 and includes technical rules for shared-custody parents and for how the CRA assesses and recovers these payments. It has received royal assent.

deepDive.heading: What the bill does
deepDive.body:
The bill's only substantive job is to increase the Goods and Services Tax/Harmonized Sales Tax credit — the quarterly, tax-free payment the CRA sends to lower- and modest-income individuals and families to offset sales tax. It does this by writing two new payment formulas into section 122.5 of the Income Tax Act, which is the section that creates the GST credit.

The first formula creates an extra payment in January 2026 that lifts the maximum credit for the 2025-2026 benefit year by 50%. The second formula raises maximum amounts by 25% for the following five years of payments. The bill's short title, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit Act, reflects the affordability framing; legally, it is simply a larger GST credit rather than a new standalone program.

deepDive.heading: The one-time January 2026 top-up
deepDive.body: New subsection 122.5(3.004) deems eligible individuals who filed a return to have made an extra payment in January 2026, calculated on the 2024 taxation year. The formula uses base figures of $1,047 for the individual, $1,047 for a spouse or common-law partner (or for a single parent's first child), and $552 for each additional qualified dependant, with a supplement for single people with no dependants tied to income above $11,337. That total is reduced by 15% of adjusted income above $45,521, then multiplied by 0.25, and the regular credit already paid for that month is subtracted — meaning the payment is a top-up on top of the normal January credit rather than a duplicate of it.

deepDive.heading: The five-year, 25% increase (July 2026 to April 2031)
deepDive.body:
New subsection 122.5(3.005) sets out amounts for 20 specified quarterly payment months: July 2026, October 2026, January 2027, April 2027, and so on through April 2031. Each payment is one-quarter of a total built from $445 for the individual, $445 for a spouse or common-law partner (or a single parent's first child), and $234 per additional dependant, with a supplement for single people with no dependants based on income above $11,564, reduced by 5% of adjusted income above $46,432.

For those months, the bill states that the ordinary GST credit amount under subsection 122.5(3) is deemed to be nil — the new, higher calculation replaces the usual one rather than being paid in addition to it. The bill also adds these dollar figures to the Income Tax Act's annual indexation list (subsection 117.1(2)), so they are adjusted for inflation for taxation years beginning after 2026, and it updates the existing rule that lets certain amounts be paid out in advance.

deepDive.heading: Who it affects and how the money arrives
deepDive.body:
The increases go to people who already qualify for the GST credit — that is, people whose income falls below the phase-out thresholds set out in the formulas. Payments are automatic for those who file an income tax return; the bill repeatedly conditions eligibility on having filed a return for the relevant taxation year. January and April payments are based on the second preceding tax year, while July and October payments use the immediately preceding year.

Special rules (new subsections 122.5(3.05) and (3.06)) apply to shared-custody parents, who receive half of the combined amounts calculated with and without the shared-custody adjustment — consistent with how other child-related benefits are split. The bill also updates administrative sections of the Income Tax Act (sections 152 and 160.1) so the CRA can assess, determine, redetermine and recover these new amounts the same way it handles the existing credit.

deepDive.heading: Context and process
deepDive.body:
The bill was sponsored by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and carries a royal recommendation, meaning it authorizes the spending of public money. Coverage at the time indicated the measure moved quickly through Parliament — CTV News reported that MPs unanimously approved a Conservative motion to fast-track the GST relief bill — and the Parliamentary Budget Officer published a costing of the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit. Later reporting (Yahoo News Canada) described roughly 12 million Canadians receiving a one-time bonus payment from the CRA.

The bill also contains coordinating amendments tied to Bill C-15, the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, which simply keep cross-references in the Income Tax Act consistent if that other bill also becomes law. Note that a CPAC headline listed above referring to "Bill C-19, the Budget Implementation Act" is from 2024 and concerns a different bill from an earlier Parliament.
